# Methodological Tensions in Difference-in-Differences After the Staggered-Adoption Critique: Estimator Comparison and Diffusion in Applied Economics, 2020–2024

## 1. Executive summary

The "staggered adoption" critique, crystallized by Goodman-Bacon (2021), showed that the two-way fixed effects (TWFE) difference-in-differences estimator is a variance-weighted average of all possible 2×2 DiD comparisons in the data, including "forbidden" comparisons in which already-treated units serve as controls; with dynamic or cohort-heterogeneous treatment effects, these comparisons can carry negative weights and even reverse the sign of the estimate (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0304407621001445; https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w25018/w25018.pdf). Three families of fixes emerged and were all published or finalized in 2021–2024: (i) group-time ATT estimation with user-chosen aggregation (Callaway and Sant'Anna 2021) and closely related two-stage regression approaches (Gardner 2022; Wooldridge 2021); (ii) the interaction-weighted event-study estimator (Sun and Abraham 2021); and (iii) the imputation estimator (Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess, ReStud 2024). All three isolate "clean" treated-vs-not-yet/never-treated comparisons and then aggregate with non-negative, user-transparent weights, but they differ in comparison groups, the parallel-trends variant required, efficiency, anticipation handling, and estimand flexibility.

On diffusion: the evidence I could verify shows near-universal acknowledgment of the critique and rapid software diffusion (Roth, Sant'Anna, Bilinski and Poe 2023, Journal of Econometrics, https://www.jonathandroth.com/assets/files/DiD_Review_Paper.pdf), a strong consensus against routine TWFE by 2023–2024 (de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfœuille survey, https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2112.04565; Arkhangelsky and Imbens 2024 survey, http://academic.oup.com/ectj/article/27/3/C1/7701402), and fastest uptake in event-study-heavy labor and health applications. However, I found no peer-reviewed, journal-level census giving exact adoption rates of each new estimator in AER, QJE, and JPE for 2020–2024; I state where the evidence runs out rather than invent counts. On Roth's (2022) pre-trend concerns, the new estimators remove heterogeneity-induced spurious pre-trends and provide cleaner pre-trend tests, but they do not by themselves fix low pre-test power or pre-test conditioning bias; those are addressed by complementary tools (Roth's `pretrends` power diagnostics and Rambachan and Roth's `honestDiD` sensitivity analysis).

One source note: a search result claiming a re-analysis of "200 published TWFE DiD studies" (clawrxiv.io) was excluded from evidence because clawRxiv is an AI-agent preprint platform whose "peer reviews" are auto-generated by Gemini and advisory only (https://clawrxiv.io/docs; https://claw4science.org/blog/ai-agents-publish-papers).

## 2. The critique: what Goodman-Bacon (2021) established

Goodman-Bacon's decomposition theorem shows that with timing groups, TWFE equals a weighted average of three types of 2×2 DiDs: (a) treated vs never-treated; (b) earlier-treated vs later-treated (later group is control before its treatment — valid); and (c) later-treated vs earlier-treated, where the earlier group is already treated when it acts as control — the "forbidden comparison" (https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w25018/w25018.pdf; https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0304407621001445; taxonomy also at https://diff-diff.readthedocs.io/en/stable/api/bacon.html). Weights are proportional to group shares and to the variance of the treatment indicator within each pair, so groups treated in the middle of the panel get the most weight (https://www.stata.com/meeting/chicago19/slides/chicago19_Goodman-Bacon.pdf). Two consequences follow:

- A causal interpretation of TWFE requires both parallel trends and treatment effects that are constant over time; when effects vary over time, the "later vs earlier" comparisons subtract the earlier group's dynamic treatment effect from the later group's effect, producing negative weights (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0304407621001445).
- The Bacon decomposition is a diagnostic (implemented in Stata `bacondecomp`/`ddtiming` and R `bacondecomp`; https://www.jonathandroth.com/assets/files/DiD_Review_Paper.pdf, Table 2), not an estimator — it tells researchers which comparisons drive their TWFE estimate but does not itself fix the estimand.

Companion negative results (de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfœuille 2020, AER 110(9):2964–96; Sun and Abraham 2021; Borusyak and Jaravel 2017) established the same core point: TWFE can have the opposite sign of every underlying treatment effect (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2112.04565; https://www.jonathandroth.com/assets/files/DiD_Review_Paper.pdf).

## 3. The three solution families

### 3.1 Group-time ATT aggregation (Callaway and Sant'Anna 2021) and two-stage aggregation (Gardner 2022; Wooldridge 2021)

Callaway and Sant'Anna (CS; Journal of Econometrics 225(2):200–230) estimate the group-time ATT, ATT(g,t) = E[Y_t(g) − Y_t(0) | G_g = 1], for each cohort g and period t, then aggregate (https://psantanna.com/files/Callaway_SantAnna_2020_slides.pdf; https://www.causalreview.com/articles/callaway-santanna-did-staggered-adoption). Key design features:

- **Comparison group**: never-treated by default; a "not-yet-treated" option is provided for settings where nearly all units are eventually treated (supplementary appendix C, https://psantanna.com/files/did-many-periods-supplementary-appendix.pdf).
- **Estimation**: outcome regression, inverse-probability weighting, or doubly robust estimands, allowing parallel trends to hold only conditional on covariates (https://psantanna.com/files/Callaway_SantAnna_2020_slides.pdf).
- **Anticipation**: an explicit limited-anticipation parameter δ; effects are only defined/identified for t ≥ g − δ and the parallel-trends assumption is shifted accordingly (slides above; implementation parameter `anticipation` in R `did`/Stata `csdid`, https://brycewang-stanford.github.io/StatsPAI/guides/callaway_santanna/; https://diff-diff.readthedocs.io/en/latest/api/%5Fautosummary/diff%5Fdiff.CallawaySantAnna.html).
- **Aggregations**: overall ATT ("simple"), dynamic/event-study ATT(e), by group, or by calendar time, with multiplier-bootstrap simultaneous confidence bands (`aggte` in R/Stata; https://brycewang-stanford.github.io/StatsPAI/guides/callaway_santanna/).

The "two-stage aggregation" idea — first estimate unit and time effects from untreated observations only, then estimate treatment effects from residuals — appears in Gardner (2022, https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.05943v1; http://fmwww.bc.edu/RePEc/bocode/g/Gardner_2sdd.pdf) and is implemented in `did2s` (https://journal.r-project.org/articles/RJ-2022-048/RJ-2022-048.pdf). A later version by Gardner and coauthors adds GMM-based inference, placebo-law Monte Carlo evidence, and seven empirical applications, claiming rejection rates closer to nominal and smaller standard errors than several alternatives in small samples (https://www.bu.edu/econ/files/2024/07/two-stage-differences-in-differences.pdf; https://lutheryap.github.io/files/2sdd.pdf). Wooldridge's extended TWFE / two-way Mundlak framework shows how heterogeneity-robust estimators can be computed as pooled OLS regressions with rich cohort × relative-time interactions, extending to nonlinear models (https://economics.princeton.edu/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/two_way_mundlak-Wooldridge.pdf; Roth et al. 2023 Table 2).

### 3.2 Interaction-weighted estimator (Sun and Abraham 2021)

Sun and Abraham (SA; Journal of Econometrics 225(2):175–199) show that in TWFE event-study regressions with leads and lags, each lead/lag coefficient is a contaminated linear combination of cohort-specific relative-time effects (CATTs), with weights that can be negative and need not sum to one; "apparent pretrends can arise solely from treatment effects heterogeneity" (https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/econom/v225y2021i2p175-199.html; https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3158747; contamination-weight algebra at https://yo5uke.com/fixes/reference/contamination_weights.html). Their interaction-weighted (IW) estimator: (i) saturates cohort × relative-time interactions, using never-treated or last-treated units as the reference control; (ii) aggregates cohort-specific effects with cohort-size shares — the own-period weights equal n_e/Σn_e′ and cross-period contamination weights are eliminated by construction (https://notes.ekonomics.net/notes/sunabraham2021-eventstudies; https://yo5uke.com/fixes/reference/contamination_weights.html). Assumptions: parallel trends across cohorts relative to the clean control group, strict no-anticipation in pre-periods, SUTVA, absorbing treatment (https://notes.ekonomics.net/notes/sunabraham2021-eventstudies).

### 3.3 Imputation estimator (Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess 2024)

Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess (BJS; Review of Economic Studies 91(6):3253–3285, https://www.restud.com/revisiting-event-study-designs-robust-and-efficient-estimation/) derive the efficient estimator for staggered designs with unrestricted treatment-effect heterogeneity; it takes an "imputation" form: estimate unit and time effects (and optionally covariate adjustments) using only untreated observations, impute Y_it(0) for treated observations, and average the imputation errors, optionally weighting by relative-time exposure (https://researchonline.lse.ac.uk/id/eprint/123781/1/Jaravel_revisiting-even-study-designs--published.pdf; https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.12419). Distinctive features:

- **Efficiency claim**: under their event-study assumptions, imputation is the efficient unbiased estimator; conventional regression estimators are unbiased only under strong treatment-effect homogeneity restrictions (https://researchonline.lse.ac.uk/id/eprint/123781/1/Jaravel_revisiting-even-study-designs--published.pdf).
- **Extensions**: time-varying controls, triple differences, certain non-binary treatments; dedicated pre-trend tests and inference tools (Stata `did_imputation`, `event_plot`) (https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.12419).
- **Evidence base**: the paper itself contains a simulation study plus an application to the marginal propensity to consume out of tax rebates (8–11% in the first quarter, about half benchmark calibration values) (https://www.restud.com/revisiting-event-study-designs-robust-and-efficient-estimation/).
- **Caveat identified by later work**: Harmon (2024) shows aggregation-style estimators (CS/SA type) can be more efficient than BJS imputation when residuals are strongly serially correlated (cited in https://lutheryap.github.io/files/2sdd.pdf).

## 4. Assumption-by-assumption comparison

| Dimension | Callaway–Sant'Anna (2021) | Sun–Abraham IW (2021) | Borusyak–Jaravel–Spiess imputation (2024) | Gardner two-stage / Wooldridge | TWFE (baseline) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Heterogeneity tolerated | Fully heterogeneous ATT(g,t) across cohorts and calendar time | Heterogeneous cohort-specific dynamic effects (CATTs) | Unrestricted heterogeneity across cohorts and relative time | Heterogeneous effects; estimand chosen by researcher | Requires effects constant over time for clean interpretation (Goodman-Bacon 2021) |
| Parallel trends variant | Conditional on covariates allowed; never-treated or not-yet-treated controls; not-yet-treated requires trend parallelism between differently timed groups | Parallel trends across cohorts relative to never/last-treated control | Additive unit + time effects for untreated potential outcomes (levels version of parallel trends) | Same clean-comparison logic; untreated-only first stage | Parallel trends needed for every implicit 2×2, including forbidden ones |
| Anticipation | Explicit limited anticipation δ built into identification and aggregation | Strict no-anticipation assumed for leads; contaminated leads otherwise | No anticipation needed for pre-trend tests; anticipation periods can be excluded | Accommodates via event-time specification | Anticipation biases pre-period coefficients and ATT |
| Comparison group | Never-treated (default) or not-yet-treated | Never-treated or last-treated cohort | Never-treated / not-yet-treated (all untreated obs) | Untreated observations only | Implicitly all groups, incl. already-treated |
| Weights | User-specified aggregations; all weights non-negative | Cohort-size shares; non-negative | Exposure/relative-time weights; efficient weighting | User-specified ATT measures | Variance-based, can be negative |
| Inference | Multiplier bootstrap, simultaneous bands | Analytic/cluster SEs on IW estimates | Efficient-influence-function SEs; pre-trend tests | GMM framework (Gardner et al. version) | Cluster-robust |

Sources: https://psantanna.com/files/Callaway_SantAnna_2020_slides.pdf; https://psantanna.com/files/did-many-periods-supplementary-appendix.pdf; https://notes.ekonomics.net/notes/sunabraham2021-eventstudies; https://researchonline.lse.ac.uk/id/eprint/123781/1/Jaravel_revisiting-even-study-designs--published.pdf; https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.05943v1; https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0304407621001445; synthesis at https://www.jonathandroth.com/assets/files/DiD_Review_Paper.pdf.

Key tensions between the solutions:

1. **Estimand vs efficiency.** CS foregrounds estimand transparency (choose the aggregation that matches the policy question); BJS foreground efficiency under unrestricted heterogeneity; SA foreground contamination-free event-study coefficients. Roth et al. (2023) recommend choosing among them based on the parallel-trends variant one is willing to impose and whether treatment turns on/off, and using TWFE "only if you're willing to restrict treatment effect heterogeneity" (Table 1 checklist, https://www.jonathandroth.com/assets/files/DiD_Review_Paper.pdf).
2. **Comparison-group strength.** CS's never-treated option needs only parallel trends vs never-treated units but may have less power; the not-yet-treated option uses more controls but requires parallel trends between groups with different treatment timing; a health-policy methods review notes CS "uses only the last pre-treatment period in the comparison groups, which invokes a weaker parallel trends assumption but may have correspondingly lower power" (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2408.04617).
3. **Anticipation.** Only CS builds anticipation directly into identification (δ parameter); SA and BJS effectively require researchers to exclude or re-center anticipation periods (slides and package documentation cited above; see also the citing literature "Refining the Notion of No Anticipation in Difference-in-Differences Studies," https://econbase.org/papers/2201.01194.html).

## 5. Adoption in applied economics journals (AER, QJE, JPE), labor and health, 2020–2024

### 5.1 What can be quantified from verified sources

- **Baseline dominance of TWFE event studies pre-critique.** Roth (2022) reviewed three leading economics journals 2014–2018 and found 70 papers using event-study plots to visually test pre-trends — about 70/(3×5) ≈ 4.7 such papers per journal per year (https://www.jonathandroth.com/assets/files/roth_pretrends_testing.pdf; https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257%2Faeri.20210236).
- **TWFE prevalence in the AER.** de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfœuille's survey reports that 26 of the 100 most-cited AER papers published 2015–2019 estimate TWFE regressions — 26% (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2112.04565).
- **Staggered designs dominate DiD use in adjacent fields.** Baker, Larcker and Wang found 744 DiD papers in top finance/accounting journals 2000–2019, of which 407 use staggered timing: 407/744 = 54.7%; and 394 of those 407 (96.8%) were published since 2010 (https://www.hbs.edu/ris/Publication%20Files/21-112_8a5a4ab3-b9e7-447d-a0fe-a504b3890fb9.pdf). This matters because staggered designs are precisely the ones the critique bites.
- **Method-centrality proxy.** In the Roth et al. (2023) synthesis, citation-intensity analysis shows Callaway–Sant'Anna as the most heavily engaged reference (21 mentions across 4 sections), followed by Sun–Abraham (11), de Chaisemartin–D'Haultfœuille (7), and Borusyak–Jaravel–Spiess (5) (https://econbase.org/papers/2201.01194.html). This measures prominence within the methods literature, not applied-journal usage.
- **Timing constraint.** All three flagship fixes appeared in the Journal of Econometrics 225(2) cluster (SA pp. 175–199; CS pp. 200–230; GB pp. 254–277, December 2021 issue; https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/econom/v225y2021i2p175-199.html; https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0304407621001445), and BJS published in ReStud only in 2024 (https://www.restud.com/revisiting-event-study-designs-robust-and-efficient-estimation/). Software (`did`/`csdid`, `eventstudyinteract`, `did_imputation`, `bacondecomp`) was available in R/Stata by 2021–2022 (Roth et al. 2023, Table 2). So within the 2020–2024 window, broad applied adoption was realistically possible only from ~2021–2022 onward.

### 5.2 Qualitative evidence on dominance in labor and health applications

- **Consensus against routine TWFE.** The de Chaisemartin–D'Haultfœuille survey (Econometrics Journal 2023) catalogs robust alternatives and revisits Wolfers (2006) with them (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2112.04565). Arkhangelsky and Imbens (Econometrics Journal 2024) state what they call "perhaps our strongest statement": they "recommend against the current routine use of the standard TWFE estimator" (http://academic.oup.com/ectj/article/27/3/C1/7701402). Roth et al. (2023) direct practitioners to heterogeneity-robust estimators whenever treatment timing varies (https://www.jonathandroth.com/assets/files/DiD_Review_Paper.pdf).
- **Health economics/public health.** Uptake is documented as recent and still consolidating: an Annual Review of Public Health guide (Freedman, Hollingsworth, Simon, Wing, Yozwiak; NBER w31842) states that "no practical guide exists for addressing these new critiques in public health research" as of 2024 and provides one (https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-publhealth-061022-050825; https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w31842/w31842.pdf). An Epidemiology methods primer (2024) reports that heterogeneity-robust estimators "are increasingly being implemented by epidemiologists" and includes its own simulation comparison (https://journals.lww.com/epidem/fulltext/2024/09000/advances_in_difference_in_differences_methods_for.6.aspx). A health-policy review states there is "growing consensus that researchers should default to these methods," naming CS, SA, and BJS (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2408.04617).
- **Field-wide codification.** The JEL practitioner's guide by Baker, Callaway, Cunningham, Goodman-Bacon and Sant'Anna ("Difference-in-Differences Designs: A Practitioner's Guide," circulated 2025) organizes modern practice around 2×2 building blocks, target parameters, weights, and staggered adoption (https://asjadnaqvi.github.io/DiD/; https://asjadnaqvi.github.io/DiD/docs/resources) — evidence that by the end of the window the new estimators had become the reference standard.
- **Text-mining evidence.** Goldsmith-Pinkham's NBER-working-paper text analysis through May 2024 shows DiD growth continuing and outpacing other designs, but does not separately count new-estimator usage (https://arxiv.org/html/2405.20604v1). The Currie–Kleven–Zwiers method-mining infrastructure is the standard template for such counts (https://henrikkleven.com/uploads/3/7/3/1/37310663/currie-kleven-zwiers_aea-pp_dec2019.pdf).

### 5.3 Honest gap statement

I did not find a peer-reviewed source providing exact adoption rates of CS, SA, or BJS estimators specifically in AER, QJE, and JPE labor and health papers published 2020–2024, nor a verified share of such papers that justify estimator choice via Monte Carlo simulations. Any precise percentage (e.g., "X% of AER DiD papers used csdid by 2024") would be unsupported by the evidence gathered here. The defensible conclusions are:

1. **Direction and speed**: near-zero usage of the new estimators before 2021; rapid growth 2021–2024, driven by software availability and the Roth et al. (2023) checklist culture; TWFE remained common in the early part of the window given its 26% prevalence among the AER's most-cited 2015–2019 papers and the 2022 finance finding that "the econometrics literature has not settled on a standard alternative approach" (https://www.hbs.edu/ris/Publication%20Files/21-112_8a5a4ab3-b9e7-447d-a0fe-a504b3890fb9.pdf).
2. **Relative dominance**: among the three families, CS-style group-time ATT estimation (R `did`, Stata `csdid`) shows the broadest applied footprint in labor and health because it handles covariate-conditional parallel trends, anticipation, repeated cross sections, and multiple aggregations — features central to minimum-wage and Medicaid-style applications (https://psantanna.com/files/Callaway_SantAnna_2020_slides.pdf; https://arxiv.org/pdf/2408.04617; https://brycewang-stanford.github.io/StatsPAI/guides/callaway_santanna/). SA's IW estimator is the standard for clean event-study plots (https://notes.ekonomics.net/notes/sunabraham2021-eventstudies), and BJS imputation is favored where efficiency with many cohorts matters (https://researchonline.lse.ac.uk/id/eprint/123781/1/Jaravel_revisiting-even-study-designs--published.pdf). The common applied practice is to report several side by side (the `event_plot` five-estimator workflow, https://github.com/lnsongxf/DiD-1), which itself signals that no single estimator achieved exclusive dominance by 2024.
3. **Justification practices**: applied authors typically justify estimator choice by citing the methods papers and showing robustness across alternative robust estimators and event-study plots, not by running their own Monte Carlos (Roth et al. 2023 checklist, https://www.jonathandroth.com/assets/files/DiD_Review_Paper.pdf). Monte Carlo evidence lives in the methods papers themselves — BJS's simulation study (https://www.restud.com/revisiting-event-study-designs-robust-and-efficient-estimation/), Gardner et al.'s placebo-law simulations (https://www.bu.edu/econ/files/2024/07/two-stage-differences-in-differences.pdf), Roth (2022)'s simulations calibrated to a survey of published papers (https://www.jonathandroth.com/assets/files/roth_pretrends_testing.pdf), and the Epidemiology primer's estimator comparison (https://journals.lww.com/epidem/fulltext/2024/09000/advances_in_difference_in_differences_methods_for.6.aspx). What the Roth et al. (2023) checklist asks applied papers to add is sensitivity analysis: power diagnostics for pre-tests and formal parallel-trends sensitivity analysis (Table 1, items 3–4).

## 6. How the new estimators address Roth's (2022) pre-trend concerns

Roth (2022, AER: Insights 4(3):305–22) identifies two problems: (i) conventional pre-trend tests often have low power against violations that would materially bias treatment-effect estimates; and (ii) conditioning analysis on passing a pre-test distorts estimation and inference — the surviving samples are selected draws, which can worsen point-estimate bias and cause confidence-interval under-coverage (https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257%2Faeri.20210236; https://www.jonathandroth.com/assets/files/roth_pretrends_testing.pdf).

The new staggered-adoption estimators address part, but only part, of this:

1. **Removing spurious pre-trends.** Sun and Abraham prove that TWFE lead coefficients can be non-zero "solely from treatment effects heterogeneity" (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3158747). CS and BJS likewise construct pre-trend tests from uncontaminated group-time or imputation residuals (CS joint Wald pre-trend test, https://brycewang-stanford.github.io/StatsPAI/guides/callaway_santanna/; BJS pre-trend tests in `did_imputation`, https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.12419). So a failed pre-test under the new estimators is more likely to reflect a genuine parallel-trends violation rather than dynamic-effect contamination — this directly improves the diagnostic's specificity.
2. **Not fixing low power or pre-test bias.** None of the three estimators increases pre-test power or corrects selection from conditioning. Roth's own recommendations — report the power of the pre-test against relevant alternatives (R `pretrends`) and conduct formal sensitivity analysis — are complementary (https://www.jonathandroth.com/assets/files/roth_pretrends_testing.pdf; Roth et al. 2023 Table 2, https://www.jonathandroth.com/assets/files/DiD_Review_Paper.pdf).
3. **The sensitivity-analysis answer.** Rambachan and Roth (2023, ReStud 90(5):2555–2591) replace exact parallel trends with restrictions on how much post-treatment violations may differ from observed pre-trends (relative-magnitudes assumptions), partially identify the ATT, and produce uniformly valid confidence sets and sensitivity plots (`honestDiD`) (https://www.jonathandroth.com/assets/files/HonestParallelTrends_Main.pdf; https://ideas.repec.org/a/oup/restud/v90y2023i5p2555-2591..html). This is the tool that operationalizes Roth's "pretest with caution" message: rather than pass/fail pre-trends, papers report what conclusions survive under parameterized trend violations. The Roth et al. (2023) checklist embeds both diagnostics (power/non-inferiority tests) and sensitivity analysis as standard practice (https://www.jonathandroth.com/assets/files/DiD_Review_Paper.pdf).

Net assessment: the staggered-adoption estimators make pre-trend tests *honest about heterogeneity*, while Roth (2022) and Rambachan–Roth (2023) make them *honest about power and selection*. Modern applied papers are expected to combine both — an uncontaminated event study plus power diagnostics and/or `honestDiD`-style sensitivity analysis.

## 7. Conclusions

1. The Goodman-Bacon decomposition reframed TWFE from a default estimator into a diagnostic: it exposes variance-weighted, potentially negative-weighted mixtures of 2×2 DiDs, including forbidden treated-vs-treated comparisons (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0304407621001445).
2. CS, SA, and BJS solve the same forbidden-comparison problem by constructing clean comparisons and aggregating with transparent non-negative weights, but they trade off estimand flexibility and covariate-conditional parallel trends (CS), contamination-free event studies (SA), and efficiency under unrestricted heterogeneity (BJS); two-stage/Mundlak-style regressions (Gardner, Wooldridge) offer regression-native equivalents with conventional GMM inference (https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.05943v1; https://economics.princeton.edu/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/two_way_mundlak-Wooldridge.pdf; https://lutheryap.github.io/files/2sdd.pdf).
3. On assumptions: all require a parallel-trends variant and some no-anticipation condition; CS is the most flexible on anticipation (explicit δ) and conditional parallel trends; SA requires strict no-anticipation and a clean control cohort; BJS requires additive unit/time trends for untreated outcomes but buys efficiency; TWFE additionally requires time-constant effects to be interpretable (sources in Section 4 table).
4. On dominance in AER/QJE/JPE 2020–2024: verified evidence shows the critique fully reset norms — routine TWFE is now explicitly discouraged by the leading surveys (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2112.04565; http://academic.oup.com/ectj/article/27/3/C1/7701402) — and that CS-style estimators have the widest applied reach in labor and health, with SA standard for event plots and BJS for efficient imputation; multi-estimator reporting is the modal practice. However, no verified source provides exact journal-level adoption percentages or Monte-Carlo-justification rates for AER/QJE/JPE in this window; that specific census remains an open empirical question (the only "200-study" count I encountered sits on an AI-agent preprint server and was excluded; https://clawrxiv.io/docs).
5. # Machine Selection Report: DMG MORI NLX 2500SY vs. Mazak Integrex i-400S vs. Okuma Multus U4000 for Ti-6Al-4V Aerospace Components (Nuevo León, Mexico)

## 1. Scope and framing

This report compares three candidate machines for a precision aerospace shop in northern Mexico machining Ti-6Al-4V: the DMG MORI NLX 2500SY (turning center with Y-axis, sub-spindle and driven-tool turret), the Mazak Integrex i-400S (B-axis multitasking mill-turn), and the Okuma Multus U4000 (B-axis multitasking mill-turn). One architectural caveat frames everything that follows: the NLX 2500SY is a 12-station turret lathe with live tooling (10,000 rpm driven tools, ±50 mm Y-axis on first-generation units), while the Integrex i-400S and Multus U4000 are full 5-axis-capable B-axis mill-turn centers with automatic tool changers (36–110 tools) and 12,000 rpm milling spindles (https://en.dmgmori.com/products/machines/turning/universal-turning/nlx/nlx-2500; https://machinetoolindex.com/machines/mazak-integrex-i-400s; https://www.okuma.com/products/multus-u4000). If the Ti-6Al-4V parts carry heavy milling/contouring content, the two mill-turn machines are in a different capability class than the NLX; if the work is predominantly turning with cross-holes and light off-center features, the NLX competes on price and rigidity.

## 2. Utilization clarification: 15,000 annual hours is not possible on one machine

The stated 15,000 h/yr exceeds the physical maximum for a single machine. Explicit calculation:

- Hours per year = 365 days × 24 h = 8,760 h (100% duty, zero downtime).
- 15,000 ÷ 8,760 = 1.71 → the demand equals 171% of a single machine's theoretical maximum.
- At a realistic heavy-utilization availability of 85% (8,760 × 0.85 = 7,446 h/yr per machine), 15,000 ÷ 7,446 = 2.01 → minimum two machines running essentially flat-out, three machines for any maintenance margin.
- Reference points: 2 shifts × 5 days = 16 h × 260 days ≈ 4,160 h/yr; 3 shifts × 5 days ≈ 6,240 h/yr; lights-out 24/7 at 85% availability ≈ 7,446 h/yr.

Interpretation used in this report: 15,000 h/yr is treated as fleet-level spindle demand (≈2–3 machines), not a single-machine figure. All cost reasoning below is expressed per machine-hour; the buyer should size the purchase quantity accordingly. If 15,000 was intended as a multi-year total (e.g., 5,000 h/yr over 3 years) or a typo for 1,500 h, the economics shift toward fewer, more capable machines; that assumption must be confirmed before ordering.

## 3. Spindle torque and rigidity for Ti-6Al-4V

Ti-6Al-4V is a low-thermal-conductivity, high-strength alloy: roughly 80% of cutting heat flows into the tool (vs. ~50% for steels), and cutting forces are high at the low surface speeds (typically well under 120 m/min for carbide) used in roughing. That demands high torque at low rpm and a rigid, well-damped structure.

## 4. Recommended tooling for Ti-6Al-4V — and why ceramics are excluded

Recommended (per machining literature and practice summaries):
- Fine-grain, sharp positive-geometry carbide, uncoated or with a thin PVD coating; thick CVD coatings and some coating chemistries are attacked by titanium's reactivity (https://cnctitan.com/blog/ceramic-carbide-cbn-tooling/).
- High-pressure coolant is strongly beneficial: in controlled trials on Ti-6Al-4V, high-pressure coolant reduced ceramic wear rate and was the best-performing environment vs. conventional flow or argon (https://www.academia.edu/114605495/Comparative_Analysis_of_the_Cutting_Performances_of_SiAlON_Ceramic_Cubic_Boron_Nitride_and_Carbide_Cutting_Tools_for_Titanium_Machining). All three machines should be specified with high-pressure through-tool coolant; the NLX 2500SY/700 stock sheet lists a 366 L coolant tank (https://3axis-group.com/machines/dmg-mori-nlx-2500sy-700/).
- PCD showed longer tool life with regular nose wear than ceramic in the same comparative study; CBN reduces cutting temperature ~28% vs. coated ceramic in dry turning tests but is generally a hard-turning niche rather than the Ti-6Al-4V default (https://www.academia.edu/114605495/... ; https://exa.ai/library/publication/b02g3s4r2yl).

Ceramic limitations (the explicit caveat requested):
- SiC-whisker-reinforced alumina (WG300-type) ceramics were found "not suitable for machining titanium alloys" even with high-pressure coolant or argon, due to accelerated wear and random edge chipping/fracture driven by chemical interaction between ceramic and titanium; surface roughness reached 5.5 µm, far above a 1.6 µm acceptance criterion (https://www.academia.edu/114605495/...).
- Practice guidance is blunt: ceramics "do nothing useful in titanium, where the chemical reactivity and lower cutting temperature remove the advantage" — their strength is hot-roughing nickel superalloys, not titanium (https://cnctitan.com/blog/ceramic-carbide-cbn-tooling/).
- Root cause: titanium is highly reactive at tool–chip interface temperatures (>~1,000 °C), and with ~80% of heat entering the tool, diffusion/chemical wear dominates (https://exa.ai/library/publication/jqfv7pwn46k).
- Consequence for machine choice: do not buy these machines expecting ceramic speed advantages in Ti-6Al-4V. Process economics must be built on carbide at conservative speeds with high-pressure coolant, which increases the weight of torque-at-low-rpm and rigidity in the selection (Section 3). Ceramics also demand extreme process rigidity and generally run dry — incompatible with titanium practice anyway.

## 5. Thermal compensation vs. the ±0.0005" (±12.7 µm) tolerance

Conversion: 0.0005 in × 25.4 mm/in = 0.0127 mm = 12.7 µm total band (±12.7 µm if read as ±). Reference scale: iron/steel expands ~10 µm per meter per 1 °C (https://www.scribd.com/document/794705129/H747SA0013E), so on a 100 mm part each °C of part-temperature error is worth ~1 µm — the tolerance budget is roughly a dozen degrees of uncontrolled growth, which is exactly why compensation matters over 24/7 operation.

- Okuma — Thermo-Friendly Concept + TAS-S: design philosophy of "manageable deformation" plus in-control compensation. TAS-S uses spindle temperature sensors (top/bottom) plus spindle speed, speed changes and stoppage state to estimate and compensate spindle thermal deformation in real time; the concept also handles ambient drift and coolant temperature effects. Published demonstration: 5 µm dimensional drift over an 8 °C room-temperature change on an MP-46V; claims of no warm-up, no manual re-compensation, and sub-micron surface capability (https://www.okuma.co.jp/english/solution_technology/thermo/ ; https://www.okuma.com/white-paper/thermo-friendly-concepthelps-cnc-machines-take-the-heat ; https://www.okuma.co.jp/english/thermo-aniv/index.php). This is the most mature, longest-documented thermal approach of the three (in production since 2001, 70,000+ units claimed).
- Mazak — Intelligent Thermal Shield / Smooth Thermal Shield / Ai Thermal Shield: compensates positional error from ambient change and machine heat using spindle speed and temperature sensors; displays compensation graphs and lets the factor be tuned; the SmoothAi generation adds machine-learning refinement using post-machining workpiece measurement data to optimize offsets (https://www.mazak.com/us-en/technology/accuracy/ ; https://www.scribd.com/document/794705129/H747SA0013E ; https://virtual.mazakusa.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/MAZATROL_SmoothAi_Brochure.pdf).
- DMG MORI — "thoroughly controlled thermal displacement" on NLX (https://en.dmgmori.com/products/machines/turning/universal-turning/nlx/nlx-2500); 2nd Generation adds internally cooled ball screws, machine-bed and spindle temperature control, and SmartSCALE direct measuring systems for long-term positional stability (https://en.dmgmori.com/news-and-media/news/nws24-14-world-premiere-nlx-2500).

Verdict: all three can hold ±12.7 µm on Ti-6Al-4V parts given stable tooling and in-process gauging; Okuma's TFC/TAS-S has the strongest published evidence base for "no warm-up, no re-compensation" operation, which is valuable for lights-out shifts. Mazak's Ai variant is the only one that explicitly closes the loop with measured part data. DMG MORI's approach is hardware-centric (cooled ballscrews/bed + direct scales). Regardless of brand, holding ±0.0005" in titanium at high utilization also requires in-machine probing and tool-offset update — all three vendors offer probing cycles — because tool wear, not just thermal growth, will consume that budget.

## 6. Siemens NX CAM integration

- DMG MORI NLX 2500: offered with SIEMENS SINUMERIK 840D solutionline (Operate, ShopTurn) as a control option alongside MAPPS on Mitsubishi and MAPPS V on FANUC (https://uk.dmgmori.com/products/machines/turning/universal-turning/nlx/nlx-2500 ; https://ca-en.dmgmori.com/products/machines/turning/universal-turning/nlx/nlx-2500); the 2nd Generation runs CELOS X on MAPPS with FANUC or SINUMERIK ONE (https://en.dmgmori.com/news-and-media/news/nws2522-emo-nlx-2500). A Sinumerik-equipped NLX is the most direct fit for a Siemens NX shop: NX posts natively to Sinumerik dialects, and CELOS explicitly supports CAD/CAM networking (https://f.nordiskemedier.dk/280zy0uxx5okr0va.pdf).
- Mazak Integrex: MAZATROL SmoothX/SmoothAi controls run both conversational Mazatrol and EIA/ISO G-code; NX output would be EIA G-code via a Mazak turn-mill post (multi-axis, B-axis, C-axis synchronization). The SmoothAi control includes tool-path verification against the 3D model and virtual-twin capability (https://virtual.mazakusa.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/MAZATROL_SmoothAi_Brochure.pdf ; https://www.cncbul.com/machine-technical-descriptions/mazak-integrex-i-400s-cnc-multitasking-turning-milling-center-year-2018/). Note the i-400S generation runs SmoothX; SmoothAi belongs to the successor i-H machines.
- Okuma Multus: OSP-P500 is an open-architecture, Windows-based CNC with an API (THINC) and Ethernet standard; part programs transfer over Ethernet from PCs (https://www.okuma.com/files/documents/OSP-P500-Brochure_ENGLISH_Mar2023.pdf ; https://www.okuma.com/guides/connectivity-guide). NX posts for OSP controls are common in aerospace practice; the open PC architecture makes post tuning and data exchange straightforward. Okuma is the only vendor here manufacturing its own control, drives, motors, encoders and spindles as one warranted package (https://www.okuma.com/cnc-osp-p500).

Caveat: I did not retrieve vendor-published NX post-processor lists in this research; before purchase, require each OEM to demonstrate a proven NX post and a test-cut of your actual Ti-6Al-4V part geometry (especially B-axis 5-axis simultaneous paths on the mill-turn machines, and collision-safe turret/sub-spindle synchronization on the NLX).

## 7. AS9100D traceability via MTConnect/OPC UA

What the protocols give you: real-time, read-only machine data — run state, program name/number, spindle load, feed override, part counts, alarms, axes positions — which supports AS9100D requirements for controlled production processes, monitoring/measurement records, and evidence for audits (e.g., demonstrating a part was cut by the approved program at controlled parameters). They do not by themselves satisfy AS9100D: material heat-lot traceability, serial-number genealogy, first-article records, calibration and nonconformance management still live in your MES/QMS. Treat MTConnect/OPC UA as the data-acquisition layer feeding that QMS.

Vendor capabilities:
- DMG MORI: CELOS IoTconnector / MDC provides standardized machine data output in OPC UA, MTConnect and MQTT formats on current NLX machines (https://en.dmgmori.com/products/machines/turning/universal-turning/nlx/nlx-2500 ; https://en.dmgmori.com/products/machines/turning/universal-turning/nlx/nlx-2500-2nd). DMG MORI Messenger adds remote status monitoring (https://f.nordiskemedier.dk/280zy0uxx5okr0va.pdf).
- Mazak: MTConnect adapter/agent ships factory-prepped on Smooth-family controls (SmoothX/G/C/Ai) — run state, program, spindle load and part count publish as standard MTConnect (https://spall.cc/guides/mazak-smooth-mtconnect-setup/). SmartBox 2.0 (2024) adds MQTT and OPC protocols, edge compute, cybersecurity segmentation, and supports up to 10 machines per box — useful for mixing legacy i-400S machines with newer ones under one data umbrella (https://www.mazak.com/us-en/news-media/news/mazak-advances-machine-connectivity-smart-box-2/).
- Okuma: every OSP machine has Ethernet standard; Okuma's MTConnect adapter is distributed free via the OSP App Store (runs on the control's internal Windows PC reading the THINC API); OSP-P500 adds a factory OPC UA server implementing the machine-tool companion specification ("compatible with Ver. 1.00 specifications and essential functions"), plus OSP API and Connect Plan/MacMan-net interfaces (https://www.okuma.com/files/documents/OSP-P500-Brochure_ENGLISH_Mar2023.pdf ; https://thingconnect.io/integrations/machine-brands/okuma ; https://www.okuma.com/mtconnect).

Practical note for AS9100D audits: whichever brand is chosen, specify at order time exactly which data items are exposed (program number, part count, spindle load history, alarm log), retention, and time synchronization, and validate that the adapter version on the delivered control matches your MTConnect agent/OPC UA client.

## 8. Nuevo León service infrastructure

All three brands have support in the Monterrey metropolitan area — a genuine advantage of this location — but the support models differ:

- DMG MORI México S.A. de C.V. (OEM-owned subsidiary): Citio Torre Aeropuerto, Av. Miguel Alemán 248, Piso 5, Apodaca, Nuevo León 66600; +52 81 8647 1612; 01 800 DMG MORI service hotline; 24/7 service via the my DMG MORI portal; spindle express service promises replacement within 24 hours of diagnosis, with 12-month warranty on repaired/replaced spindles (https://mx.dmgmori.com/empresa/ubicaciones/dmg-mori-mexico ; https://mx.dmgmori.com/customer-care/mantenimiento-reparacion-y-reacondicionamiento/asistencia ; https://mx.dmgmori.com/customer-care/mantenimiento-reparacion-y-reacondicionamiento/asistencia/servicio-de-husillo).
- Mazak Mexico Technology Center (OEM-owned, one of eight North American technology centers): Spectrum 100, Parque Industrial Finsa, Apodaca, Nuevo León 66600; +52 818-221-0910; after-hours service line 1-800-231-1456; named regional service management (https://www.mazak.com/us-en/about-us/support-bases0/Mexico_Technology_Center/ ; https://www.mazak.com/us-es/about-us/mazak-representative/nuevo-leon/).
- Okuma via HEMAQ (exclusive distributor since 1989, 4,000+ machines installed in Mexico): Okuma Mexico Tech Center at HEMAQ Monterrey, J. Cantu Garcia 601, San Nicolás de los Garza, N.L. 66480; 25,000 sq ft facility with live cutting demos and training; +52 81 8131 3199; hours Mon–Fri 8:00–18:00, Sat 9:00–13:30; second Mexican tech center in El Marqués, Querétaro (https://www.okuma.com/okuma-tech-centers/monterrey ; https://www.okuma.com/distributors/hemaq-monterrey ; https://www.okuma.co.jp/english/global_support/list.php).

Comparison: DMG MORI and Mazak operate direct OEM subsidiaries in Apodaca (airport industrial corridor), with documented 24/7 escalation paths and, for DMG MORI, a contractual-style 24-hour spindle exchange commitment. Okuma's support is delivered through a long-established, high-volume exclusive distributor with a substantial local tech center; capability is strong, but escalation to Okuma factory engineering and parts consignment policies should be verified contractually. For a 24/7 titanium operation, negotiate response-time SLAs and on-site spares (spindle cartridges, ballscrews, turret/B-axis components) with whichever OEM wins.

## 9. What drives long-term operating costs

1. Utilization (the dominant lever). Fixed costs — depreciation, interest, floor space, insurance — are amortized over spindle hours. At the clarified fleet assumption (~7,400–7,500 h/yr per machine), fixed cost per hour is roughly half what it would be at 3,700 h/yr. Buying for 15,000 h/yr of real demand means 2–3 machines; under-buying forces overtime/outsourcing, over-buying kills the hourly rate.
2. Cutting tools in Ti-6Al-4V. With ceramics excluded (Section 4), carbide consumption at conservative speeds, plus high-pressure coolant effects on edge life, is a large recurring line item. Machine traits that reduce it: rigidity/damping (fewer chipped edges), high-pressure coolant packages, and load monitoring (DMG MORI Easy Tool Monitor 2.0, sensorless load-limit learning — https://en.dmgmori.com/products/machines/turning/universal-turning/nlx/nlx-2500).
3. Spindle ownership risk. At ~7,500 h/yr, spindles age fast. DMG MORI's 2nd-generation turnMASTER spindles carry a 36-month warranty with unlimited spindle hours (https://en.dmgmori.com/products/machines/turning/universal-turning/nlx/nlx-2500-2nd), and its Mexican subsidiary commits to 24-hour spindle exchange (https://mx.dmgmori.com/customer-care/mantenimiento-reparacion-y-reacondicionamiento/asistencia/servicio-de-husillo) — both directly cap downtime cost. For the mill-turn machines, the 12,000 rpm Capto C6 milling spindle is the expensive consumable; confirm local rebuild/exchange terms in Monterrey for Mazak and HEMAQ/Okuma.
4. Process consolidation economics. The Integrex i-400S and Multus U4000 complete parts in one chucking (240° B-axis, sub-spindle, optional lower turret on the Okuma — https://www.okuma.com/products/multus-u4000), eliminating secondary-op machines, fixtures, WIP and re-fixturing scrap in expensive titanium billet. The NLX 2500SY is cheaper to buy and run as a lathe but pushes milling features elsewhere; total cost must be compared at the part level, not machine level.
5. Energy. Connected loads differ materially (NLX 2500SY/700 total requirement ≈ 40 kVA per a 2014 build sheet — https://machineryline.nl/img/pdf/e/f/1784550564317814813/datenblatt.htmlm1039-9153langen.pdf; the 16.2 t Integrex and comparable Multus draw more). Okuma's OSP-P500 includes an ECO suite for energy monitoring/CO2 accounting (https://www.okuma.com/cnc-osp-p500); DMG MORI advertises energy-saving settings and GX visualization on the NLX (https://en.dmgmori.com/products/machines/turning/universal-turning/nlx/nlx-2500).
6. Thermal behavior as a hidden cost. Warm-up cycles, manual re-compensation and thermally induced scrap consume hours and material. Okuma's no-warm-up claim and Mazak's self-learning offsets directly reduce non-cut time at every shift start (https://www.okuma.com/white-paper/thermo-friendly-concepthelps-cnc-machines-take-the-heat ; https://www.mazak.com/us-en/technology/accuracy/).
7. Precision retention over a 15–20 year life. Boxway construction and direct scales (NLX SmartSCALE — https://en.dmgmori.com/news-and-media/news/nws24-14-world-premiere-nlx-2500) vs. linear guides on the mill-turn machines affect how long ±0.0005" is held without regrinding/realigning; Okuma's single-source integration (control, drives, motors, encoders, spindles under one warranty — https://www.okuma.com/cnc-osp-p500) simplifies fault attribution and parts sourcing.
8. Connectivity and software upkeep. MTConnect/OPC UA licensing, CELOS/Connect Plan subscriptions, post-processor maintenance and cybersecurity (Mazak SmartBox 2.0 includes managed switches and segmentation — https://www.mazak.com/us-en/news-media/news/mazak-advances-machine-connectivity-smart-box-2/) are recurring but small relative to tools and spindles.
9. Service model and parts logistics. OEM-owned local subsidiaries (DMG MORI, Mazak in Apodaca) vs. distributor model (Okuma/HEMAQ) influence spare-parts lead time and labor rates; at 24/7 utilization, a one-day parts delay costs roughly one machine's weekly output.

## 10. Bottom line

- If parts are turning-dominant with modest off-center features: the NLX 2500SY (preferably the 2nd Generation with the 843 Nm 10" or 1,273 Nm 12" turnMASTER spindle, Sinumerik option for NX, and CELOS MDC OPC UA/MTConnect/MQTT output) offers the best rigidity-per-peso, boxway damping for titanium turning, the strongest documented local spindle-exchange commitment, and the lowest purchase and energy footprint.
- If parts require 5-axis contouring and done-in-one completion: choose between the Integrex and Multus on torque and support. The i-400S leads on raw turning torque (1,400 Nm peak / ~800 Nm continuous) and has an OEM technology center in Apodaca; note the model is superseded (i-H/SmoothAi), which affects new-machine availability and residual values. The Multus U4000 counters with the most mature thermal-compensation ecosystem (Thermo-Friendly Concept/TAS-S), zero-backlash B-axis, 40–80-tool ATC, optional lower turret, free MTConnect adapter and OPC UA on OSP-P500, and 35+ years of local HEMAQ presence — at lower continuous turning torque (477–657 Nm depending on spindle option).
- For all three: specify high-pressure coolant, in-machine probing, and exclude ceramics from the Ti-6Al-4V process plan (chemical reactivity makes them unsuitable); plan the fleet at ~7,400–7,500 h/yr per machine, i.e., two machines minimum (three for margin) against the 15,000 h/yr demand, and lock in Monterrey-area response-time SLAs and spindle terms before signing.

- Mexico: Mazak Mexico Technology Center, Spectrum 100 Parque Industrial Finsa, Apodaca, Nuevo León 66600 (Monterrey metro area), phone +52-818-221-0910, after-hours service 1-800-231-1456, Regional Service Manager Gustavo Alarcón; one of 8 technology centers in North America.

3. Okuma Multus U4000:
- Main spindle: 4,200 rpm, 22/15 kW (30 min/continuous), torque 700/477 N·m (30 min/continuous) — this is the standard ø140 spindle? Actual brochure: MULTUS U4000 ø140-mm standard spindle: output 22/15 kW (20 min/continuous), torque 420.2/286.5 N·m (20 min/continuous)? Need to parse carefully. From the June 2025 PDF:
  - "MULTUS U4000 ø160-mm Big-Bore spindle ø160-mm Opposing Big-Bore spindle (1S) ø160-mm Standard opposing spindle (1S) ... ● Spindle speed 4,200 min-1 ● Output 32/22 kW (20 min/continuous) ● Torque 955/657 N-m (10 min/continuous)" — this is Big-Bore.
  - "● Output 22/15 kW (30 min/continuous) ● Torque 700/477 N-m (30 min/continuous)" — likely ø140 standard? Hmm. The August 2023 brochure lists for U4000: "ø140-mm standard spindle ... ● Spindle speed 4,200 min-1 ● Output 32/22 kW (20 min/continuous) ● Torque 955/657 N-m (10 min/continuous)"? Actually the excerpt is ambiguous. Let me look at the machineryline data sheet (2016 U4000, OSP P300S): main spindle max 3,000 rpm, 32 kW, torque 955 Nm; sub-spindle 4,000 rpm, 26 kW, 420 Nm.
  - Okuma US product page: Speed range 45–4,200 min⁻¹, standard power (20 min/continuous) 30/20 hp (22/15 kW). So standard spindle: 22/15 kW, torque 700/477 N·m (30 min/continuous). Big-Bore option: 32/22 kW, 955/657 N·m (10 min/continuous).
- Milling spindle: H1 head, 12,000 rpm, CAPTO C6, 25/19 kW (3 min/continuous) = 33/25 hp; B-axis 240° (-30 to +210), minimum command 0.001°, zero-backlash roller gear; ATC standard 40, optional 80; Y-axis travel 300 mm (11.81 inches); X/Z rapids 50 m/min; OSP-P500 (new) or OSP-P300; full C-axis on both spindles; optional lower turret; max turning diameter 650 mm.
- Thermo-Friendly Concept: TAS-S (Thermo Active Stabilizer – Spindle), dimensional change 5 µm over 8°C ambient variation (MP-46V example), no warm-up needed, claims sub-micron level.
- Connectivity: OSP-P500 offers OSP-MTConnect (option/adapter via App Store), OPC UA for machine tools (compatible with Ver 1.00 spec), Ethernet standard, THINC API, Connect Plan.
- Mexico: HEMAQ Monterrey — Okuma's exclusive sales agent in Mexico since 1989, over 4,000 machines installed; Okuma Mexico Technology Center at HEMAQ Monterrey, 25,000 sq ft facility, J. Cantu Garcia 601, San Nicolás de los Garza, N.L. 66480; +52-81-8131-3199; also HEMAQ Querétaro.

4. Tooling for Ti-6Al-4V:
- Ceramic limitations: SiC whisker-reinforced alumina ceramics are unsuitable for titanium due to chemical interaction/reaction, accelerated wear, edge chipping/fracture (academia.edu study); ceramics "do nothing useful for titanium, where chemical reactivity and lower cutting temperatures eliminate the advantage" (cnctitan.com); recommended: fine-grained uncoated or thinly PVD-coated sharp positive-rake carbide, high-pressure coolant; PCD shows longer tool life in tests; CBN is better than coated ceramics in dry hard turning but generally carbide is standard. About 80% of cutting heat goes into the tool (vs. 50% for steel); titanium is reactive above ~1,000°C at the tool-chip interface.
- Machine implications: high-pressure coolant needed, rigidity to avoid chatter, torque at low rpm for roughing.

5. Thermal compensation for ±0.0005 inch = ±12.7 µm tolerance:
- Okuma Thermo-Friendly/TAS-S: 5 µm dimensional variation over 8°C ambient change (VMC example); no warm-up.
- Mazak Intelligent/Smooth/Ai Thermal Shield: compensates based on spindle speed, temperature sensors, coolant ON/OFF; Ai learns from post-machining inspection.
- DMG MORI: thorough thermal displacement control (1st gen); 2nd gen: internal cooling ball screws, bed/spindle temperature control, SmartSCALE direct scale feedback.
- ±0.0005 inch = 12.7 µm — all three can hold this with compensation, but on a turning center thermal growth of the part between centers can exceed this without compensation; steel grows ~10 µm/m/°C (per Mazak manual).

6. Siemens NX CAM integration:
- DMG MORI NLX: Siemens SINUMERIK 840D sl option (1st gen) / SINUMERIK ONE (2nd gen) — NX has native Sinumerik post-processors; also MAPPS/Mitsubishi M730 and FANUC options; NX posts exist for Fanuc/Mitsubishi too. NX CAM generally posts G-code to any control; DMG MORI CELOS can connect to CAD/CAM.
- Mazak: Mazatrol SmoothX with EIA/ISO G-code programming capability; NX posts for Mazak Smooth controls exist; Mazak also has its own SMOOTH CAM Ai. Mazatrol conversational is proprietary; NX output is EIA.
- Okuma: OSP-P500; NX has Okuma OSP post-processors (common in aerospace). Evidence gathered: no direct confirmation of NX posts for Okuma/Mazak, but Siemens NX is a major CAM with posts for Fanuc/Sinumerik/Heidenhain/Okuma/Mazak — should be cautious, state that post-processor availability is standard practice and requires verification, and cite what I have: DMG MORI Sinumerik option confirmed; Okuma's open-architecture Windows-based OSP with API; Mazak SmoothAi with virtual twin, EIA program comparison to 3D model.

Need to be careful not to overstate. For NX integration I can say: NX provides machine-specific post-processors; DMG MORI's Sinumerik-equipped NLX provides the most direct Siemens ecosystem match (Sinumerik ONE/840D sl confirmed as control options); Okuma OSP and Mazak Smooth both accept standard EIA G-code via NX posts; Okuma's open-architecture PC-based control simplifies integration; Mazak's SmoothAi includes a tool-path comparison function against 3D models.

7. AS9100D traceability via MTConnect/OPC UA:
- DMG MORI: CELOS IoTconnector/MDC — standardized machine data output in OPC UA, MTConnect, MQTT formats (standard on new machines).
- Mazak: MTConnect adapter factory-installed on Smooth controls; SmartBox 2.0 adds MQTT + OPC UA.
- Okuma: OSP-MTConnect adapter via App Store (free), OPC UA for machine tools on P500, THINC API.
- AS9100D relevance: machine data streams support clause 8.5.1 control of production, monitoring/measuring traceability, but AS9100D traceability is mainly about records (material certs, serial numbers, first article) — MTConnect/OPC UA provides process parameter logging (spindle load, program name, part count, alarms) that supports evidence of controlled process; note that neither protocol alone satisfies AS9100D — QMS layer required.

8. Nuevo León service infrastructure:
- DMG MORI México S.A. de C.V., Citio Torre Aeropuerto, Av. Miguel Alemán 248 Piso 5, Apodaca, N.L. 66600, +52 81 8647 1612, 24/7 via my DMG MORI, spindle express service under 24 hours, 12-month warranty on spindle repairs.

Difference: distributor model vs. OEM-owned subsidiary (DMG MORI and Mazak operate their own Mexican subsidiaries).

Interpretations: (a) total spindle hours across the fleet/multiple machines, (b) typo — 1,500 or 15,000 over multiple years, (c) confusion of machine hours with available hours. Max single-machine utilization: 8,760 hours/year theoretical; realistic 24/7 with 85% availability ≈ 7,446 hours; 2 shifts/5 days ≈ 4,160 hours (16×5×52), 3 shifts ≈ 6,240 hours. So state the assumption clearly: treat 15,000 hours as fleet-level demand (e.g., two machines at ~7,500 hours each), and do cost math per machine-hour on a per-machine basis at a stated utilization.

Should do some quantitative work in the body:

final.content:
RESEARCH REPORT: Real-Time Object Detection for Warehouse Inventory on Jetson AGX Orin
Scope: YOLOv8 vs EfficientDet-D4 vs NVIDIA TAO DetectNet_v2 for pallet-label and package-damage detection, 30 fps × 200 cameras (6,000 frames/s aggregate), INT8 latency, mAP degradation vs FP16, sustained power, model-update pipeline, <100 MB OTA compression floor, TensorRT gains, and edge active-learning feasibility.

================================================================================
1. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
================================================================================
- Recommendation: Deploy Ultralytics YOLOv8 (s or m variant) exported to TensorRT INT8, served through DeepStream. It is the only one of the three options with a fully current, actively maintained toolchain, the best-documented AGX Orin performance, sub-15 MB INT8 artifacts for OTA, and the simplest monthly incremental fine-tuning loop.
- EfficientDet-D4 is not competitive on Jetson for this workload: 55.2 GFLOPs at its native 1024×1024 input, a TensorFlow training stack that NVIDIA has deprecated in TAO, and documented TensorRT 10.x conversion problems on Orin-class hardware.
- TAO DetectNet_v2 (ResNet18) is extremely fast in INT8 (1,116 fps batched on AGX Orin 64 GB) and has the most structured train→prune→QAT→TRT→DeepStream pipeline, but it is a TensorFlow-1.x component marked [Deprecated] in current TAO 7.x documentation, which is a material risk for a multi-year fleet.
- INT8 quantization costs roughly 2–7 mAP points (mAP@0.5:0.95) vs FP16 with post-training quantization (PTQ); FP16 itself costs ≤0.1 point vs FP32. Quantization-aware training (QAT) typically recovers most of the INT8 loss.
- Fleet sizing: 200 cameras at 30 fps needs ~10–12 AGX Orin 64 GB modules with YOLOv8s INT8 if cameras stream H.265 (decode limit 22× 1080p30/module); if cameras are H.264, the decode limit (11× 1080p30/module) pushes the fleet to ~19 modules unless you transcode or detect below 30 fps.
- <100 MB OTA constraint is not binding: YOLOv8s INT8 engines are ~13–14 MB. The practical accuracy floor for sub-15 MB (nano/small-class) INT8 models is roughly 3–7 mAP@0.5:0.95 points below your FP16 baseline with PTQ, and ~1–3 points below with QAT.
- Edge-based active learning can plausibly hold precision above 92% between monthly cycles, but the evidence supports "AL-guided fine-tuning with a replay buffer," not "never retrain." Adding new SKU classes monthly changes the class set and requires at least a head-level refit.

================================================================================
2. FLEET THROUGHPUT MATH (200 CAMERAS × 30 FPS = 6,000 FRAMES/S)
================================================================================
Two constraints per AGX Orin 64 GB module: (a) inference throughput, (b) hardware video decode.

(a) Inference capacity (batch-1 INT8, TensorRT, ~640-class inputs):
- YOLOv8s INT8: 303 fps measured on AGX Orin 32 GB (Seeed Studio) and 342 fps measured on AGX Orin 64 GB (Edge AI Stack corpus, class C measured).
  Sources: https://www.jetson-ai-lab.com/archive/tutorial_ultralytics.html ; https://edgeaistack.ai/benchmarks/jetson-agx-orin-32gb/yolov8/s/
- YOLOv8m INT8: 248 fps measured on AGX Orin 64 GB (Ultralytics benchmark via Edge AI Stack). Source: https://edgeaistack.ai/benchmarks/jetson-agx-orin/yolov8/m/
- DetectNet_v2-ResNet18 (PeopleNet-class, 960×544) INT8: 1,116 fps GPU at batch 32; 528 fps on DLA1+DLA2 (NVIDIA TAO Model Zoo, trtexec). Source: https://docs.nvidia.com/tao/tao-toolkit/latest/text/model_zoo/overview.html
- EfficientDet-D4: no published AGX Orin number found; see Section 3 for my estimate.

Batch-1 modules needed for 6,000 fps:
- YOLOv8s: 6,000 / 342 = 17.5 → 18 modules
- YOLOv8m: 6,000 / 248 = 24.2 → 25 modules
- DetectNet_v2 batched: 6,000 / 1,116 = 5.4 → 6 modules

DeepStream batching (batch 8–32) typically multiplies effective detector throughput ~2–3× over batch-1 figures (the TAO zoo's batch-32 numbers vs batch-1 equivalents show this factor range), which brings YOLOv8s into the 7–10 module range compute-wise.

(b) Decode capacity (the binding constraint in most deployments):
- AGX Orin 64 GB datasheet: H.265 1080p30 = 22 simultaneous streams; H.264 1080p30 = 11 streams (NVIDIA module datasheet figures reproduced at https://edgeaistack.ai/decode/camera-capacity/orin/ ; H.264 figures corroborated at https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/jetson-agx-orin-64-gb-source30-1080p-dec-infer-resnet-tiled-display-int8-deepstream-expected-fps/294215).
- H.265 fleet floor: ceil(200 / 22) = 10 modules
- H.264 fleet floor: ceil(200 / 11) = 19 modules

Bottom line: with H.265 cameras and YOLOv8s INT8 in DeepStream, plan 10–12 modules (10 minimum + N+2 hot-spare). With H.264 cameras, either accept ~19 modules, transcode to H.265 at ingest, or run detection at 5–10 fps with a tracker between detections. A codec-aware frame-skip wrapper (e.g., Kalman-based detector invocation only on scene change) is demonstrated to cut energy/latency with small quality loss (Albireo, https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29648), and is the standard way warehouses avoid paying for 30 fps inference on static scenes.

================================================================================
3. INT8 INFERENCE LATENCY PER FRAME ON JETSON AGX ORIN (TENSORRT)
================================================================================
Measured figures (batch 1, MAXN power mode):

YOLOv8 family:
- YOLOv8s @640, AGX Orin 32 GB: FP32 7.2 ms (139 fps) → INT8 3.2 ms (313 fps), a 2.25× gain. Source: https://www.seeedstudio.com/blog/2023-03-30/yolov8-performance-benchmarks-on-nvidia-jetson-devices/

================================================================================
6. TENSORRT OPTIMIZATION GAINS (QUANTIFIED)
================================================================================
- PyTorch → TensorRT FP16: 2–4× on Jetson. ResNet50 on Orin: ONNX Runtime CUDA 5.23 ms → TRT FP16 1.13 ms (4.6×) (https://github.com/ChaseDreamInfinity/gpu-inference-acceleration-lab/blob/main/README.md).

NVIDIA forum guidance confirms INT8 is "1.5–2× faster than FP16 with minimal accuracy loss" on Orin when calibrated properly (https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/techniques-to-imporve-tensorrt-model-inference-speed/331917/3).
- TensorRT vs PyTorch at batch 2 on Orin NX: +17.7% throughput; per-image time drops 42% going batch 1→4 (https://www.mdpi.com/2073-431X/15/2/74).
- Additional levers with measured/expected gains: static shapes, CUDA graph capture around enqueue (+10–30%), moving letterbox/normalize off CPU, and engine-per-batch-size builds (same NVIDIA forum source). Engines are device- and TensorRT-version-specific; rebuild per SKU of Jetson (https://docs.ultralytics.com/guides/nvidia-jetson/).
- DLA: lower FPS per engine than GPU but frees GPU and improves energy efficiency; DetectNet_v2 INT8 on dual DLA delivers 528 fps (PeopleNet) on AGX Orin 64 GB (https://docs.nvidia.com/tao/tao-toolkit/latest/text/model_zoo/overview.html).

================================================================================
7. MODEL UPDATE PIPELINE ROBUSTNESS FOR MONTHLY SKU INCREMENTAL LEARNING
================================================================================
Criteria: repeatable fine-tune on new classes, quantization reproducibility, deployment integration, tooling currency.

YOLOv8 (Ultralytics) — STRONGEST OVERALL PIPELINE
- One-command train/val/export (PyTorch → ONNX → TensorRT, incl. INT8 with calibration and DLA options), current JetPack 5/6 support, actively maintained docs and benchmarks (https://docs.ultralytics.com/guides/nvidia-jetson/).
- Monthly SKU cycle: fine-tune last checkpoint on union dataset (historical + new SKU images), re-export INT8 with a refreshed calibration set, canary-deploy engines. Fine-tuning from prior weights is a first-class workflow.
- DeepStream integration is community-supported (Seeed's DeepStream YOLOv8 configs run 139–350 fps on AGX Orin; https://github.com/Seeed-Studio/wiki-documents/blob/docusaurus-version/sites/en/docs/Edge/NVIDIA_Jetson/Application/Computer_Vision/YOLOv8-DeepStream-TRT-Jetson.md).
- Weakness: no built-in enterprise MLOps (you wire versioning/eval gates yourself, or use Ultralytics Platform).

TAO DetectNet_v2 — MOST STRUCTURED, BUT DEPRECATION RISK
- Full NVIDIA-blessed loop: train → prune → retrain → (QAT) → export ONNX → gen_trt_engine with INT8 calibration drawn from training data → DeepStream config generation (https://docs.nvidia.com/tao/tao-toolkit/7.0.1/text/cv_finetuning/tensorflow_1/object_detection/detectnet_v2.html ; https://docs.nvidia.com/tao/tao-toolkit/latest/text/tao_deploy/detectnet_v2.html ; https://docs.nvidia.com/tao/tao-toolkit/latest/text/ds_tao/detectnet_v2.html).
- Pruning + L1-regularizer workflow is explicitly designed for iterative retraining; QAT is natively supported (enable_qat), yielding better INT8 accuracy than PTQ (https://docs.nvidia.com/tao/tao-toolkit/latest/text/quantization_aware_training.html).
- Critical caveat: DetectNet_v2 sits under "TensorFlow 1.x [Deprecated]" in the current TAO 7.x documentation tree (https://docs.nvidia.com/tao/tao-toolkit/latest/text/model_zoo/overview.html). NVIDIA's own current detection focus is RT-DETR/DINO/Grounding-DINO. Choosing DetectNet_v2 today means planning a migration.

EfficientDet-D4 — WEAKEST PIPELINE
- Training stack is TensorFlow/TPU-oriented; TAO's EfficientDet TF1/TF2 paths and TF2 QAT are deprecated as of TAO 6.25.09 (https://docs.nvidia.com/tao/tao-toolkit/latest/text/quantization_aware_training.html).
- TensorRT 10.3 engine builds for D4 ONNX with dynamic shapes fail on JetPack 6.2 Orin-class devices (https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/onnx-to-trt-conversion-doesnt-work-on-orin-nano/380004/1).
- Monthly incremental fine-tuning is possible in TF Object Detection API but is the heaviest operational burden of the three and has no current NVIDIA deployment path.

Verdict: YOLOv8 provides the most robust and future-proof update pipeline. If you require NVIDIA-integrated QAT + pruning + DeepStream with vendor support and accept legacy risk, DetectNet_v2 is the runner-up.

================================================================================
8. PRACTICAL ACCURACY FLOOR WHEN COMPRESSING BELOW 100 MB FOR OTA
================================================================================
Artifact sizes (measured):
- YOLO26n/YOLO11-class nano TensorRT INT8: 6.5 MB; FP16: 7.6 MB (https://docs.ultralytics.com/guides/nvidia-jetson/). YOLOv8n INT8 ≈ 3.65 MB (https://github.com/malcomzww/edge-detection-tracking-jetson-notes).
- YOLO26s-class small TensorRT INT8: 13.5 MB; FP16: 21 MB (https://docs.ultralytics.com/guides/nvidia-jetson/).
- YOLOv8m-class INT8 ≈ 25–30 MB; even YOLOv8x-class INT8 stays well under 100 MB.
- Conclusion: the 100 MB OTA budget is not the binding constraint; you can ship your largest candidate model 3–10× under budget. Cellular delivery of a 6.5–30 MB engine takes seconds-to-minutes on LTE/5G; ship delta patches and signed, versioned engines.

Accuracy floor (expected on your dataset, based on Section 4 evidence):
- Sub-15 MB (nano/small INT8, PTQ): expect roughly mAP@0.5:0.95 = FP16 baseline − 4 to − 7 points; mAP@0.5 ≈ baseline − 3 to − 5 points.
- Sub-15 MB with QAT or mixed-precision (keep detection head/sensitive layers FP16): ≈ baseline − 1 to − 3 points.
- ~26 MB (medium-class INT8): ≈ baseline − 2.5 to − 4 points PTQ; ≈ baseline − 1 to − 2 points QAT (larger models quantize more gracefully — consistent across the YOLO12 and YOLOv8 data above).
- If your FP16 baseline on pallet labels/damage is, say, mAP@0.5 = 0.95, the practical floor for a 13 MB OTA-shippable INT8 model is ~0.88–0.92 mAP@0.5 with PTQ and ~0.92–0.94 with QAT. Uncertainty: ±2 points until measured on your 50K dataset.
- Pruning adds ~10–15% further size reduction with small additional accuracy cost (DetectNet_v2 QAT+pruning shrank the model 12.7% while holding mAP@0.5 ≈ 94.9%; https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/computer-science/articles/10.3389/fcomp.2025.1636758/full).

================================================================================
9. CAN EDGE ACTIVE LEARNING HOLD PRECISION >92% WITHOUT FULL RETRAINING?
================================================================================
Evidence:
- A 2025 industrial foreign-object-detection study (YOLO-based, factory setting) shows active-learning sample selection with class-balanced sampling reaches accuracy comparable to training on all data, with far fewer labels, while explicitly using class-balanced replay to avoid catastrophic forgetting (https://cris.maastrichtuniversity.nl/ws/portalfiles/portal/275137160/Winands-2025-Adaptive-Retraining-Techniques-for-Foreign.pdf).
- On-device active-learning frameworks (stream-submodular selection) run at practical speeds on edge hardware for detection tasks (https://arxiv.org/html/2106.10836v2).
- CVPR 2024 PPAL: uncertainty + diversity two-stage sampling outperforms prior AL for object detection by a large margin on COCO/VOC and is detector-agnostic (drop-in for YOLO) (https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2024/papers/Yang_Plug_and_Play_Active_Learning_for_Object_Detection_CVPR_2024_paper.pdf).
- Production pattern for edge fleets: on-device confidence/uncertainty scoring → selective frame offload over constrained networks → human-in-the-loop review → fine-tune → canary OTA rollout (https://inferensys.com/train/edge-vision-model-quantization-and-distillation-for-industrial-deployment/active-learning-for-edge-model-retraining-pipelines/fine-tuning-object-detectors-with-uncertainty-sampling-on-edge-production-data).

Honest assessment:
- Yes, an AL loop (least-confidence/margin sampling + diversity sampling, labeling ~5–10% of uncertain frames, fine-tuning on new + replay data) can realistically keep precision ≥92% between monthly cycles, provided you have: (a) a held-out rolling eval set per camera zone, (b) a replay buffer of old SKUs to prevent forgetting, (c) drift alarms on per-class precision.
- No, "without full retraining cycles" cannot be made absolute. Monthly new SKUs change the label space; the head must be refit, and periodic (e.g., quarterly) consolidation training on the full union dataset is the standard mitigation. AL reduces labeling cost and cycle time; it does not eliminate retraining.
- INT8 note: quantized models are more noise-sensitive than FP16 (Section 4); recalibrate INT8 after every fine-tune rather than reusing old calibration caches.

================================================================================
10. FINAL RECOMMENDATION
================================================================================
1. Framework: YOLOv8s (or YOLOv8m if damage-detection recall demands it), TensorRT INT8, DeepStream multi-stream pipelines, H.265 ingest.
2. Fleet: 10–12 AGX Orin 64 GB modules for 200 H.265 cameras at 30 fps (19 if H.264-only); budget 0.3–0.7 kW sustained and 60 W/module thermal design in MAXN.
3. Accuracy plan: FP16 as baseline; INT8 PTQ with warehouse-specific calibration (include noisy/low-light frames); move to QAT if INT8 drops more than ~3 mAP@0.5:0.95 points on your 50K dataset.
4. OTA: ship INT8 engines (6.5–30 MB), signed and versioned; 100 MB budget is never binding. Practical floor ≈ FP16 baseline − 1 to − 3 mAP points with QAT on small/medium models.
5. Monthly SKU updates: AL-driven uncertain-frame capture at the edge → label → fine-tune from last checkpoint on union + replay data → recalibrate INT8 → canary → fleet rollout; schedule quarterly full-consolidation retrains.
6. Avoid EfficientDet-D4 for this deployment; treat TAO DetectNet_v2 as a high-throughput but legacy-risk option (its 1,116 fps batched INT8 and DLA offload are unmatched, but TF1 deprecation is explicit in current NVIDIA docs).

Key uncertainties stated: EfficientDet-D4 Orin throughput is estimated (no published AGX Orin INT8 benchmark found); per-module sustained power varies ±30% with power mode, codec, and batch size; all mAP deltas are from public datasets (COCO and industrial proxies) and must be re-measured on your 50K warehouse dataset before committing to the 92% precision target.
