RESEARCH REPORT: Adaptive Input Systems for Musicians with Hand Tremor in DAW Environments

==========================================================================
0. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY AND VERIFICATION VERDICTS
==========================================================================

This investigation began by verifying the three named product features in the task. Two of the three do not exist as described, and several of the requested empirical data sets (false-positive rates for tremor-specific gesture rejection in MIDI, composition completion times under threshold calibrations, motor-skill retention studies for musicians switching adaptive/standard interfaces) could not be located in any indexed literature. The honest headline findings are:

1. Ableton Live has NO "MIDI velocity smoothing" feature. Its Velocity MIDI effect is a static range remapper (clip/gate/fixed modes, Drive, Compand, Random), not a temporal smoothing or tremor filter (https://www.ableton.com/en/live-manual/12/live-midi-effect-reference/).

2. Logic Pro's Smart Controls have NO tremor compensation. Apple's official guide describes Smart Controls purely as a mappable macro panel of onscreen knobs for channel-strip and plug-in parameters (https://support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/smart-controls-overview-lgcp7e59f24b/mac; https://help.apple.com/pdf/logicpromac/en_US/logic-pro-mac-user-guide.pdf).

3. SteadyMouse is real and accurately described: Windows-only anti-tremor mouse software with tremor-band motion filtering, accidental-click blocking, and an Icon Targeting snap system (https://www.steadymouse.com/; https://www.steadymouse.com/enterprise/). It is a pointing-device tool, not a MIDI/music tool, and macOS has no equivalent built-in tremor filter (https://inputconfig.com/guides/tremor-and-limited-range).

4. Genuine HCI/robotics research on real-time tremor filtering exists (Riviere & Thakor's WFLC line; Casiez et al.'s 1€ filter), but it targets pointing, surgery, and generic noisy input — not MIDI capture or the tremor-vs-vibrato distinction. No published study was found that distinguishes pathological tremor from intentional vibrato in real-time MIDI.

5. The core technical problem is real and quantifiable: documented vibrato rates (roughly 4.9–7.8 Hz) fall entirely inside the essential-tremor band (4–12 Hz), so frequency-domain filtering alone cannot separate them (see Section 4 for the arithmetic).

==========================================================================
1. VERIFICATION OF THE THREE NAMED SYSTEMS
==========================================================================

1.1 Ableton Live "MIDI velocity smoothing" — DOES NOT EXIST

The Ableton Reference Manual v12 enumerates every stock MIDI effect: Arpeggiator, CC Control, Chord, Note Length, Pitch, Random, Scale, and Velocity (https://www.ableton.com/en/live-manual/12/live-midi-effect-reference/). The Velocity device's documented controls are:

- Velocity Curve grid remapping incoming (1–127) velocities into an Out Low/Out High range;
- Mode toggles: Clip (clamp to range), Gate (drop out-of-range notes entirely), Fixed (constant output velocity);
- Random (adds random velocity modulation), Drive (pushes values to extremes), Compand (expands/compresses the curve) (same URL).

None of these is a temporal smoothing filter; all operate per-event on Note On/Off values. The manual contains no tremor, accessibility, or smoothing parameter for MIDI input. The only "velocity smoothing" controls found in the Ableton ecosystem belong to third-party plug-ins, e.g., Aftertone Formfactor's "Velocity Smoothing (0–100%)" CC-follower parameter (https://aftertone.co/formfactor/docs.html) and Anukari's modulator smoothing time (https://anukari.com/manual/objects/midi-velocity) — neither is an Ableton feature nor tremor-specific.

What Ableton actually offers that a tremor user could repurpose: Velocity in Gate mode to suppress weak (possibly accidental) note-ons; Note Length to standardize durations; quantization and the Live 12 MIDI editor's ability to "shape velocities smoothly" after recording (https://magneticmag.com/2023/11/ableton-12s-announcement/). These are post-hoc or threshold tools, not real-time tremor discrimination.

1.2 Logic Pro "Smart Controls with tremor compensation" — DOES NOT EXIST

Apple's Smart Controls documentation describes "a simplified set of visual controls that you can use to quickly modify the sound of the current patch without having to edit individual channel strip or plug-in settings," with features limited to mapping, layouts, parameter-mapping graphs, hardware assignment, and automation (https://support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/smart-controls-overview-lgcp7e59f24b/mac; Logic Pro User Guide PDF, "Use Smart Controls" section, https://help.apple.com/pdf/logicpromac/en_US/logic-pro-mac-user-guide.pdf). No tremor, filtering, stabilization, or accessibility-compensation feature appears anywhere in the Smart Controls chapter or its sub-pages. Searches coupling "Logic Pro Smart Controls" with tremor compensation return only third-party accessibility guides and unrelated products.

What Logic actually offers adjacent to the claim: the Velocity Processor MIDI FX plug-in and a MIDI FX compressor, which forum users employ to even out uneven velocity (https://www.logicprohelp.com/forums/topic/94694/; https://www.logicprohelp.com/forums/topic/136875/) — dynamic compression of velocity, not tremor-aware smoothing.

1.3 SteadyMouse — REAL, BUT A POINTER TOOL, NOT A MIDI TOOL

Verified facts (https://www.steadymouse.com/; https://www.steadymouse.com/about/; https://www.steadymouse.com/enterprise/; https://essentialtremor.org/assistive-devices/steadymouse-hand-tremor-mouse-accessibility-software/):

- Project started 2005 after the developer's grandfather was diagnosed with Parkinson's; SteadyMouse 2 launched October 2016; 30+ releases since; Windows only; nine languages; 70-day refund policy.
- Feature set: (a) anti-tremor filtering that "detects and removes shaking motion before it reaches your cursor," with adjustable strength and multiple filter profiles; (b) automatic blocking of unintentional clicks; (c) Icon Targeting System that snaps the cursor to intended targets on a key tap; (d) global on/off toggle via Num-Lock.
- Positioned for Essential Tremor, Parkinson's, and MS; listed in the VA Technical Reference Model (Tool ID 11407) and registered on sam.gov (enterprise page).
- The developer describes the core engineering as DSP learned specifically to "remove the tremor while leaving intended cursor motion intact" (about page).

Independent confirmation of platform scope: "macOS has no tremor filter of its own, and SteadyMouse, the best-known anti-tremor app, is Windows software" (https://inputconfig.com/guides/tremor-and-limited-range). That same guide documents the workaround Mac users adopt: mapping a gamepad stick to the pointer with a dead zone "that swallows the shake," a slow curve, and a click that "waits for the hand to settle" — a useful description of threshold-based rejection in practice.

Implication for the comparison the task requests: SteadyMouse filters continuous 2-D pointer motion in the time domain; DAW MIDI streams are discrete event streams (Note On/Off, velocity, CC). SteadyMouse's approach cannot be dropped onto MIDI pitch-bend or velocity data unchanged, and no evidence was found that SteadyMouse has ever been applied to musical input.

==========================================================================
2. WHAT THE COMPARISON ACTUALLY SHOWS: THREE FILTERING PHILOSOPHIES
==========================================================================

Given the verification results, the meaningful comparison is between three genuinely existing approaches to unintended-input filtering:

A. SteadyMouse-style band/dynamics rejection (pointer domain).
   - Strategy: identify oscillatory motion characteristic of tremor and subtract it; separately gate clicks by requiring deliberate actuation; assist target acquisition with snapping.
   - Intentional-gesture preservation: relies on tremor being quasi-periodic and on intended motion being slower/larger; user-configurable strength/profiles "to fit personal tremor characteristics" (https://www.steadymouse.com/enterprise/).
   - No published false-positive/false-negative rates were found on the vendor site or in indexed literature.

B. DAW-native MIDI processing (Ableton Velocity Gate/Clip; Logic Velocity Processor/compressor; quantize).
   - Strategy: per-event amplitude thresholding or range compression; timing quantization after the fact.
   - Intentional-gesture preservation: none — these tools are expression-agnostic. A Gate set to drop low velocities will drop a genuine pianissimo as readily as a tremor-induced brush; velocity compression flattens both tremor spikes and intended accents. There is no frequency analysis and no vibrato awareness.

C. Adaptive signal filters from HCI/robotics (WFLC; 1€ filter), applicable to continuous controllers (pitch bend, mod wheel, ribbon, theremin-style interfaces).
   - WFLC (weighted-frequency Fourier linear combiner): models tremor online as a modulating sinusoid, tracking frequency, amplitude, and phase with zero phase lag, and subtracts it. Developed explicitly for "computer input filtering, clinical tremor quantification, and active tremor canceling" (Riviere & Thakor, IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Magazine, 15(3):29–36, 1996, https://publications.ri.cmu.edu/modeling-and-canceling-tremor-in-human-machine-interfaces). Quantified result: in 25 benchtop tests, WFLC compensation reduced RMS tip motion in the 6–16 Hz tremor band by 67% and reduced RMS error against an a posteriori estimate of voluntary motion by 30% (Riviere, Rader & Thakor, IEEE Trans. Biomedical Engineering 45(7):839–846, 1998, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9644892/). The CMU MICRON lab page reports "average rms amplitude reduction of 69%" in preliminary 1-DOF experiments and notes the algorithm "has also been used for canceling of pathological tremor in assistive computer interfaces" (https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~micron/filtering.htm).
   - 1€ filter (Casiez, Roussel & Vogel, CHI 2012, https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2207676.2208639): first-order low-pass with speed-adaptive cutoff — low cutoff at low speed kills jitter, raised cutoff at high speed minimizes lag; two tunable parameters (mincutoff fcmin and beta). Tuning guidance: decrease fcmin if slow-speed jitter is the problem; increase beta if fast-motion lag is (https://gery.casiez.net/1euro/). This is the canonical HCI formalization of the smoothing-vs-latency trade-off that any tremor filter for musical controllers must manage. It is already appearing in music tools: the KAOS hand-gesture MIDI controller exposes "One Euro min cutoff — silky glides with no tremor, or crisp immediate tracking" and advertises that "your hand never sits perfectly still — but your MIDI output will. Jitter disappears at rest, responsiveness kicks in when you move" (https://kaoscontrol.co.uk/).

Key comparative point: only approach C has peer-reviewed quantitative validation; only approach A is a shipped product purpose-built for tremor; approach B is what DAW users actually have today, and it is the least tremor-aware of the three.

==========================================================================
3. CLINICAL GROUND TRUTH: TREMOR FREQUENCIES
==========================================================================

The task's 4–12 Hz figure for pathological tremor is correct for essential tremor and consistent with the literature:

- Essential tremor: "4–12 Hz action tremor" of bilateral upper extremities is a core diagnostic feature (Tremor Syndromes: An Updated Review, Frontiers in Neurology, 2021, https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/neurology/articles/10.3389/fneur.2021.684835/full).
- Parkinson's disease: UK Brain Bank criteria include "4–6-Hz rest tremor" (Distinguishing essential tremor from Parkinson's disease, PMC3475963, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3475963/). An EMG differential-diagnosis study of 25 PD, 20 ET, and 20 enhanced-physiological-tremor patients found PD tremor at 4–6 Hz, ET also largely in that range, and enhanced physiological tremor at 6–12 Hz with overlap (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5573102/).
- Physiological tremor: 6–12 Hz, low amplitude, present in everyone (https://clevelandclinicmeded.com/medicalpubs/diseasemanagement/neurology/tremors/).
- The 1995 Riviere/Cameron adaptive-interface paper likewise cites pathological tremor as spanning roughly 2–12 Hz across conditions including parkinsonian tremor (https://publications.ri.cmu.edu/storage/publications/pub_files/pub3/riviere_cameron_1995_2/riviere_cameron_1995_2.pdf).

Additional clinical discriminators beyond frequency (relevant to Section 4): PD rest tremor is typically alternating (flexor/extensor) while ET postural tremor is typically synchronous (PMC5573102; PMC3656631, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3656631/); PD "re-emergent" tremor shows a latency of roughly 9–13 seconds after assuming posture versus 1–2 seconds for ET (Cleveland Clinic, above; PMC3656631). These are EMG/latency signatures, not features available in a MIDI stream.

==========================================================================
4. THE CORE PROBLEM: PATHOLOGICAL TREMOR VS. INTENTIONAL VIBRATO
==========================================================================

4.1 Documented vibrato rates

- Violin vibrato: 5.5–7 pulses/s in 1930s studies; historical vocal vibrato 5.9–7.8 pps; modern singers 4.9–6 pps (Acoustic parameters of violin vibrato, JASA 80(S1):S87, https://pubs.aip.org/asa/jasa/article/80/S1/S87/731036/Acoustic-parameters-of-violin-vibrato).
- Artist-level violinist case study: mean vibrato rate ≈5.7 Hz (first position) and ≈6.3 Hz (fifth position); width ≈40–108 cents (Performance Practice of Violin Vibrato: An Artist-Level Case Study, 2009, https://exa.ai/library/publication/s5gb7rcj4tl).
- String/vocal vibrato literature reviews confirm rates clustering around 5–7 Hz with pitch-height effects of only ~0.3 Hz (FSU thesis, https://repository.lib.fsu.edu/islandora/object/fsu%3A181053/datastream/PDF/view).

4.2 Explicit overlap calculation (my arithmetic from the cited ranges)

| Signal                        | Band (Hz)   |
|-------------------------------|-------------|
| Essential tremor (action)     | 4–12        |
| Parkinson's rest tremor       | 4–6         |
| Enhanced physiological tremor | 6–12        |
| Violin vibrato                | 5.5–7       |
| Vocal vibrato (full range)    | 4.9–7.8     |

- Vibrato band ∩ ET band: 4.9–7.8 Hz lies 100% inside 4–12 Hz. Every documented vibrato rate is also a valid essential-tremor rate.
- Violin vibrato ∩ PD band: 5.5–6.0 of 5.5–7.0 Hz ≈ 33% of the violin vibrato band overlaps the Parkinson's rest-tremor band.
- Consequence: any notch/low-pass filter tuned to remove 4–12 Hz tremor will, by construction, remove essentially all conventional vibrato; a narrower 4–6 Hz PD notch still destroys roughly one third of typical violin vibrato frequencies. Frequency content alone is provably insufficient to distinguish the two.

4.3 What could distinguish them (and why it is hard in MIDI)

No HCI study was found that solves this for real-time MIDI capture. From the gathered evidence, candidate discriminators are:

- Voluntary vs. involuntary context: vibrato is initiated/ceased at note-level musical boundaries (the artist case study observed vibrato stopping during slurred-note transitions; https://exa.ai/library/publication/s5gb7rcj4tl). Tremor persists across task phases. A system would need performance-phase awareness (note held vs. hand at rest vs. transport between notes).
- Onset latency: ET postural tremor appears within 1–2 s of posture assumption; PD re-emergent tremor after ~9–13 s (Cleveland Clinic; PMC3656631). Intentional vibrato has a deliberate, musically timed onset. Latency-to-context features are in principle detectable but unstudied for MIDI.
- EMG contraction pattern (alternating vs. synchronous; PMC5573102): requires sensors beyond any DAW's capture path.
- Amplitude/stationarity: pathological tremor is relatively stationary and load-sensitive (weight loading changes EPT; PMC5573102), while vibrato width/rate are expressively modulated with dynamics and pitch height (FSU thesis). Again, no MIDI-domain study exists.

4.4 The latency cost of naive filtering (derived, standard filter theory)

A first-order low-pass with cutoff fc has a (DC) time constant τ = 1/(2π·fc):
- fc = 4 Hz → τ ≈ 40 ms
- fc = 3 Hz → τ ≈ 53 ms
- fc = 1 Hz → τ ≈ 159 ms
Filtering at or below the tremor/vibrato band therefore adds tens to >100 ms of effective lag — audible and performance-destroying for real-time playing. This is precisely the trade-off the 1€ paper formalizes (jitter reduction vs. lag; https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2207676.2208639) and what Riviere & Thakor addressed with zero-phase WFLC estimation (1996 paper, above). The MTIC whitepaper likewise argues that aggressive <10 Hz filtering "removes high-frequency components of the motor command signal, resulting in a perceptible delay and a 'numbed' haptic experience" — but note this is a self-published, simulation-only whitepaper claiming a 40% latency reduction (p < 0.001) without independent replication; treat it as low-evidence-strength (https://michaelrapoport.github.io/My-AI-Related-Whitepapers/micro-tremor-intentionality-controller.html).

==========================================================================
5. HCI RESEARCH THAT DOES EXIST (ADJACENT, NOT MIDI-VIBRATO-SPECIFIC)
==========================================================================

- Riviere & Thakor, WFLC line (1995–1998): adaptive tremor modeling/cancellation for human-machine interfaces, including "input filters" for a mouse or glove; 67% RMS tremor-band reduction, 30% reduction in error vs. estimated voluntary motion (URLs in Section 2C). This is the closest body of work to "distinguishing pathological tremor from intended motion in real time," but it was never evaluated on musical gestures.
- Casiez, Roussel & Vogel, 1€ filter, CHI 2012: the standard speed-adaptive low-pass for noisy interactive input; less lag than alternatives for a given jitter reduction (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2207676.2208639). Already marketed for tremor smoothing in a gesture-to-MIDI controller (KAOS, https://kaoscontrol.co.uk/).
- Smartphone tremor input correction (IMWUT/UbiComp 2018): motion-sensor fusion to correct tremor-affected taps produced "up to 40% fewer misses" across two empirical studies with persons with tremor (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3161169). Related: Zhong et al., W4A 2015, reducing fine pointing/steady tapping demands on Android (cited therein); mouse tremor-smoothing adapter ease-of-use study with ET users (UAHCI 2007, https://dlnext.acm.org/doi/10.5555/1766311.1766384).
- Gesture rejection-threshold research (general, not tremor-specific):
  * VKM (Taranta et al., 2022): synthetic-data-driven rejection-threshold selection for custom gestures in high-activity data; notes "loose boundaries can lead to high false positive rates and degrade user experience" (https://www.cs.ucf.edu/icerc/isuelab/publications/pubs/Taranta2022.pdf; https://www.cs.ucf.edu/icerc/isuelab/research/vkm/).
  * Bi-level thresholding (Negulescu, Ruiz & Lank, MobileHCI 2012, https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2371574; TOCHI 2019, https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3181672): a tight threshold limits false positives while a loose threshold prevents repeated false negatives; Wizard-of-Oz studies showed significantly lower NASA-TLX workload and lower accelerometer variance, and improved precision/recall on a real wrist/finger dataset. This is the best available proxy evidence that rejection-policy design changes user workload — a precondition for any flow-state argument.
  * MAGIC 2.0 (Kohlsdorf et al.): predicting accidental triggering of candidate gestures against a >1.5M-second "Everyday Gesture Library" (http://danielashbrook.com/pubs/2011%20Kohlsdorf-Magic%202.pdf).

==========================================================================
6. REQUESTED DATA SETS THAT DO NOT EXIST IN THE LOCATED LITERATURE
==========================================================================

Stated plainly, with search scope:

- False-positive rates for tremor-specific gesture rejection in real-time MIDI capture, and documented case studies of their impact on creative flow states: NONE found. No indexed study reports FP/FN rates for tremor filtering in musical performance, and no study links rejection errors to flow measurement (e.g., FSS) in musicians with movement disorders. The closest evidence is (a) the general gesture-rejection literature in Section 5, which shows false positives degrade UX and that bi-level thresholding lowers workload, and (b) the 40% miss reduction in smartphone tremor input (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3161169). Any specific percentages for MIDI gesture rejection would be fabricated; I report none.

- Sensitivity-threshold calibration effects on composition completion time and user satisfaction among professional musicians with movement disorders: NO controlled study found. The nearest relevant empirical work:
  * SIGACCESS 2013, "Toward accessible technology for music composers and producers with motor disabilities" (https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/2513383.2513412): an initial user study with three motor-impaired musicians (a composer with degenerative motor neuron disease, a post-stroke guitarist, and a student with impaired finger movement) who adapted conventional music software and identified limitations — control-surface layout optimization, novel interfaces, repurposed text input. Qualitative; no completion-time or satisfaction-score statistics reported in the abstract.
  * ASSETS 2025 vibrotactile EQ study with six blind/visually-impaired producers in Reaper: >94% information-recognition accuracy in all conditions and NO significant differences in task completion time or perceived workload between haptics, screen reader, and hybrid (https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3663547.3746374) — a cautionary null result showing alternative feedback does not automatically speed creative tasks. (Population is VIB, not tremor.)
  * SteadyMouse vendor documentation describes configurable sensitivity but publishes no timed/satisfaction benchmarks (https://www.steadymouse.com/enterprise/).

- Motor skill retention when transitioning between adaptive and standard interfaces: NO music- or tremor-specific study found. Adjacent rehabilitation evidence:
  * MS VR transfer trial (n=56 MS, 41 controls): practicing on the harder "abstract" (Kinect) interface led to successful transfer to the concrete (touchscreen) interface, while acquisition gains were retained across a retention phase (https://exa.ai/library/publication/yqglbxc2pb5).
  * Myoelectric prosthesis training (12 limb-intact participants, 5 sessions): prosthesis-control improvement correlated with the retention metric from training, not with pre-test performance — i.e., retention-designed training transfers (https://google.iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1741-2552/ae2803).
  * AR prosthesis training: limb loading during virtual training increased skill transfer to physical tasks (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12984-023-01136-5).
  * Wheelchair-extender interface study (61 participants): a familiar interface applied to changed dynamics produced LONGER task times and MORE collisions than a new interface, attributed to erroneous mental models (https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s42452-021-04854-4.pdf). Directionally, this warns that musicians returning from an adaptive (stabilized) interface to a standard one may carry maladapted expectations about how much correction the system provides.
  These support general principles (retention predicts transfer; changed dynamics break calibrated mental models) but none measures musicians, tremor, or musical tasks.

==========================================================================
7. WHAT DOES EXIST FOR TREMOR AND MUSIC (CASE MATERIAL)
==========================================================================

- Tremors vs. Tremors (UCL Queen Square Institute of Neurology, 2024): accelerometric tremor recordings from five people with Parkinson's were transformed into musical elements driving instruments and melodies in five bespoke songs; qualitative reports of positive emotional impact and condition acceptance (https://www.ucl.ac.uk/news/2024/mar/researchers-transform-parkinsons-tremors-music; http://www.tremorsvstremors.com/). Notably, this treats tremor as expressive material rather than noise to reject — the opposite design stance from filtering.
- Ayre (student hackathon project, 2026): webcam-based hand-gesture arpeggiator/drum machine with an explicit "tremor smoothing — adjustable stabilization slider" for Parkinson's/muscle weakness, one-hand mode, and voice-only mode (https://github.com/0xrpheus/ayre). Low evidence strength (no evaluation data), but it demonstrates the emerging pattern: a user-adjustable stabilization slider, i.e., threshold calibration left to the performer.
- KAOS gesture MIDI controller: ships a 1€-filter min-cutoff control explicitly framed as tremor-vs-responsiveness trade-off (https://kaoscontrol.co.uk/).
- InputConfig's Mac tremor guide: practical dead-zone/slow-curve/settle-before-click calibration guidance for gamepad-stick-as-mouse (https://inputconfig.com/guides/tremor-and-limited-range).
- DAW accessibility research more broadly is dominated by blindness/VIB work (20 VIB sound creatives interviewed on haptic opportunities, MDPI Arts 2023, https://www.mdpi.com/2076-0752/12/4/154; convivial-tools analysis, TACCESS 2025, https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/3733606; BCU vibrotactile thesis, https://www.open-access.bcu.ac.uk/17118/). Motor-impairment-specific DAW research remains limited essentially to the SIGACCESS 2013 study above.

==========================================================================
8. SYNTHESIS: ANSWERING THE TASK'S QUESTIONS DIRECTLY
==========================================================================

Q: How do Ableton's velocity smoothing, Logic's tremor-compensating Smart Controls, and SteadyMouse compare in filtering unintended input vs. preserving vibrato?
A: The first two features do not exist. The defensible comparison is: Ableton/Logic offer only per-event thresholding, range compression, and post-hoc quantization — none of which can distinguish tremor from intended dynamics; SteadyMouse offers genuine tremor-band DSP plus click gating, but only for pointer input on Windows; the only validated real-time tremor-vs-intent filters (WFLC: 67% tremor-band RMS reduction with 30% preservation error reduction; 1€: speed-adaptive jitter/lag optimization) live in research code or are just entering gesture-MIDI products like KAOS. None of them models vibrato.

Q: What HCI research exists on distinguishing pathological tremor (4–12 Hz) from musical expression in real-time MIDI?
A: None directly. The applicable foundations are Riviere & Thakor's WFLC (zero-phase adaptive tremor cancellation for human-machine input, 1995–1998) and Casiez et al.'s 1€ filter (CHI 2012). The frequency-overlap arithmetic in Section 4 shows why a purely spectral solution is impossible: vibrato (≈4.9–7.8 Hz) is fully contained in the ET band (4–12 Hz).

Q: Documented false-positive rates for gesture rejection and impact on flow?
A: No tremor/MIDI-specific rates exist in the located literature. General HCI evidence shows loose rejection thresholds cause high false-positive rates that degrade UX (VKM, 2022), and bi-level thresholding reduces workload (NASA-TLX) and repeated errors (MobileHCI 2012; TOCHI 2019). Flow-state measurements in this context are entirely absent.

Q: How do sensitivity-threshold calibrations affect composition completion times and satisfaction among professional musicians with movement disorders?
A: Unknown — no such study was found. Adjacent evidence: 40% fewer misses from tremor-aware input correction on smartphones (IMWUT 2018); a null effect of feedback modality on completion time in an ASSETS 2025 DAW study with blind producers; qualitative needs reports from three motor-impaired musicians (SIGACCESS 2013). Reporting invented completion-time or satisfaction figures would be unsupported.

Q: Motor skill retention when transitioning between adaptive and standard interfaces?
A: No music-domain data exist. Rehabilitation studies indicate retention is achievable and predicts transfer when training is designed for it (myoelectric, 2025), that harder/abstract practice can transfer better (MS VR trial, 2024), and that familiar mappings applied to altered dynamics increase errors and time (wheelchair extender study, 2021) — suggesting tremor users switching off stabilization may experience a recalibration cost, but this is inference, not measurement.

==========================================================================
9. PRACTICAL IMPLICATIONS AND RESEARCH GAPS
==========================================================================

1. Because tremor and vibrato are spectrally indistinguishable, a viable real-time MIDI system would need context features: note-phase awareness (vibrato occurs on sustained, intended notes; tremor also appears between notes and during transport), onset-intent cues, per-user calibration, and an explicit performer-controlled mode switch (the "stabilization slider" pattern in Ayre/KAOS/InputConfig).
2. Latency budgets matter: naive low-pass filtering at tremor frequencies implies ~40–160 ms of lag (Section 4.4); zero-phase adaptive estimation (WFLC) or speed-adaptive filtering (1€) are the evidenced ways to stay inside musical timing tolerances.
3. DAW vendors currently provide nothing tremor-specific; the realistic today-stack for a tremor user is: SteadyMouse (Windows, pointing) + hardware with dead zones/slow curves + per-event MIDI gating/compression + post-recording quantization/velocity editing.
4. Open research gaps, all confirmed empty by this review: (a) labeled data sets of tremor vs. intentional vibrato in MIDI/continuous-controller streams; (b) FP/FN reporting for tremor-aware gesture rejection with flow-state outcomes; (c) controlled calibration studies with composition completion time and satisfaction endpoints in professional musicians with ET/PD; (d) longitudinal retention/transfer studies of stabilized vs. standard musical interfaces.

EVIDENCE-STRENGTH NOTES: Peer-reviewed sources (IEEE T-BME, CHI, IMWUT, MobileHCI/TOCHI, Frontiers, PMC clinical journals, ACM SIGACCESS/ASSETS) anchor the claims above. Vendor claims (Steadymouse.com; KAOS marketing) are reported as vendor statements. The MTIC whitepaper (self-published, simulation-only) and the Ayre GitHub project (unevaluated hackathon work) are flagged low-strength where used. All "not found" statements reflect the searches performed for this report and remain subject to the usual limits of search coverage.

# Data Breach Insurance Comparison: Chubb vs. Coalition vs. Cowbell Cyber
## For a 15-Employee Austin, TX Business with Dual PCI-DSS and HIPAA Exposure

---

## EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

This report compares three cyber insurance carriers—Chubb, Coalition, and Cowbell Cyber—across the coverage dimensions most relevant to a small Austin business that simultaneously handles customer payment card data (triggering PCI-DSS obligations) and employee health records (triggering HIPAA obligations as either a covered entity or business associate). All three carriers offer regulatory fine and PCI assessment coverage, but they differ materially in how sublimits are structured, how incident response is delivered, and what exclusions apply to e-commerce operations. For a $2–5M revenue business with dual PCI/HIPAA exposure, expect annual premiums in the range of roughly $3,500–$9,000+ for a $1M policy, rising to $7,000–$20,000+ for $2–5M in limits, depending heavily on security controls, revenue tier, and data sensitivity.

---

## 1. REGULATORY FINE COVERAGE AND SUBLIMIT STRUCTURE

### 1A. Chubb — Cyber Enterprise Risk Management (Cyber ERM)

Chubb's Cyber ERM policy (sample form PF-48169, 02/19) provides regulatory fine and payment card coverage through its third-party liability insuring agreement, **Insuring Agreement E: Cyber, Privacy and Network Security Liability**. The policy's definition of "Damages" explicitly includes three categories relevant to this business:

- **Regulatory Fines**: Defined as "any civil monetary fine or penalty imposed by a government or regulatory body, including an official governmental entity in such entity's regulatory or official capacity pursuant to its order under a Regulatory Proceeding." The definition expressly excludes "any civil monetary fines or penalties that are not insurable by law, criminal fines, disgorgement of profits or multiple damages." (Source: Chubb Cyber ERM V2.2, https://lmalloyds.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Chubb-Cyber-ERM-V2.2-Policy-Documents-1-003-International.pdf; also https://studio.chubb.com/connect/files/NA_CyberSmallBusiness_Sample.pdf)

- **Payment Card Loss**: Defined as "monetary assessments, fines, penalties, chargebacks, reimbursements, and fraud recoveries that You become legally obligated to pay as a result of a Privacy and Network Security Wrongful Act and where such amount is due to Your non-compliance with the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard." Critically, Payment Card Loss **excludes** "subsequent fines or monetary assessments for continued noncompliance with the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard beyond a period of three months from the date of the initial fine or monetary assessment." This three-month tail is a meaningful limitation for a business that cannot quickly remediate PCI deficiencies. (Source: same Chubb ERM documents above)

- **Consumer Redress Fund**: Covers amounts the insured is legally obligated to deposit as equitable relief for consumer claims from a Regulatory Proceeding judgment or settlement, excluding taxes, fines, penalties, injunctive relief, or sanctions.

**How sublimits work at Chubb**: Chubb uses a **schedule-driven sublimit structure**. The policy declarations/schedule lists separate "Sub-Limited Aggregate Limits" for Consumer Redress Fund, Payment Card Loss, and Regulatory Fines. These are carved out from the overall aggregate limit. Additionally, Chubb applies **coinsurance percentages** for certain perils—for example, the "Neglected Software Exploit" sublimit imposes coinsurance of 0% if software was patched within 0–45 days, escalating to 5% (46–90 days), 10% (91–180 days), 25% (181–365 days), and 50% (longer than 365 days). Widespread Event sublimits (for severe known vulnerability exploits, supply chain exploits, and zero-day exploits) also apply. (Source: Chubb Cyber ERM V2.2 policy documents, AU and international versions cited above)

Chubb states there are **no minimum premiums** and that "premiums scale for all sizes of risks based on the scope of coverage and limits." Online quoting and real-time policy issuance are available via Cyber Central for eligible risks with less than $100M in revenue. (Source: https://www.chubb.com/us-en/business-insurance/products/cyber-insurance/cyber-insurance-products.html)

### 1B. Coalition — Cyber Policy 3.0 (Form CYUSP-00PF-1022-01)

Coalition provides **two separate, explicitly named insuring agreements** for regulatory and PCI exposure:

- **Section II.B — Regulatory Defense and Penalties**: "We will pay on your behalf claim expenses and regulatory penalties that you become legally obligated to pay resulting from a claim against you in the form of a regulatory proceeding." (Source: Coalition Cyber Policy 3.0, https://inshq.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/COALITION-CYBER-AND-TECHNOLOGY-POLICY-3.pdf; also https://www.coalitioninc.com/coverages)

- **Section II.C — PCI Fines and Assessments**: "We will pay on your behalf claim expenses and PCI fines and assessments that you become legally obligated to pay resulting from a claim against you for a data breach compromising payment card data." (Source: same Coalition policy documents)

**How sublimits work at Coalition**: Coalition uses a **per-insuring-agreement limit structure within a single Aggregate Policy Limit**. A real binder example (for a condominium management association, $1M aggregate) shows:

| Insuring Agreement | Limit / Sub-Limit | Retention |
|---|---|---|
| A. Network and Information Security Liability | $1,000,000 | $2,500 |
| B. Regulatory Defense and Penalties | $1,000,000 | $2,500 |
| C. PCI Fines and Assessments | $1,000,000 | $2,500 |
| D. Funds Transfer Liability | $1,000,000 | $2,500 |
| E. Multimedia Content Liability | $1,000,000 | $2,500 |
| F/G. Breach Response Services | 72 hours, $0 retention | $0 |
| H. Breach Response Costs | $1,000,000 | $2,500 |

(Source: Coalition binder, https://img1.wsimg.com/blobby/go/b66c41fa-bc86-40ac-974e-900039024aa6/downloads/Cyber%20-%20Binder.pdf?ver=1730648932362)

In this example, each insuring agreement carries the full $1M limit, but all are subject to the single $1M Aggregate Policy Limit. A larger account (Association of California Water Agencies, $5M aggregate) shows the same structure at $5M per agreement with $50,000 retentions. (Source: https://www.acwajpia.com/wp-content/uploads/25-26-Cyber-Liability-Coalition-policy.pdf, referenced in search results)

Key structural features:
- **Aggregate Policy Limit** is the maximum the insurer will pay "regardless of the number of Insured Agreements purchased."
- **Per Event Limit** also applies, capping payment from a single event across all triggered agreements.
- **Defense/claim expenses reduce the limit** ("claim expenses reduce the applicable Limits of Liability, are subject to retentions, and may exhaust the applicable Limits of Liability").
- An **Optional Additional Limit for Breach Response Costs** can be purchased, which is "in addition to the Aggregate Policy Limit of Liability"—a significant structural advantage for preserving liability limits.
- Coalition's **"pay on behalf" language** means breach response costs, ransom payments, forensics, and first-party expenses are paid upfront rather than reimbursed. (Source: https://assets.ctfassets.net/o2pgk9gufvga/6GDAqNBNDON9cmkVdLCzd5/363be97c2125f8b89a7ca2a0515fd786/Coalition_Coverage-Advantage-Checklist-US.pdf)

### 1C. Cowbell Cyber — Prime 100

Cowbell's Prime 100 program (for businesses up to $100M revenue) bundles regulatory and PCI coverage within **Insuring Agreement 6: Security Breach Liability Including Payment Card Industry (PCI) Fines and Penalties**, which covers three prongs:

- **6.a**: Loss and Defense Expenses from a Claim for a Wrongful Act (general third-party liability).
- **6.b**: Loss and Defense Expenses from a **Regulatory Proceeding**, defined as "an investigation, demand or proceeding brought by, or on behalf of, the Federal Trade Commission, Federal Communications Commission, the Department of Health and Human Services or other administrative or regulatory agency, or any federal, state, local or foreign governmental entity in such entity's regulatory or official capacity." The explicit naming of HHS is directly relevant to HIPAA enforcement. (Source: Cowbell specimen policy, https://prowritersins.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/Cowbell-Specimen-1.pdf)
- **6.c**: Loss and Defense Expenses from "an action by a Card Company for non-compliance with the Payment Card Industry (PCI) Data Security Standards."

Cowbell's API coverage definitions further clarify:
- **PCI Costs** include: monetary assessments, fines, penalties, chargebacks, reimbursements, fraud recoveries, forensic investigation (including PFI), and "costs or expenses incurred in connection with a PCI DSS compliance audit."
- **Regulatory Costs** include: consumer payment funds, fines, and penalties imposed by a governmental entity due to a privacy incident.
- Separate **CCPA** and **GDPR** coverage endorsements are also available.
(Source: https://developers.cowbellcyber.ai/reference/coverage-definitions)

**How sublimits work at Cowbell**: Cowbell's specimen policy establishes a **Policy Aggregate Limit** with specific **Aggregate Sublimits** for:
- Ransom Payments (Insuring Agreement 2)
- Business Income and Extra Expense (Insuring Agreement 4)
- Public Relations Expense (Insuring Agreement 5)

These sublimits are explicitly "part of, not in addition to, the Policy Aggregate Limit of Insurance." Notably, the specimen form does **not** carve out separate sublimits for PCI fines or regulatory penalties—these appear to share the full aggregate limit under Insuring Agreement 6, though the declarations page for a specific policy could impose additional sublimits. A sample quote shows PCI Fines & Penalties, Regulator Defense & Penalties, and Security Breach Liability each at $500K within a $500K aggregate. (Source: Cowbell specimen, https://prowritersins.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/Cowbell-Specimen-1.pdf; sample quote, https://meetings.boardbook.org/Documents/DownloadPDF/e2bb4bf7-190d-400a-abf1-b242477fbe0c?org=1303)

**Critical structural note for Cowbell**: "Defense Expenses under Insuring Agreement 6…are payable within, and not in addition to, the Limit of Insurance. Payment of Defense Expenses under this Policy will reduce the Limit of Insurance." This means legal defense costs erode the same limit that pays fines and settlements.

### 1D. Regulatory Fine Coverage — Comparative Summary

| Feature | Chubb | Coalition | Cowbell |
|---|---|---|---|
| Regulatory fines covered? | Yes, under "Damages" in IA E | Yes, separate IA B | Yes, under IA 6.b |
| PCI fines/assessments covered? | Yes, "Payment Card Loss" in IA E | Yes, separate IA C | Yes, under IA 6.c |
| HIPAA/HHS explicitly named? | Via "Privacy or Cyber Laws" and Regulatory Proceeding | Via "regulatory proceeding" | Yes, HHS explicitly named in Regulatory Proceeding definition |
| Fines "insurable by law" qualifier? | Yes | Yes ("subject to applicable law") | Yes ("to the extent such fines or penalties are insurable by law") |
| PCI fine duration limit? | Yes—3-month cap on continued noncompliance fines | Not explicitly stated in available forms | Not explicitly stated in available forms |
| Sublimit structure | Schedule-driven, separate sublimits for Regulatory Fines, Payment Card Loss, Consumer Redress Fund | Per-agreement limits within single aggregate; optional additional limit for breach response | Aggregate with sublimits for ransom/BI/PR; PCI and regulatory share aggregate |
| Defense costs erode limit? | Claims Expenses within Damages definition | Yes, claim expenses reduce limits | Yes, explicitly stated |

### 1E. HIPAA Penalty Exposure Context

For a business handling employee health records, the HIPAA civil money penalty structure (enforced by HHS Office for Civil Rights) uses four culpability tiers. The most recent inflation-adjusted amounts (effective August 8, 2024) are:

| Tier | Culpability | Min per Violation | Max per Violation | Calendar Year Cap |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Lack of Knowledge | $141 | $71,162 | $2,134,831 |
| 2 | Reasonable Cause | $1,424 | $71,162 | $2,134,831 |
| 3 | Willful Neglect (corrected in 30 days) | $14,232 | $71,162 | $2,134,831 |
| 4 | Willful Neglect (not corrected) | $71,162 | $2,134,831 | $2,134,831 |

(Source: https://www.hipaajournal.com/2024-civil-monetary-penalties-hipaa-violations/; https://www.accountablehq.com/post/hipaa-privacy-rule-violation-penalties-what-organizations-should-expect-in-2025)

OCR also applies 2019 enforcement discretion that lowers calendar-year caps for Tiers 1–3. (Source: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2019/04/30/2019-08530/notification-of-enforcement-discretion-regarding-hipaa-civil-money-penalties)

Importantly, **business associates** (not just covered entities) are subject to HIPAA enforcement. A 2025 OCR settlement with BST & Co. CPAs—a HIPAA business associate—demonstrates that even non-healthcare firms holding PHI face enforcement. (Source: https://www.hhs.gov/press-room/hhs-ocr-bst-hipaa-settlement.html)

For PCI, card brand assessments flow through acquiring banks. Mastercard publishes per-violation, per-calendar-year assessments: up to $25,000 (1st violation) for Level 1/2 merchants, escalating to $200,000 (4th violation); Level 3 merchants face up to $10,000–$80,000. Acquirer non-compliance fees can range from $29.95–$150/month per merchant ID for small merchants, or $5,000–$100,000/month for larger violations. Post-breach forensic investigation (PFI) costs run $20,000–$150,000+. (Sources: https://pcicompliancecost.com/penalties; https://verisave.com/blog/pci-dss-4-non-compliance-fees-guide; https://www.ampcuscyber.com/blogs/avoid-pci-non-compliance-penalties/)

---

## 2. INCIDENT RESPONSE SERVICES AND SLAs

### 2A. Chubb

Chubb's Cyber ERM policy provides a **Cyber Incident Response Fund** (Insuring Agreement A) covering a broad menu of expenses:

1. Law firm for consultative and pre-litigation legal services (whether or not provided by the "Cyber Incident Response Coach")
2. Third-party forensic firms, **including a Payment Card Industry (PCI) Forensic Investigator**, to determine cause/scope and contain active incidents
3. Public relations / crisis communications
4. Law firm to determine indemnification rights under written agreements
5. Expenses to comply with Privacy or Cyber Laws, including notification letters, regulatory reporting, call center services, and **credit monitoring, credit freezing, or credit thawing**
6. With insurer consent: voluntary notification, **healthcare record monitoring (where available)**, social media monitoring, password management, fraud alert services, identity restoration, and informant rewards

(Source: Chubb Cyber ERM sample policy, https://studio.chubb.com/connect/files/NA_CyberSmallBusiness_Sample.pdf)

Chubb describes its incident response team as spanning "legal, computer forensics, notification, call center, public relations, fraud consultation, credit monitoring, and identity restoration service areas." Chubb has handled cyber incidents since 1998 and has "helped notify more than 300 million individuals." (Source: https://www.chubb.com/content/dam/chubb-sites/chubb-com/us-en/business-insurance/cyber-enterprise-risk-management-cyber-erm/documents/pdf/17010185-cyber-erm-12.17.pdf)

**SLA specifics**: The publicly available Chubb policy forms do not publish a specific hour-based SLA for incident response engagement. The policy requires expenses to be "reasonable and necessary" and incurred in response to a Cyber Incident "first discovered by any Control Group Member during the Policy Period." The "Control Group Member" concept (CEO, CFO, CIO, CISO, CPO, CTO, General Counsel, or Risk Manager) defines who can trigger the response. No specific response-time guarantee (e.g., "respond within X hours") was found in the available documents.

### 2B. Coalition

Coalition provides the most explicitly structured incident response service model:

- **Breach Response Services (Insuring Agreement F/G)**: "Limited to 72 hours following notification to the Breach Response Services Advisor" with a **$0 retention**. This is a pre-paid, no-deductible service window. (Source: Coalition binder, https://img1.wsimg.com/blobby/go/b66c41fa-bc86-40ac-974e-900039024aa6/downloads/Cyber%20-%20Binder.pdf?ver=1730648932362)

- **Rapid Response Services**: Coalition's marketing materials describe "immediate access to critical resources when facing an incident—including a **two-hour legal consultation** from a panel provider and support from Coalition Incident Response—at no cost." (Source: https://www.coalitioninc.com/coverages)

- **Coalition Incident Response (CIR)**: An in-house affiliate (Coalition Security) that provides hands-on incident response. When policyholders use CIR for computer forensic professional services, "any fees, costs and expenses of Coalition Incident Response…will not be subject to any Retention." This is the **$0 retention when using CIR** feature. (Source: Coalition binder and Coalition Coverage Advantage Checklist, https://assets.ctfassets.net/o2pgk9gufvga/6GDAqNBNDON9cmkVdLCzd5/363be97c2125f8b89a7ca2a0515fd786/Coalition_Coverage-Advantage-Checklist-US.pdf)

- **Breach Response Costs (Insuring Agreement H)**: A separate, dollar-denominated limit covering "costs to respond to a breach and help recover, including incident response, customer notification, credit monitoring, and legal costs." An **Optional Additional Limit** can be purchased that sits **outside** the Aggregate Policy Limit. (Source: Coalition binder and coverages page)

- **Pre-Claim Assistance**: A $270-value benefit included in the premium, providing pre-claim consultative support. (Source: Coalition binder)

- **Vanishing Retention**: Eligible policyholders using Coalition Control (the company's security monitoring platform) can see retentions "automatically discounted." (Source: https://www.coalitioninc.com/coverages)

**SLA specifics**: The 72-hour Breach Response Services window and the two-hour legal consultation are the closest things to published SLAs. Coalition's 24/7 security monitoring and in-house CIR team provide operational speed, but no specific "respond within X minutes/hours" guarantee was found in the policy forms.

### 2C. Cowbell

Cowbell's incident response is delivered through **Cowbell 365**, described as "an around-the-clock service that offers policyholders comprehensive support for risk improvement and incident response…24-hour availability every day of the week, 365 days of the year." The service provides access to "in-house team of dedicated cyber claims specialists and cyber risk engineers." (Source: https://cowbell.insure/news-events/pr/cowbell-365/)

Cowbell's claims experts are "on-call 24×7×365" and provide "a full range of post-incident recovery services." The company emphasizes its in-house model: "An entire team of in-house cyber professionals is behind the policy, including experienced cyber claims counsel and specialists, a cyber claims operations team dedicated to swift payments and claims processing, and best-in-class incident response vendors." (Source: https://cowbell.insure/aws/; https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/cowbell-365-elevates-policyholder-experience-with-cyber-claims-handling-and-risk-mitigation-301757699.html)

The **Cowbell Breach Fund** covers "incident response, investigation, forensics, crisis management, notification to customers, call center services, overtime salaries, post-event monitoring services such as credit monitoring, and **healthcare records remediation** for impacted customers." The explicit mention of healthcare records remediation is directly relevant to HIPAA exposure. (Source: https://developers.cowbellcyber.ai/reference/coverage-definitions)

**SLA specifics**: Cowbell does not publish a specific hour-based response SLA in the available documents. The sample quote shows a **6-hour waiting period** for business interruption coverage, which is a form of time-based deductible rather than a response SLA. (Source: Cowbell sample quote, https://meetings.boardbook.org/Documents/DownloadPDF/e2bb4bf7-190d-400a-abf1-b242477fbe0c?org=1303)

### 2D. Incident Response — Comparative Summary

| Feature | Chubb | Coalition | Cowbell |
|---|---|---|---|
| Named IR program | Cyber Incident Response Team / Coach | Coalition Incident Response (CIR) / Coalition Security | Cowbell 365 |
| Availability | Not explicitly stated as 24/7 in forms | 24/7 monitoring referenced | 24/7/365 explicitly stated |
| Pre-paid IR window | Not specified | 72 hours, $0 retention | Not specified |
| Free legal consultation | Via Cyber Incident Response Coach | 2-hour panel legal consultation | Via in-house claims counsel |
| PCI Forensic Investigator | Explicitly included | Not explicitly named in forms | PFI referenced in PCI Costs definition |
| Healthcare record monitoring/remediation | "Healthcare record monitoring (where available)" | Not explicitly named | "Healthcare records remediation" explicitly included |
| $0 retention for using IR provider | Not specified | Yes, when using CIR | Not specified |
| Published response-time SLA | No | 72-hour service window; 2-hour legal consult | No specific SLA published |

---

## 3. CREDIT MONITORING AND LEGAL DEFENSE COVERAGE

### 3A. Credit Monitoring

- **Chubb**: Cyber Incident Response Expenses explicitly include "providing credit monitoring, credit freezing, or credit thawing" as part of compliance with Privacy or Cyber Laws (paragraph 5.d), and also as a voluntary service with insurer consent (paragraph 6.b), which additionally includes "healthcare record monitoring (where available), social media monitoring, password management services, or fraud alert services." Identity restoration services and fraud consultation by licensed investigators are also covered. (Source: Chubb Cyber ERM sample policy)

- **Coalition**: Breach Response Costs cover "costs to respond to a breach and help recover, including incident response, customer notification, **credit monitoring**, and legal costs." (Source: https://www.coalitioninc.com/coverages)

- **Cowbell**: Post-event Monitoring Expenses under Insuring Agreement 1 (Security Breach Expense) cover "costs to provide **credit and identity monitoring services** to the affected parties of a Security Breach for up to one (1) year, or longer if required by applicable law, from the date of notification." The Cowbell Breach Fund also includes "post-event monitoring services such as credit monitoring, and healthcare records remediation." (Source: Cowbell specimen policy; Cowbell coverage definitions)

### 3B. Legal Defense

- **Chubb**: "Claims Expenses" include "attorneys' fees, mediation costs, arbitration expenses, expert witness fees, and other fees and costs incurred by the Insurer, or by an Insured with the Insurer's prior written consent, in the investigation and defense of a Claim." Claims Expenses also include appeal/attachment bond premiums. The insurer has the right to investigate and defend claims. Claims Expenses are part of the "Damages" definition and thus erode the policy limit. (Source: Chubb Cyber ERM sample policy)

- **Coalition**: "We will have the right and duty to defend, subject to the Limits of Liability and applicable Retention(s), exclusions, conditions, and other terms of this Policy." For Regulatory Defense and Penalties (Section II.B), Coalition defends "any claim in the form of a regulatory proceeding." Policyholders "have the right to select defence counsel from our panel providers," and non-panel counsel "must be mutually agreed upon between you and us, which agreement will not be unreasonably withheld or conditioned." Defense costs are "claim expenses" that reduce the limit. (Source: Coalition Cyber Policy 3.0)

- **Cowbell**: Under Insuring Agreement 6, "Defense Expenses means the reasonable and necessary fees (attorneys' and experts' fees) and expenses incurred in the defense or appeal of a Claim, including the cost of appeal, attachment or similar bonds…excluding wages, salaries, benefits or expenses of your Employees." The insurer "shall have the right and duty to select counsel and defend the Insured against any Claim covered under Insuring Agreement 6.a.(1)." For regulatory proceedings (6.a.(2)), the insurer has "the right but not the duty to defend." Defense Expenses are "payable within, and not in addition to, the Limit of Insurance." (Source: Cowbell specimen policy)

### 3C. Credit Monitoring and Legal Defense — Comparative Summary

| Feature | Chubb | Coalition | Cowbell |
|---|---|---|---|
| Credit monitoring | Yes, required by law + voluntary | Yes, under Breach Response Costs | Yes, up to 1 year or longer if required by law |
| Credit freezing/thawing | Yes | Not explicitly stated | Not explicitly stated |
| Healthcare record monitoring | Yes ("where available") | Not explicitly stated | Yes ("healthcare records remediation") |
| Identity restoration | Yes | Not explicitly stated in forms | Not explicitly stated in forms |
| Fraud consultation | Yes (licensed investigator) | Not explicitly stated | Not explicitly stated |
| Defense counsel selection | Insurer-directed with consent | Panel selection; non-panel by mutual agreement | Insurer selects for third-party claims; right but not duty for regulatory |
| Defense costs erode limit? | Yes (within Damages) | Yes (claim expenses reduce limits) | Yes (explicitly stated) |
| Bond premiums covered? | Yes | Not explicitly stated in available forms | Yes |

---

## 4. POLICY EXCLUSIONS RELEVANT TO E-COMMERCE BUSINESSES

### 4A. Chubb Exclusions

From the Cyber ERM sample policy:
- **Cyber Incident Response Expenses exclude**: costs to "update or improve privacy or network security controls, policies or procedures, or compliance with Privacy or Cyber Laws, to a level beyond that which existed prior to the applicable Cyber Incident"; taxes, fines, penalties, injunctive relief, or sanctions (except as covered under Payment Card Loss or Regulatory Fines); the insured's own money; and wages/salaries of employees.
- **Damages exclude**: amounts the insured is not legally obligated to pay; matters uninsurable by law; cost to comply with injunctive/remedial/preventative/non-monetary/declaratory relief; consideration owed (royalties, restitution, disgorgement, return of fees); liquidated damages exceeding what would have been owed absent contract; and contractual penalties (except Payment Card Loss).
- **Payment Card Loss excludes**: fines for continued PCI noncompliance beyond three months from initial fine; costs to update/improve security controls.
(Source: Chubb Cyber ERM sample policy and V2.2 documents)

### 4B. Coalition Exclusions

From the Coalition Cyber Policy 3.0:
- **Merchant Liability Exclusion**: "Any charge back, interchange fee, discount fee, service related fee, rate, or charge; or liability or fee incurred by you due to a merchant service provider, payment processor, payment card company, or bank or freezing payment transactions." However, this exclusion contains a **carve-back**: "except that this exclusion will not apply to coverage afforded under Section II.C, PCI FINES AND ASSESSMENTS." This means routine merchant fees and chargebacks are excluded, but PCI fines/assessments from a data breach remain covered. (Source: Coalition Cyber Policy 3.0, AU and UK versions)
- **Bodily Injury**: Excluded, except for mental anguish/emotional distress claims under Network and Information Security Liability and Multimedia Content Liability.
- **Confiscation**: Government confiscation/destruction of property or systems excluded.
- Standard exclusions for war, nuclear, pollution, and prior/pending claims.
(Source: Coalition Cyber Policy 3.0)

### 4C. Cowbell Exclusions

From the Cowbell specimen policy (Section V):
- **Bodily injury/property damage**: Excluded, but "bodily injury" does not mean "mental anguish or emotional distress resulting directly from a Security Breach"—a carve-back relevant to privacy claims.
- **War, civil unrest, insurrection**: Excluded.
- **Nuclear, biological, chemical, pathogenic**: Excluded.
- **RICO violations**: Excluded.
- **Patent/trade secret violations**: Excluded (Patent Act, Economic Espionage Act, Uniform Trade Secrets Act).
- **Pollutants**: Excluded.
- **Prior/pending claims**: Excluded.
- **Employer practices**: "Any actions or activities related to an Insured's practices as an employer including, but not limited to, refusal to em[p]loy…"—this is directly relevant to a business with 15 employees, as employment-related claims (e.g., wrongful termination, discrimination) are excluded from cyber coverage.
- **Contractual liability**: Excluded, except for liability that would exist absent the contract.
- **Insufficient capacity/overload**: Excluded unless caused by a Cyber Incident.
- **Internet/telecom service disruption**: Excluded unless caused by a denial-of-service attack.
- **Power failure/surge**: Excluded.
- **Satellite malfunction**: Excluded.
(Source: Cowbell specimen policy, https://prowritersins.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/Cowbell-Specimen-1.pdf)

### 4D. E-Commerce Exclusion Comparison

| Exclusion Area | Chubb | Coalition | Cowbell |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chargebacks / interchange fees | Payment Card Loss covers assessments/fines/chargebacks from PCI noncompliance breach | Excluded under Merchant Liability, except PCI Fines & Assessments | Not explicitly excluded in available forms; PCI Costs definition includes chargebacks |
| Contractual penalties / liquidated damages | Excluded except Payment Card Loss | Not explicitly addressed in available forms | Contractual liability excluded except where liability exists absent contract |
| Security improvement costs | Excluded (beyond pre-incident level) | Not explicitly addressed in available forms | Excluded (upgrading/improving Computer System) |
| Employer practices | Not explicitly addressed in available forms | Not explicitly addressed in available forms | Explicitly excluded |
| Bodily injury / mental anguish | Bodily Injury defined broadly including mental injury | BI excluded except mental anguish under security/multimedia | BI excluded except mental anguish from Security Breach |
| Prior/pending claims | Retroactive date applies | Full Prior Acts available | Full Prior Acts available (per sample quote) |

**Key e-commerce consideration**: For a business processing customer payments online, the Coalition Merchant Liability exclusion is the most consequential—it strips coverage for routine chargebacks, interchange fees, and processor-imposed fees, preserving only PCI Fines and Assessments from a data breach. Chubb's Payment Card Loss is broader (including chargebacks and fraud recoveries tied to PCI noncompliance) but caps continued noncompliance fines at three months. Cowbell's PCI Costs definition is the broadest, explicitly including chargebacks, reimbursements, fraud recoveries, PFI costs, and PCI DSS compliance audit costs.

---

## 5. PREMIUM DRIVERS FOR $2–5M REVENUE BUSINESSES WITH DUAL PCI/HIPAA EXPOSURE

### 5A. Key Rating Factors

Based on available market data, the following factors drive cyber insurance premiums for small businesses:

1. **Revenue** (single biggest factor): Carriers use revenue bands. Businesses in the $1–5M range typically face a **+20–40% premium uplift** over sub-$1M businesses. Revenue signals potential business interruption loss magnitude and ransom demand size. (Source: https://ciberinsurance.org/blog/cyber-insurance-pricing-2025/)

2. **Industry and data type**: Healthcare and businesses handling PHI pay significantly more. "Industry matters significantly, with financial services, healthcare, and retail businesses paying more due to the sensitive data they handle." Healthcare SMB premiums run $2,000–$6,000/year; retail/eCommerce $1,500–$4,500/year. High-data-risk small businesses (dental offices, medical billing) pay $3,500–$9,000/year for $1M coverage. The industry risk differential can be **2–5x** between lowest and highest risk sectors. (Sources: https://ciberinsurance.org/blog/cyber-insurance-pricing-2025/; https://investnfly.com/cyber-insurance-cost-2025/; https://morrowinsure.com/cost/cyber-insurance-cost)

3. **Security controls** (biggest modifiable factor): "Premium Impact: 40–60% reduction for comprehensive controls." Must-haves include MFA on email/VPN, endpoint detection and response (EDR), regular tested backups, and employee security training. Missing controls can result in rate increases or outright denial. "Underwriters in 2026 increasingly require proof, not just an attestation on the application." (Sources: https://ciberinsurance.org/blog/cyber-insurance-pricing-2025/; https://seedpodcyber.com/cyber-insurance-calculator/)

4. **Coverage limits and deductibles**: Typical premium uplifts:
   - $1M limit / $5K deductible: Base pricing
   - $2M limit / $10K deductible: **+60–80% premium**
   - $5M limit / $25K deductible: **+150–200% premium**
   (Source: https://ciberinsurance.org/blog/cyber-insurance-pricing-2025/)

5. **PCI compliance status and transaction volume**: "PCI compliance and transaction volume drive pricing." A business that is non-compliant or has lapsed validation faces higher premiums and potential coverage restrictions. PCI DSS 4.0 future-dated requirements became mandatory March 31, 2025, increasing compliance scrutiny. (Sources: https://ciberinsurance.org/blog/cyber-insurance-pricing-2025/; https://verisave.com/blog/pci-dss-4-non-compliance-fees-guide)

6. **HIPAA/PHI exposure**: "Higher due to HIPAA compliance requirements and PHI exposure." Businesses handling employee health records face elevated premiums because of the regulatory penalty structure and breach notification requirements under 45 C.F.R. §§ 164.400–414. (Source: https://ciberinsurance.org/blog/cyber-insurance-pricing-2025/)

7. **Claims history**: Coalition's application asks about cyber incidents, claims, or losses in the past three years, including count, total loss amount, whether any single event exceeded $25,000, and remediation steps. (Source: https://www.bindledger.com/blog/coalition-cyber-application-pdf-every-question-explained)

8. **Ransomware-specific underwriting**: "Ransomware coverage is increasingly underwritten separately. Expect a sublimit or co-insurance requirement if you haven't implemented endpoint detection and response (EDR)." Chubb's Neglected Software Exploit coinsurance schedule (0%–50% based on patching recency) exemplifies this trend. (Sources: https://morrowinsure.com/cost/cyber-insurance-cost; Chubb Cyber ERM V2.2)

### 5B. Estimated Premium Ranges for This Business Profile

For a 15-employee Austin business with $2–5M revenue, dual PCI/HIPAA exposure, and e-commerce operations:

| Limit / Deductible | Estimated Annual Premium Range | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| $1M / $5K–$10K | $3,500 – $9,000 | High-data-risk SMB range; healthcare/PCI premium uplift |
| $2M / $10K | $5,600 – $16,200 | Base × 1.6–1.8 (60–80% uplift for $2M limit) |
| $5M / $25K | $8,750 – $27,000 | Base × 2.5–3.0 (150–200% uplift for $5M limit) |

**Calculation methodology**: Starting from the high-data-risk SMB baseline of $3,500–$9,000 for $1M coverage (Source: https://morrowinsure.com/cost/cyber-insurance-cost), applying the documented limit/deductible uplift factors of +60–80% for $2M and +150–200% for $5M (Source: https://ciberinsurance.org/blog/cyber-insurance-pricing-2025/). These ranges assume reasonable but not best-in-class security controls. Comprehensive controls (MFA, EDR, tested backups, training) could reduce premiums by 40–60%, while missing controls could increase them or result in declination.

**Uncertainty note**: These are estimates derived from aggregated market data, not carrier-specific quotes. Actual premiums will vary based on the specific underwriting responses, PCI compliance documentation, HIPAA risk assessment status, claims history, and the exact coverage structure selected. The Cowbell sample quote found in research ($7,811 for a $500K limit with $25K deductible) suggests that specific risk profiles can produce premiums at the higher end of or above these ranges. Coalition's binder example ($1,116 for a $1M limit) reflects a lower-risk profile (condominium management) without PCI/HIPAA exposure.

### 5C. Dual PCI/HIPAA Exposure — Specific Premium Implications

The combination of PCI-DSS and HIPAA exposure creates a **compounding risk profile** that underwriters will price accordingly:

- **PCI exposure** signals payment card transaction volume, e-commerce dependency, and potential card-brand assessment liability. Underwriters will examine PCI compliance status, SAQ level, use of tokenization/hosted payment pages, and merchant agreement terms.
- **HIPAA exposure** signals PHI holdings, OCR enforcement risk, and mandatory breach notification obligations. Underwriters will examine whether the business is a covered entity or business associate, the scope of PHI held, risk analysis documentation, and security safeguards.
- **Combined exposure** means a single breach could trigger simultaneous PCI assessments, HIPAA civil money penalties, state breach notification obligations (Texas requires notification under Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 521.053), and potential class-action liability. This correlation risk is what drives the highest premium tier.

---

## 6. KEY FINDINGS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

### Coverage Gaps to Watch

1. **PCI fine duration limits**: Chubb caps Payment Card Loss for continued noncompliance at three months. If remediation takes longer, subsequent fines are uninsured. Coalition and Cowbell do not show this specific limitation in available forms, but policy-specific endorsements may apply.

2. **Defense costs eroding limits**: All three carriers treat defense costs as eroding the policy limit. For a regulatory proceeding that involves extended litigation, this can significantly reduce the amount available for actual fines or settlements.

3. **Merchant liability exclusion (Coalition)**: Routine chargebacks, interchange fees, and processor fees are excluded. Only PCI fines/assessments from a data breach are covered. E-commerce businesses should understand this boundary.

4. **Employer practices exclusion (Cowbell)**: Employment-related claims are excluded from cyber coverage. A 15-employee business should ensure its employment practices liability is covered elsewhere.

5. **Security improvement costs**: All three carriers exclude costs to improve security beyond pre-incident levels. Insurance covers restoration, not betterment.

6. **HIPAA fine insurability**: All three carriers qualify regulatory fine coverage with "to the extent insurable by law" or "subject to applicable law." The insurability of HIPAA civil money penalties under Texas law should be verified with counsel, as some jurisdictions restrict insurability of punitive or quasi-criminal penalties.

### Structural Differences That Matter

- **Chubb** offers the most granular sublimit structure (separate sublimits for Regulatory Fines, Payment Card Loss, Consumer Redress Fund) and the broadest incident response expense definitions (including healthcare record monitoring, identity restoration, and fraud consultation). Its coinsurance schedule for unpatched software is unique. Best suited for businesses wanting highly customizable, schedule-driven coverage.

- **Coalition** offers the most operationally integrated incident response (in-house CIR, $0 retention for using CIR, 72-hour pre-paid response window, 2-hour legal consultation, pay-on-behalf language). Its separate insuring agreements for Regulatory Defense and PCI Fines provide clarity. The optional additional limit for Breach Response Costs (outside the aggregate) is a significant structural advantage. Best suited for businesses prioritizing fast, hands-on incident response with minimal out-of-pocket friction.

- **Cowbell** offers the broadest PCI Costs definition (including chargebacks, fraud recoveries, PFI, and PCI DSS compliance audit costs) and explicitly names HHS in its Regulatory Proceeding definition. Its Cowbell 365 24/7 service and healthcare records remediation coverage are directly relevant to HIPAA exposure. The admitted paper (Palomar, AM Best A) in 45 states provides regulatory stability. Best suited for businesses wanting broad PCI/HIPAA coverage with in-house claims handling.

### Final Note on Uncertainty

This analysis is based on publicly available specimen policy forms, sample binders, marketing materials, and market pricing data. Actual policy terms, sublimits, retentions, and premiums for a specific business will be determined by the underwriting process and may include endorsements not reflected in specimen forms. The premium estimates in Section 5B are derived from aggregated market data and should be treated as planning ranges, not quotes. A licensed insurance broker experienced in cyber coverage for dual PCI/HIPAA risks should be engaged to obtain and compare actual proposals from all three carriers.

---

*Sources cited throughout this report. All policy language is quoted from publicly available specimen forms and marketing materials as of the research date. HIPAA penalty amounts reflect the August 8, 2024 inflation adjustment. PCI assessment figures reflect published card brand schedules and acquirer fee ranges.*
