# CI/CD Orchestration for a 200+ Service Fintech: GitLab DAG vs GitHub Actions Reusable Workflows vs Buildkite Dynamic Pipelines

## 1. Executive Summary

For a fintech platform with 200+ microservices, 50–100 production deployments daily, and a polyglot stack (Java/Go/Python), the three approaches differ less in raw single-pipeline speed (all three converge on a ~40–45 minute critical path for the reference service) and more in **concurrency behavior at peak, centralization of pipeline logic, and compliance machinery**:

- **GitLab CI DAG (`needs`)** gives the most complete *built-in* compliance/audit stack (Ultimate-tier compliance frameworks, enforced compliance pipelines, audit event streaming) and native canary/incremental-rollout templates, but GitLab.com-hosted compute is the most expensive per-minute option found ($10 per 1,000 compute minutes; ~$1,100 per 1,000 reference runs). Self-managed runners eliminate per-minute fees. (https://about.gitlab.com/pricing/faq-compute-minutes/, https://docs.gitlab.com/user/compliance/compliance_frameworks/)
- **GitHub Actions reusable workflows** centralize logic cleanly and have the strongest *secrets-rotation* story via OIDC federation (short-lived cloud credentials, no long-lived keys), but carry structural limits (10 nesting levels, 50 called workflows per file, environment secrets not passable through `workflow_call`) and hard concurrency ceilings (500 concurrent jobs on standard Enterprise-hosted runners). Cost for the reference pipeline on GitHub-hosted 2-core Linux runners is ~$660 per 1,000 runs. (https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/reusing-workflow-configurations, https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/limits, https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/security/openid-connect)
- **Buildkite dynamic pipeline generation** is the only one with published, named evidence of operating at far greater scale than this scenario requires (Shopify: 8,000 pipelines, 300M jobs in 10 months, ~10,000 concurrent agents; 75% build-time reduction), with effectively unbounded self-hosted concurrency and a single central generator script as the reuse mechanism across hundreds of services. Its gaps: thin native compliance/audit features in the evidence gathered, and you own more plumbing. Per-minute platform cost is $0 on self-hosted agents; hosted Linux agents run ~$0.004/vCPU-min. (https://buildkite.com/resources/case-studies/shopify/, https://buildkite.com/docs/pipelines/configure/dynamic-pipelines, https://pricingsaas.com/companies/buildkite)

**Bottom line:** If minimizing developer wait time at high concurrency and minimizing per-service maintenance are the dominant goals, the evidence favors **Buildkite-style dynamic pipeline generation on self-hosted agents, paired with a progressive-delivery controller (Flagger/Argo Rollouts) for canary + automated rollback** — this is the pattern proven at Shopify-class scale. If the organization is already GitHub-centric, **reusable workflows + OIDC + ArgoCD/Argo Rollouts (GitOps)** is the lowest-friction equivalent, with a real fintech case study showing 15-minute average deployments and canary/blue-green at 99.99% uptime. If turnkey compliance evidence collection is the overriding constraint and the org runs GitLab as SCM, **GitLab Ultimate with DAG + parent-child pipelines + enforced compliance pipelines** is the strongest single-vendor option. Details, math, and caveats below.

---

## 2. Scenario Definition and Modeling Assumptions

Reference pipeline per service (as specified in the task):
- 1 build job: **15 min**
- 8 parallel test jobs: duration **not specified in the task; assumed 10 min each** (sensitivity range 6–14 min tested below)
- 3 sequential deployment stages (e.g., staging → canary → production): **assumed 5 min each = 15 min**

Volume context: 50–100 production deployments/day = ~1,500–3,000 production pipelines/month; with PR/branch CI across 200+ repos, total monthly runs are plausibly 10–50× that. All three vendors' pricing models make **self-hosted compute the norm at this scale**, which is reflected in the cost analysis.

These test/deploy durations are assumptions; every derived figure scales linearly with them and the formulas are shown so readers can substitute real values.

---

## 3. Mechanism Comparison

### 3.1 GitLab CI DAG pipelines
GitLab's `needs` keyword converts the default stage-ordered pipeline into a directed acyclic graph: "Jobs run as soon as their dependencies are met, regardless of the pipeline's stages configuration," supporting fan-out, fan-in, and diamond dependencies; `needs: []` starts a job immediately (https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/yaml/needs/). GitLab explicitly positions four architectures: basic, `needs`-based DAG, parent-child pipelines (recommended for monorepos/many components), and multi-project pipelines ("Good for larger products that have cross-project interdependencies, like those with a microservices architecture") (https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/pipelines/pipeline_architectures/). GitLab's own docs note the failure modes of scale: stage barriers cause waits, `include:`-based config grows complex, and "namespace collisions where jobs are unintentionally duplicated" (https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/pipelines/pipeline_architectures/).

### 3.2 GitHub Actions reusable workflows
A reusable workflow is triggered by `on: workflow_call` and accepts typed inputs, secrets, and outputs; callers invoke it with a single `uses:` line, so "the caller workflow file may contain just a few lines of YAML" (https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/workflows-and-actions/reusing-workflow-configurations). Documented limitations relevant to a 200-service platform (https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/reusing-workflow-configurations):
- Max **10 levels of nesting**; max **50 unique reusable workflows** callable from one workflow file.
- Workflow-level `env` from the caller does **not** propagate to called workflows (outputs must be used instead).
- **Environment secrets cannot be passed** through `workflow_call` (the called workflow's job-level environment wins); `secrets: inherit` is the workaround (https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/reuse-automations/reuse-workflows).
- Reusable workflows are called at job level only, not step level.

Unlike composite actions, reusable workflows log every job/step separately and can define their own runners — good for auditability (https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/workflows-and-actions/reusing-workflow-configurations).

### 3.3 Buildkite dynamic pipeline generation
Buildkite's model: a bootstrap step runs a generator script whose YAML/JSON output is piped to `buildkite-agent pipeline upload`; "The generated steps are inserted into the running build immediately after the bootstrap step," each scheduled as its own job on any matching agent/queue (https://buildkite.com/docs/pipelines/configure/dynamic-pipelines). Key properties:
- Limit of **500 steps per uploaded file**; larger pipelines split across multiple uploads (https://buildkite.com/docs/agent/cli/reference/pipeline).
- `--replace` swaps the bootstrap step with the generated pipeline; the "handler pattern" reads runtime state (meta-data, artifacts, git diff, API responses) mid-build and uploads the next phase — the documented foundation for pipelines that adapt in flight, including rollback branches (https://github.com/buildkite/skills/blob/main/skills/buildkite-pipelines/references/dynamic-pipeline-patterns.md).
- A multi-language **Buildkite SDK** (Go/Python/TypeScript examples in docs) generates steps programmatically — directly relevant to polyglot Java/Go/Python estates (https://buildkite.com/docs/pipelines/configure/dynamic-pipelines/sdk).
- Centralized-generator pattern: each service repo's tiny `pipeline.yml` just clones and invokes one org-level generator repo (https://github.com/buildkite/skills/blob/main/skills/buildkite-pipelines/references/dynamic-pipeline-patterns.md).

---

## 4. Pipeline Execution Time for the Reference Service

### 4.1 Critical-path math (zero queue wait)

Critical path = build + slowest parallel test + sequential deploy stages.

| Model | Formula | All tests = 10 min | Tests vary 6–14 min |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stage-based (GitLab w/o `needs`, or any stage barrier) | 15 + max(tests) + 15 | **40 min** | **44 min** |
| GitLab DAG / GH Actions `needs` / Buildkite `depends_on` | same critical path when deploy requires all tests green | **40 min** | **44 min** |

**Important honest finding:** for this single-service pipeline, DAG scheduling does *not* shorten the critical path, because deployment inherently requires all tests to pass. DAG/dynamic-generation wins come from three places:

1. **Independent side jobs start immediately.** `needs: []` lint/secret-scan/SAST jobs run concurrent with the build instead of waiting for stage barriers (https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/yaml/needs/). This doesn't cut the critical path but removes tail latency from feedback on cheap checks.
2. **Partial-dependency deploys.** If the first deploy stage (e.g., dev/staging) only needs unit tests (say the 6-min job), DAG scheduling starts it at minute 21 instead of 29 — **up to ~8 min saved** on the path to the first environment.
3. **Multi-service fan-out (the dominant effect at 200 services).** In a stage-based pipeline triggered by multi-repo or monorepo changes, all builds must finish before any test starts; with per-service DAG paths (GitLab) or per-service generated steps (Buildkite), each service flows independently and wall time equals the slowest single-service path (~40 min) rather than accumulating stage-barrier synchronization across services. GitLab's docs use exactly this example: "deploy_a could run and deploy before build_b completes" (https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/yaml/needs/).

### 4.2 Platform-specific overheads

- **Buildkite dynamic generation** adds one serial bootstrap step before anything else runs (generator script + upload). Typical generator runtimes are seconds to a couple of minutes; call it **~1 min added**, i.e., ~41 min for the reference pipeline. The `--replace` variant hides this step from the UI but not its latency (https://github.com/buildkite/skills/blob/main/skills/buildkite-pipelines/references/dynamic-pipeline-patterns.md).
- **GitHub Actions reusable workflows** add per-job runner allocation and artifact transfer between jobs; each called workflow runs "as if it was part of the caller workflow" (https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/workflows-and-actions/reusing-workflow-configurations). I found no authoritative per-job overhead figure in the evidence gathered; treat added seconds-to-a-minute per job as an estimate (uncertainty stated).
- **Queue wait, not critical path, is the real differentiator at this scale.** With 200+ services and bursty PR activity, nominal concurrency caps bind:
  - GitHub Actions Enterprise: **500 concurrent jobs** on standard GitHub-hosted runners (1,000 on larger runners); concurrency groups queue at most 100 pending runs per group (https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/limits, https://github.blog/changelog/2026-05-07-github-actions-concurrency-groups-now-allow-larger-queues/). A vendor-run load test by CircleCI (clearly a competitor source; treat with caution) reported that an Enterprise org with 500-job capacity "never exceeded approximately 124 concurrent jobs and limited processing to roughly 6 workflows simultaneously" when replaying 24h of commits on a large repo (https://circleci.com/blog/ci-cd-at-scale-circleci-vs-github-actions/). Whether this reproduces with self-hosted runners and many repos is uncertain, but it flags throughput risk worth piloting.
  - Buildkite self-hosted: concurrency is limited only by agent fleet size; Shopify ran **~10,000 concurrent agents** (https://buildkite.com/resources/case-studies/shopify/).
  - GitLab self-managed runners: concurrency is likewise fleet-limited (no per-minute cap applies to self-managed runners; https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/pipelines/compute_minutes/).

**Execution-time verdict:** ~40–45 min critical path on all three for one service; Buildkite and self-hosted GitLab have the clearest headroom for peak concurrency; GitHub Actions needs careful sizing against its 500-job standard ceiling.

---

## 5. Cost per 1,000 Pipeline Runs

### 5.1 Compute consumption of the reference pipeline
Job-minutes per run = 1×15 (build) + 8×10 (tests) + 3×5 (deploys) = **110 job-minutes** (+ ~1 min Buildkite bootstrap).
Per 1,000 runs = **110,000 job-minutes**.

### 5.2 Platform rates found

| Platform | Rate (evidence) | Cost per 1,000 reference runs |
|---|---|---|
| GitHub-hosted, Linux 2-core | $0.006/min (https://docs.github.com/en/billing/reference/actions-runner-pricing) | 110,000 × $0.006 = **$660** |
| GitHub-hosted, Linux 1-core slim | $0.002/min (same source) | **$220** (only if 1-core suffices — unlikely for Java builds) |
| GitHub self-hosted (from 2026-03-01) | $0.002/min platform charge; listed hosted rates cut ~40% with the charge bundled (https://github.com/resources/insights/2026-pricing-changes-for-github-actions) | **$220 platform fee** + own infra |
| GitLab.com instance runners (overage) | $10 per 1,000 compute minutes; cost factor 1.0 for standard projects (https://about.gitlab.com/pricing/faq-compute-minutes/, https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/pipelines/compute_minutes/) | 110,000 compute-min → **$1,100** |
| GitLab self-managed + own runners | No per-minute GitLab charge; license is Premium $29/user/mo (10,000 compute-min/mo included, irrelevant on own runners) / Ultimate custom (50,000 incl.) (https://about.gitlab.com/pricing/) | **$0 to GitLab** + own infra + license |
| Buildkite self-hosted | No per-minute charge; Pro $30/active user/mo; Enterprise custom (30-user min) (https://buildkite.com/pricing/, https://pricingsaas.com/companies/buildkite/diffs/2024Q4) | **$0 to Buildkite** + own infra + seats |
| Buildkite hosted Linux agents | $0.004/vCPU-min; add-ons seen at $0.01/min (Small), $0.03/min (Medium) (https://pricingsaas.com/companies/buildkite) | 2 vCPU assumption: 110,000 × 2 × $0.004 = **$880**; Small-instance rate: **$1,100** |

Verification of arithmetic: 110,000 × 0.006 = 660 ✓; 110,000 × 0.002 = 220 ✓; (110,000/1,000) × 10 = 1,100 ✓; 110,000 × 2 × 0.004 = 880 ✓.

### 5.3 Monthly-scale projection (illustrative)
Assume 30,000 total pipeline runs/month (mid estimate for 200 services with active PR CI): 30,000 × 110 = **3.3M job-minutes/month**.
- GitHub-hosted 2-core: 3.3M × $0.006 ≈ **$19,800/month**
- GitLab.com overage packs: 3.3M/1,000 × $10 ≈ **$33,000/month**
- Self-hosted on any of the three: cloud infra cost only (plus GitHub's new $0.002/min self-hosted charge ≈ $6,600/month from March 2026 — a material change to note: "Beginning March 1, 2026, self-hosted runners will be included within your free usage quota, and will consume available usage based on list price" — https://github.com/resources/insights/2026-pricing-changes-for-github-actions).

**Cost verdict:** At this volume all three push you to self-hosted compute; on hosted compute, GitHub 2-core ($660/1k) is cheapest found, GitLab.com overage ($1,100/1k) most expensive, Buildkite hosted in between (~$880–1,100/1k). Included quotas (GitHub Enterprise Cloud 50,000 min/mo — https://docs.github.com/en/enterprise-cloud@latest/billing/concepts/product-billing/github-actions; GitLab Premium 10,000/Ultimate 50,000 min/mo — https://about.gitlab.com/pricing/) offset only ~1–3% of this workload. Uncertainty: real costs swing with test duration, caching effectiveness, spot-instance use, and artifact storage, none of which I could quantify from sources.

---

## 6. Operational Overhead of Pipeline Definitions Across 200+ Services

**GitLab.** Reuse via `include:` (project/instance templates), parent-child pipelines, and multi-project pipelines (https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/pipelines/pipeline_architectures/). Ultimate adds **compliance pipelines**: a compliance framework can "enforce compliance pipeline configuration" on every project assigned to it (https://docs.gitlab.com/user/compliance/compliance_frameworks/) — i.e., the platform team can inject mandatory CI into all 200 services without editing each repo. Overhead risk documented by GitLab itself: `include:` complexity and namespace collisions duplicating jobs unintentionally (https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/pipelines/pipeline_architectures/).

**GitHub Actions.** One reusable workflow repo per concern (build-java, build-go, test, deploy); each service repo carries a caller file of a few lines (https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/workflows-and-actions/reusing-workflow-configurations). Maintenance friction points from the docs: environment secrets can't traverse `workflow_call` (forces `secrets: inherit` or org-level secret sprawl), env vars don't propagate, and the 10-level/50-workflow caps constrain deep platform layering (https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/reusing-workflow-configurations). Updating the central reusable workflow propagates automatically to callers (versioned by ref), but 200 caller files still exist and must be kept pointing at current refs.

**Buildkite.** The lowest per-service footprint in evidence: each repo's `.buildkite/pipeline.yml` is a 2–3 line bootstrap that invokes a **single centralized generator** (cloned from an infra repo), and all policy/logic lives in that generator (https://github.com/buildkite/skills/blob/main/skills/buildkite-pipelines/references/dynamic-pipeline-patterns.md). Enterprise plan adds pipeline templates (https://buildkite.com/pricing/feature-comparison/). The trade-off: the generator is code you write, test, and version — more power, more ownership — and agent fleet management (autoscaling stacks, secret buckets) is yours (https://buildkite.com/docs/agent/self-hosted/aws/elastic-ci-stack). Shopify operated 8,000 pipelines on this model (https://buildkite.com/resources/case-studies/shopify/).

**Overhead verdict:** Buildkite's central-generator pattern minimizes per-service YAML to near zero and concentrates logic in one tested codebase; GitLab Ultimate's enforced compliance pipelines are the strongest *governance* lever; GitHub reusable workflows sit in between, with documented propagation limits around secrets/env.

---

## 7. Secrets Rotation

- **GitHub Actions — strongest evidence.** OIDC federation: "your cloud provider issues a short-lived access token that is only valid for a single job, and then automatically expires"; no duplicated long-lived cloud credentials to rotate; trust is bound to repo/branch/environment claims (https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/security/openid-connect). Practitioner write-ups confirm the pattern removes stored AWS keys entirely and makes each assumed session attributable in CloudTrail (https://matthewpalma.dev/blog/github-actions-oidc-aws-short-lived-ci-credentials, https://teninvent.ai/en/blog/github-actions-oidc-deploy-roles-per-aws-account). For a fintech, this directly addresses OWASP-style long-lived-secret risk (https://nhimanagement.com/implement/github-actions-aws-oidc.html). Caveat: mis-scoped `sub` claim conditions widen blast radius (same source).
- **GitLab.** The evidence gathered covers secret *detection* as an enforceable compliance control and "secure secrets storage" referenced among GitLab Credits add-on features (https://docs.gitlab.com/user/compliance/compliance_frameworks/, https://about.gitlab.com/pricing/), but I did not retrieve GitLab's CI/CD variables/OIDC documentation in this session — treat GitLab's rotation mechanics as unverified here rather than weak.
- **Buildkite.** The hybrid model's pitch: the open-source agent "keeps customers' proprietary code and secrets secure from any third parties, including Buildkite" (https://buildkite.com/resources/blog/introducing-the-scale-out-delivery-platform/); the Elastic CI Stack provides per-pipeline S3 secret storage with SSE encryption (https://buildkite.com/docs/agent/self-hosted/aws/elastic-ci-stack). Rotation practice therefore centers on your own cloud IAM/secret manager; OIDC support was not in the evidence gathered.

---

## 8. Compliance Audit Trails

- If minimizing wait time at very high concurrency and polyglot flexibility is top priority (and you'll self-host compute anyway): Buildkite dynamic pipelines — Shopify-class evidence.
Overall recommendation that minimizes both wait time and maintenance with progressive delivery: Buildkite-style dynamic pipeline generation on self-hosted agents (proven at Shopify scale, unlimited concurrency, single central generator = low per-service maintenance), combined with a progressive delivery controller (Flagger/Argo Rollouts) for canary/auto-rollback — with the caveat that if the org needs turnkey compliance audit features, GitLab Ultimate is strongest; if already on GitHub, reusable workflows + GitOps is the lowest-friction path. Should present a decision matrix and clear primary recommendation with conditions.

Let me do the quantitative calculations explicitly.

**Execution time model (assumptions stated):**
- Build: 15 min (1 job)
- Tests: 8 parallel jobs, assume 10 min each (range 6–14)
- Deploy: 3 sequential stages, assume 5 min each = 15 min
- Scheduling/queue overhead: variable

Critical path (ideal, no queue): 15 + max(tests) + 15.
- If all tests 10 min: 40 min.
- If tests vary 6–14 min: stage-based and DAG both wait for slowest test before deploy (deploy needs all tests green) → 44 min.

DAG savings in this single-service pipeline:
- Start lint/scan immediately (needs:[]) — doesn't affect critical path unless long.
- If deploy only needs a subset (e.g., deploy to dev after unit tests, integration tests continue), DAG can overlap: e.g., deploy-dev starts at 15+6=21 min instead of 29 min → saves up to 8 min.
- Main gain: multi-service fan-out. Example: 5 services changed in one push, each with own build/test/deploy path: stage-based forces all builds to complete before any tests; DAG lets each service flow independently → wall clock = slowest single-service path (~40 min) rather than sum of stage barriers; also avoids head-of-line blocking.

GitHub Actions reusable workflows: same logical graph; adds per-job runner allocation. Evidence: CircleCI vendor test showed GitHub Actions throttled to ~124 concurrent jobs against nominal 500 in their setup — flag as vendor-reported.

Buildkite dynamic: adds bootstrap generation step (assume ~1 min) → ~41 min; but unbounded agent concurrency reduces queue wait at peak (50–100 deploys/day means bursts).

**Cost per 1000 runs:**
Job-minutes per run = 15 + 8×10 + 3×5 = 110 min. Per 1000 = 110,000 job-minutes.

- GitHub-hosted Linux 2-core: 110,000 × $0.006 = $660. (Listed rate includes $0.002 platform fee from Jan 2026.) 1-core slim: $220 (if sufficient). Windows/macOS not applicable.
- Self-hosted on GitHub from March 1, 2026: $0.002/min platform fee → 110,000 × $0.002 = $220 per 1000 runs + your own infra.
- GitLab.com hosted runners: 110,000 compute minutes (cost factor 1) → additional packs $10/1000 → $1,100 per 1000 runs; included quota offsets (Premium 10k/month ≈ ~91 runs/month free). Self-managed GitLab with own runners: $0 per-minute charge to GitLab; you pay infra + license ($29/user/month Premium, Ultimate custom).
- Buildkite self-hosted: $0 per-minute charge to Buildkite (Pro $30/active user/month; Enterprise custom). Hosted agents: $0.004/vCPU-min; at 2 vCPU per job → $880 per 1000 runs; Small $0.01/min → $1,100.

Caveats: artifact storage, caching affect real cost; test durations are assumption.

Monthly volume context: 50–100 production deploys/day → 1,500–3,000 production pipelines/month; with CI runs on PRs/branches, total easily 10x–50x. At say 30,000 runs/month → 3.3M job-minutes/month. GitHub-hosted 2-core ≈ $19,800/month; GitLab additional packs ≈ $33,000/month; Buildkite self-hosted ≈ infra only. This shows why self-hosted compute dominates at this scale.

Let me double-check the arithmetic with simple numbers:
- 110,000 × 0.006 = 660 ✓
- 110,000 × 0.002 = 220 ✓
- 110 × 10 = 1,100 ✓
- 110,000 × 2 × 0.004 = 880 ✓
- 30,000 runs × 110 min = 3,300,000 min; × $0.006 = $19,800 ✓; × $0.01/1000 (GitLab $10/1000) = $33,000 ✓

Concurrency check: 50–100 deploys/day is modest as deploys, but CI pipelines across 200 services with PRs can peak at hundreds of concurrent jobs. GitHub Enterprise standard hosted cap of 500 concurrent jobs (larger runners 1000) is relevant.

Report structure:
1. Executive summary / conclusion
2. Scenario definition and assumptions
3. Mechanism comparison (DAG vs reusable workflows vs dynamic generation)
4. Pipeline execution time analysis (with calculations)
5. Cost per 1000 runs (with calculations)
6. Operational overhead across 200+ services

8. Compliance audit trail
9. Rollback orchestration and progressive delivery
10. Evidence from similar-scale companies
11. Recommendation and decision matrix
12. Uncertainties and gaps

Cite URLs inline. Make uncertainty explicit. No tool calls. Plain text with headings. Will be long but complete.

# Vertical Integration Strategies of Barry Callebaut, Cargill, and Olam/ofi in Cocoa (2018–2024): Upstream Investment, Sustainability, EUDR Compliance, and Competitive Positioning

---

## 1. Executive Summary

The three largest global cocoa processors—Barry Callebaut, Cargill, and ofi (formerly Olam Cocoa)—pursued distinct but converging vertical integration strategies between 2018 and 2024. All three expanded origin-country processing capacity in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana, deepened direct sourcing relationships with farming cooperatives, and invested heavily in traceability infrastructure ahead of the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR). Barry Callebaut leads in farm-level mapping (83% of direct supply chain plots mapped by FY2023/24), Cargill leads in single-site processing scale (its $100M Yopougon expansion created Africa's largest grinding plant), and ofi achieved 100% direct supply chain traceability earliest (2020). All three companies positioned EUDR readiness as a competitive differentiator for premium manufacturing contracts, though the regulation's application was ultimately delayed from December 2024 to December 2025.

---

## 2. Sourcing Structure: Direct vs. Indirect/Broker Purchasing

### Barry Callebaut
Barry Callebaut describes itself as "fully vertically integrated along the entire value chain," sourcing cocoa directly from smallholder farmers in Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana, Cameroon, Indonesia, Brazil, Ecuador, and Nigeria, supplemented by third-party suppliers from main producing countries (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/system/files/2024-11/Report%20on%20non-financial%20matters%20according%20to%20Swiss%20Co.%202023_24_1628.pdf). The company does not publish a single consolidated percentage split between direct and broker-purchased volumes. However, its disclosures indicate that in 2022/23, 29% of cocoa and non-cocoa volumes sourced from third-party suppliers had child labor risk "adequately addressed," implying a substantial indirect channel remains (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/en/sustainability/reporting/forever-chocolate-progress-report-202223). The company maintained 1,600 staff on the ground in origin countries interacting daily with farmers (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/system/files/2024-11/Forever%20Chocolate%20Progress%20Report_1.pdf). In Côte d'Ivoire alone, Barry Callebaut purchases approximately 210,000 tonnes of beans from around 250,000 cocoa farmers (https://www.incotedivoire.net/economic/new/Barry%20Callebaut%20plans%20to%20triple%20chocolate%20production%20capacity%20in%20C%C3%B4te%20d%E2%80%99Ivoire). Total beans processed were approximately 991,007 tonnes in FY2022/23 (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/system/files/2023-11/Barry_Callebaut_Annual_Report_2022-23_4.pdf).

### Cargill
Cargill's IDH case study states that "globally, approximately 60% of Cargill's cocoa supply chain is directly sourced, and 40% indirectly, although this varies by country" (https://www.idhsustainabletrade.com/uploaded/2021/06/Case-Study-Cargill_FinalVersion.pdf). The company directly sources from five producing countries—Brazil, Côte d'Ivoire, Ecuador, Ghana, and Indonesia—with 19 additional origins sourced indirectly (https://www.cargill.com/sustainability/doc/1451373894196/2025-cargill-impact-report-cocoa.pdf). The Cargill Cocoa Promise program, its direct sustainability supply chain, accounts for "about one third of the cocoa we source" per KPMG-assured 2024 reporting (https://www.cargill.com/sustainability/doc/1432271059750/2024-impact-report-cocoa.pdf). In Ghana, Cargill established a licensed buying company (LBC) in 2016 to trade directly with farmers (https://www.cargill.com/2021/cargill-commissions-us$13-million-cocoa-processing-plant).

### ofi (Olam Food Ingredients)
ofi's cocoa business sources from a network of approximately 650,000 smallholder farmers (https://5.imimg.com/data5/SELLER/Doc/2024/6/429805471/IP/FD/UP/44270845/olam-cocoa-mass.pdf). The company achieved 100% traceability in its direct supply chain in 2020, tracking "approximately 12% of the world's cocoa beans back to an individual farm or community" across nine countries (https://www.olamgroup.com/news/all-news/press-release/olam-cocoa-hits-100-percent-traceability-target-across-its-direct-global-supply-chain.html). ofi defines its direct supply chain as volumes "procured directly from farmers, farmer groups, or local buying agents or aggregators restricted to a specific group of farmers," while acknowledging indirect channels including "exchange traded volumes, government entities" (https://downloads.ctfassets.net/yzlb24ni1fxz/37uF0nYZ3aF62YUDaFrJ6K/dba5dd3dd8b302279fb64d4a12134ff7/ofi_Cocoa_Compass_Report_2024.pdf). ofi is described as "the leading exporter of cocoa beans from the continent" of Africa (https://5.imimg.com/data5/SELLER/Doc/2024/6/429805471/IP/FD/UP/44270845/olam-cocoa-mass.pdf).

**Data limitation:** None of the three companies publishes a single, audited percentage of total cocoa volume split between direct-sourced and broker/trader-purchased in a directly comparable format. Cargill's ~60/40 split is the most explicit figure available.

---

## 3. Capital Expenditures on Origin-Country Processing Facilities

### Barry Callebaut – Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana

| Investment | Amount | Details | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| SACO Abidjan expansion (announced 2019) | CHF 55 million (FCFA 30 billion) over 5 years | +40% cocoa bean processing capacity by 2022; new grinding unit at Zone 4C plant; 45 direct + 120 indirect jobs created | https://www.barry-callebaut.com/en/about-us/media/news-stories/barry-callebaut-expands-its-cocoa-processing-capacities-cote-divoire |
| 10-year Côte d'Ivoire growth programme (announced ~2023) | Undisclosed total; plans to triple chocolate production capacity | CEO Hein Schumacher announced programme "based on Côte d'Ivoire"; current grinding capacity 230,000 tonnes | https://www.incotedivoire.net/economic/new/Barry%20Callebaut%20plans%20to%20triple%20chocolate%20production%20capacity%20in%20C%C3%B4te%20d%E2%80%99Ivoire |
| BC Next Level (2023–2025) | CHF 500 million net investment total; CHF 200–250M capex component | Company-wide programme including plant infrastructure, quality/food safety, digitalization; not exclusively origin-focused | https://www.barry-callebaut.com/system/files/2024-11/Barry%20Callebaut_FY%2023%2024%20Presentation%20FINAL.pdf |

Barry Callebaut operates two industrial facilities in Côte d'Ivoire (Abidjan and San Pedro), which are its "two most important cocoa grinding factories" globally, mobilizing about 3,000 people. The company has operated in Côte d'Ivoire through subsidiary SACO since 1964 (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/en/about-us/media/news-stories/barry-callebaut-expands-its-cocoa-processing-capacities-cote-divoire). In Ghana, Barry Callebaut operates Nyonkopa, a licensed buying company (https://au.marketscreener.com/quote/stock/BARRY-CALLEBAUT-AG-408710/news/Barry-Callebaut-Annual-Report-2023-24-Barry-Callebaut-Annual-Report-2023-24-48267986/).

### Cargill – Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana

| Investment | Amount | Details | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Yopougon, Côte d'Ivoire expansion (completed Nov 2021) | US$100 million | +50% production capacity; became "single largest cocoa-grinding plant in Africa"; dedicated Gerkens dark brown powder capacity; ~100 full-time jobs created | https://www.cargill.com/2021/cargill-completes-us$100m-cocoa-processing-expansion |
| Tema, Ghana expansion (completed Nov 2021) | US$13 million | +20% grind capability; annual capacity raised to 90,000 tonnes; largest cocoa processing facility in Ghana | https://www.cargill.com/2021/cargill-commissions-us$13-million-cocoa-processing-plant |
| Sustainability/traceability programs (announced Dec 2019) | US$12.3 million over 3 years | $7.7M Côte d'Ivoire + $3.4M Ghana + $1.2M mapping technology | https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/cargill-invests-113-million-in-ivory-coast-and-ghana-site-expansions-12-3-million-towards-sustainability-and-traceability-programs-300969258.html |
| Additional Côte d'Ivoire sustainability (2021) | US$13 million over one year | $6M farmer coaching/training; $3.5M traceability projects | https://www.cargill.com/2021/cargill-completes-us$100m-cocoa-processing-expansion |

**Total disclosed Cargill origin investment 2019–2021: ~US$138.3 million** (processing capex + sustainability programs).

Cargill operates 27 processing facilities globally, including two in West Africa (https://www.cargill.com/sustainability/doc/1451373894196/2025-cargill-impact-report-cocoa.pdf). The Yopougon plant has operated since 2000; Tema since 2008.

### ofi (Olam) – Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana

| Investment | Amount | Details | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| San Pedro OCP facility (commissioned July 2014, inaugurated March 2015) | US$75 million | 75,000 MT/year grind capacity; produces whole bean and nib roasted liquor, cocoa butter, cocoa cake; 450 employees; partly powered by cocoa shell biomass | https://www.olamgroup.com/news/all-news/press-release/ouattara-olam-cocoa-processing-facility-cote-divoire.html |
| Abidjan greenfield processing (announced 2010, commissioned ~2012) | US$43.5 million | 60,000 MT capacity for liquor, butter, cake; plus primary processing/warehousing in San Pedro | https://www.olamgroup.com/news/all-news/press-release/greenfield-cocoa-processing-facility-processing-warehousing-cote-divoire.html |
| ADM Cocoa acquisition (2014) | Undisclosed | Acquired ADM's eight cocoa processing factories, including Abidjan plant | https://www.confectionerynews.com/Article/2015/03/09/Olam-opens-75m-Cote-d-Ivoire-cocoa-plant/ |
| Olam Agri Côte d'Ivoire expansion (reported 2025/26) | US$200 million | Expansion of grinding capacity for liquor, butter, powder export | https://www.billionaireroom.com/471/ |

**Note:** The $75M San Pedro and $43.5M Abidjan investments pre-date the 2018 window but constitute the operational base on which ofi built during 2018–2024. The $200M expansion was reported in early 2026 and falls outside the study period but signals continued commitment. FMO/Proparco/DEG co-financed the San Pedro plant with a EUR 33.6 million term facility within a EUR 50 million total project (https://www.fmo.nl/project-detail/32467).

---

## 4. Sustainability Certification Programs and Farmer Income

### Barry Callebaut – Forever Chocolate / Cocoa Horizons

Barry Callebaut's flagship program is **Forever Chocolate** (launched 2016), with **Cocoa Horizons** as its "preferred vehicle to drive impact" (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/en/sustainability/reporting/forever-chocolate-progress-report-202223). Key metrics across the study period:

| KPI | 2018/19 | 2019/20 | 2020/21 | 2021/22 | 2022/23 | 2023/24 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Farmers in sustainability program | 302,239 | 262,791 | 406,628 | 343,023 | 462,471 | 594,608 |
| Farmers receiving Farm Services | 46,176 | 71,972 | 125,593 | 171,710 | 169,981 | 197,763 |
| Farmers above poverty line | 169,460 | 104,645 | 143,233 | 214,124 | 269,762 | 475,752 |
| % farmer groups with CLMRS | 21.3% | 42.2% | 61.4% | 80.6% | 76.5% | 91.0% |
| % plots mapped (direct chain) | 72.3% | 66.0% | — | 79.7% | 78.9% | 83.0% |
| % products with certified/verified cocoa | — | — | 37.0% | 42.6% | 49.4% | 51.5% → 55.5% |

(Source: https://www.barry-callebaut.com/system/files/2024-11/ESG%20Datasheet%202023_24.pdf)

**Farmer income:** Barry Callebaut reports farmers "above poverty line" using the World Bank $2.15/day threshold (updated from $1.90 in September 2022). The jump from 269,762 (2022/23) to 475,752 (2023/24) reflects both methodology changes and record cocoa farmgate prices. The company generated **CHF 43.5 million in premiums** from Cocoa Horizons products in 2023/24, with 100% flowing to the Cocoa Horizons Foundation (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/en-ZA/sustainability/reporting/forever-chocolate-progress-report-202324; https://www.barry-callebaut.com/system/files/2024-02/CDP%20Forests%20report%202023_Barry%20Callebaut.pdf).

**Data limitation:** Barry Callebaut does not publish per-farmer income deltas in absolute dollar terms. The "above poverty line" metric is a binary threshold measure, not a continuous income measure.

### Cargill – Cocoa Promise

Cargill's **Cocoa Promise** (launched 2012) is its cornerstone sustainability program. In 2023, Cargill celebrated 10 years of the program, reporting:
- 100% of cocoa in direct supply chain traceable to first point of purchase
- 72% of farms in direct supply chain GPS polygon mapped
- ~50% of all cocoa sourced is certified sustainably (third-party or Cargill Promise Verified)
(https://kennedysconfection.co.uk/celebrating-10-years-of-cargills-cocoa-promise-sustainable-growth-in-chocolate/)

The 2024 Impact Report (KPMG-assured) shows:
- **54% sustainable cocoa volumes sold**
- **76.6% of farmers delivering volume through digital First Mile Traceability** within the Promise supply chain
- 100% of cocoa in direct supply chain traceable to first point of purchase
(https://www.cargill.com/sustainability/doc/1432271059750/2024-impact-report-cocoa.pdf)

Cargill trained "all Cargill Cocoa Promise farmers on sustainable cocoa production practices" and "helped families find new ways to increase their household income" but does not publish a specific percentage income change figure (https://kennedysconfection.co.uk/celebrating-10-years-of-cargills-cocoa-promise-sustainable-growth-in-chocolate/). In Indonesia, Cargill reached ~25,000 farmers with training over 10 years (https://www.cargill.com/2023/cargill-cocoa-promise-10y).

### ofi – Cocoa Compass

ofi's **Cocoa Compass** (launched 2019) set 2030 goals including 100% traceable/sustainable direct supply chain volumes and living income targets. Key data:
- **30,168 farmers earning a living income** (2022 data), on track toward 2030 target of 150,000 (https://www.ofi.com/en-gb/news-and-events/press-release/ofi-cocoa-shares-how-transparency-and-traceability-are-driving-sustainability-impact-for-food-and-beverage-sector)
- **9.8 million trees distributed** for agroforestry systems 2018–2024 (https://downloads.ctfassets.net/yzlb24ni1fxz/37uF0nYZ3aF62YUDaFrJ6K/dba5dd3dd8b302279fb64d4a12134ff7/ofi_Cocoa_Compass_Report_2024.pdf)
- Six active landscape partnerships
- 100% traceability and deforestation monitoring in direct supply chain achieved 2020 (https://www.olamgroup.com/news/all-news/press-release/olam-cocoa-hits-100-percent-traceability-target-across-its-direct-global-supply-chain.html)
- 325,000+ farmers using ofi's OFIS sustainability technology (https://www.olamgroup.com/news/all-news/press-release/olam-cocoa-hits-100-percent-traceability-target-across-its-direct-global-supply-chain.html)

**Data limitation:** ofi reports "farmers earning a living income" as a count but does not disclose baseline income or percentage change. The living income benchmark differs from Barry Callebaut's poverty-line metric, making direct comparison impossible.

---

## 5. EUDR Compliance Responses

### Regulatory Context
The EUDR (EU 2023/1115) entered into force June 29, 2023, originally applicable December 30, 2024. It requires cocoa imports to be: (1) deforestation-free (no production on land deforested after December 31, 2020), (2) legal under country-of-production laws, and (3) covered by a Due Diligence Statement with geolocation data (https://www.twobirds.com/en/insights/2024/global/from-bean-to-bar). On October 2, 2024, the European Commission proposed a 12-month delay, making the law applicable **December 30, 2025** for large companies and June 30, 2026 for micro/small enterprises (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/system/files/2024-11/Forever%20Chocolate%20Progress%20Report_1.pdf). Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana are expected to be classified "high risk," requiring full due diligence and 9% import checks (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/system/files/2024-09/EUDR%20Investor%20Webinar%20-%20Barry%20Callebaut.PDF).

### Barry Callebaut

**Position:** Barry Callebaut was an "ardent supporter" of EUDR for three years prior to implementation and publicly urged legislators not to delay or dilute it: "We still call for the swift implementation of this critical legislation and urge the legislators to dismiss all proposed amendments which would dilute the impact of the regulation" (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/en/about-us/media/news-stories/statement-eudr). When the European Cocoa Association voted to request a delay in September 2024, **Barry Callebaut abstained** rather than supporting the delay (https://www.hrw.org/sites/default/files/media_2024/09/Reactive%20Statement%2C%20ECA%20letter%20requesting%20the%20delay%20of%20EUDR%20implementation_JC.pdf).

**Traceability implementation:**
- Mapped **669,174 cocoa farm plots** in FY2023/24, a +22.2% increase year-over-year (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/en-ZA/sustainability/reporting/forever-chocolate-progress-report-202324)
- **83% of plots mapped** within direct cocoa supply chain (2023/24), up from 78.9% (2022/23) and 79.7% (2021/22) (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/system/files/2024-11/ESG%20Datasheet%202023_24.pdf)
- Farmer database covers **80% of direct cocoa supply chain**, "resulting in traceability to farm level" (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/system/files/2024-11/Forever%20Chocolate%20Progress%20Report_1.pdf)
- **46.5% of raw material volume proven deforestation-free** in 2023/24 (up from 34.1% in 2022/23) (ESG Datasheet)
- 1,600 staff on the ground in origin countries
- Participated in European Commission's **Deforestation Information System (DIS) pilot testing** (https://cocoaradar.com/european-commission-to-open-eudr-registry-to-operators-and-traders-from-november-2024/)
- Stated it "will be EUDR compliant by the application date" (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/system/files/2024-11/Forever%20Chocolate%20Progress%20Report_1.pdf)
- Committed to cover "all technical compliance costs for farmers and farmer groups" (https://www.barry-callebaut.com/system/files/2024-11/Forever%20Chocolate%20Progress%20Report_1.pdf)

# Edge Computing’s Transformation of Industrial IoT Architectures (2024): Manufacturing Predictive Maintenance, Autonomous Mobile Robots, and Energy Distribution

## 0. Market and architectural context

Edge computing moved from pilot rhetoric to budgeted infrastructure in 2024. IDC’s Worldwide Edge Spending Guide put global spending at **$232 billion in 2024, up 15.4% over 2023**, with growth sustained to nearly **$350 billion by 2027** (https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20240314632794/en/New-IDC-Spending-Guide-Forecasts-Edge-Computing-Investments-Will-Reach-%24232-Billion-in-2024); IDC’s September 2024 update pegged 2024 at **$228B (+14%) rising to ~$378B by 2028** (https://www.eetasia.com/global-spending-on-edge-computing-projected-to-reach-378b-in-2028/). The common thread across all three use cases below is the same architectural inversion: **move latency-critical inference and control to the data source; keep the cloud for model training, fleet orchestration, and long-horizon analytics.**

---

## 1. Manufacturing predictive maintenance

### 1a. Before vs. after architecture

**Before (cloud-centric, ~2015–2021 pattern):**
- Sensors/PLCs → gateways → plant network → WAN/internet → centralized cloud historian + analytics.
- Vibration and process data streamed raw (often 4–10 kHz accelerometer sampling) to cloud for FFT/anomaly detection.
- Anomaly detection latency dominated by the cloud round trip: one documented manufacturing deployment measured **200–800 ms round-trip latency to the cloud**, which "meant anomalies were detected too late to prevent failure," compounded by intermittent factory connectivity (https://www.amtarc.com/resources/case-studies/iot-predictive-maintenance).
- Failure modes: WAN outage = blind spot; raw-data egress costs scale with sensor count; alerts arrive as advisories to humans, not as control actions.

**After (edge-distributed, 2024 pattern):**
- Three-tier stack: (1) smart sensors/gateways run quantized ML inference locally (TensorFlow Lite/INT8 models, TinyML on MCUs); (2) plant-level edge servers or industrial PCs host apps, buffer data, and can trigger PLC actions; (3) cloud receives only anomalies, features, and aggregates, and pushes retrained model weights back via OTA/blue-green deployment (https://www.amtarc.com/resources/case-studies/iot-predictive-maintenance; https://www.rapidcircuitry.com/case-studies/industrial-iot-predictive-maintenance).
- Vendor platforms formalized this split: Siemens Industrial Edge + AWS IoT SiteWise Edge (launched on the Siemens Industrial Edge Marketplace at re:Invent 2023, used by machine builder Frontmatec for predictive-maintenance services) (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/industries/the-power-of-edge-to-cloud-integration-in-manufacturing-how-frontmatec-accelerates-time-to-value-of-machine-digital-services-with-siemens-and-aws/); Microsoft Azure Stack HCI + Azure Arc + AKS at Emirates Global Aluminium (https://www.microsoft.com/en/customers/story/1777264680029793974-ega-azure-arc-discrete-manufacturing-en-united-arab-emirates); VMware Edge Compute Stack consolidating IPCs/PLCs at Audi’s Böllinger Höfe plant (https://www.edgeir.com/audi-using-vmware-edge-compute-stack-at-the-industrial-edge-20241010).

### 1b. Quantified impacts

**Latency (targets and measured values):**
| Deployment | Before | After | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Generic manufacturing firm (Amtarc case) | 200–800 ms cloud round trip | <50 ms on-device inference, no cloud dependency | https://www.amtarc.com/resources/case-studies/iot-predictive-maintenance |
| Automotive plant robotic arms (Inovasense) | Cloud monitoring "too much latency" | <100 ms sensor-to-action loop; **<10 ms** edge-to-PLC emergency stop via Profinet | https://inovasense.com/projects/predictive-maintenance |
| Steel plant vibration PdM (Rapid Circuitry) | Reactive maintenance | **<50 ms** edge inference, 94% fault classification | https://www.rapidcircuitry.com/case-studies/industrial-iot-predictive-maintenance |
| Emirates Global Aluminium smart-crane video AI (Microsoft) | >1 s response | **13× faster → ~77 ms equivalent** (1,000 ms ÷ 13), subsecond and more consistent "because there's less hops involved" | https://www.microsoft.com/en/customers/story/1777264680029793974-ega-azure-arc-discrete-manufacturing-en-united-arab-emirates |
| Audi vPLC robot-cell control (VMware ECS) | Dedicated IPCs per function | vPLC command execution in **5–10 µs**, total performance budget **250 µs**; non-real-time VDI/MES workloads targeted at 25 ms from an edge cloud 200 m–10 km away | https://www.edgeir.com/audi-using-vmware-edge-compute-stack-at-the-industrial-edge-20241010 |

Arithmetic check on EGA: a 13× improvement on a >1 s baseline yields ≤ ~77 ms; EGA describes the result qualitatively as "subseconds," consistent with that bound.

**Bandwidth reduction (% data reduction):**
- Peer-reviewed edge–cloud hybrid PdM framework: **60% bandwidth reduction**, 35% latency reduction, 28% energy reduction vs. cloud-only (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39771653/).
- Ademero Manufacturing case: edge anomaly detection cited at **90% data reduction** with <100 ms local processing (https://www.ademero.com/ai-resources/case-studies/manufacturing-predictive-maintenance).
- Inovasense: **only anomaly events are uploaded**; quantified as **€40k/year saved per production line in data-transmission costs**; "raw vibration data never leaves the factory floor" (https://inovasense.com/projects/predictive-maintenance).
- Siemens/Scottish Water: FFT computed on the MindConnect Nano edge device; **only FFT results are sent to the cloud** (https://assets.new.siemens.com/siemens/assets/api/uuid:862a0188-342a-4426-ae4c-c6d9aa0fce04/dimc-b10107-00-7600scottishwaterdigitaltransformation-144.pdf).
- Upper-bound illustration (vendor math, verified here): SF2 Systems’ "State Fingerprint" approach — 50 sensor channels × 100 samples/s = 5,000 metrics/s = 432M metrics/day × 4 bytes ≈ **1.73 GB/day raw**; replaced by 1 KB state updates once per minute = 1.44 MB/day → reduction = (1,728 − 1.44)/1,728 ≈ **99.9%** (https://www.firmenpresse.de/pressrelease742617/99-9-data-reduction-why-send-gigabytes-to-the-cloud-when-asset-state-is-determined-at-the-edge.html). Treat 99.9% as an architectural ceiling for state-summary schemes, not a typical deployment figure.

**Availability / SLA improvements (unplanned-downtime reductions):**
- Octapharma + Siemens Industrial Edge: **up to 50% reduction in unplanned downtime**, up to 10% machine-performance gain (https://resources.sw.siemens.com/en-US/e-book-data-driven-predictive-maintenance-and-production-transparency/).
- Aluminum producer + Senseye (Siemens): **20% unplanned-downtime reduction, ROI in 4–6 months** (https://assets.new.siemens.com/siemens/assets/api/uuid:f92396c6-8b8a-4d42-b531-036b91e3cd04/Aluminium_original.pdf).
- Siemens Predictive Service Analyzer edge app: plant availability **up to +30%**, productivity up to +10% for drive systems (https://www.electricalsinformed.com/amp/news/ai-based-service-edge-app-siemens-co-1639146574-ga.1652461970.html).
- Case-study integrators report larger point results: 78% unplanned-downtime reduction in an Indian steel plant (https://www.rapidcircuitry.com/case-studies/industrial-iot-predictive-maintenance), 73% in an automotive plant with detection ~2 weeks before failure (https://inovasense.com/projects/predictive-maintenance), 70% with 91% prediction accuracy across 140+ edge devices (https://www.amtarc.com/resources/case-studies/iot-predictive-maintenance).
- Availability also improved structurally: EGA’s platform is designed to run "fully disconnected, if necessary" (https://www.microsoft.com/en/customers/story/1777264680029793974-ega-azure-arc-discrete-manufacturing-en-united-arab-emirates), and edge buffering bridges connectivity gaps (https://www.rapidcircuitry.com/case-studies/industrial-iot-predictive-maintenance).

### 1c. Trade-offs: cost, security, maintainability

**Cost.** Edge shifted PdM economics from egress/cloud-inference fees to on-prem capex plus orchestration. EGA reports an **86% cost reduction** for image/video analytics versus running the same workloads in public cloud, plus release cadence moving "from weeks and months between releases to multiple a day" (https://www.microsoft.com/en/customers/story/1777264680029793974-ega-azure-arc-discrete-manufacturing-en-united-arab-emirates). Siemens Erlangen electronics factory cut ML training/retraining time 80% (≈30 min → ≈5 min) and storage costs >90% by pairing cloud training (SageMaker) with edge inference on Industrial Edge devices (https://findausecase.com/use-cases/siemens-electronics-factory-erlangen-reduces-machine-learning-deployment-time-by-80-with-aws-and-siemens-industrial-ai-on-industrial-edge). Counterweight: Audi noted a typical plant carries **10,000+ industrial PCs and 4,000 HMIs**, so edge consolidation is itself a cost program — energy, troubleshooting, and maintenance of scattered devices is expensive (https://www.edgeir.com/audi-using-vmware-edge-compute-stack-at-the-industrial-edge-20241010).

**Security.** Local inference is a data-sovereignty feature: EGA explicitly wants AI decisions made "with as little outside exposure and with as little reliance on networks and the internet as possible" (Microsoft case study, above); Inovasense keeps raw vibration data entirely on-prem (https://inovasense.com/projects/predictive-maintenance). But edge also enlarges the attack surface: Audi cited "complexity of patching different systems" across many IPCs as a security risk that consolidation addresses (https://www.edgeir.com/audi-using-vmware-edge-compute-stack-at-the-industrial-edge-20241010).

**Maintainability.** The win is centralized model management with distributed runtime: Siemens Industrial Edge lets Schuler deploy/update press-shop apps remotely to on-site edge PCs (https://www.siemens.com/en-gb/company/insights/schuler-pressen-industrial-edge-smart-factory/); the Amtarc deployment pushes retrained INT8 models OTA every 30 days with blue/green rollout and automatic rollback (https://www.amtarc.com/resources/case-studies/iot-predictive-maintenance). The risk is fleet heterogeneity and vendor lock-in; Broadcom/VMware licensing backlash is already affecting edge spending decisions (https://www.edgeir.com/audi-using-vmware-edge-compute-stack-at-the-industrial-edge-20241010).

---

## 2. Autonomous mobile robots (AMRs)

### 2a. Before vs. after architecture

**Before (two legacy poles):**
- *Onboard-heavy AGVs/AMRs:* all perception, SLAM, and control on the vehicle; fleet manager in a back-office server room; vehicles unaware of each other, causing deadlock and suboptimal routing — exactly the condition Bosch described at its Reutlingen semiconductor plant before cloud/edge control (https://5gsmart.eu/wp-content/uploads/5G-SMART-D4.4-v1.0.pdf).
- *Cloud-robotics experiments:* everything offloaded to a distant cloud; limited by unbounded WAN latency and Wi-Fi dead zones. A 2024 logistics-industry analysis concluded safety-relevant, fast-response functions must stay on the robot, while cross-vehicle functions (traffic control, task assignment, mapping, path planning) are the right candidates for offload (https://exa.ai/library/publication/mxn90432nwv).

**After (2024 edge-distributed pattern):**
- **On-robot edge:** SLAM, obstacle avoidance, and safety stops run on onboard NPUs/GPUs (e.g., a 4-TOPS NPU compute board in a Rapid Circuitry AMR design; on-device quantized models) (https://www.rapidcircuitry.com/case-studies/edge-ai-warehouse-robotics).
- **On-site edge/MEC server or factory cloud:** fleet orchestration, traffic management, map fusion, and heavy perception offload, reached over private 5G or Wi-Fi 6 with single-digit-to-low-double-digit ms latency — validated at Bosch Reutlingen over a private 5G SA network (https://5gsmart.eu/wp-content/uploads/5G-SMART-D4.4-v1.0.pdf; https://exa.ai/library/publication/5kywwkd6462) and piloted by BMW at Landshut ("Robot in the Cloud": camera-based localization computed in a data cloud over 5G, millimeter-precision coordinates, onboard compute removed) (https://www.press.bmwgroup.com/global/article/detail/T0396773EN/intelligent-connected-factory-with-5g-technology:-autonomous-logistics-at-bmw-group-plant-landshut-calculates-data-in-the-cloud?language=en).
- **Public cloud:** analytics, simulation, model training, OTA updates, multi-site benchmarking (Locus LocusHub/LocusIntelligence) (https://locusrobotics.com/platform/locusone/).
- Standardization cemented the split: **VDA 5050** (MQTT/JSON interface between master control and vehicles, designed for ≥1,000 vehicles; v2.1.0 published August 2024) assumes unreliable wireless and lets robots finish orders if the broker connection drops (https://www.vdma.eu/documents/34570/3317035/24-08-20_PI_VDMA_VDA5050_EN.pdf/67a56bb6-1ca8-4fa9-40b6-e240eb217e08; https://github.com/VDA5050/VDA5050/blob/release/2.1.0/VDA5050_EN.md).

### 2b. Quantified impacts

**Latency:**
| Function | Cloud-centric | Edge-distributed (2024) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Safety-rated stop command | ~100 ms (network-dependent) | **<10 ms** local loopback | https://inferensys.com/differences/physical-ai-and-humanoid-robotics-software/autonomous-mobile-robot-amr-fleet-managers/cloud-based-vs-on-premise-fleet-management-server |
| Collision avoidance for AMR at 2 m/s | 50–200 ms cloud round trip "too slow" | single-digit ms on-device inference | https://www.vcow.com/next-generation-amr-agv-with-edge-ai-computer/ |
| AGV control loop over wireless | — | **<20 ms** target with private 5G for campus AGVs | https://jacar.es/en/private-5g-networks-in-factories-when-it-makes-sense/ |
| Wireless determinism (lab) | Wi-Fi jitter 14.8 ms std-dev | private 5G SA jitter **2.1 ms** std-dev | https://cdn.techscience.press/files/cmc/2026/TSP_CMC-89-2/TSP_CMC_88224/TSP_CMC_88224.pdf |
| Bosch Reutlingen cloud-controlled AMRs | Wi-Fi baseline | Validated over 5G SA using RTT, packet loss, reaction time, handover KPIs; concluded "5G technology is ready" for the application | https://5gsmart.eu/wp-content/uploads/5G-SMART-D4.4-v1.0.pdf |

**Bandwidth:**
- The dominant flow reverses: instead of uploading everything, robots keep raw sensor streams local and exchange compact state (VDA 5050 state/visualization topics at QoS 0 to "reduce communication overhead") (https://github.com/VDA5050/VDA5050/blob/release/2.1.0/VDA5050_EN.md).
- BMW Landshut deliberately streams camera frames to the on-site cloud over 5G — high bandwidth, but consumed inside the plant rather than over WAN, and it deletes the need for expensive onboard compute (https://www.press.bmwgroup.com/global/article/detail/T0396773EN/intelligent-connected-factory-with-5g-technology:-autonomous-logistics-at-bmw-group-plant-landshut-calculates-data-in-the-cloud?language=en).
- Research prototypes show task-oriented point-cloud compression for cooperative UGVs cutting communication overhead (https://arxiv.org/html/2410.01515v1) and ROS-level caching cutting perception latency by ~82% via object reuse (https://arxiv.org/html/2402.19410).
- Offloading perception to an edge GPU cut one robot platform’s compute-related power draw by **5 W (~40%)** — a battery-life analog of bandwidth savings (https://cdn.techscience.press/files/cmc/2026/TSP_CMC-89-2/TSP_CMC_88224/TSP_CMC_88224.pdf).

**Availability / SLA:**
- Edge autonomy is the availability mechanism: robots continue missions when WAN/cloud drops; a cloud-dependent fleet stops entirely in a server outage (https://www.vcow.com/next-generation-amr-agv-with-edge-ai-computer/; https://reemanbot.com/posts/edge-ai-in-autonomous-mobile-robots-on-device-inference-explained).
- Bosch/Qualcomm Salzgitter trial reported private 5G supporting **99.9999% (six-nines) reliability** with microsecond time sync and centimeter positioning for AGV/robot workloads (https://www.gsma.com/5GHub/images/5G-Case-Study-Manufacturing-digital-version.pdf).
- Scale proof points: Locus LocusONE orchestrates **800+ robots at a single site** and reports predictive robot pre-positioning improving throughput **15–20%** vs reactive routing (https://locusrobotics.com/platform/locusone/; https://robotomated.com/learn/vs/locus-robotics-vs-6-river-systems).

### 2c. Trade-offs: cost, security, maintainability

**Cost.** Two opposing cost curves: (1) onboard edge compute raises vehicle BOM but removes per-inference cloud fees, which otherwise "scale linearly" with fleet size (https://www.vcow.com/next-generation-amr-agv-with-edge-ai-computer/); (2) a quantified 3-year TCO comparison for a 50-robot fleet puts **cloud fleet management at $180k–$250k vs. $350k–$500k on-premise**, while on-prem caps out near ~200 robots per server versus 1,000+ for cloud platforms (https://inferensys.com/differences/physical-ai-and-humanoid-robotics-software/autonomous-mobile-robot-amr-fleet-managers/cloud-based-vs-on-premise-fleet-management-server). BMW’s cloud/edge split explicitly aims to remove costly processors from the vehicles themselves (https://www.press.bmwgroup.com/global/article/detail/T0396773EN/intelligent-connected-factory-with-5g-technology:-autonomous-logistics-at-bmw-group-plant-landshut-calculates-data-in-the-cloud?language=en). Private 5G adds material upfront cost (typically six-to-seven figures per campus) and only beats Wi-Fi 6 for large, mobility-dense sites (https://jacar.es/en/private-5g-networks-in-factories-when-it-makes-sense/).

**Security.** On-prem edge/private 5G keeps telemetry inside the perimeter — Nokia/MiR emphasized that "all data remaining securely within the network" was a selling point of private 5G AMR connectivity (https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-and-mobile-industrial-robots-mir-showcase-real-time-robot-fleet-management-using-private-5g-wireless-at-logimat-germany/), and on-prem servers are the recommended path for ITAR/GDPR data-residency (https://inferensys.com/differences/physical-ai-and-humanoid-robotics-software/autonomous-mobile-robot-amr-fleet-managers/cloud-based-vs-on-premise-fleet-management-server). The flip side: edge servers and OTA update channels become new attack surfaces requiring hardened supply chains and progressive canary rollouts (https://bitbox.cloud/infrastructure-for-warehouse-automation-deploying-robot-orch).

**Maintainability.** Offloading control to edge/cloud centralizes software updates ("ease of maintenance of the control software and improved resiliency to software and hardware failures" was Bosch’s stated rationale at Reutlingen) (https://5gsmart.eu/wp-content/uploads/5G-SMART-D4.4-v1.0.pdf). But the operator now owns a distributed compute fleet: the on-prem option "assumes full responsibility for hardware maintenance, security patching, and high-availability clustering, which requires a dedicated IT/OT engineering team" (https://inferensys.com/differences/physical-ai-and-humanoid-robotics-software/autonomous-mobile-robot-amr-fleet-managers/cloud-based-vs-on-premise-fleet-management-server). VDA 5050 reduces multi-vendor lock-in and integration burden (https://www.vdma.eu/documents/34570/3317035/24-08-20_PI_VDMA_VDA5050_EN.pdf/67a56bb6-1ca8-4fa9-40b6-e240eb217e08).

---

## 3. Energy distribution (grid edge)

### 3a. Before vs. after architecture

**Before (cloud/SCADA-centric):**
- RTUs/IEDs poll-and-report to a central SCADA/ADMS over serial or low-bandwidth WAN; AMI meters report 15- or 60-minute interval data, day-later.
- Fault handling: centralized FLISR decisions in the control room, or dumb recloser timers; restoration measured in minutes-to-hours; low-voltage (LV) grid essentially invisible.
- Itron’s framing: real-time LV visibility at 1-second resolution requires **"a minimum of 20,000 times more data than utilities currently manage from AMI sources"** — infeasible to backhaul centrally ("thousands of people throwing handfuls of hay onto a stack") (https://apac.itron.com/documents/d/asset-library-120736/positive-proof-for-distributed-intelligence-at-the-grid-edge-webpdf3410).

**After (edge-distributed, 2024 pattern):**
- **Device edge:** distributed-intelligence (DI) apps run inside smart meters, recloser controls, and transformer monitors — 1-second sampling, local anomaly detection (bypass theft, high impedance, neutral faults), local voltage/VAR decisions (https://apac.itron.com/documents/d/asset-library-120736/positive-proof-for-distributed-intelligence-at-the-grid-edge-webpdf3410; https://na.itron.com/w/itron-and-pge-collaborate-to-enable-control-of-ev-charging).
- **Substation/feeder edge:** IEC 61850-based automation with local fast self-healing; Schneider EcoStruxure Advanced Protection & Automation detects, isolates, and restores MV open-loop faults **in under 300 ms** at the edge (https://productinfo.se.com/esxp_digital_apps_iec/apa/English/ESXP2GE019EN-05_Advanced_Protection_Automation.pdf); 5G+MEC FLISR demonstrated in China as "the first case with integrated 5G and MEC in DA applications," shortening fault processing time vs centralized feeder automation (https://exa.ai/library/publication/c8ykk94jzd9); Irish FLISR-with-edge research targets CML/CI reduction (https://arxiv.org/html/2407.17497).
- **Cloud/control-room:** orchestration and optimization (GE Vernova GridOS + Itron data fabric, announced Feb 2024, unifying edge-to-core data models) (https://na.itron.com/w/itron-and-ge-vernova-pioneer-unification-of-grid-edge), DERMS aggregation (Itron Aggregator DERMS contracted by Xcel Energy, Dec 2024) (https://investors.itron.com/news-releases/news-release-details/itron-and-xcel-energy-collaborate-manage-growing-number).

### 3b. Quantified impacts

**Latency:**
| Application | Before | After | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| LV grid anomaly visibility (AMI) | 15–60 min intervals, day-later | **1-second** resolution analytics on-meter | https://apac.itron.com/documents/d/asset-library-120736/positive-proof-for-distributed-intelligence-at-the-grid-edge-webpdf3410 |
| MV fault isolation & restoration | Centralized FLISR: minutes (PNNL simulated distributed FLISR restoration times of 3:32–6:19 depending on comms delays) | Schneider fast self-healing **<300 ms**; edge-based restoration research reports ~2.89-minute recovery with >95% success vs slower centralized baselines | https://productinfo.se.com/esxp_digital_apps_iec/apa/English/ESXP2GE019EN-05_Advanced_Protection_Automation.pdf; https://www.pnnl.gov/main/publications/external/technical_reports/PNNL-35420.pdf; https://www.inderscience.com/info/inarticle.php?artid=152365 |
| Protection messaging over WAN | Fiber-only GOOSE | Routable GOOSE (R-GOOSE) over public/private 5G with local-breakout latency judged acceptable for FLISR and PMU schemes (Swedish field study, 2024) | https://exa.ai/library/publication/71h13zd31wk |
| EV charging load control | Cloud integrations exchanging data "only a few times a day" | **Real-time, on-meter** edge control loop keeping charging within panel limits (PG&E EV Connect pilot) | https://na.itron.com/w/itron-and-pge-collaborate-to-enable-control-of-ev-charging |

**Bandwidth reduction:**
- The core economic argument is avoidance: running DI at the meter sidesteps backhauling the 20,000× data growth that 1-second LV visibility would otherwise require (https://apac.itron.com/documents/d/asset-library-120736/positive-proof-for-distributed-intelligence-at-the-grid-edge-webpdf3410).
- Edge–cloud PMU fault-localization designs detect faults at the edge and upload only events/results, eliminating steady-state data transfer and packet-loss exposure (https://exa.ai/library/publication/mx39lttjtl7). A later (2026) cloud-edge fault-diagnosis paper quantifies the pattern at **31.5 kB uplink per event** with 118 ms median decision latency — directionally consistent but post-dating 2024 (https://exa.ai/library/publication/vf860xyfqmq).
- SMUD’s NET2GRID EnergyAI Edge runs EV-disaggregation analytics **inside Itron Riva meters**, so high-frequency raw data never traverses the network (https://na.itron.com/documents/d/asset-library-120736/1020128cs-01-smud-n2g-ev-awareness-case-study).

**Availability / SLA (reliability outcomes):**
- Itron/TEC blind lab test: DI edge apps were **100% accurate with 0 false positives** on meter-bypass, neutral-fault, and high-impedance detection, versus cloud analytics at **58% (with 7 false positives), 0%, and 0%** respectively (https://apac.itron.com/documents/d/asset-library-120736/positive-proof-for-distributed-intelligence-at-the-grid-edge-webpdf3410).
- Field validation at Tampa Electric: apps OTA-deployed to **200,000 meters**; field inspections confirmed visible fault conditions in **>86%** of sampled alarms (13 of 15); fleet grew to **800,000+ DI meters, ~720,000 running grid-edge apps, ~2.2 million app instances** (same source).
- Itron states Grid Edge Essentials can enhance grid capacity **by as much as 20%** via optimization of existing assets (non-wires alternative) (https://investors.itron.com/node/24511/pdf; https://na.itron.com/w/itron-to-showcase-innovative-grid-edge-intelligence-portfolio-at-distributech-2024).
- Substation-side efficiency as an availability proxy: Dominion Energy’s IEC 61850 "DICE" mass-producible digital substation eliminates ~**75% of protection panels**, cuts panel-to-panel wiring ~60%, and saves ~4 weeks of fabrication/installation per substation (https://www.pacw.org/rolling-the-dice-on-iec-61850).

### 3c. Trade-offs: cost, security, maintainability

**Cost.** The grid-edge model reuses already-purchased AMI hardware: TEC’s rationale was that DI apps add ROI incrementally over a 15–20-year meter life without new point solutions (https://apac.itron.com/documents/d/asset-library-120736/positive-proof-for-distributed-intelligence-at-the-grid-edge-webpdf3410). PG&E’s on-meter EV control avoids costly customer panel/service upgrades (https://na.itron.com/w/itron-and-pge-collaborate-to-enable-control-of-ev-charging), and Itron cites deferred infrastructure capex via the ~20% capacity gain (https://investors.itron.com/node/24511/pdf). Costs shift to network engineering and app lifecycle management; 5G+MEC FLISR requires new ICT investment (https://exa.ai/library/publication/c8ykk94jzd9).

**Security.** Utilities are the most security-conservative of the three domains. IEC 61850 substation designs increasingly use SDN segmentation and zero-touch deployment to contain the expanded Ethernet attack surface (ELES Slovenia case with SEL: https://selinc.com/api/download/138803/?lang=en-us). Edge keeps customer-level consumption data local (disaggregation in the meter rather than the cloud — SMUD/NET2GRID), which is a privacy advantage, but downloadable apps on revenue meters create a new firmware-supply-chain surface that must be managed OTA at scale (https://apac.itron.com/documents/d/asset-library-120736/positive-proof-for-distributed-intelligence-at-the-grid-edge-webpdf3410).

**Maintainability.** The decisive maintainability evidence is OTA app management at scale: Itron pushed three DI apps over the air to 200,000 production meters "without negatively impacting the AMI system’s core meter-to-cash operations," and added voltage analytics within weeks of an engineer request (https://apac.itron.com/documents/d/asset-library-120736/positive-proof-for-distributed-intelligence-at-the-grid-edge-webpdf3410). Dominion’s DICE pushes maintainability into factory assembly (mass-produced, offsite-tested enclosures) (https://www.pacw.org/rolling-the-dice-on-iec-61850). The standing risk is heterogeneous IED firmware and standards drift across vendors, which is why SDN-based centralized network management is being adopted (https://selinc.com/api/download/138803/?lang=en-us).

---

## 4. Cross-cutting synthesis and uncertainty statement

**The common 2024 architecture** across all three domains is a three-layer split: (1) millisecond/microsecond control and safety at the device or adjacent edge node (<10 ms AMR safety stops; <50 ms PdM inference; 5–10 µs vPLC cycles; <300 ms grid self-healing); (2) site-level orchestration on private wireless or plant edge clouds (10–100 ms class); (3) cloud for training, simulation, fleet analytics, and model distribution. Bandwidth reductions cluster at **60% (measured in peer-reviewed hybrid PdM)** to **90–99.9% (event/state-only upload schemes)**, with the upper bound applying only when raw data is genuinely discarded rather than buffered.

**Caveats.** (1) Several headline percentages (78%, 73%, 70% downtime cuts; 99.9% data reduction) come from vendor or integrator case studies without independent audit; I flagged vendor math where I could re-verify it (SF2: 99.92% confirmed by calculation; EGA 13× → ~77 ms confirmed as an upper bound). (2) A few corroborating academic results cited here were published after 2024 (2025–2026); they are labeled as such and used only as directional support. (3) Six-nines wireless reliability (Bosch/Qualcomm) is a trial claim, not a field SLA. (4) TCO comparisons for AMR fleet management come from a single vendor analysis and should be treated as order-of-magnitude guidance.

**Bottom line:** as of 2024, edge computing transformed industrial IoT from "send everything to the cloud and hope the network holds" into a deterministic, tiered architecture where latency targets are met locally (ms to µs), 60–99% of raw data volume never traverses the WAN, and availability improves both statistically (20–50%+ downtime reductions in named deployments) and structurally (offline-capable robots, disconnected-capable plants, on-meter grid analytics). The price paid is a new distributed-systems burden: edge hardware capex, expanded patch/attack surface, and orchestration complexity — which is precisely what the 2024 platform generation (Azure Arc/Azure Stack HCI, Siemens Industrial Edge, VMware ECS, Itron DI, VDA 5050, IEC 61850 + SDN) was built to manage.
