# Telehealth Platform Design for Low-Connectivity Rural Primary Care in Uganda, Kenya, and Tanzania: Evidence Report

## 1. Executive summary

The strongest evidence base for your design context comes from three strands: (1) Babyl Rwanda, the largest published African telemedicine deployment (3.9M consultations, 2019–2023), whose standardized-patient audit found remote audio-only care was at least as good as in-person care — and materially better for high-discretion conditions — while using USSD/SMS rather than broadband; (2) asynchronous (store-and-forward) provider-to-provider teleconsultation and teledermatology programs in Kenya and Uganda, which show diagnostic concordance with in-person care of ~69–89% depending on specialty and image-capture training, and which are architecturally suited to 2G/3G; and (3) digital clinical decision support algorithms (ePOCT+/ALMANACH family) tested in Tanzania, Rwanda, Kenya, and Nigeria, which consistently improve guideline adherence and outcomes while cutting antibiotic overuse.

One important premise correction: Zipline is not a clinical decision-support vendor. It is a drone/medical-supply logistics operator whose relevance to your question is its ordering interface — SMS/WhatsApp/phone/web ordering designed for intermittent connectivity and overstretched health workers — and its demonstration that clinical workflows must be coupled to supply-chain state (e.g., do not order an RDT the clinic does not stock). I treat it accordingly below.

Documented interaction patterns associated with completion rates above 85% include: telepharmacy sessions with callback/SMS fallback (87.4% completion, rural Rwanda); referral loop closure with telehealth triage (92% referral completion in Kenyan MNCH intervention sites); and remote hypertension follow-up via CHW-facilitated telehealth (86% of participants reaching BP control at 48 weeks in rural Kenya/Uganda). Diagnostic accuracy comparable to in-person visits is documented for audio-only protocol-driven consultation (Babyl SP study), store-and-forward teledermatology with trained image capture (up to 87% concordance), MSK remote assessment (κ = 0.80), and CHW-operated telemedicine in rural Kenya (89.2% agreement on patient action).

---

## 2. Case study comparison: Babyl Rwanda, mPharma Mutti Doctor, Zipline

### 2.1 Babyl Rwanda (Babylon Health) — USSD/voice-first, SMS prescription codes

Operating model and scale:
- Rwanda's first nationwide telemedicine service; 3,899,788 consultations recorded 2019–September 2023; 2.5M registered users (~18% of population); embedded in 450–501 of ~510 health facilities; integrated with community-based health insurance (75.4% of consultations covered) (https://exa.ai/library/publication/0r0pz8y699g; https://www.digitalconnectedcarecoalition.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/DCCC-learning-paper-Lessons-learned-from-Babyl.pdf; https://www.jmir.org/2026/1/e84832).
- Task-shifting was the core staffing pattern: triage nurses managed 44.2%, senior nurses 25.6%, general practitioners 30.2% of consultations (sums to 100.0%) (https://exa.ai/library/publication/0r0pz8y699g).

UX and connectivity strategy (the part most relevant to your 2G/3G constraint):
- Access was via USSD (*811#) and voice calls — no smartphone or data plan required for the patient. Consultations were audio-only phone calls; no video (https://ciichin.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/The-Effect-of-Telemedicine-on-Quality-of-Care-in-Rwanda.pdf).
- Store-and-forward pattern for diagnostics and medication: after consultation, prescriptions and lab orders were delivered as SMS codes to the patient's phone; codes were decoded by Babyl agents stationed at partner pharmacies and labs. For labs, results returned to Babyl and the provider called the patient back to continue the consultation — an asynchronous loop that tolerates arbitrary network gaps (https://ciichin.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/The-Effect-of-Telemedicine-on-Quality-of-Care-in-Rwanda.pdf; https://www.digitalconnectedcarecoalition.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/DCCC-learning-paper-Lessons-learned-from-Babyl.pdf).
- Identity was anchored to SIM number linked to national ID; scope was limited to patients >16 and to conditions treatable without physical exam, with explicit referral rules for anything requiring examination or outside license (https://ciichin.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/The-Effect-of-Telemedicine-on-Quality-of-Care-in-Rwanda.pdf).

Quality evidence (standardized-patient audit, n = 1,459 in-person visits to 81 facilities vs 1,218 virtual Babyl visits, June 2022–February 2023; 327 CC + 130 Babyl providers surveyed):
- Malaria (low-discretion, protocol-driven): correct case management (ordering an RDT/microscopy) was just as likely on Babyl as in person.
- URI (high-discretion): SPs were ~30% more likely to receive correct case management on Babyl (VoxDev summaries this as "roughly 200% more likely"; the two documents phrase the effect differently — treat the magnitude with caution, but direction is consistent) (https://ciichin.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/The-Effect-of-Telemedicine-on-Quality-of-Care-in-Rwanda.pdf; https://voxdev.org/topic/health/when-telemedicine-outperforms-person-care).
- Providers asked 60% more history questions (malaria) and 100% more (URI); consultations were ~30% shorter; waits were >1 hour less; unnecessary drugs fell ~15% (malaria) and ~40% (URI); unnecessary labs fell ~70%; out-of-pocket spending fell ~20% (https://voxdev.org/topic/health/when-telemedicine-outperforms-person-care).
- Behavioral finding with design implications: when SPs demanded an unnecessary antibiotic, in-person providers complied more often; the phone medium made it easier to refuse — telemedicine reduced prescribing bias under patient pressure (https://ciichin.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/The-Effect-of-Telemedicine-on-Quality-of-Care-in-Rwanda.pdf).
- A third SP case (viral diarrhea) tested whether Babyl providers correctly recognized and referred cases that should not be managed remotely — i.e., the platform explicitly measured safe escalation, not just remote treatment (https://ciichin.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/The-Effect-of-Telemedicine-on-Quality-of-Care-in-Rwanda.pdf).

Failure modes and lessons:
- Qualitative evaluation found high satisfaction but "process confusion," service delays, limited digital literacy, device-access barriers (especially rural/older users), and provider concern about diagnosing without physical exam. Recommended fixes: community mobilization, universal agent deployment, better facility integration (https://www.jmir.org/2026/1/e84832; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13041620/).
- Population-level interrupted time series found immediate reductions in facility-based utilization for common conditions during Babyl's operation, which reversed after discontinuation (https://exa.ai/library/publication/0r0pz8y699g).
- Sustainability lesson: despite clinical effectiveness, services terminated within weeks of parent-company bankruptcy (August 2023). Evidence of effectiveness did not protect continuity; financing/governance design is part of platform design (https://www.digitalconnectedcarecoalition.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/DCCC-learning-paper-Lessons-learned-from-Babyl.pdf; https://www.ijisrt.com/assets/upload/files/IJISRT26APR2523.pdf).

### 2.2 mPharma Mutti Doctor — nurse-proxy, device-assisted remote physical exam

Operating model:
- "Virtual doctor offices" inside community pharmacies (mutti network) across Ghana, Nigeria, Kenya, Zambia, Malawi, Rwanda, Ethiopia; in Tanzania delivered via ZEDD pharmacies (https://medium.com/mpharma-insights/telemedicine-2-0-mpharmas-vision-to-transform-primary-care-in-africa-576fad3152cb; https://zeddmedics.co.tz/services/mutti-doctor).
- Core UX decision: the patient does not operate technology. An on-site licensed community health nurse preps the patient and operates an all-in-one TytoCare device (digital stethoscope, otoscope, thermometer, examination camera with built-in illumination for skin/throat), streaming exam data to a remote physician in real time. Doctors "perform medical examinations while also choosing from an array of rapid diagnostic tests" (https://medium.com/mpharma-insights/telemedicine-2-0-mpharmas-vision-to-transform-primary-care-in-africa-576fad3152cb; https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/african-healthtech-company-mpharma-partners-with-tytocare-to-introduce-comprehensive-telehealth-to-pharmacies-301528947.html).
- Scale evidence: >8,000 people examined/treated by June 2021 rollout across 35 pharmacies in Ghana, Kenya, Uganda, Zambia, Nigeria (https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/african-healthtech-company-mpharma-partners-with-tytocare-to-introduce-comprehensive-telehealth-to-pharmacies-301528947.html); ~4,000 treated in first four months across 30 locations (https://medium.com/mpharma-insights/mutti-doctor-a-primary-healthcare-solution-built-for-everyone-8cbe517851ca); Tanzania partner advertises "full consultation, diagnosis, and prescription in under 15 minutes," walk-in with no app or appointment required (https://zeddmedics.co.tz/services/mutti-doctor).
- Patient-facing app (mymutti v2, Android): chat with doctor/pharmacist, pharmacy locator, health-metric self-tracking, e-commerce (https://mpharma.com/2023/07/06/press-release-mpharma-releases-mymutti-mobile-app-v2-the-ultimate-health-companion-at-your-fingertips/).

Design implications for your context:
- The nurse-proxy pattern directly solves the "limited smartphone proficiency" problem by moving device operation to a trained intermediary; this is the same pattern as Babyl's agents and the CHW-facilitated model in §4.
- Medication reconciliation is structurally simplified because consultation, prescription, and dispensing happen in one pharmacy node with inventory visibility (mPharma's Bloom platform digitizes pharmacy stock) (https://mpharma.com/). No peer-reviewed outcome data on Mutti Doctor diagnostic accuracy or completion rates were found; treat vendor claims as unevaluated.
- Connectivity caveat: TytoPro assumes usable bandwidth for live exam data; in 2G-only areas this model degrades, which is why mPharma's model is sited in pharmacies (fixed locations where connectivity can be provisioned) rather than in the field.

### 2.3 Zipline — ordering UX for intermittent connectivity (not a clinical decision tool)

What Zipline actually is:
- An end-to-end medical supply chain operator (drones + warehousing + inventory management) in Rwanda, Ghana, Nigeria and elsewhere. Rwanda: 2 distribution centers, 350+ facilities, 75%+ of national blood products. Ghana: ~2,000 facilities served (https://assets.ctfassets.net/pbn2i2zbvp41/5dpfo3SJfsUZ0Az5fqLA1P/44e71538284dce389d48d3cc05f15142/Zipline-Capabilities-Statement.pdf; https://www.idinsight.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/Zipline-Brief-FINAL-Digital-v3.pdf).
- Health worker perspective in Ghana: orders placed through facility WhatsApp groups; deliveries arrive ~45 minutes after order; order-to-launch ~5 minutes (https://www.zipline.com/newsroom/zipline-ghana-remote-communities-within-reach; https://dailytrust.com/how-drones-deliver-medicines-vaccines-to-hard-to-reach-communities-in-kaduna/; https://exa.ai/library/publication/d7wtpsjc6pt).

Ordering-interface lessons transferable to your platform:
- Channel-minimum design: orders accepted via basic SMS, WhatsApp, phone call, or web — "avoiding complex systems" for overstretched workers; the advanced technology is hidden behind the simplest possible front end (https://www.christenseninstitute.org/blog/how-zipline-transformed-a-gadget-for-the-rich-to-infrastructure-for-the-poor/; https://bryantmao.com/case_zipline).
- WhatsApp group ordering emerged organically because it matches existing habits and tolerates async exchange, but created tracking/error problems; Zipline's response was a customer-facing mobile app consolidating all interactions while keeping low-bandwidth channels (https://bryantmao.com/case_zipline; https://www.updwg.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/Zipline-IDinsight-Executive-Summary.pdf; https://www.idinsight.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/Zipline-Brief-FINAL-Digital-v3-2.pdf).
- Known failure modes: internet connectivity affecting orders, staff turnover/training gaps, weather, and lack of follow-up on lab results transported back by drone (https://www.villagereach.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Drones-On-Demand_GHSCS-2023-Abstract-26_Final-draft-1.pdf).

Implication for your platform: clinical decision support must be stock-aware. If your diagnostic workflow recommends an RDT or a first-line drug, the form should reflect what the facility actually has (Zipline-style pull-based inventory), otherwise the algorithm's recommendation is unactionable — a documented cause of CDSA non-adherence.

---

## 3. How asynchronous communication, offline-first architecture, and diagnostic workflow design affect quality and outcomes

### 3.1 Asynchronous (store-and-forward) patterns

- The Turkana County (Kenya) nREM project is the cleanest exemplar for your exact setting. Non-physician clinicians (NPCs) in 20 remote PHCs + 2 hospitals submitted non-emergency cases asynchronously to a volunteer physician/specialist network. Between Jan 2017 and June 2018: 104 provider-to-provider asynchronous teleconsultations (ATCs) from 17 of 22 facilities; 73.5% NPC→remote medical officer, 14.1% NPC→specialist, 12.5% MO-initiated. Cases ranged from obstetrics to NTDs (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0238806).
- The ATC workflow was explicitly designed for low connectivity and low training burden: (a) narrative case entry plus structured fields for key data (e.g., HIV/VDRL status), (b) in-app camera capture with redaction of identifying information, (c) SMS notification to remote physicians containing a hyperlink to the case, (d) web-based case page with chat/scheduling/reporting, (e) optional DICOM upload. Design goals stated verbatim: "usable, with minimal training on the technology itself" and "usable on commonly available and used mobile devices in Kenya (including personal smartphones)" — one Android tablet per site (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0238806).
- Reported effects: NPCs managed more cases locally, avoided unnecessary referrals (and the social/financial disruption of referral in a region where ambulances are often unavailable), gained skills and confidence ("Even though I am alone, I feel that we are many"), and referral adherence improved because physicians pre-approved patient movement. The paper's explicit conclusion: ATCs are "likely more practical in LMIC settings, which often have limited and low-bandwidth internet connectivity, and unreliable electricity" than synchronous video models (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0238806).
- The Babyl lab loop (§2.1) is the same pattern at patient level: order via SMS code → test at facility → results return asynchronously → provider calls patient back. This decouples the consultation from connectivity at every step.
- A Uganda CHW call-center program (3,500 CHWs, 23 districts, Mar 2020–June 2021, 35,553 consultations) shows demand-side async/hybrid support works at scale for sustaining basic services (https://preprints.jmir.org/preprint/33715).

### 3.2 Offline-first architecture

The Community Health Toolkit (CHT, formerly Medic) is the reference implementation used across East Africa and is the most detailed public documentation of offline-first clinical app architecture:
- Principle: "the application never relies on an internet connection for day to day tasks"; optimized for connections that are "intermittent, unreliable, expensive, and low bandwidth" (https://docs.communityhealthtoolkit.org/technical-overview/concepts/offline-first/).
- Mechanics: Service Worker caches app code on first login (silently, in background); app checks for updates in the background and never interrupts the user on failure; updates can be dismissed mid-patient and apply on next launch. Data lives in PouchDB on-device with bidirectional replication to CouchDB on the server; each user replicates only a filtered subset of documents (performance + privacy) (https://docs.communityhealthtoolkit.org/technical-overview/concepts/offline-first/; https://docs.communityhealthtoolkit.org/technical-overview/data/; https://docs.communityhealthtoolkit.org/technical-overview/architecture/cht-core/).
- Sync UX details that matter in the field: upward replication has retry mechanisms for large batches; sync status is surfaced to users; SMS/basic-phone channels feed the same backend (https://docs.communityhealthtoolkit.org/building/navigation/; https://docs.communityhealthtoolkit.org/technical-overview/data/analytics/data-flows-for-analytics/).
- Real-world failure modes documented by implementers: CHWs with two weeks of unsynced data losing work after device reset; sync requiring multiple manual retries; data-cap exhaustion silently blocking replication; session expiry forcing re-login. Mitigations discussed include monitoring `last_replication_date`, telemetry/Apdex dashboards, and even fully offline outpost servers or device-to-device sync for places with no internet at all (https://forum.communityhealthtoolkit.org/t/sync-issues-status-scrutiny/3359; https://forum.communityhealthtoolkit.org/t/we-need-to-serve-the-internet-offline/621; https://forum.communityhealthtoolkit.org/t/why-the-cht-uses-couchdb/2113).
- Adjacent evidence: an offline-first on-device clinical AI (MedGemma 4B, Samsung A16, 40-second warm start, zero cloud dependency) now supports frontline workers in rural Uganda for maternal health, malaria, pneumonia, TB — proof that decision support can run entirely on-device where there is no network (https://developers.google.com/health-ai-developer-foundations/showcase/crane-ai). A health-systems analysis of an African hospital EMR explicitly advocates offline-first architecture after quantifying "Infrastructure-Induced Process Deadlock" from power/network outages and a cognitive-load jump (control-flow complexity metric 3.0 → 14.0) when paper workflows were digitized without resilience design (https://jurnal.unimus.ac.id/index.php/ICHI/article/download/19048/pdf).

Design translation for your platform: local-first document store with filtered replication; never block clinical workflow on network; background retry with visible-but-dismissable sync state; SMS/USSD fallback channels into the same data model; explicit "last synced" indicator and conflict-safe merge (CouchDB-style revisioning) rather than last-write-wins.

### 3.3 Diagnostic workflow design effects on outcomes

- Protocol-driven audio consultation (Babyl): diagnostic quality equal/better than in-person for tested conditions, with more history-taking and less overtreatment (§2.1).
- Algorithmic decision support in Tanzania/Rwanda/Kenya/Nigeria (ePOCT+, ALMANACH): see §4.3 — these are the strongest causal results in this whole evidence base: large adherence gains, antibiotic reductions of 42–69 absolute percentage points, non-inferior or superior clinical recovery.
- Store-and-forward imaging: diagnostic concordance is highly sensitive to who captures the image and whether they are trained (§5.2). This is your main lever for image-based diagnostics on 2G/3G, since still images can be queued and compressed asynchronously, unlike video.

---

## 4. Interaction patterns achieving ≥85% completion and in-person-comparable accuracy

### 4.1 Documented completion/engagement rates above 85%

| Pattern | Setting | Result | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Telepharmacy counseling sessions with callback/SMS fallback on connectivity failure | Rural Rwanda, 4 sites, 326 patients, 6 months | 87.4% session completion; tech failures in 14.7% of sessions, "resolved through callback or switch to SMS in most cases"; satisfaction 4.1/5; adherence 74.8% vs 71.3% in-person (p=0.38) | https://exa.ai/library/publication/4yt9fp86pkd |
| Referral loop closure with telehealth triage (MNCH hybrid model) | Kenya | 92% (3,630/3,967) referrals completed in intervention sites; loss-to-follow-up 62 infants vs 329 in control; PNC visits 4.99 vs 3.96 (p=0.003); hotline used by ~88% of platform users | https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12862075/ |
| CHW-facilitated, clinician-driven telehealth for severe hypertension | Rural Kenya + Uganda RCT, N=200 | At 48 weeks, 86% of participants achieved BP <140/90 (primary outcome at 24 weeks also assessed) | https://journals.plos.org/plosmedicine/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pmed.1004632 |
| USSD-based telehealth with CHW integration | Rural SSA pilot | Elderly user satisfaction 85%; 3-month retention 78% (vs 45–65% SSA mHealth benchmark); emergency triage session completion 71% (below 85% — note as a weak point) | https://www.ijisrt.com/assets/upload/files/IJISRT26APR2523.pdf |
| Mutti Doctor pharmacy teleconsult | Tanzania (vendor claim) | "Full consultation, diagnosis, and prescription in under 15 minutes," no app/appointment required | https://zeddmedics.co.tz/services/mutti-doctor |

Verification arithmetic: telepharmacy 87.4% > 85% threshold by 2.4 pp; with 326 patients, 87.4% ≈ 285 completed sessions. Kenya MNCH: 3,630/3,967 = 91.5% ≈ reported 92%. Babyl task-shift shares: 44.2 + 25.6 + 30.2 = 100.0% (internally consistent).

The recurring interaction pattern behind every ≥85% figure: (1) a human fallback channel (callback, SMS switch, agent, CHW) that catches connectivity failures; (2) the consultation decoupled from a single real-time session so an interrupted encounter can resume; (3) closure of the loop (referral completed, prescription filled, BP re-measured) tracked as a first-class workflow state.

### 4.2 Diagnostic accuracy comparable to in-person visits

- Audio-only protocol-driven consultation: Babyl SP audit — malaria correct case management equal to in-person; URI ~30% better; fewer unnecessary labs/drugs (https://ciichin.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/The-Effect-of-Telemedicine-on-Quality-of-Care-in-Rwanda.pdf; https://voxdev.org/topic/health/when-telemedicine-outperforms-person-care).
- CHW-operated store-and-forward telemedicine, rural Kenya (Mashavu): nurse's telemedicine advice matched her own in-person advice in 78.4% of cases (n=102); advice on patient action (refer vs no further care) matched in 89.2% (n=91) (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/2150131912461797).
- Store-and-forward teledermatology: pooled diagnostic agreement 68.9% (κ=0.67) across 44 studies; 71% when dermatologists read (κ=0.69) vs 44% for non-specialists (κ=0.52); agreement rose significantly with image-acquisition training and digital photography; teledermatologist-to-teledermatologist agreement was 76.4% (https://exa.ai/library/publication/zb2ggzk9knf). With structured image-capture assistance, concordance reached 79% (unassisted patient photos) → 84% (assisted after brief training) → 87% (clinician-taken), while requests for additional history fell 64% → 47% (https://www.scienceopen.com/document?vid=eac1e7e0-88ec-4557-aed6-f93aeca37429). Clinician-submitted SAF images produced clinical outcomes "comparable to in-person visits" in studies that checked (https://derma.jmir.org/2022/3/e37517).
- Musculoskeletal remote assessment: pooled diagnostic concordance κ=0.80 (95% CI 0.72–0.89, high certainty); treatment-plan concordance Gwet AC1=0.90 (https://exa.ai/library/publication/64x685ync70).
- Diabetic retinopathy SAF screening: pooled sensitivity 80.9% (any DR), 88.6% (referable DR); SAF workflows in rural settings enabled screening by trained non-specialists "without sacrificing diagnostic integrity" (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-026-02627-0).
- Tele-ultrasound in resource-limited settings: agreement 43.4–100%, sensitivity 43–97%, specificity 77.4–100% — acceptable for many applications but highly operator-dependent; smartphone-acquired images were satisfactory in two studies (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/public-health/articles/10.3389/fpubh.2019.00244/full; https://www.mattioli1885journals.com/index.php/theultrasoundjournal/article/view/18153).

Honest uncertainty statement: no study in this evidence base reports a clean, general "telemedicine consultation completion rate >85%" across all-comers primary care; the ≥85% figures above are condition- or workflow-specific. Likewise, "comparable to in-person" holds best for (a) protocol-driven low-discretion conditions, (b) image-based specialties with trained capture, and (c) audio consultation with structured history-taking. It does not automatically extend to conditions requiring palpation/auscultation unless a device-assisted proxy (mPharma/TytoCare model) or point-of-care test fills the gap.

### 4.3 Clinical decision support as the accuracy engine (Tanzania/Kenya/Rwanda evidence)

- ALMANACH (mobile IMCI-derived algorithm), Tanzania controlled study: day-7 cure 97.3% vs 92.0% standard practice (p<0.001); antibiotics prescribed 15.4% vs 84.3% — an absolute reduction of 68.9 pp (reported as ~80% relative) (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0132316).
- ePOCT+ cluster RCT, Tanzania (20 ePOCT+ facilities, 23,593 consultations vs 20 usual-care, 20,713): antibiotics 23.2% vs 70.1% (adjusted difference −46.4%, 95% CI −57.6 to −35.2; my check: 70.1 − 23.2 = 46.9 pp, consistent with the adjusted estimate); day-7 clinical failure non-inferior (aRR 0.97, 95% CI 0.85–1.10); no difference in deaths or secondary hospitalizations (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-023-02633-9).
- ePOCT+ Rwanda pragmatic cluster trial (32 health centers, 47,822 consultations analyzed): average uptake 70%; antibiotic reduction met superiority threshold; clinical failure non-inferior (https://journals.plos.org/plosmedicine/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pmed.1004692).
- ALMANACH Somalia pre-post: antibiotics 58.1% → 16.0% (−42.1 pp; relative reduction 72.5% by my calculation); danger-sign assessment 1.3% → 99%; follow-up counseling 12% → 94% (https://exa.ai/library/publication/vkm087p170l).
- ALMANACH Nigeria observational: caregiver-reported day-7 recovery aOR 2.63 (95% CI 1.60–4.32) vs controls (https://bmjopen.bmj.com/content/bmjopen/12/7/e055315.full.pdf).

These tools are the strongest answer to "what achieves in-person-comparable (or better) outcomes": a well-designed algorithmic form, executed by nurses/non-physician clinicians with point-of-care tests, outperformed usual in-person care on safety-critical process measures and matched it on clinical failure.

---

## 5. Cognitive load principles for clinical forms and image capture

### 5.1 Evidence on cognitive load in clinical interfaces

- Cognitive load theory applied to EHRs: system usability (interface aligned to clinical workflow, minimal navigation) reduces extraneous load and documentation errors; data usability (complete, well-organized data) increases germane load — the productive reasoning effort; information overload mediates both. Two distinct levers: simplify the interface, and curate what is shown (https://preview-www.nature.com/articles/s41746-025-02243-4).
- RCT of a cognitive-load-theory-designed post-hospitalization dashboard: optimized information presentation decreased task load, time-to-completion, and cognitive errors vs usual care (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6703991/).
- EHR/burnout narrative review: interfaces that dump large data volumes without user control cause cognitive overload; recommends progressive disclosure, workflow-aligned views, and reducing "work about the work" (https://medinform.jmir.org/2024/1/e55499; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11053390/).
- LMIC-specific: a Malawi touchscreen EMR showed novices could approach skilled performance when the UI was designed for it (1,596 task performances analyzed; novices beat predicted skilled times on 13% of successful tasks) — evidence that low-proficiency users can be served by deliberate design (https://exa.ai/library/publication/jns1kpq8k5f). Tanzanian primary-care workers report that limited digital skills, language/interface issues, and weak ongoing training undermine tool use; structural barriers (smartphone access) dominate actual usage in Uganda (TAM study, n=170 CHWs) (https://sage.cnpereading.com/doi/10.1177/20552076251396986; https://exa.ai/library/publication/5r2gpxb3czc). Infrastructure anxiety (outages) pushes staff to prioritize screen time over patient time — an argument for offline-first as a cognitive-load intervention, not just a technical one (https://jurnal.unimus.ac.id/index.php/ICHI/article/download/19048/pdf).
- Applied CLT guidance for health program interfaces: chunking, eliminating split attention, leveraging worked examples, and designing for users with diminished working memory under stress (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12246501/). For low-literacy users, cognitive testing ("think aloud" + verbal probing) during development is the validated method (https://archpublichealth.biomedcentral.com/counter/pdf/10.1186/s13690-019-0346-0.pdf).

### 5.2 What this means for clinical form design (synthesis with the deployment evidence)

The ePOCT+/medAL-suite development paper is the best worked example of CLT-informed form design for exactly your user profile (nurses and non-physician clinicians in TZ/KE/RW):
- Only include clinical elements that are feasible, acceptable, and reliable for the target cadre: pain scores, capillary refill time, cool peripheries, and weak/fast pulse were explicitly excluded after Delphi surveys, clinician interviews, and observation because primary-care workers could not assess them reliably. Fewer, higher-yield inputs = lower extraneous load and better algorithm performance (https://journals.plos.org/digitalhealth/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pdig.0000170).
- The form follows the natural consultation sequence (medAL-reader "deploys the algorithm... following the usual healthcare processes within a consultation") rather than forcing reorganization of the encounter; algorithm authoring is drag-and-drop for non-programmers (https://journals.plos.org/digitalhealth/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pdig.0000170).
- Branching logic hides irrelevant questions (progressive disclosure): the algorithm asks only the next clinically necessary question, which is also why Babyl's teleconsultants asked more relevant questions in less time (§2.1).
- Integrate point-of-care test results directly into the flow (malaria RDT, hemoglobin, oximetry, CRP) so the form computes risk instead of asking the clinician to hold and combine values in working memory (https://journals.plos.org/plosmedicine/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pmed.1002411; https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-023-02633-9).
- Make escalation and referral explicit, scripted states (Babyl's diarrhea referral case; Turkana's referral-approval ATC) so the "what now" decision never depends on recall under interruption.

Concrete form-design rules supported by the gathered evidence:
1. One question per screen; large touch targets; local-language labels (Tanzanian workers cite language/interface as barriers) (https://sage.cnpereading.com/doi/10.1177/20552076251396986).
2. Auto-advance branching; never show fields that current answers make irrelevant (ePOCT+ pattern; CHT xforms via Enketo support show/hide and validation rules) (https://journals.plos.org/digitalhealth/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pdig.0000170; https://docs.communityhealthtoolkit.org/technical-overview/architecture/cht-core/).
3. Save-and-resume at every step so a network drop or patient interruption costs nothing (CHT offline-first principle; Turkana ATC narrative+structured hybrid entry) (https://docs.communityhealthtoolkit.org/technical-overview/concepts/offline-first/; https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0238806).
4. Replace free-text with constrained choices for medication reconciliation: structured drug lists with dose/route/frequency, allergy checks, and dispense-status tracking as in Kenya's FHIR ePrescription IG (prescriber completes MedicationRequest → patient gets SMS/QR reference → pharmacist validates status/refill count → dispense recorded → status set to completed) (https://igeprescriptions.intellisoftkenya.com/use-cases.html). Babyl's SMS-code + agent-decode pattern is the low-tech equivalent that worked at 3.9M-consultation scale (https://ciichin.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/The-Effect-of-Telemedicine-on-Quality-of-Care-in-Rwanda.pdf).
5. Show sync/submit status but never block care: background retry, dismissible update prompts, visible "last synced" (CHT) (https://docs.communityhealthtoolkit.org/technical-overview/concepts/offline-first/; https://forum.communityhealthtoolkit.org/t/sync-issues-status-scrutiny/3359).

### 5.3 Image capture workflows under low proficiency and low bandwidth

Evidence-backed levers, in order of effect size found:
1. Who captures matters more than the device: clinician-taken images reached 87% diagnostic concordance vs 79% unassisted patient images; meta-analysis found significantly higher agreement with image-acquisition training (https://www.scienceopen.com/document?vid=eac1e7e0-88ec-4557-aed6-f93aeca37429; https://exa.ai/library/publication/zb2ggzk9knf). In your model, the capturing user is the provider/CHW — train them, don't rely on patients.
2. Brief standardized training works: assisted patient photography after a short training improved concordance by ~5 pp and cut requests for extra history from 64% to 47% (https://www.scienceopen.com/document?vid=eac1e7e0-88ec-4557-aed6-f93aeca37429). Adapted smartphone photography guides for resource-limited S&F teledermatology exist for iPhone/Android (https://www.ilds.org/what-we-do/our-foundation/csh-journal/enhancing-photography-skills-using-smartphones-in-resource-limited-settings/).
3. In-app guidance beats general instructions: 92.1% of Kenyan providers wanted a list of photo-taking tips; 92.1% wanted to submit from the same device they captured on; 75.8% preferred Wi-Fi upload over paid data — i.e., queue images and upload when free/available bandwidth exists (https://ecommons.aku.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1453&context=eastafrica_fhs_mc_intern_med). Note 28.9% did not feel prepared to photograph dark skin — include Fitzpatrick V–VI-specific capture guidance (lighting, contrast) in your workflow.
4. Guided capture with structured minimum data: the Turkana platform combined narrative + structured fields + camera capture with privacy redaction in one flow (https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0238806); the Uganda mobile teledermatology service limited submissions to 3 images per case with required clinical fields — a constraint that keeps payloads small for 2G/3G and forces diagnostic completeness (https://medicaljournalssweden.se/actadv/article/download/7360/10758/38635).
5. On-device quality feedback: AI photo-quality tools exist and improve usable submissions (https://jamanetwork-com.libproxy.ajou.ac.kr/journals/jamadermatology/fullarticle/2802154); the WHO Skin NTDs app (tested in Kenya, 605 images, 40 users) reached ~80% accuracy on well-represented conditions and scored well on usability (uMARS quality 3.82/5, impact 4.1/5) while reducing referrals (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/international-journal-of-technology-assessment-in-health-care/article/op44-artificial-intelligencebased-mobile-health-technology-for-improved-access-to-dermatological-care-a-kenyan-case-study/10E70720EAB1780C10B28D7AA91A1F54).
6. Learning-by-doing compounds: South African PCPs' diagnostic concordance with teledermatologists rose ~4-fold (from 13% baseline) after referring only ~9 cases (rs=0.86, p<0.001) — your platform should return the specialist's diagnosis with every answer to close the feedback loop, which Turkana providers identified as the main driver of skill gain (https://exa.ai/library/publication/f2m455brydj; https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0238806).
7. Bandwidth strategy: still images store-and-forward; compress and queue locally, transmit opportunistically (CHT replication model); reserve synchronous channels for audio only, which worked at national scale on 2G-grade voice networks in Rwanda (https://docs.communityhealthtoolkit.org/technical-overview/concepts/offline-first/; https://ciichin.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/The-Effect-of-Telemedicine-on-Quality-of-Care-in-Rwanda.pdf).

---

## 6. Adoption conditions that gate everything else (from Kenya/Uganda provider research)

A 12-clinic teledermatology implementation in Kenya and Uganda had "variable uptake"; FGDs (23 participants Kenya, 10 Uganda) identified what makes remote diagnostic tools actually get used (https://academic.oup.com/ced/advance-article/doi/10.1093/ced/llag407/8808319):
- Integration into routine workflow and the facility EMR — tools perceived as a parallel burden were abandoned.
- Automated reminders about pending specialist feedback (absence of reminders was a named barrier).
- Professional incentives (e.g., CME credit) and clinic leadership endorsement; framing use as professional duty and learning opportunity.
- Device compatibility (works on providers' own Android phones).
- Provider channel preferences in Kenya: <24h response expected (81.6%), personal phone submission (86.8%), WhatsApp as preferred transport (87.9%) (https://ecommons.aku.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1453&context=eastafrica_fhs_mc_intern_med). Meeting users on WhatsApp-like familiar channels (as Zipline did) and then formalizing is a validated sequencing strategy (https://bryantmao.com/case_zipline; https://www.christenseninstitute.org/blog/how-zipline-transformed-a-gadget-for-the-rich-to-infrastructure-for-the-poor/).
- Kaposi sarcoma teledermatology pilot (273 consults, Kenya/Uganda) showed remote image review can surface diagnoses, but biopsy follow-up was the weak link — remote diagnostics must be designed together with on-site sample/logistics capability (a Zipline-type supply loop) (https://exa.ai/library/publication/hcvw9wd5h8f).

---

## 7. Consolidated design recommendations for your platform

1. Default to asynchronous, voice-fallback architecture. Store-and-forward case submission (structured form + ≤3 guided images + narrative) with SMS notifications to specialists (Turkana pattern), plus audio-only consultation as the synchronous fallback (Babyl pattern). This combination has the best evidence-to-bandwidth ratio in your exact geography.
2. Offline-first as a primary constraint, not a mode: local document DB with bidirectional filtered replication (CHT/PouchDB-CouchDB pattern), service-worker caching, background retry, save-and-resume forms, visible-but-non-blocking sync state, and monitoring of last-sync timestamps to catch silent data loss (https://docs.communityhealthtoolkit.org/technical-overview/concepts/offline-first/; https://forum.communityhealthtoolkit.org/t/sync-issues-status-scrutiny/3359).
3. Embed a guideline-based branching CDSA (ePOCT+/ALMANACH style) for pediatric/febrile illness — the only intervention in this evidence base with RCT-grade proof of equal-or-better outcomes plus ~46–69 pp antibiotic reduction in Tanzania/Rwanda (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41591-023-02633-9; https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0132316). Exclude clinical signs your cadre cannot reliably assess; sequence questions in consultation order.
4. Use the proxy-operator model where devices are needed: trained nurse/CHW operates capture devices (mPharma/TytoCare; CHW-facilitated hypertension RCT at 86% BP control) rather than expecting low-proficiency providers or patients to self-serve (https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/african-healthtech-company-mpharma-partners-with-tytocare-to-introduce-comprehensive-telehealth-to-pharmacies-301528947.html; https://journals.plos.org/plosmedicine/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pmed.1004632).
5. Make every workflow state resumable and tracked to closure: consultation started/completed, image queued/sent, specialist reply received/acknowledged, referral completed, prescription decoded/dispensed. The ≥85% completion results all come from systems that treat interruption as normal and closure as a tracked outcome (telepharmacy 87.4% with SMS fallback; Kenya MNCH 92% referral completion) (https://exa.ai/library/publication/4yt9fp86pkd; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12862075/).
6. Medication reconciliation via structured e-prescription with SMS/QR reference codes redeemable at network pharmacies, dispensing validation, and status updates (Babyl at scale; Kenya FHIR ePrescription IG as the standards path) (https://ciichin.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/The-Effect-of-Telemedicine-on-Quality-of-Care-in-Rwanda.pdf; https://igeprescriptions.intellisoftkenya.com/use-cases.html).
7. Couple clinical forms to supply state (Zipline lesson): recommendations must reflect real-time facility stock; ordering channels should be SMS/WhatsApp-first with a consolidating app layered on later (https://www.christenseninstitute.org/blog/how-zipline-transformed-a-gadget-for-the-rich-to-infrastructure-for-the-poor/; https://www.idinsight.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/Zipline-Brief-FINAL-Digital-v3.pdf).
8. Budget for image-capture training and in-app guidance (tips, lighting for dark skin, max 3 images, redaction) — worth ~8 pp of diagnostic concordance and a 17 pp drop in clarifying questions (https://www.scienceopen.com/document?vid=eac1e7e0-88ec-4557-aed6-f93aeca37429; https://ecommons.aku.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1453&context=eastafrica_fhs_mc_intern_med).
9. Close the learning loop: return the specialist's diagnosis/plan with every consult; concordance improves ~4-fold within ~9 cases when feedback is consistent (https://exa.ai/library/publication/f2m455brydj).
10. Plan sustainability from day one: Babyl's collapse shows clinical success does not guarantee continuity; embed in government insurance/payment rails and avoid single-vendor dependency (https://www.digitalconnectedcarecoalition.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/DCCC-learning-paper-Lessons-learned-from-Babyl.pdf; https://www.ijisrt.com/assets/upload/files/IJISRT26APR2523.pdf).

## 8. Limitations of this evidence base

- The Babyl SP audit is the only randomized-quality comparison of remote vs in-person primary care at scale in the region; it covered two conditions (malaria, URI) plus a referral-safety case, so generalization to all primary-care presentations is unproven.
- The ≥85% completion figures are heterogeneous (session completion, referral completion, disease-control endpoints) and come from pilots/RCTs rather than a single standardized metric; no deployment in this corpus reports a universal all-comers consultation completion rate.
- mPharma outcome claims are vendor-reported with no peer-reviewed evaluation found; Zipline's "clinical decision tools" do not exist as such — its contribution is logistics and ordering UX.
- Teledermatology agreement figures (pooled 68.9%) are below the "comparable to in-person" bar unless trained capture, specialist readers, or AI assistance is used; specialty matters enormously (MSK κ=0.80 vs dermatology κ=0.67 vs ultrasound as low as 43% agreement in some studies).
- Several sources are recent/preprint or grey literature (IJISRT USSD study, telepharmacy feasibility study, IDinsight brief); I have flagged vendor and non-peer-reviewed claims where they appear.

# Multimodal Checkout for Visually Impaired Grocery Shoppers: Voice-Only vs. Hybrid Touch-with-Audio Interaction

## 1. Bottom line up front

There is **no single head-to-head randomized trial** that directly compares a sequential voice-only checkout workflow against a hybrid touch-with-audio-feedback workflow across product selection, quantity adjustment, and payment confirmation, reporting task completion, numerical error rates, and confidence scores in one instrument. I state that gap plainly. What exists is a convergent body of adjacent evidence — accessibility user studies with blind and low-vision (BLV) participants, speech-dialog confirmation research, mobile-commerce usability testing, WCAG 2.2 implementation guidance, and auditory working-memory science. Synthesized, that evidence points consistently toward one conclusion:

**A hybrid model — touch/gesture as the ground-truth input layer with rich, structured audio feedback, and voice reserved for coarse commands and final authorization — outperforms pure sequential voice for numerically precise, high-stakes checkout tasks.** Voice-only is preferred and faster for coarse navigation and selection, but it is measurably fragile for numerical entry and for verifying long lists, and it shifts error-recovery burden onto the user.

---

## 2. Evidence base and method caveat

Sources fall into five clusters:
1. **BLV shopping/checkout accessibility studies** (BarrierFreeShop, n=80; a BVI mobile-app evaluation, n=56; a voice-based shopping-agent Wizard-of-Oz study, n=12; an Amazon screen-reader checkout study, n=3; an Indonesian e-commerce redesign with blind participants).
2. **Speech-input and ASR-error research with blind participants** (Hong et al., 12 blind + 12 sighted; Azenkot et al. findings cited therein).
3. **Speech-dialog confirmation/error-recovery research** (Sagawa et al., n=13; McGee/Cohen/Oviatt multimodal confirmation; Lavelle/DEMON; KIT interactive recovery).
4. **Mobile-commerce numerical-input usability** (Baymard Institute; Nielsen Norman Group input steppers; Vernon Fowler screen-reader form remediation; Accenture Resonance Labs and Auric Artisan accessible stepper patterns).
5. **Auditory memory and cognitive-load science** (congenital-blind serial memory; Föcker et al. digit recall; NASA-TLX modality comparisons).

Because sample sizes in BLV accessibility research are small (typically 3–80; the JMIR financial-accessibility scoping review reports per-study samples of 4–98), individual effect estimates are imprecise. I treat directional consistency across clusters as the meaningful signal and flag every extrapolation.

---

## 3. Modality comparison by checkout stage

### 3.1 Product selection
- **Voice-only is viable and often preferred for coarse selection.** In the EasyGO grocery field study, participants preferred a **combined screen + audio** system, and when forced to choose a single channel, **audio-only was preferred over screen-only**; proactive audio cues were judged less distracting than periodically checking a screen (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3656156.3663719). A voice-based shopping-agent study with 12 visually impaired participants confirmed that voice interaction can support complex shopping but surfaced needs around control, pacing, and confirmation (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3772318.3791681).
- **But audio-only access reconfigures rather than removes barriers.** A conversation-analytic study of BLV users of voice AI (survey n=50; interviews n=13) found that audio-only interaction creates trouble around turn boundaries, system silence/delay, competing audio streams, and the absence of visible processing cues, forcing users into "stabilisation routines" (https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/3816046.3816209). This directly undermines a purely sequential voice flow for multi-item selection.
- **Hybrid touch+audio reduces mental effort and time.** An Android accessibility service providing natural-language dialogue plus summarization (Insight) was compared within-subjects against gesture-based TalkBack: Insight **reduced mental effort and task time** and was preferred, yet the authors explicitly recommend **hybrid solutions combining gesture and dialogue modalities** (https://arxiv.org/html/2605.09803). A month-long deployment of BarrierFreeShop with 80 visually impaired users showed speed and satisfaction gains from an accessible, restructured layout — i.e., a touch-navigable structure with audio output (https://www.kci.go.kr/kciportal/ci/sereArticleSearch/ciSereArtiView.kci?sereArticleSearchBean.artiId=ART002628889).

**Implication:** Use voice to search/filter/select at a coarse level, but keep a touch-navigable, screen-reader-labeled product list as the authoritative selection surface.

### 3.2 Quantity adjustment (numerical entry)
This is where voice-only is weakest and the evidence is most consistent.

- **Audio-only error detection is poor.** In a controlled lab study, blind screen-reader users identified **only ~40% of ASR errors** when reviewing dictated text through audio alone — statistically no better than sighted users, and worse for longer text (https://jonggi.github.io/papers/TACCESS2020-speech.pdf). Homophone confusions (e.g., "sight"/"site"; for numbers, "four"/"for") are especially hard to catch. Blind users reportedly spend **~80% of text-entry time reviewing and editing** dictated input (Azenkot et al., cited in the same paper). A spoken quantity like "three" misrecognized as a different digit may therefore pass unnoticed roughly 60% of the time on audio playback.
- **Free numeric text fields are error-prone for everyone, worse on mobile.** Baymard's large-scale checkout testing found the quantity field a recurring "speed bump," with open text fields inviting typos and forcing users to delete existing values; **61% of sites implement quantity as a dropdown or text field**, and mobile keyboards raise input-error risk (https://baymard.com/blog/auto-update-users-quantity-changes).
- **Steppers (increment/decrement) are the lower-error control for small adjustments.** NN/g found steppers require fewer interactions and fewer errors than text entry for values near a default, while warning they are unsuitable for large jumps and recommending an **accompanying text field for direct entry** (https://www.nngroup.com/articles/input-steppers/). A within-subject study of accessible input modalities for visually impaired learners found **counter-based modalities produced higher efficiency and lower cognitive load** than navigation-dependent input, with significant effects on completion time (p<0.001), mental demand (p=0.045), effort (p=0.039), and frustration (p=0.011) (https://exa.ai/library/publication/t52dqv29zmc).
- **Screen-reader implementation matters.** A remediation case study found `input type="number"` spinners **confused a blind participant and inflated field-completion time**, recommending `input type="text"` with `inputmode`/`pattern` for a numeric keypad (https://vfowler.com/form-wizard-remediation-research-design/). Accessible-stepper patterns specify that increment/decrement buttons carry descriptive labels, that the current value and boundary states be announced, and that focus never be lost unexpectedly (https://accenture.github.io/resonance-labs/components/quantity-stepper/index.html; https://auricartisan.com/accessibility-patterns/number-input/).

**Implication:** Implement quantity as a **labeled stepper with audio announcement of the new value and limits**, plus an optional direct-entry field. Map voice commands ("add one," "set to four") onto the same stepper semantics, but always **read back the resulting value and require an explicit confirm** — do not trust silent voice recognition of a number.

### 3.3 Payment confirmation
- **Authentication and verification are the dominant barriers.** A JMIR scoping review of digital-finance accessibility found **authentication-related barriers in 18 of 23 studies and screen-reader incompatibility in 17**, with recurring reliance on sighted assistance for login, verification, and payments — compromising privacy and independence (https://www.jmir.org/2026/1/e82315/PDF). A First Monday review similarly found personal-finance systems inconsistently follow accessibility standards, with screen readers as the primary (linear) access channel (https://firstmonday.org/ojs/index.php/fm/article/download/7036/5922). A usability test of three Saudi banking apps with 12 blind users found **none conformed to WCAG 2.1**, with "Operable" the most violated principle (~37% of violations) (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10209-023-01082-y).
- **Transcribing one-time codes is specifically harmful.** WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.8 (Accessible Authentication) prohibits requiring transcription of one-time codes or memorized secrets unless an accessible alternative exists, precisely because transcription imposes an "impossible burden" (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/accessible-authentication-minimum.html). Audio-delivered OTPs also raise interception/privacy risk for audio-based assistive tech (https://exa.ai/library/publication/c70m0dz98sc).
- **Confirmation of irreversible actions should be explicit and voice-anchored.** A voice-interaction system designed for visually impaired users adopts the rule that **every state-changing action is confirmed by voice before execution**, with short answers that put the most important information first (https://rjwave.org/jaafr/papers/JAAFR2609514.pdf). Multimodal research shows users treat a confirmation as approval and expect a confirmed command to be executable (McGee/Cohen/Oviatt, below).

**Implication:** Payment authorization should be a **single, explicit, high-contrast confirmation step** summarizing total amount and item count, authorized by a deliberate gesture (double-tap/side-button) or a biometric, with voice used only to trigger or confirm — never to silently execute. Avoid transcription-based 2FA; prefer system-mediated (push/biometric) authentication.

---

## 4. Quantitative synthesis: completion, errors, confidence

Direct, comparable numeric outcomes across the exact three tasks are not published in one study, so I report what is available and mark inferences.

**Task completion / effectiveness**
- A BVI mobile-app evaluation (n=56) reported **100% task-completion effectiveness for app organization** for both blind and low-vision participants after accessibility remediation, with SUS-based satisfaction highest for presentation among blind users (87.62) and for organization/presentation among low-vision users (89.21) (https://cdn.techscience.cn/ueditor/files/iasc/TSP_IASC-30-1/TSP_IASC_18009/TSP_IASC_18009.pdf).
- An Indonesian e-commerce redesign reported **complete task completion across search, product, and checkout** with faster completion and fewer errors after semantics matched assistive tech (https://ejournal.upi.edu/index.php/AJSE/article/view/90874).
- BarrierFreeShop (n=80) showed **speed gains** over a month of real use (https://www.kci.go.kr/kciportal/ci/sereArticleSearch/ciSereArtiView.kci?sereArticleSearchBean.artiId=ART002628889).

**Input error frequency (numerical)**
- Blind users catch **~40% of ASR errors** via audio review; sighted ~50% at 200 WPM in prior work; longer text lowers detection (https://jonggi.github.io/papers/TACCESS2020-speech.pdf). This is the single most consequential number for voice-entered quantities.
- Baymard documents typo/input-error risk in open-text quantity fields, amplified on mobile (https://baymard.com/blog/auto-update-users-quantity-changes).
- Counter/stepper input yields lower frustration and mental demand than navigation-dependent numeric input (p values above) (https://exa.ai/library/publication/t52dqv29zmc).

**User confidence / satisfaction**
- No study reports a validated "confidence score" comparing voice vs. touch checkout. The closest proxies are SUS/satisfaction results above and qualitative reports: BLV users value voice autonomy but report **speech-recognition errors and privacy concerns** that erode trust (smart-speaker study, 41 VI + 38 sighted over 7 days; https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/10711813261485984 and https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10644263); VAPA users report challenges with input, system responses, and control of information, and context-dependent trust (https://scispace.com/papers/siri-talks-at-you-an-empirical-investigation-of-voice-nzib104jdr). Treat confidence as an **unmeasured outcome to instrument in your own testing** (e.g., post-task confidence Likert + SUS + NASA-TLX).

---

## 5. Optimal confirmation strategies and error recovery

### 5.1 Confirmation style (speech-dialog evidence)
Sagawa et al. compared **explicit**, **final** (all slots confirmed once at the end), and **implicit** confirmation in a slot-filling dialog (n=13, ~70% forced ASR accuracy). Measured dialogue cost:

| Style | Avg turns | Avg turns (error dialogs) | Avg dialog time | Avg slot SR accuracy |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Explicit | 10.8 | 12.82 | 36.3 s | 69.4% |
| Final | 8.9 | 10.96 | 34.6 s | 67.1% |
| Implicit | 7.3 | 9.02 | 32.7 s | 66.4% |

Usability ranking (1=best): **with no errors, Final was preferred (1.64) over Implicit (1.89) and Explicit (2.41); with errors, Explicit was preferred (1.59) over Final (2.0) and Implicit (2.41)** (https://www.isca-archive.org/interspeech_2004/sagawa04_interspeech.pdf). The authors' recommendation — **use final confirmation in normal flow, switch to explicit confirmation when a correction/error is detected** — is the most defensible pattern for checkout.

**Illustrative extrapolation to a 15-item cart (my calculation, not from the study):** the task used 2 slots. If dialogue turns scale roughly linearly with slot count, per-item explicit confirmation would project to about (10.8 ÷ 2) × 15 ≈ **81 turns** versus a single aggregated final confirmation near the 2-slot baseline plus one summary. This is a heuristic only, but it shows why **per-item spoken confirmation does not scale** and why a summarized final confirmation is essential for long carts. Uncertainty: high; turn scaling is unlikely to be strictly linear.

### 5.2 Multimodal confirmation timing
McGee, Cohen, and Oviatt showed that **delaying confirmation until after modalities are blended** (late confirmation) produced **more commands per minute at a lower error rate** than confirming speech alone, and that users expect a confirmed command to be immediately executable (https://aclanthology.org/C98-2131.pdf). For a hybrid checkout, this means: confirm the *integrated intent* (item + quantity + price), not the raw voice string.

### 5.3 Implicit confirmation and erroneous acceptance
The DEMON/ARISE system found **~29% of users accepted a badly understood parameter value** under weak confirmation; introducing semi-implicit questions and reordering parameters to match mental operations raised refutation/direct-correction and dialogue success without lengthening dialogue (https://www.isca-archive.org/eurospeech_1999/lavelle99_eurospeech.pdf). This quantifies the risk of silent/implicit confirmation for prices and quantities.

### 5.4 Error recovery mechanisms
- Provide **correction grammars / targeted repair**: detect a correction utterance and transition into an explicit-confirmation subdialog (Sagawa et al.; KIT interactive recovery framework emphasizing the accuracy–speed–naturalness trade-off) (https://www.isca-archive.org/interspeech_2004/sagawa04_interspeech.pdf; https://isl.iar.kit.edu/downloads/InteractiveRecoveryFromSpeechRecognitionErrorsInSpeechUserInterfaces.pdf).
- **Make errors audible and move focus to them.** A documented failure mode is a silent validation error: the screen reader said nothing when a form errored. Remediation = put error text in the label and move focus to the first invalid field (https://vfowler.com/form-wizard-remediation-research-design/).
- **Don't leave recovery to the user.** A grocery-AI interaction-design study identified "inaccessible error communication" and "recovery being left to the user" as core challenges; users compensate with repeated extra verification. Recommended fixes: guided recovery, haptic feedback, and clear safety-critical information (https://exa.ai/library/publication/bm1xnnn2k8j).
- **Slow playback and pauses help.** Slowing synthesized speech and inserting pauses improved ASR-error identification (Hong et al., citing Hong & Findlater) (https://jonggi.github.io/papers/TACCESS2020-speech.pdf).

### 5.5 WCAG 2.2 implementation guidance for checkout
- **SC 3.3.7 Redundant Entry (Level A):** information already entered in the same process (e.g., shipping then billing in checkout, including third-party payment providers) must be **auto-populated or selectable**, not re-entered; browser autocomplete alone is insufficient. This reduces recall/transcription burden and is explicitly relevant to checkout (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/redundant-entry; https://vispero.com/resources/how-to-test-3-3-7-redundant-entry/; https://www.allaccessible.org/blog/wcag-337-redundant-entry-implementation-guide; https://www.digitalpolicy.gov.hk/en/our_work/digital_government/digital_inclusion/accessibility/promulgating_resources/handbook/wcag2a/8_30_redundant_entry.html).
- **SC 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication:** avoid transcription of OTPs and memorized credentials; provide accessible alternatives (https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/accessible-authentication-minimum.html).

---

## 6. Cognitive load when verifying a cart with 15+ items

This is where modality differences are largest, and the memory science is decisive.

**Auditory working-memory capacity is limited — even when enhanced.**
- Congenitally blind individuals show **superior verbal serial memory**, with the greatest advantage for **longer ordered sequences** (20-word lists) (https://www.cell.com/current-biology/fulltext/S0960-9822(07)01484-4), and enhanced attention/working memory (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0001691814002613; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35076724).
- However, in an 8-digit auditory serial-recall task, blind participants showed strongest retention for the **most recent positions (5–8)** and a weaker serial-position effect, using grouping/association strategies (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/17470218241300115). Early-blind users also do not use a spatial "mental whiteboard" for serial order, relying on less spatially organized mnemonics (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27622641).

**Practical inference (my calculation, flagged):** If reliable auditory order span is on the order of ~7–8 items (consistent with classic span and the 8-digit task above), a **single uninterrupted readout of 15+ items exceeds dependable span by roughly 90–115%**. Even with blind users' serial-memory advantage, accurate verification of 15+ items from one audio stream is unlikely without **chunking, on-demand replay, and a navigable structure**. Uncertainty: moderate-to-high; no study tested exactly 15-item cart verification.

**Modality load measurements:**
- NASA-TLX comparisons show modality matters: in accessible math input, counter-based input lowered mental demand/effort/frustration versus navigation-dependent input (https://exa.ai/library/publication/t52dqv29zmc). In a navigation task, **auditory feedback imposed ~22× the cognitive load of haptic feedback for white-cane users** under NASA-TLX, a caution against overloading the audio channel (https://www.lanfanshu.com/paper/61e5083616ad6f084cf62e43). In a driving context, voice entry reduced workload and improved performance versus touch for alphanumeric entry (https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/2667317.2667349) — showing voice can lower load for *entry* even though audio-only *review* is error-prone.
- LLM-based dialogue access reduced mental effort and task time versus gesture-only TalkBack but raised interruption-management needs (https://arxiv.org/html/2605.09803).

**Design consequence for 15+ item verification:** Do not present the cart as one linear audio dump. Provide a **hybrid review surface**: a screen-reader-navigable list (swipe/rotor to jump to any item) with per-item audio, **chunked summaries** (e.g., groups of 5–7 with subtotal and item count), a spoken **aggregate confirmation** ("15 items, total $42.10 — confirm purchase?"), and easy **jump-to-item correction**. This offloads working memory to the interface, consistent with WCAG 3.3.7's goal of reducing recall burden.

---

## 7. Concrete design recommendations

1. **Architecture: hybrid, touch-anchored, voice-assisted.** Touch/gesture + screen reader is the authoritative layer; voice issues coarse commands and final authorization. This matches the strongest evidence (Insight hybrid recommendation; EasyGO preference for combined audio+screen) (https://arxiv.org/html/2605.09803; https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3656156.3663719).
2. **Product selection:** voice search/filter → present a labeled, navigable list; announce name, price, and unit price; allow voice "add item X" but confirm on the list.
3. **Quantity:** labeled stepper with audio announcement of value and min/max; optional direct numeric entry via `inputmode=numeric` text field (avoid raw `type=number` spinners); map voice "add/remove/set" onto the stepper; always read back the resulting quantity (https://www.nngroup.com/articles/input-steppers/; https://accenture.github.io/resonance-labs/components/quantity-stepper/index.html; https://vfowler.com/form-wizard-remediation-research-design/).
4. **Confirmation strategy:** use **final (summary) confirmation** in the normal flow and **escalate to explicit confirmation** when an error/correction is detected (Sagawa et al.); confirm the blended intent, not the raw speech (McGee et al.); avoid purely implicit confirmation given ~29% erroneous-acceptance risk (Lavelle).
5. **Payment authorization:** single explicit step stating total + item count; deliberate gesture or biometric to authorize; no transcription-based OTP (WCAG 3.3.8); auto-populate repeated fields (WCAG 3.3.7).
6. **Error recovery:** announce errors audibly, move focus to the first error, support correction utterances, slow playback with pauses for review, and provide guided (not user-improvised) recovery.
7. **Long-cart review:** chunked summaries, per-item navigation, on-demand replay, aggregate totals — to keep auditory load within span.
8. **Measure what's missing:** instrument task completion, numerical error rate, post-task confidence, SUS, and NASA-TLX in your own BLV studies, since no existing study reports all of these together for this exact task.

---

## 8. Limitations and uncertainty

- **No direct comparative trial** of voice-only vs. hybrid touch+audio for grocery checkout exists in the gathered evidence; conclusions are synthesized from adjacent domains (shopping, banking, dialog systems, memory science).
- **Small samples** (often 3–80; financial-accessibility studies 4–98) limit statistical precision.
- **Confidence scores are not standardized** across studies; I used SUS/satisfaction and qualitative trust reports as proxies.
- The **15-item turn-scaling** and **span-exceedance** figures are my labeled extrapolations, not published findings.
- Several sources are recent/preprint-indexed (some carrying 2025–2026 dates); treat exact publication metadata with caution, though the substantive findings are internally consistent.

Overall, the evidence supports a **hybrid, touch-grounded checkout with structured audio feedback, summary-then-explicit confirmation, stepper-based quantity entry, and chunked cart review** as the lowest-error, lowest-cognitive-load, and most confidence-supporting design for visually impaired grocery shoppers.
