# Error Prevention and Recovery in E-Commerce Checkout Flows: Japan, Germany, and Brazil

## 1. Executive Summary

This report examines how checkout error-prevention and recovery mechanisms in Japan (Rakuten), Germany (Otto), and Brazil (Mercado Livre) reflect and accommodate differing cultural attitudes toward mistakes, uncertainty, and system trust, using Hofstede's Uncertainty Avoidance Index (Japan 92, Germany 65, Brazil 76) and Hall's high-/low-context framework as analytical lenses.

Key findings:

1. **Each market has codified a different "mistake philosophy" into law, and platform UX largely implements that law.** Germany mandates *pre-commitment error prevention* via the Button-Lösung (§ 312j BGB): no valid contract exists unless the final button explicitly says "zahlungspflichtig bestellen" (or equivalent) (https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/bgb/__312j.html). Japan mandates a *final confirmation screen with correction opportunity* and uses the presence of that screen to allocate mistake risk (Act on Specified Commercial Transactions, amended June 1, 2022; Electronic Consumer Contract Act) (https://www.no-trouble.caa.go.jp/pdf/20171201ac06.pdf, https://nagaoka-law.com/column/592/). Brazil relies primarily on *post-purchase statutory recovery*: a 7-day no-justification "right of regret" (direito de arrependimento, CDC Art. 49) with immediate full refund (https://smartlex.net.br/legislacao/cdc/artigo/49).

2. **The three platforms embody these models.** Rakuten enforces a mandatory multi-step flow ending in an explicit "注文を確定する" (confirm order) screen with per-section change buttons, a ~30-minute self-service cancellation window, then human-mediated recovery through the individual shop (https://ichiba.faq.rakuten.net/detail/000007221, https://ichiba.faq.rakuten.net/detail/000007081). Otto runs a 5-step checkout terminating in "Jetzt zahlungspflichtig bestellen," after which no changes are possible and recovery proceeds through formal rights (returns, revocation) rather than in-flow undo (https://www.otto-office.com/de/Bestellung/faq_bestellung/c?notracking=0). Mercado Livre pairs a fast "Comprar agora" entry path with a mandatory final review screen ("Confirmar a compra"), then layers self-service pre-shipment cancellation, the 7-day legal regret window, and the Compra Garantida buyer-protection escrow (https://www.techtudo.com.br/dicas-e-tutoriais/2018/05/como-comprar-no-mercado-livre.ghtml, https://inovaonline3.com/como-comprar-com-seguranca-no-mercado-livre-passo-a-passo-completo/).

3. **True one-click purchasing is legally constrained in Germany, structurally absent at Rakuten, and softened into "fast path + confirmation" at Mercado Livre.** The German Federal Court of Justice (BGH, 9 Oct 2025, I ZR 159/24) confirmed that contracts concluded without a compliant confirmation button are void — no retroactive healing (https://www.otto-schmidt.de/blog/it-recht-blog/button-vorhanden-vertrag-nicht-der-bgh-zieht-durch-ITBLOG0008038.html).

4. **Quantitative outcomes differ but cannot be causally attributed to confirmation patterns alone.** Japan's measured cart abandonment (~62.9%, n=4,374 sites) is *below* the global average of 70.19% (Baymard); Germany sits at 64.6% (ECDB) to 68.9% (Statista via Searchlab); Brazil reaches up to ~82% (E-commerce Radar), with 78% of Brazilians reporting abandonment and 83% reporting abandonment due to checkout distrust (Opinion Box). Confounders — payment localization, shipping cost, fraud rates, trust infrastructure — are large and documented.

5. **Documented micro-findings with cross-cultural relevance:** specific (not generic) error messages measurably reduce checkout failure (Baymard); confirmation dialogs prevent errors only if not overused, because habituation turns them into automated clicks (NN/g); uncertainty avoidance moderates how strongly trust and satisfaction convert into reuse intention, meaning mistake recovery that preserves trust has outsized repeat-purchase effects in high-UAI cultures (Drake multi-level model, 3,500+ consumers, 38 countries; Virginia Tech three-country study).

6. **Evidence gaps, stated plainly:** no public per-platform A/B data exist for Rakuten, Otto, or Mercado Livre linking confirmation-dialog design to accidental-purchase frequency or customer-service contact volume. Those two metrics are reconstructed below from legal, behavioral, and market-level proxies, with uncertainty flagged.

---

## 2. Cultural Baselines: Uncertainty Avoidance and Communication Context

### 2.1 Hofstede UAI scores confirmed

The task's stated scores are verified against Hofstede comparison sources: Japan 92, Germany 65, Brazil 76 (https://www.hofstedeinsightsoy.com/country-comparison-tool, https://classwrites.com/hofstede-compare/japan-vs-germany, https://classwrites.com/hofstede-compare/germany-vs-brazil).

Simple gap arithmetic (computed here):
- Japan − Germany = 92 − 65 = **27 points** — classified as a "large difference" in cross-cultural design terms (https://classwrites.com/hofstede-compare/japan-vs-germany).
- Brazil − Germany = 76 − 65 = **11 points** — "small difference; broadly similar expectations" (https://classwrites.com/hofstede-compare/germany-vs-brazil).
- Japan − Brazil = 92 − 76 = **16 points**.

Interpretive note from the source material: Brazil's profile description emphasizes that high-UAI societies want rules and elaborate legal systems "to make the world a safer place," yet "the individual's need to obey these laws, however, is weak" (https://www.hofstedeinsightsoy.com/country-comparison-tool). This is behaviorally significant: Brazil's high UAI expresses itself as demand for *protective rights and guarantees* (e.g., the 7-day regret right, buyer-protection escrows) more than as demand for procedural rigidity at the interface. Japan's extreme UAI (92) expresses itself as demand for *exhaustive pre-commitment verification and process completeness*. Germany's moderate-high UAI (65) expresses itself as *explicit, legally precise verbalization of obligations*.

### 2.2 Hall's high-/low-context placement

Hall's framework places Japan at the extreme high-context end, German-speaking cultures at the low-context end, and Latin America (including Brazil) in the high-context zone (https://education.alberta.ca/media/1626285/studies-on-cultural-patterns.pdf, https://mycourses.aalto.fi/pluginfile.php/1189342/mod_resource/content/3/nishimuranevgitella299.pdf, https://classwrites.com/high-and-low-context-cultures-countries). Practical implications used below: high-context cultures prefer relational recovery, face-saving error framing, and meaning carried by the situation (guarantees, brand, intermediaries); low-context cultures prefer everything spelled out in explicit text (the German legal requirement that the button literally verbalize the payment obligation is a quintessentially low-context mechanism).

**Caveat:** a systematic review questions whether Hall's country classifications rest on rigorous evidence, noting "mixed and often contradictory findings" (https://sage.cnpereading.com/doi/10.1177/1470595811398797). I use Hall's framework as a directional lens, not as a measured variable.

---

## 3. Three Institutional Models of Mistake Handling (Law as Codified UX)

The strongest evidence in this research is that each country's consumer law *mandates* a specific error-handling architecture, and the leading platforms implement it. This means cultural accommodation is not merely a design preference but a compliance requirement.

### 3.1 Germany: prevention through mandatory explicit confirmation (Button-Lösung)

- Since 2012, § 312j(3) BGB requires that the consumer "expressly confirms" the payment obligation; a button satisfies this only if legibly labeled with nothing other than "zahlungspflichtig bestellen" or an unambiguous equivalent (e.g., "Kaufen"). Labels like "Bestellen," "Bestellung abschicken," "Bezahlen," or "Jetzt Mitglied werden" are insufficient (https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/bgb/__312j.html, https://www.otto-schmidt.de/blog/it-recht-blog/die-button-losung-im-online-handel-aktuelle-anforderungen-und-rechtliche-vorgaben-ITBLOG0007859.html).
- § 312j(2) BGB requires that essential contract information (product characteristics, total price, delivery, cancellation conditions) appear on the order-summary page *immediately before* the button, visible without scrolling (https://www.ihk.de/stuttgart/fuer-unternehmen/recht-und-steuern/it-recht/ecommerce/ecommerce-vertrag-4642418, https://www.verbraucherzentrale-berlin.de/wissen/digitale-welt/onlinehandel/preisangabe-kaufenbutton-etc-so-kommt-online-ein-vertrag-zustande-6762).
- Consequence of non-compliance: **no contract comes into existence** (§ 312j(4) BGB). The BGH (9 Oct 2025, I ZR 159/24) ended attempts at judicial softening: "Keine Schwebezustände, keine nachträgliche Heilung" — no suspended states, no retroactive healing (https://www.otto-schmidt.de/blog/it-recht-blog/button-vorhanden-vertrag-nicht-der-bgh-zieht-durch-ITBLOG0008038.html). The CJEU (Conny, C-400/22, 30 May 2024) left national consequences to member states (same source). The KG Berlin (5 Sept 2024, 5 U 42/21) applied the rule to the immediate ordering situation (https://recht.nulegal.eu/rechtsprechung/kg/2024-09-05/5-u-42-21).
- Cultural reading: this is low-context, high-explicitness error prevention. The system prevents accidental purchases by forcing the user to *verbally acknowledge the obligation* at the moment of commitment. The law was a response to subscription-trap ("Abo-Falle") and accidental-order problems — i.e., it treats mistake prevention as a design specification.

### 3.2 Japan: mandatory final confirmation screen + statutory risk allocation for misclicks

- The 2022 amendment of the Act on Specified Commercial Transactions (特定商取引法, Art. 12-6, effective June 1, 2022) requires the **final confirmation screen (最終確認画面)** — the screen where clicking the button completes the order — to display, in one viewable place: quantity, price, payment timing/method, delivery timing, and cancellation/return conditions. Misleading or missing display gives the consumer a **right to cancel the declaration of intent** (Art. 15-4; exercisable for 1 year from recognition / 5 years from contract) (https://www.caa.go.jp/policies/policy/consumer_transaction/meeting_materials/assets/consumer_transaction_cms101_220628_15.pdf, https://lawplayer.com/jp/article/351AC0000000057/15_4, https://www.no-trouble.caa.go.jp/pdf/20241119la02_09.pdf).
- The accompanying guideline on "acts causing application against the customer's intent" (Ordinance Art. 16) specifies compliant and non-compliant patterns. Compliant: a final screen titled "注文内容の確認" (order content confirmation) where clicking "この内容で注文する" (order with this content) is the first moment the order is placed, **with easy means to confirm and correct** the content (change/back buttons). Non-compliant: a final button labeled merely "送信" (send) with no indication it is a paid order (https://www.no-trouble.caa.go.jp/pdf/20171201ac06.pdf).
- The **Electronic Consumer Contract Act** adds a distinctive risk-allocation rule: consumers can normally rescind for mistake even with gross negligence (an exception to Civil Code Art. 95), **but this protection disappears if the business provided a final confirmation screen or equivalent intent-confirmation measure**. In other words, the presence of the confirmation screen legally shifts misclick risk back to the consumer (https://nagaoka-law.com/column/592/).
- There is **no cooling-off for mail-order sales** in Japan; instead, if no return policy is clearly displayed, consumers get a statutory 8-day return right from delivery at their own shipping cost (Art. 15-3) (https://nagaoka-law.com/column/592/).
- Cultural reading: Japan's UAI-92 anxiety is addressed by *process completeness before commitment* (multi-step verification, one-screen summary, correction affordances) rather than by generous post-hoc exit. The legal architecture explicitly trades: "we force the platform to make you check; in exchange, your misclick is your responsibility." Mistake acknowledgment is institutionalized as a *risk-allocation device*, not as forgiveness.

### 3.3 Brazil: recovery through statutory regret (direito de arrependimento)

- CDC Art. 49 (Lei 8.078/1990): for purchases made outside a physical establishment — expressly including internet purchases — the consumer may **withdraw within 7 days** of signing or of receiving the product/service, **without justification**, with all amounts paid refunded "de imediato, monetariamente atualizado" (immediately, inflation-adjusted) (https://smartlex.net.br/legislacao/cdc/artigo/49, https://www.jusbrasil.com.br/topicos/10601327/artigo-49-da-lei-n-8078-de-11-de-setembro-de-1990).
- Case law confirms the right overrides sector regulations (e.g., airline resolution 400/2016 could not defeat Art. 49 for online airfare purchases) (same Jusbrasil source).
- Cultural reading: the word itself — *arrependimento* (regret/repentance) — legitimizes the mistake as an expected emotional state. Brazil's UAI-76 need for safety is satisfied by an *unconditional exit right* plus intermediated payment (Mercado Pago escrow) rather than by pre-commitment ritual. This fits the Hofstede description of Brazilian high UAI: strong demand for protective rules, flexible adherence, and emphasis on relational reassurance (https://www.hofstedeinsightsoy.com/country-comparison-tool).

---

## 4. Platform Comparison: Confirmation Patterns, Undo Capability, Error Tone

### 4.1 Rakuten Ichiba (Japan)

**Confirmation pattern.** Mandatory multi-step flow: cart → "ご購入手続き" (purchase procedure) → "注文内容の確認" (order content confirmation) → "注文を確定する" (finalize order) → completion screen. On the confirmation screen, each section (payment, shipping, etc.) has its own "変更" (change) button. Upon clicking finalize, an automatic order-confirmation email is sent immediately (subject: 【楽天市場】注文内容ご確認(自動配信メール)) (https://ichiba.faq.rakuten.net/detail/000007221). A merchant-facing notice makes the stakes explicit: once "注文を確定する" is clicked, the order is fixed instantly and cannot be changed by the customer; users are asked to verify payment method, shipping, and fees first (https://www.rakuten.ne.jp/gold/dtc/faq/order.html). This matches the CAA guideline's compliant pattern exactly.

**Undo capability.** Narrow and partly human-mediated:
- Cancellation may be possible **within ~30 minutes** of ordering in some cases; otherwise the user must contact the individual shop (https://ichiba.faq.rakuten.net/detail/000007081).
- **Payment method cannot be changed after finalization** for most flows; the standard remedy is shop-side cancellation and re-order (same source).
- Rakuten's marketplace structure means recovery is a *conversation with the shop* — consistent with high-context, relationship-based resolution.
- On the seller side, orders unconfirmed for 14 days auto-cancel (RMS workflow), showing the platform builds time-boxed states throughout (https://manual.sokuhan.jp/renkei/mallcart/rakuten/pay-conf/).

**Error message tone.** Rakuten's guidance for errors at the finalize step is notably face-saving and process-oriented: if an error appears, the order *may already have gone through*; do not immediately re-order (to avoid duplicates); wait, then check the confirmation email or purchase history (which may take ~10 minutes to reflect, longer during sales events) (https://ichiba.faq.rakuten.net/detail/000006565). The framing protects the user from double-action without bluntly accusing them of error, and it treats system ambiguity (not user fault) as the default narrative — a high-context, harmony-preserving tone.

### 4.2 Otto (Germany)

**Confirmation pattern.** Otto's documented order process is a linear 5-step wizard: (1) Login, (2) customer/order data, (3) payment method selection, (4) "Bestellung überprüfen" — full review of all inputs with the ability to make changes, acceptance of AGB, then "Jetzt zahlungspflichtig bestellen," (5) completion page with print/view/save options and confirmation email (https://www.otto-office.com/de/Bestellung/faq_bestellung/c?notracking=0). This is the Button-Lösung implemented verbatim. Note the review step explicitly offers correction *before* commitment and the completion page offers *documentation* (print/save) — low-context: the record, not the relationship, is the safety net. Contract formation typically requires the retailer's explicit acceptance (Auftragsbestätigung) after the auto-receipt email; some German shops bind the customer's offer for seven days (https://www.shop.floetotto.de/mediafiles/Sonstiges/2023/FLOETOTTO_AGB_Onlineshop_2022.pdf) — a two-beat contract formation that adds a second, system-side confirmation layer.

**Undo capability.** After the final button, "Änderungen an Ihrer Bestellung sind nun nicht mehr möglich" (changes are no longer possible) (https://www.otto-office.com/de/Bestellung/faq_bestellung/c?notracking=0). Recovery is channeled into *formal rights* — order cancellation before dispatch where offered, statutory revocation/returns after receipt — rather than in-flow undo. Germany's return culture is heavy: ECDB benchmarks put overall German returns at 9.2% and fashion returns at 18.6% (https://static.ecdb.com/media/2026/07/ecdb-e-commerce-kpi-and-benchmarks-report-2026-14366.pdf). The German model effectively says: commit explicitly once, then use codified, impersonal reversal rights.

**Error/confirmation tone.** The legally prescribed vocabulary ("zahlungspflichtig bestellen," "Kaufen") and the prohibition of softer labels ("Bestellen," "weiter") show the system's theory of error: ambiguity itself is the hazard, so language must be maximally explicit (https://www.verbraucherzentrale-berlin.de/wissen/digitale-welt/onlinehandel/preisangabe-kaufenbutton-etc-so-kommt-online-ein-vertrag-zustande-6762). This is the opposite of high-context indirectness; the mistake is prevented by *saying the consequence in words*.

### 4.3 Mercado Livre (Brazil)

**Confirmation pattern.** Two entry paths: "Adicionar ao carrinho" or "Comprar agora" (buy now), the latter skipping the cart and going directly to checkout. The flow then proceeds: address → shipping method/cost → payment method → CPF for nota fiscal → final review of items, address, payment, and detailed price → "Confirmar a compra" (https://www.techtudo.com.br/dicas-e-tutoriais/2018/05/como-comprar-no-mercado-livre.ghtml, https://descontostop.com/guias-compras/como-comprar-mercado-livre/). Important: "Comprar agora" is a *fast path, not a one-click purchase* — commitment still requires the final review and explicit "Confirmar a compra." The platform thus offers speed for experienced users while retaining the confirmation screen that Brazilian trust conditions demand (83% have abandoned checkouts they distrusted; see §5.3).

**Undo capability.** The richest self-service recovery stack of the three:
- Self-service cancellation before shipment via "Minhas compras" → "Cancelar pedido" (https://digitei.com/mercado-livre-entrar-acesse-sua-conta-e-compre-agora/, https://inovaonline3.com/como-comprar-com-seguranca-no-mercado-livre-passo-a-passo-completo/).
- Statutory 7-day regret right after receipt (CDC Art. 49).
- **Compra Garantida** buyer protection: for wrong/defective products or non-delivery, the platform mediates and refunds via Mercado Pago; funds are held in the payment ecosystem rather than released immediately to sellers (https://inovaonline3.com/como-comprar-com-seguranca-no-mercado-livre-passo-a-passo-completo/). Cancellations executed outside the official system may forfeit refund eligibility — the platform pulls recovery *into* the system (same source).
- Payment rails matter for error recovery: Pix now carries ~40% of Brazilian e-commerce volume (2024) and is instant, replacing the boleto bancário, which took 1–3 days to clear; PIX "has materially reduced abandonment for boleto-replacement cases" (https://paymentscmi.com/insights/mercado-comercio-eletronico-no-brasil/, https://areza.digital/markets/brazil/ecommerce/). Boleto volume fell an estimated 50–70% between 2020 and 2025 (https://areza.digital/markets/brazil/ecommerce/).

**Error/confirmation tone.** Brazilian help and guidance content around the platform is emotionally reassuring and anxiety-reducing: order tracking is described as removing "inseguranças" and bringing "tranquilidade," designed "para facilitar a vida até de quem está comprando online pela primeira vez… sem mistério" (https://www.barrasvirtual.com.br/acompanhar-pedidos-mercado-livre-3-passos-simples/). Trust is carried by intermediaries and guarantees (escrow, buyer protection, reputational systems) rather than by procedural solemnity — consistent with high-context trust formation and with research showing culture shapes *trust* as the key mediator for (high-context) Asian-style consumers, while (low-context) Europeans respond more to usability/risk information (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43039-021-00022-z).

### 4.4 Comparative summary

| Dimension | Rakuten (JP, UAI 92, high-context) | Otto (DE, UAI 65, low-context) | Mercado Livre (BR, UAI 76, high-context) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Confirmation pattern | Mandatory multi-step; explicit final confirmation screen with per-section change buttons (CAA-compliant) | 5-step wizard; legally prescribed "zahlungspflichtig bestellen" button; full info re-displayed pre-button | Fast path ("Comprar agora") but mandatory final review + "Confirmar a compra" |
| One-click purchase | Absent (structurally and legally discouraged) | Effectively prohibited for consumer contracts without compliant explicit button (BGH 2025) | Fast entry, but never one-click commitment |
| Order modification window | ~30 min self-service in some cases; otherwise shop negotiation; payment method generally locked post-order | None after final button; correction only pre-commitment | Self-service cancel pre-shipment; 7-day legal regret post-receipt |
| Payment reversal | Shop-mediated cancellation/re-order; konbini/bank-transfer flows add async windows | Formal revocation/return rights; refund after return | Escrow (Mercado Pago); instant Pix refunds; Compra Garantida mediation |
| Mistake acknowledgment style | Face-saving, system-ambiguity framing ("don't re-click; check email first") | Explicit verbalization of obligation; documentation (print/save) | Reassurance + unconditional exit right ("arrependimento"); intermediary absorbs risk |
| Recovery channel | Human (shop contact) — high-context relationship | Formal rights — low-context rules | Platform mediation + statutory right — high-context intermediary |

Sources as cited in §4.1–4.3.

---

## 5. Multi-Step Confirmation vs. Streamlined One-Click: Effects on Abandonment, Accidental Purchases, and Service Contacts

### 5.1 Cart abandonment benchmarks (quantitative work shown)

Data gathered, by market:

- **Global:** Baymard's 14-year tracked average = **70.19%**; ~70% of users abandon after adding to cart (https://baymard.com/research/checkout-usability, https://baymard.com/research-articles/current-state-of-checkout-ux).
- **Japan:** CART RECOVERY survey of 4,374 e-commerce sites (monthly sales >¥5M), 2025: average abandonment **62.9%** (−0.4 pts YoY); apparel ~70%; opportunity loss ≈ **2.6× monthly sales** (https://en.submit.ne.jp/cartrecovery/column/2025research). Komoju corroborates ~62.9% average, "lower than the global average" (https://en.komoju.com/conversion/cart-abandonment-in-japan/).
- **Germany:** ECDB 2026 benchmark: **64.6%** (transaction-modeled) (https://static.ecdb.com/media/2026/07/ecdb-e-commerce-kpi-and-benchmarks-report-2026-14366.pdf); Statista via Searchlab 2026: **68.9%** (https://searchlab.nl/en/statistics/cart-abandonment-statistics-2026). Methodological spread: 68.9 − 64.6 = **4.3 percentage points** between two reputable measures of the same market — a useful reminder of measurement uncertainty.
- **Brazil:** up to **82%** (E-commerce Radar) (https://www.ecommerceupdate.org/en/noticias/descubra-por-que-82-abandonam-suas-compras-online-e-como-mudar-esse-cenario/); Opinion Box 2023: **78%** have abandoned at the final stage; **83%** have abandoned because they distrusted the checkout (https://www.revistavarejobrasil.com.br/maioria-dos-consumidores-desiste-da-compra-no-checkout-veja-como-impulsionar-as-vendas/); only **22%** of carts at traditional Brazilian e-commerce complete (Poli Pay industry claim, same ecommerceupdate source).
- Statista's cross-country Q1 2026 ranking places Mexico highest (93%) and South Korea/Spain at 88%, with Germany and Japan at the low-abandonment end (https://www.statista.com/statistics/546885/cart-abandonment-rate-region/).

Simple comparisons (computed here):
- Brazil high estimate vs. Japan: 82% − 62.9% ≈ **19-point gap**.
- Germany (ECDB) vs. Japan: 64.6% − 62.9% = **1.7 points** — essentially equivalent.
- Japan vs. global average: 70.19% − 62.9% ≈ **7.3 points lower** than global.

**Interpretation with explicit caution:** Japan's *lower-than-global* abandonment coexists with the world's most mandatory multi-step confirmation regime. This directly challenges any simple claim that explicit confirmations raise abandonment. Germany's abandonment is comparable to Japan's despite a lighter (single explicit-button) confirmation regime. Brazil's markedly higher abandonment coincides with a recovery-oriented regime — but also with high shipping-cost sensitivity (41% cite freight cost/time; https://www.ecommerceupdate.com.br/pt/pesquisa-revela-habitos-de-consumo-online-dos-brasileiros-75-finalizariam-compras-com-cupons-de-desconto/), fraud rates of ~2.5–3.5% of transaction attempts (https://areza.digital/markets/brazil/ecommerce/), and checkout distrust (83%, above). **Abandonment differences between these markets are not demonstrated to be caused by confirmation patterns; the evidence supports treating confirmation design as one moderating factor among several.**

### 5.2 What the UX research says about confirmation vs. streamlining trade-offs

- NN/g: confirmation dialogs prevent user errors **before actions with serious, hard-to-undo consequences (including "costing large amounts of money")**, but overuse causes habituation — repeated dialogs become automated clicks and lose protective power. For the most dangerous operations, require non-standard responses (e.g., typing a word) (https://www.nngroup.com/articles/confirmation-dialog/). Applied to checkout: a single, well-designed, specific final confirmation (the German/Japanese model) fits the guideline; stacking multiple dialogs would backfire.
- NN/g heuristic #3 (user control and freedom): support clearly marked "emergency exits," back/cancel, and undo; undo must be discoverable. Prevention is better than recovery, but recovery capability reduces anxiety (https://www.nngroup.com/articles/user-control-and-freedom/, https://www.nngroup.com/articles/proximity-consequential-options/). Mercado Livre's pre-shipment cancel and Brazil's regret right implement "undo" at the transaction level; Otto and Rakuten concentrate undo *before* commitment.
- Baymard: **specific error details improve error-recovery time for all users and dramatically reduce the share of users who get completely stuck and give up** (https://baymard.com/research-articles/current-state-of-checkout-ux). This is the strongest documented link between error-message quality and completed purchases, and it holds across markets.
- Baymard friction points that interact with confirmation design: 18% abandon when forced to create an account (disproportionately first-time buyers); strict password rules can cause up to 19% abandonment among existing account users; >70% resist providing phone numbers without explanation (https://baymard.com/research-articles/current-state-of-checkout-ux, https://baymard.com/research/checkout-usability).

### 5.3 Accidental purchase frequency and customer-service contact volume

**Direct, public per-platform metrics for accidental purchases and CS contact volume were not found in this research; I state this plainly rather than fabricate figures.** The available evidence is structural and legal:

- **Germany:** the Button-Lösung exists *because* accidental/hidden-obligation orders (subscription traps) were a documented mass problem; the legal consequence (no contract without compliant button) means accidental "purchases" via ambiguous buttons are legally non-existent rather than serviced after the fact (https://www.otto-schmidt.de/blog/it-recht-blog/die-button-losung-im-online-handel-aktuelle-anforderungen-und-rechtliche-vorgaben-ITBLOG0007859.html). The BGH's strict stance (2025) shifts accidental-purchase risk entirely onto merchants' UI compliance. Expected effect: low accidental-purchase incidence at compliant shops; CS contacts shift from "I didn't mean to buy" to returns/revocation processing (Germany's 9.2% overall return rate is the visible outlet; https://static.ecdb.com/media/2026/07/ecdb-e-commerce-kpi-and-benchmarks-report-2026-14366.pdf).
- **Japan:** the Electronic Consumer Contract Act creates a measurable legal incentive structure: platforms that display a proper final confirmation screen are *insulated* from misclick rescission claims (https://nagaoka-law.com/column/592/). This predicts (a) near-universal adoption of confirmation screens (Rakuten's flow confirms), and (b) accidental-purchase disputes being rare but high-stakes when the screen was defective — the 2022 Art. 15-4 cancellation right was introduced precisely for "I thought it was a one-time purchase but it was a subscription" cases (https://lawplayer.com/jp/article/351AC0000000057/15_4). Rakuten's duplicate-order guidance (wait before re-clicking after an error) indicates duplicate/accidental ordering is a known failure mode that the platform manages through messaging rather than undo tooling (https://ichiba.faq.rakuten.net/detail/000006565). Because post-order changes require contacting the shop, Japan's model likely *converts* accidental-purchase events into CS contacts (shop messages/calls) rather than eliminating them via self-service undo — a plausible but unquantified inference.
- **Brazil:** the 7-day no-justification regret right plus Compra Garantida means accidental purchases are *expected and absorbed*: the system does not need to prevent every mistake because reversal is cheap and unilateral. Mercado Livre's own survey shows 72% of consumers habitually fill carts and abandon them, 50% using the cart as a save-for-later device, and only 44% returning to complete (https://www.ecommerceupdate.com.br/pt/pesquisa-revela-habitos-de-consumo-online-dos-brasileiros-75-finalizariam-compras-com-cupons-de-desconto/) — indicating low commitment anxiety at the cart stage. The 83% distrust-driven abandonment figure (https://www.revistavarejobrasil.com.br/maioria-dos-consumidores-desiste-da-compra-no-checkout-veja-como-impulsionar-as-vendas/) suggests that in Brazil, *trust signals* (guarantees, escrow, familiar payment rails like Pix) move abandonment more than confirmation-step count.

### 5.4 Synthesis: explicit multi-step confirmation vs. one-click

1. **Explicit confirmation does not measurably raise abandonment in these markets** — Japan (most confirmation steps) has abandonment below the global average, and Germany (mandatory explicit button) is at or below many Western European peers (62.9–64.6–68.9% vs. 70.19% global; sources in §5.1).
2. **One-click streamlining is legally bounded in Germany and structurally absent in Japan**, so the natural experiment the task posits cannot be observed within Rakuten/Otto; the closest observable is Mercado Livre's "Comprar agora" fast path, which still terminates in a confirmation screen. The evidence thus supports a convergence thesis: **all three markets converge on "one explicit, specific, final confirmation," and differentiate primarily on what happens after commitment** (Germany: formal rights; Japan: shop negotiation + narrow windows; Brazil: unilateral regret + escrow).
3. **Where streamlining demonstrably helps:** payment localization and rail speed. Cart abandonment ran **32% higher** for merchants not offering localized APAC payment options (PYMNTS via Komoju, https://en.komoju.com/conversion/cart-abandonment-in-japan/); in Japan, shoppers are "less likely to retry a failed payment and switch to a competitor" (https://en.komoju.com/blog/general-advice/how-payment-analytics-help-merchants/); in Brazil, replacing 1–3-day boleto with instant Pix materially reduced abandonment (https://areza.digital/markets/brazil/ecommerce/). Friction reduction at *payment* has better evidence than confirmation-step reduction at *commitment*.

---

## 6. Payment Reversal, Modification Windows, and Mistake Acknowledgment: Effects on Confidence and Repeat Purchase (First-Time vs. Experienced; High- vs. Low-Context)

### 6.1 Documented mechanisms and their confidence effects

**Payment reversal / escrow (Brazil).** Mercado Pago's hold-and-release model plus Compra Garantida means first-time buyers face bounded downside: money is recoverable if the product is wrong, defective, or never arrives, and refunds route back into the wallet (https://inovaonline3.com/como-comprar-com-seguranca-no-mercado-livre-passo-a-passo-completo/). Combined with CDC Art. 49's unconditional 7-day exit (https://smartlex.net.br/legislacao/cdc/artigo/49), this is a *recovery-first trust architecture*. Cross-cultural evidence supports its weight in high-context/high-UAI markets: in a 38-country, 3,500+ consumer study, uncertainty avoidance **moderated the trust → e-loyalty relationship** (and information quality → perceived usefulness), with stronger effects for high-UA consumers (https://escholarshare.drake.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/50e037b6-fb17-4842-841b-5770bb2c678d/content). A Virginia Tech three-country study similarly found UA moderates **satisfaction → reuse intention** (https://vtechworks.lib.vt.edu/items/f817b8aa-53a9-4abe-a9b1-e3f0de007ed5/full). Implication: in Brazil (and Japan), a recovery experience that preserves trust converts disproportionately into repeat purchase; a bad recovery is more costly to loyalty than in lower-UA markets.

**Order modification windows (Japan).** Rakuten's ~30-minute cancellation window and shop-mediated changes (https://ichiba.faq.rakuten.net/detail/000007081) create a short, high-context "grace period." For first-time shoppers in a UAI-92 culture, the *existence* of the confirmation screen plus immediate auto-confirmation email (https://ichiba.faq.rakuten.net/detail/000007221) provides the certainty they need; the limited post-order undo reflects the legal logic that once confirmation has been offered, the mistake risk is the consumer's (Electronic Consumer Contract Act, https://nagaoka-law.com/column/592/). For experienced shoppers, the cost is friction: payment-method lock-in and shop-by-shop cancellation heterogeneity. Japan's konbini/bank-transfer payment mix adds asynchronous windows (payment completes at the convenience store later), which both extends the de facto reconsideration period and creates a distinct failure mode — konbini selections that are never paid (https://en.komoju.com/blog/general-advice/how-payment-analytics-help-merchants/).

**Pre-commitment correction + post-commitment formal rights (Germany).** Otto's model concentrates all undo capability before the button and offers documentation (print/save) after (https://www.otto-office.com/de/Bestellung/faq_bestellung/c?notracking=0). For low-context users, confidence comes from *explicitness and records*, not from reversibility warmth. Germany's purchase frequency (12.4 orders/year; https://static.ecdb.com/media/2026/07/ecdb-e-commerce-kpi-and-benchmarks-report-2026-14366.pdf) and Otto's position (GMV €7.9bn, conversion 2.86%, AOV €171, frequency 2.7×/yr, +9.9% growth; same source) indicate the model sustains repeat business among experienced, high-basket generalist shoppers. The 18.6% fashion return rate (same source) shows Germans exercise reversal rights heavily when they exist — consistent with low-context cultures using codified rights rather than negotiation.

### 6.2 First-time vs. experienced shoppers

- **First-time friction is dominated by account and identity demands, not confirmation steps:** 18% abandonment from forced account creation; phone-number reluctance >70% (Baymard, https://baymard.com/research-articles/current-state-of-checkout-ux). Rakuten mitigates with guest purchase plus an order-confirmation lookup form for non-members (https://ichiba.faq.rakuten.net/detail/000007221); Mercado Livre's guidance explicitly targets first-timers ("até de quem está comprando online pela primeira vez… sem mistério," https://www.barrasvirtual.com.br/acompanhar-pedidos-mercado-livre-3-passos-simples/).
- **Experienced shoppers optimize for speed and use carts strategically:** 72% of surveyed Brazilians fill-and-abandon carts, half as save-for-later; 75% say a coupon would complete the purchase; ~30% wait for proprietary promo dates (Mercado Livre survey, https://www.ecommerceupdate.com.br/pt/pesquisa-revela-habitos-de-consumo-online-dos-brasileiros-75-finalizariam-compras-com-cupons-de-desconto/). For this segment, "Comprar agora" fast paths and one-tap Pix payment reduce friction where it matters; extra confirmation dialogs would add nothing.
- **Market maturity predicts repeat-purchase frequency:** ECDB shows purchase frequency rising with online-share maturity (Germany 12.4×/yr at 18.7% online share; US 27.7× at ~30%) (https://static.ecdb.com/media/2026/07/ecdb-e-commerce-kpi-and-benchmarks-report-2026-14366.pdf). In less mature segments, confidence-building recovery mechanisms are the leading indicator of repeat-purchase growth (same source's guidance: "treat rising online share as your leading indicator").

### 6.3 High-context vs. low-context interaction patterns

- **Mistake acknowledgment:** In high-context Japan, platform language avoids attributing blame to the user (Rakuten's duplicate-order guidance frames the ambiguity as systemic: "the order may already be confirmed; please check before re-ordering," https://ichiba.faq.rakuten.net/detail/000006565). In low-context Germany, the mistake is preempted by forcing the user to *say the costly thing in words* ("zahlungspflichtig bestellen," https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/bgb/__312j.html). In high-context Brazil, the mistake is normalized emotionally ("arrependimento") and absorbed institutionally (escrow + 7-day right, https://smartlex.net.br/legislacao/cdc/artigo/49).
- **Recovery channel:** relationship (Japan: message the shop) vs. rules (Germany: exercise rights) vs. intermediary (Brazil: platform mediates). This maps cleanly onto Hall's framework (https://classwrites.com/high-and-low-context-cultures-countries), with the caveat that Hall's country classifications themselves have contested validity (https://sage.cnpereading.com/doi/10.1177/1470595811398797).
- **Trust formation:** cross-cultural SEM evidence indicates culture acts primarily on *trust* for high-context-leaning consumers and on *usability/perceived risk* for low-context-leaning Europeans (Alibaba study, 350 consumers, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s43039-021-00022-z); national culture explains ~23% of variance in general disposition to trust (China/Finland study, 616 consumers, https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/ininma/v38y2018i1p97-106.html); and website-design → trust/satisfaction → loyalty paths differ across Canada/Germany/China samples (JMIS 2008, 571 participants, https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.2753/MIS0742-1222240402). Design consequence: error-recovery messaging in Japan/Brazil should foreground relationship and guarantee cues; in Germany, precision, completeness, and reference to rights.

---

## 7. Limitations and Uncertainty

1. **No public per-platform experiments** link Rakuten/Otto/Mercado Livre confirmation-dialog variants to abandonment, accidental purchases, or CS contact volume. All platform-level causal claims here are inferences from law, documented flows, and market benchmarks.
2. **Abandonment figures are not methodologically comparable:** ECDB (transaction-modeled, Germany 64.6%) vs. Statista (68.9% Germany) vs. CART RECOVERY (62.9%, Japanese sites >¥5M monthly sales) vs. E-commerce Radar/Opinion Box (82%/78%, Brazil, survey-based). Cross-country gaps of a few points are within method noise; only the Brazil-vs-Japan/Germany gap (~12–19 pts) is large enough to be meaningful, and even it is confounded by freight cost, fraud, payment mix, and trust.
3. **ECDB's benchmark table covers Germany but not Japan or Brazil** among the three target markets (https://static.ecdb.com/media/2026/07/ecdb-e-commerce-kpi-and-benchmarks-report-2026-14366.pdf); Japan and Brazil KPIs come from secondary industry sources.
4. **Hofstede scores are national averages** and do not segment by age, device, or shopper experience; Hall's classifications are contested (https://sage.cnpereading.com/doi/10.1177/1470595811398797).
5. **Otto.de's current consumer checkout UI was documented via Otto Office (B2B arm) FAQ and German legal/commerce sources**; I could not directly inspect otto.de's live consumer checkout in this session.
6. The German 14-day distance-selling withdrawal right (EU Consumer Rights Directive) is standard background context for the German recovery model but was not independently re-verified in this session; the evidence gathered here covers the Button-Lösung and contract-formation side in detail.

---

## 8. Design Implications (Synthesis)

1. **Keep exactly one explicit, specific, final confirmation** — legally required wording in Germany (https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/bgb/__312j.html), CAA-compliant confirmation screen in Japan (https://www.no-trouble.caa.go.jp/pdf/20171201ac06.pdf), review screen in Brazil. Stacking additional dialogs invites habituation without added safety (https://www.nngroup.com/articles/confirmation-dialog/).
2. **Invest in recovery, not just prevention, proportional to culture:** high-UAI/high-context markets (Japan 92, Brazil 76) reward visible, low-effort reversal paths because UA moderates trust→loyalty and satisfaction→reuse (https://escholarshare.drake.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/50e037b6-fb17-4842-841b-5770bb2c678d/content, https://vtechworks.lib.vt.edu/items/f817b8aa-53a9-4abe-a9b1-e3f0de007ed5/full). In Brazil, that means escrow visibility, instant Pix refunds, and prominent "arrependimento" framing; in Japan, a short self-service grace window plus respectful, non-blaming shop-contact paths; in Germany, precise rights information and documentation.
3. **Make error messages specific everywhere** — this is the single best-documented checkout error-recovery lever (Baymard, https://baymard.com/research-articles/current-state-of-checkout-ux) — but tune tone: face-saving and process-oriented in Japan, explicit and rights-referencing in Germany, reassuring and guarantee-led in Brazil.
4. **For first-time shoppers, remove account/identity friction and show the safety net before commitment** (guest checkout, guarantee badges, refund-window statements); for experienced shoppers, offer fast paths ("Comprar agora"-style) that still terminate in the mandatory confirmation.
5. **Do not expect confirmation-step reduction to move abandonment much** in these markets; the higher-leverage, better-evidenced interventions are payment localization (32% abandonment penalty when absent for APAC, https://en.komoju.com/conversion/cart-abandonment-in-japan/), instant payment rails (Pix effect in Brazil, https://areza.digital/markets/brazil/ecommerce/), transparent shipping costs (top abandonment driver at 48% globally, https://www.emarketer.com/content/extra-costs-are-the-top-reason-consumers-abandon-online-carts, and 41% in Brazil, https://www.ecommerceupdate.com.br/pt/pesquisa-revela-habitos-de-consumo-online-dos-brasileiros-75-finalizariam-compras-com-cupons-de-desconto/), and delivery-date clarity in Japan (~40% abandoned over slow delivery estimates, https://en.komoju.com/blog/woocommerce/).

**Bottom line:** Japan, Germany, and Brazil have each institutionalized a culturally coherent answer to "what happens when a shopper makes a mistake?" — Japan prevents through exhaustive pre-commitment verification and then allocates risk; Germany prevents through mandatory verbal explicitness and then offers formal rights; Brazil permits speed and then guarantees unconditional, intermediated recovery. The leading platforms (Rakuten, Otto, Mercado Livre) implement these national logics faithfully, and the available quantitative evidence shows all three models sustain large-scale repeat purchasing — with abandonment differences driven more by payment, logistics, and trust infrastructure than by the number of confirmation steps.

# Legal Research Report: Slavery Law and the Molasses Act in the 1730s British Empire

## 0. Three corrections that matter for your novel

Before the detail, three findings that should change how you frame the book:

1. **The Molasses Act contains no slave-law language at all.** It is a fiscal-trade statute (6 Geo. 2, c. 13) about duties on foreign rum, molasses, and sugar. No clause classifies anyone as chattel. The chattel language you want lives in *colonial* assemblies' statutes, not Westminster's (see §2).
2. **South Carolina's famous "chattels personal" clause is dated May 10, 1740** — passed *after* the Stono Rebellion (September 9, 1739). During 1730–1739 the operative South Carolina code was the February 1722 act. If your novel is set in 1739, characters would be living under the 1722 law when Stono breaks out; the "chattels personal" consolidation arrives the following spring (see §3.3).
3. **Jamaica and Barbados classified enslaved people as *real estate* (attached to the plantation/freehold), while South Carolina in 1740 classified them as *chattels personal*.** That divergence is real, legally significant, and useful for characterization (§3.1–3.3).

Also note timing: the Molasses Act received royal assent on **17 May 1733**, but the duties only took effect **25 December 1733** — a character cannot be paying the duty earlier than that (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molasses_Act; https://vlex.co.uk/vid/trade-of-sugar-colonies-808173605).

---

## 1. The Molasses Act (1733): actual statutory language

**Citation:** 6 Geo. 2, c. 13; long title: *"An Act for the better securing and encouraging the Trade of his Majesty's Sugar Colonies in America."* Introduced in the Commons by Sir Robert Walpole; royal assent 17 May 1733; duties effective 25 December 1733; repeatedly continued (1737, 1745, 1753, 1756) and superseded by the Sugar Act of 1763; repealed 1867 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molasses_Act; https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Chronological_Table_and_Index_of_the_Statutes/Chronological_Table/6Geo2).

**Preamble (as enacted):**

> "WHEREAS the Welfare and Prosperity of your Majesty's Sugar Colonies in America are of the greatest Consequence and Importance to the Trade, Navigation and Strength of this Kingdom: And whereas the Planters of the said Sugar Colonies have of late Years fallen under such great Discouragements, that they are unable to improve or carry on the Sugar Trade upon an equal Footing with the foreign Sugar Colonies, without some Advantage and Relief be given to them from Great Britain…" (https://vlex.co.uk/vid/trade-of-sugar-colonies-808173605)

**The operative duty schedule (Section I)** — verified against the vLex as-enacted text:

| Commodity (foreign, i.e., non-British American produce) | Duty |
|---|---|
| Rum or spirits | 9 pence per gallon |
| Molasses or syrups | 6 pence per gallon |
| Sugars and paneles | 5 shillings per hundredweight avoirdupois |

The act specifies payment "in ready Money by the Importers thereof, before the landing" (s. II), with goods landed before entry and payment forfeited and prosecutable "in any Court of Admiralty in his Majesty's Colonies or Plantations in America" or in any court of record (s. III) (https://vlex.co.uk/vid/trade-of-sugar-colonies-808173605). A contemporaneous objection to the act's likely destruction of the North American–French West Indies trade is preserved in colonial correspondence (Franklin-era materials, Colonial Society of Massachusetts, https://www.colonialsociety.org/publications/3111/259-richard-jackson).

**Key point for your research question:** the act's text nowhere mentions enslaved people, slave discipline, or property in persons. Its subject is imperial market share in sugar products. Slavery enters the picture only indirectly, because the protected "Sugar Colonies" were slave societies and because New England rum was a currency of the slave trade (see §5).

---

## 2. Where the chattel language actually lives: archives and printed statute collections

Your instinct about sources is right, with one refinement:

- **The National Archives (Kew)** holds the *original* colonial acts transmitted to London for royal review, in the Colonial Office series — e.g., Barbados acts in **CO 30** (the 1661 slave act is CO 30/2, fos. 16–26), Jamaica and South Carolina materials in the CO 5 and Jamaica CO 137/139 series, with Board of Trade deliberations in CO 5 and the Board's journals (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144039X.2015.1123436, note 48; https://www.british-history.ac.uk/jrnl-trade-plantations/vol3/pp319-333).
- **Printed colonial "statutes at large"** are usually the practical source for verbatim text: *Acts of Assembly, Passed in the Island of Jamaica; From 1681, to 1737, inclusive* (London: John Baskett, 1738); John Lunan, *An Abstract of the Laws of Jamaica Relating to Slaves* (1819, full text at https://archive.org/stream/anabstractlawsj00britgoog/anabstractlawsj00britgoog_djvu.txt); Richard Hall, *Acts, Passed in the Island of Barbados* (London, 1764); for South Carolina, *The Statutes at Large of South Carolina* (ed. McCord) — the 1740 act is Act No. 670, printed at 7 Stat. 397 (https://openjurist.org/33/scl/536/vinyard-v-passalaigue; https://www.ccpl.org/charleston-time-machine/private-manumission-intimate-path-freedom).
- **A free, curated digital alternative:** the University of New Brunswick project *Laws of Enslavement and Freedom in the Anglo-Atlantic World* (https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/) transcribes the Barbados 1661/1668/1688 acts, Jamaica 1664/1696/1717 acts, and others, with editorial notes (CC-BY; attribute © Stefanie Hunt-Kennedy, https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/terms-use).

---

## 3. The property-classification clauses, colony by colony

### 3.1 Barbados

**The 1661 code** — *"An Act for the better ordering and governing of Negroes"* — is the founding slave code of the Anglo-Atlantic world, and its preamble contains the explicit chattel framing:

> "…the Negroes an heathenish, brutish & an uncertaine dangerous kind of people… there being in all the body of that Law [of England] noe tract to guide us where to walk nor any rule sett us how to governe such Slaves, yet we well know by the right rule of reason, and order, we are not to leave them to the arbitrary, cruel, and outrageous wills of every evil disposed person, **but soe farr to protect them as we doe many other goods and Chattels, and alsoe somewhat further as being created Men**, though without the knowledge of God in the world…" (https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/laws/barbados-1661; transcriptions also at https://slaverylawpower.omeka.net/items/show/1 and https://slaverylawpower.org/barbados-huntington/)

**Property classification:** Barbados went further with *"An Act declaring the Negro Slaves of this Island to be Real Estate"* (29 April 1668):

> "…all Negro Slaves in all Courts of Judicature and other Places within this Island, shall be held, taken, and adjudged to be Estate real, and not Chattels, and shall descend unto the Heirs and Widows of any Person dying Intestate, according to the Manner and Customs of Lands of Inheritance held in Fee-Simple." (https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/node/335/legal_article/pdf; a 1672 declaratory act followed: https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/laws?f=metadata_tags%3AReal+Estate)

**The code in force in your 1730s** was the consolidated 1688 act, *"An Act for the Governing of Negroes,"* whose preamble hardens the dehumanizing language: enslaved people are "of barbarous, wild, and salvage Natures… wholly unqualified, to be governed by the Laws, Customs and Practices of our Nations," while requiring that they "be well provided for, and guarded from the Cruelties and Insolences of themselves or other ill-tempered People or Owners" (https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/laws/barbados-1688; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbados_Slave_Code).

### 3.2 Jamaica

Jamaica's first comprehensive code (1664) was "almost an exact replica" of the 1661 Barbados law, including the "soe farr to protect them as wee doe men's other goods & chattels" preamble (https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/laws/jamaica-1664-0; https://slaverylawpower.org/nhprc-sample-documents/jamaica-slave-code-governing/).

**The statutes actually in force in the 1730s:**

- *"An Act for the better Order and Government of Slaves"* (1696): ticket/pass system ("no slave… to go out of their plantation without a Ticket or White Servant"), 40-shilling fine for failing to whip unauthorized visitors, and summary jurisdiction — "if any Slave shall offer any Violence, by striking or otherwise, to any White Person, such Slave shall be punished at the Discretion of Two Justices and Three Freeholders, who may inflict Death or any other Punishment according to their Discretion" (https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/laws/jamaica-1696).
- *"An Act for the more effectual punishing of crimes committed by slaves"* (August 1717). The Board of Trade received it in January 1718 and referred it to the Attorney General "for his opinion thereupon in point of law" — good evidence of imperial scrutiny in action (https://www.british-history.ac.uk/jrnl-trade-plantations/vol3/pp319-333). Both the 1696 and 1717 acts were later swept away by the 1788 consolidated slave law, which lists them by title in its repeal schedule (https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/node/179/legal_article/pdf). *Uncertainty note:* I could not retrieve the full verbatim text of the 1717 act online; it survives in the TNA Jamaica act books and in the 1738 Baskett printed collection cited in §2.

**Property classification:** Jamaica treated enslaved people as attached to the plantation — effectively real estate. Attorney-General of Jamaica* (1848) later confirmed the settled rule: "By the law of Jamaica, slaves could only be directly devised as real estate" (https://archive.org/stream/anabstractlawsj00britgoog/anabstractlawsj00britgoog_djvu.txt; https://vlex.co.uk/vid/rosanna-richards-rosanna-otherwise-805199653; https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/laws/jamaica-1711). ### 3.3 South Carolina

**In force during 1730–1739:** the February 1722 act, *"An Act for the Better Ordering and Governing of Negroes and other Slaves."* Its preamble: the province's estates "cannot be well and sufficiently managed and brought to use without the labor and service of negroes and other slaves," who "are of barbarous, wild and savage natures, and such as render them wholly unqualified to be governed by the laws, customs and practices of England." Its property clause: "all negroes, mulattoes, mestizoes or Indians, which at any time hereafter shall have been sold, and now are held and taken to be, or hereafter shall be bought and sold for slave, are hereby declared slaves, and they, and their children, are hereby made and declared slaves, to all intents and purposes" (https://www.postandcourier.com/georgetown/news/a-government-of-men-episode-7-the-kensington-conspiracy/article_c2bfdb33-b02b-5373-8a78-a16c320acd1b.html; https://www.ccpl.org/charleston-time-machine/private-manumission-intimate-path-freedom). > "That all Negroes and Indians, (free Indians in amity with this government, and negroes, mulattoes, and mustizoes, who are now free, excepted,) mulattoes or mustizoes who now are, or shall hereafter be, in this Province, and all their issue and offspring, born or to be born, shall be, and they are hereby declared to be, and remain forever hereafter, absolute slaves, and shall follow the condition of the mother, and **shall be deemed, held, taken, reputed and adjudged in law, to be chattels personal, in the hands of their owners and possessors, and their executors, administrators, and assigns, to all intents, constructions and purposes whatsoever**…" (https://www.scpronet.com/modjeskaschool/wp-content/uploads/2016/03/9-an-act-for-better-ordering-slavecodes1740.pdf; corroborated at https://billofrightsinstitute.org/activities/an-act-for-the-better-ordering-and-governing-negroes-and-other-slaves-south-carolina-1740/, https://ushistoryscene.com/article/excerpts-south-carolina-slave-code-1740-no-670-1740/, and in antebellum case law quoting the act, https://openjurist.org/35/scl/445/state-v-belmont)

Its preamble adds that the power of owners "ought to be settled and limited by positive laws, so that the slave may be kept in due subjection and obedience, and the owners… may be restrained from exercising too great rigour and cruelty over them" (same PDF). The act also banned teaching slaves to read/write (s. XLV), restricted movement (ss. X, XXXVI), and it is characterized in the scholarship as transforming slaves' legal status "from freehold property to chattel" while turning poor-white racial privilege into "a realistic device for control" (https://academic.oup.com/mississippi-scholarship-online/book/24303/chapter/185971504).

---

## 4. Parliament vs. the plantation codes: who governed slave control and punishment

The evidence supports a clean division of labor in the 1730s:

**Westminster legislated trade and navigation, not slave discipline.** The Molasses Act is typical: duties, customs entries, forfeiture, vice-admiralty enforcement (https://vlex.co.uk/vid/trade-of-sugar-colonies-808173605). Parliament in this decade passed no code governing the treatment, trial, or punishment of enslaved people in the colonies; that was left to the colonial assemblies, whose "better ordering and governing" acts supplied the entire apparatus of control: pass/ticket regimes, summary tribunals of justices plus freeholders with power over life and death, escalatory corporal punishment (whipping, branding, mutilation, death), and in South Carolina 1740 a literacy ban (sources in §3).

**The colonial codes delegated state violence to masters and local tribunals.** The Barbados 1661 code "left the masters with near complete dominion over the life and death of their slaves," with roughly ten of its twenty-three articles restricting movement; Jamaica 1696 gave two justices and three freeholders discretion "to inflict Death or any other Punishment" (https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/0F85444AE842C18FA1752CC4B8AA1A7A/9781108845274c12_305-322.pdf; https://slaveryandfreedomlaws.lib.unb.ca/laws/jamaica-1696). The chattel/real-estate classification reinforced this: defining slaves as property "took the slave out of the law's jurisdiction… how he treated his slaves was entirely his own affair," while real-estate treatment tied people to plantations and inheritance (http://sjchistory.weebly.com/uploads/5/1/4/6/5146401/the_slave_laws.pdf; https://vlex.co.uk/vid/rosanna-richards-rosanna-otherwise-805199653).

**Imperial oversight existed but was reactive.** Transmitted colonial acts could be reviewed by the Board of Trade, referred to the Attorney General, and disallowed by the Privy Council — exactly what happened with Jamaica's August 1717 acts, one of which was ordered repealed and another sent for legal opinion (https://www.british-history.ac.uk/jrnl-trade-plantations/vol3/pp319-333). In practice, though, the dehumanizing architecture of the codes was repeatedly confirmed; even the "protective" clauses (limits on cruelty) were weak and poorly enforced, as the eighteenth-century West Indian slave-law survey makes clear (https://revistas.upr.edu/index.php/rcs/article/download/9666/8037 — note this is Elsa Goveia's classic mid-twentieth-century essay, useful background rather than recent scholarship).

1. **"Custom and law: The Status of Enslaved Africans in Seventeenth-Century Barbados," *Slavery & Abolition* 37, no. 2 (2016)**, DOI 10.1080/0144039X.2015.1123436 (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0144039X.2015.1123436). 2. **"A 'Manifest Violation' of the Rights of Englishmen: Rights Talk and the Law of Property in Early Eighteenth-Century Jamaica," *Law and History Review* (Cambridge)** (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/law-and-history-review/article/abs/manifest-violation-of-the-rights-of-englishmen-rights-talk-and-the-law-of-property-in-early-eighteenthcentury-jamaica/05CB34BAA228CCA4D699C64054DD25E8). Directly on point for the 1700s–1730s Jamaica: the Whitchurch escheat case over "the Negro Woman Slave Commonly Called Catalina," property law, and Jamaica's transition "from a society with slaves to a slave society." *Caveat: publication year/author not shown in my retrieval; confirm on the page (it is a recent article).*
3. **Jessica Walker (attrib.), "Enslaved People in Women's Wills in Colonial Jamaica, 1661–1771," *Journal of Slavery and Data Preservation* 6, no. 3** (https://scholarlypublishingcollective.org/msup/jsdp/article-pdf/6/3/83/2318935/83walker.pdf). Peer-reviewed, recent, and thematically ideal: shows enslavers choosing to categorize captives "as fungible or personal property, rather than real estate," and how that choice intensified commodification and credit-market use of human beings.

## 6. The Molasses Act debate: trade regulation or slave control?

**What the evidence supports:** the scholarly debate is real, but it is *not* framed as "trade regulation vs. slave control." No source I found argues the act was primarily a slave-control measure. The actual lines of debate:

1. **Regulation, not revenue.** The standard account: Parliament passed the act "largely at the insistence of large plantation owners in the British West Indies… not to raise revenue but to regulate trade by making British products cheaper than those from the French West Indies" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molasses_Act; https://en-academic.com/dic.nsf/enwiki/2041804). The duty was set prohibitively (6d/gallon on foreign molasses) to channel New England purchases to British islands; Theodore Draper and John C. Miller stressed that smuggling, bribery, and intimidation "effectively nullified the law" (https://en-academic.com/dic.nsf/enwiki/2041804).
2. **The classic economic-historiography framing** is John J. McCusker's "The Molasses Act and the Market Strategy of the British Sugar Planters," *Journal of Economic History* (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-economic-history/article/abs/molasses-act-and-the-market-strategy-of-the-british-sugar-planters/F9DBE80ABEB2FFC7EE03EDC1BDF59428). He catalogues the competing interpretations — Anglo-French commercial rivalry; conflict between British colonial regions; aid to one set of colonies at another's expense; precedent for parliamentary taxation — and argues the act must be read as one element of the planters' broader program to adapt the Navigation Acts to the international sugar economy (also targeting Irish merchants and English sugar buyers). *Caveat: this article predates 2015 (it is the 1980s), but it remains the anchor of the debate.*
3. **Where slavery enters the argument:** the act protected the *slave plantation complex*, and its downstream effects touched the slave trade directly. The New England–French West Indies trade converted molasses into rum, and rum into enslaved people on the African coast — the triangular-trade description in the standard accounts makes the linkage explicit (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molasses_Act; https://revolutionarywarjournal.com/molasses-act-of-1733/). The "sugar interest" lobbying Parliament was a lobby of slaveholders (https://sciencesignal.blog/who-passed-the-molasses-act — popular, not peer-reviewed, use with care). So the defensible formulation for your novel is: **the Molasses Act was trade regulation designed by and for slave societies — an act of imperial economic policy whose purpose was to protect slave-based sugar production, not to police enslaved people.** Slave control itself was handled colony by colony, in the codes detailed in §3.
