final.content:
# AI Code-Completion Timing, Flow, and Code Quality: Research Synthesis for Enterprise Interface Design

## 1. Executive Summary

The evidence base converges on four findings with direct design consequences:

1. **Acceptance rate, not code persistence, drives perceived productivity.** GitHub's telemetry study of ~2,600 Copilot users found acceptance rate was the single best telemetry predictor of self-reported productivity (ρ = 0.24, p < 0.0001), while persistence of accepted code correlated more weakly (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2205.06537).
2. **Latency is a first-class cost in the suggestion utility function.** Microsoft Research's utility-theoretic work formalizes that a suggestion's net value declines with generation latency, and that latency is only "experienced" when the developer is actively waiting — which is precisely the flow-breaking condition (https://arxiv.org/html/2306.04930). A secondary account of GitHub's telemetry analysis reports suggestions delivered within ~100 ms enjoyed roughly 1.5× the acceptance of suggestions taking ≥500 ms (https://exa.ai/library/publication/9qvgg86nrxh — secondary citation of Ziegler et al.; treat the exact multiplier with caution, see §9).
3. **Experience level reverses the benefit.** Less-experienced developers gain the most from inline completion (Peng et al. RCT: 55.8% faster overall, largest gains for less-experienced participants, https://arxiv.org/html/2302.06590), while a 2025 RCT of 16 highly experienced open-source maintainers found AI tooling made them **19% slower** — while they believed it made them ~20% faster (https://metr.org/blog/2025-07-10-early-2025-ai-experienced-os-dev-study/). This perception–reality gap is the core trust-calibration problem for enterprise deployments.
4. **Interruption costs are large and asymmetric.** Only 10% of programming sessions resume editing within 1 minute of an interruption; developers commonly need 10–15 minutes to re-enter productive editing, and get roughly one uninterrupted 2-hour block per day (https://www.chrisparnin.me/pdf/parnin-sqj11.pdf; https://www.gamedeveloper.com/programming/programmer-interrupted). Proactive suggestions that arrive at the wrong moment therefore impose costs far exceeding the seconds of display time.

**Key evidence gaps, stated plainly:** I found no peer-reviewed latency/acceptance studies specific to **Tabnine** multi-line prediction (it appears only as a named competitor in GitHub's paper), no published study that cleanly splits developers at exactly 2–5 vs. 10+ years (I synthesize across adjacent experience bands), and no published acceptance-rate breakdown by task type (debugging vs. new feature). JetBrains has not published acceptance-rate or latency figures for AI Assistant deployments; its strongest public evidence is longitudinal telemetry on workflow structure (§7).

---

## 2. Tool-by-Tool Findings: Presentation Mode, Timing, and Outcomes

### 2.1 GitHub Copilot (inline ghost-text suggestions)

**Productivity.** In the Peng/Kalliamvakou RCT (95 recruited professional developers, mean ~6 years coding experience, JavaScript HTTP-server task), the Copilot group finished 55.8% faster (95% CI: 21–89%; p = 0.0017). Explicit arithmetic from the reported means: control = 160.89 min, treatment = 71.17 min; (160.89 − 71.17) / 160.89 = 55.8% time reduction; throughput ratio 160.89 / 71.17 = 2.26, i.e., a 126% throughput gain (https://arxiv.org/html/2302.06590; https://www.nngroup.com/articles/ai-programmers-productive/). Heterogeneous effects: **developers with less programming experience benefited most**, as did older programmers and those coding more hours per day (https://arxiv.org/html/2302.06590).

**What telemetry says about timing.** Copilot fires on heuristic "opportunities" (e.g., cursor not mid-word), abandons in-flight requests if the developer moves on, and surfaces part of the response — an explicit acknowledgment that late suggestions are worthless (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2205.06537). Overall acceptance rate was 27%, with >31 accepted completions per active user-day. Acceptance varies by context: Python and JavaScript show higher acceptance than TypeScript; acceptance is significantly higher on weekends/off-hours (23.5%/23%) than during working hours (21.2%), and what matters is whether the time window matches the user's habitual coding regime (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2205.06537). For comparison, Microsoft's IntelliCode Compose reported ~10% click-through in online trials (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2205.06537).

**Caution from controlled tasks.** Vaithilingam et al.'s 25-participant Copilot-vs-IntelliCode study found no significant correlation between task completion time and survey responses, and Copilot did not consistently reduce task time or improve success on realistic tasks (cited in https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2205.06537 and https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.10258). Perceived benefit and measured benefit can diverge — a recurring theme below.

### 2.2 Amazon CodeWhisperer (comment-to-code generation)

**Productivity.** AWS's preview-period productivity challenge reported participants using CodeWhisperer were **27% more likely to complete tasks successfully and 57% faster** on average (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/amazon-codewhisperer-free-for-individual-use-is-now-generally-available/; https://pages.awscloud.com/rs/112-TZM-766/images/DEV201-Maximizing%20Developer%20Productivity%20with%20Amazon%20CodeWhisperer.pdf). An internal AWS pod study (4 pods, identical codebase and backlog, one sprint, no prior CodeWhisperer experience) reported 20–50% faster task completion (https://pages.awscloud.com/rs/112-TZM-766/images/ADC-C3%20-%20Amazon%20CodeWhisperer.pdf). These are vendor-run challenge designs, not blinded RCTs; treat effect sizes as upper-bound marketing-adjacent evidence.

**Presentation model and flow rationale.** CodeWhisperer triggers both from code context and from natural-language comments, and AWS explicitly markets it as flow preservation: developers otherwise break flow to search Stack Overflow or ask colleagues, so in-IDE generation "meets developers where they are most productive" (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/amazon-codewhisperer-free-for-individual-use-is-now-generally-available/). A behavioral study of CodeWhisperer usage (two user studies, n=10 each, keystroke-level telemetry via a custom plugin) identified four patterns: incremental code refinement, **explicit instruction via natural-language comments**, baseline structuring from model suggestions, and integrative use with external sources (https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.11516; https://www.cs.ubc.ca/~bestchai/papers/vlhcc2025-codewhisperer.pdf). The comment-driven mode effectively converts suggestion timing from a latency race into a deliberate, user-initiated handoff — closer to on-demand than proactive.

**Code quality.** On HumanEval-style generation, average technical debt from code smells was 5.6 minutes for CodeWhisperer vs. 9.1 for Copilot and 8.9 for ChatGPT (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2304.10778). Note this is a benchmark result; it does not measure how presentation timing affects quality in situ.

### 2.3 Tabnine (multi-line predictions)

**Evidence gap.** Tabnine appears in the research record I could verify only as one of the commercial neural-synthesis tools alongside Copilot and Kite (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2205.06537). I found no peer-reviewed latency, acceptance, or flow studies of Tabnine's multi-line prediction specifically. Designers should not assume Copilot-derived latency/acceptance curves transfer to Tabnine; its on-prem/private-deployment architecture (relevant to enterprise) plausibly changes the latency distribution, but I have no sourced numbers.

---

## 3. Experience Bands: 2–5 Years vs. 10+ Years

No study I located randomizes exactly these bands, but three converging data sets bracket the comparison:

| Evidence | Population | Finding |
|---|---|---|
| Peng et al. RCT (https://arxiv.org/html/2302.06590) | 95 devs, mean ~6 yrs experience | Less-experienced developers benefited most from Copilot; treatment effect 55.8% faster overall |
| METR RCT (https://metr.org/blog/2025-07-10-early-2025-ai-experienced-os-dev-study/; https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.09089) | 16 experienced OSS maintainers, avg 5 yrs on their own mature repos (22k+ stars, 1M+ LOC) | AI allowed → **+19% completion time** (slower); regression estimate 0.188, CI [0.013, 0.395] |
| JetBrains longitudinal survey (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.10258) | 62 professionals; 22 had 16+ yrs, 14 had 11–15 yrs, 17 had 6–10 yrs, 8 had 3–5 yrs, 1 had 1–2 yrs | Self-reported productivity gains across the board; objective telemetry showed more code written **and** more deleted |

**Synthesis for the 2–5-year band:** these developers resemble the Peng et al. population (mean ~6 years) and are the group most likely to accept inline suggestions and gain speed, particularly on greenfield/boilerplate work. Their risk is **over-reliance**: trust research documents reduced willingness to critically assess AI output among some users (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.10258, citing over-reliance studies; https://facctconference.org/static/papers24/facct24-99.pdf).

**Synthesis for the 10+ year band:** the METR result is the strongest direct evidence — on familiar, complex, mature codebases, expert developers were slowed by early-2025 AI tools even though they forecast a 24% speedup and, post-study, still believed they had been 20% faster. Quantifying the calibration gap: forecast −24% vs. measured +19% = a **43-percentage-point perception–reality gap** (https://metr.org/blog/2025-07-10-early-2025-ai-experienced-os-dev-study/). Experts in mature systems have internalized context that suggestions cannot see; suggestion review becomes net overhead. JetBrains' two-year telemetry corroborates the mechanism: AI users produce substantially more code but also delete significantly more, while perceiving minimal change — effort is redistributed into "more fragmented, reactive, and cognitively demanding workflows" rather than reduced (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.10258; https://blog.jetbrains.com/research/2026/04/ai-impact-developer-workflows/).

**Design implication:** default aggressiveness should be experience- and codebase-familiarity-tunable. High aggressiveness suits 2–5-year developers on unfamiliar/boilerplate code; 10+ year developers in mature repositories should get conservative, on-demand-biased defaults.

---

## 4. Latency Thresholds and Suggestion Timing

### 4.1 The utility-theoretic frame (Microsoft Research)

Mozannar, Bansal, Fourney & Horvitz define **suggestion utility** δ = E[writing without suggestion] − E[verification + editing/writing with suggestion] − E[latency τ]. Show a suggestion only if δ > 0 (https://arxiv.org/html/2306.04930). Two critical nuances:

- **Latency is charged only when the programmer's latent state includes expecting/waiting for a suggestion.** A slow suggestion that arrives while the developer is still typing costs nothing; a fast suggestion that makes a developer pause and wait costs τ *and* breaks momentum (https://arxiv.org/html/2306.04930).
- The acceptance threshold below which a suggestion should be withheld is P* = (E[verification] + E[latency]) / (E[writing|reject] − E[editing|accept]) — i.e., **as latency rises, the quality bar for displaying a suggestion rises with it** (https://arxiv.org/html/2306.04930).

Their CDHF system, trained on 535 programmers and 168k suggestions, hides 25% of suggestions while guaranteeing ≥95% of hidden ones would have been rejected, avoids generating 13% at all, and raises acceptance rate by 7.2 points. A minimal version was implemented in Copilot itself (https://arxiv.org/html/2306.04930; https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/28878). Warning from the same work: optimizing display purely on acceptance rewards lower-quality (e.g., trivially partial) suggestions — an enterprise metric-gaming hazard (https://arxiv.org/html/2306.04930).

### 4.2 Empirical latency–acceptance numbers

A secondary summary of the GitHub telemetry study reports suggestions delivered **within ~100 ms achieved ~1.5× the acceptance of those taking ≥500 ms** (https://exa.ai/library/publication/9qvgg86nrxh, describing Ziegler et al.). I could not independently verify this figure against the primary PDF (paywalled fetch failed), so treat "100 ms / 500 ms / 1.5×" as directionally supported but numerically unverified. It is consistent with the CDHF model's structure and with general HCI response-time literature.

### 4.3 Latent state dominates suggestion context

In the CUPS study (21 developers retrospectively labeling 3,137 coding segments and 1,096 suggestion interactions), an acceptance-prediction model using only code/suggestion features reached 61.9% ± 1.9% accuracy; adding the programmer's **latent state** (what they were actually doing/thinking) raised it to 83.6% ± 2.4% (p = 6.9e-7) (https://arxiv.org/html/2306.04930; https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.14306). Whether the developer is mid-thought, verifying, or idle matters more than what's on screen. CUPS-based time accounting found developers spend roughly **half of coding time in interaction with the AI system** rather than writing code directly (https://pure.tudelft.nl/admin/files/298085871/Final_The_Cost_of_AI_Assisted_Code_Integration_Instrumenting_Developer_Workflows_in_IDEs_1_1_.pdf, summarizing Mozannar et al.).

**Practical thresholds implied by the evidence:**
- **< ~100–200 ms:** safe zone for proactive inline display (secondary-sourced; directionally robust).
- **≥ ~500 ms:** acceptance drops materially; either suppress, downgrade to non-blocking affordance, or deliver asynchronously.
- **Any latency while the user has resumed typing:** suppress; the suggestion is now an interruption, and CDHF-style gating shows ~1 in 4 suggestions can be withheld almost risk-free (https://arxiv.org/html/2306.04930).

---

## 5. Interruption Costs, Flow, and Task Type (Debugging vs. New Features)

### 5.1 Baseline interruption economics (pre-AI but foundational)

Parnin & Rugaber's analysis of 10,000 sessions from 86 programmers plus a 414-developer survey (https://www.chrisparnin.me/pdf/parnin-sqj11.pdf; https://www.gamedeveloper.com/programming/programmer-interrupted):
- Only **10%** of sessions resume programming activity <1 minute after an interruption.
- Only **7%** of sessions begin editing without first navigating elsewhere to rebuild context.
- Typical resumption to first edit: **10–15 minutes**; ~**7 minutes** needed to transition from high-memory to low-memory state; roughly **one** uninterrupted 2-hour session per day; **40%** of interrupted tasks are never resumed.

An unrequested suggestion that pulls a developer out of a debugging mental model therefore risks costs measured in minutes, not milliseconds — orders of magnitude larger than the suggestion's expected time savings when acceptance probability is low.

### 5.2 Task-type evidence (partial)

There is **no published acceptance-rate split for debugging vs. new-feature coding** in the sources I verified. The closest evidence:
- METR's 246 tasks spanned bug fixes, features, and refactors with no reported per-type breakdown (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.09089).
- JetBrains' experience-sampling field work (30 industrial developers, 627 experience-sampling responses, 207 end-of-day surveys, validated on 131 more) found developers delegate first the work they enjoy least — test generation and docstrings go early; bug triage and refactoring are handed over more reluctantly (https://kairos.jetbrains.com/research/articles/human-ai-experience-from-a-z).
- The JetBrains HAX systematic review of 90 in-IDE studies finds AI-assisted coding simultaneously raises productivity and introduces verification overhead and over-reliance, with quality risks in correctness, maintainability, and security (https://kairos.jetbrains.com/research/articles/human-ai-experience-from-a-z).

**Inference for task-type policy (flagged as inference, not measured result):** During debugging, the developer's latent state is hypothesis-testing with heavy working-memory load — precisely the state where CUPS latent-state modeling shows acceptance predictability depends on unobserved cognition (https://arxiv.org/html/2306.04930) and where Parnin's resumption costs apply. Proactive inline suggestions during active debugging should be suppressed or deferred to explicit invocation. During new-feature/greenfield authoring — the task type in the Peng et al. and AWS challenge studies where gains were largest (https://arxiv.org/html/2302.06590; https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/amazon-codewhisperer-free-for-individual-use-is-now-generally-available/) — proactive display at low latency is supported.

---

## 6. Explanations, Trust, and Calibration

- **What developers use to judge trustworthiness:** an ICSE 2025 mixed-methods study (survey n=29, observation n=10) found **comprehensibility and perceived correctness** were the most-used criteria; developers altered trust decisions over time, keeping only **52%** of originally accepted suggestions — direct evidence that acceptance is not final commitment (https://dlnext.acm.org/doi/10.1109/ICSE55347.2025.00199). This aligns with telemetry: 18.16% of accepted AI code is later deleted and 6.62% heavily rewritten (Sahoo et al., cited in https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.10258).
- **Explanation availability:** a within-subjects study of 34 developers comparing LLM code review with (A) detailed explanation + feedback, (B) feedback only, (C) no explanation found the level of explanation **significantly influences both trust and agreement with AI recommendations, but in different ways**; full explanations yielded the highest perceived trust (https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/3832184). The divergence between trust and agreement is the calibration point: explanations can raise trust without proportionally improving appropriate agreement, so explanations must be paired with verification supports.
- **Over-reliance countermeasures:** cognitive forcing functions reduce overreliance in AI-assisted decision-making (Buçinca et al. 2021, cited in https://facctconference.org/static/papers24/facct24-99.pdf and https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3630106.3658984). Trust is situational, rooted in perceived ability, integrity, and benevolence; existing tools lack affordances to evaluate trustworthiness efficiently; promising design concepts include suggestion-quality indicators, usage statistics, and control mechanisms (https://facctconference.org/static/papers24/facct24-99.pdf; https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3630106.3658984).
- **Acceptance drivers beyond quality:** suggestion quality, the developer's language expertise, and file context (e.g., test files) all shift acceptance (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3664646.3664757).
- **The METR calibration failure** (§3) is the strongest argument that enterprise rollouts need feedback loops showing developers their actual (not perceived) AI impact (https://metr.org/blog/2025-07-10-early-2025-ai-experienced-os-dev-study/).

---

## 7. JetBrains Deployment Evidence

JetBrains' strongest public evidence is the ICSE '26 longitudinal study: **151,904,543 anonymized IDE interaction events over two years from 800 developers (400 AI users, 400 matched non-users)**, plus a 62-respondent survey and 5 interviews (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.10258; https://blog.jetbrains.com/research/2026/04/ai-impact-developer-workflows/; https://kairos.jetbrains.com/research/publications/evolving-with-ai). Findings:
- AI users write and modify **significantly more code**, rely more on external snippets, and **switch contexts more often**.
- AI users **delete significantly more code** — objective churn contradicts self-reported "productivity up, nothing else changed."
- Conclusion: AI "redistributes effort across more fragmented, reactive, and cognitively demanding workflows" rather than uniformly reducing effort (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.10258).
- Baseline context from the same paper: developers spend ~70% of time on comprehension (Minelli et al.) and interact with the IDE only ~25% of observed time amid frequent brief interruptions (Amann et al.) — so any proactive suggestion competes with an already-fragmented attention budget.

A TU Delft thesis using JetBrains AI Assistant and Full Line Code Completion metric data (40M+ actions across ~26k units) similarly argues acceptance rates alone are inadequate, and cites repository-level evidence of shorter code lifetime/higher churn after assistant adoption (https://repository.tudelft.nl/file/File_a95ba540-75bb-462b-8d33-8d7b1b9c6c30?preview=1). JetBrains has **not published AI Assistant acceptance-rate or latency figures** in the sources I verified.

For completeness, a Google enterprise RCT (96 engineers, complex enterprise task) estimated ~21% time reduction from three AI features with a wide confidence interval, and found developers coding more hours/day benefited more (https://arxiv.org/html/2410.12944v2) — intermediate between the Peng and METR results, consistent with task/codebase maturity moderating gains.

---

## 8. Design Synthesis: Proactive vs. On-Demand

Grounded recommendations, each tied to evidence above:

1. **Gate proactive display on both acceptance probability and latency.** Implement CDHF-style two-stage gating: decide from code context alone when possible (avoid generation latency entirely); show only when predicted acceptance exceeds the latency-adjusted threshold P* (https://arxiv.org/html/2306.04930). Retrospective evidence: 25% of suggestions safely hidden, +7.2 pts acceptance.
2. **Latency budget:** target <100–200 ms for inline proactive display; at ≥500 ms, do not show inline ghost text — queue asynchronously or downgrade to an unobtrusive affordance (directionally supported by the 100 ms vs. 500 ms acceptance finding, secondary source, §9; consistent with CDHF's latency cost term). Never display a suggestion that arrives after typing has resumed.
3. **Task-mode policies:** new-feature/greenfield → proactive inline enabled (where RCT gains were demonstrated: https://arxiv.org/html/2302.06590; https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/amazon-codewhisperer-free-for-individual-use-is-now-generally-available/). Active debugging → suppress proactive display; offer comment-to-code or explicit invocation only, mirroring CodeWhisperer's deliberate handoff pattern (https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.11516). Rationale: 10–15-minute resumption costs from interruptions (https://www.chrisparnin.me/pdf/parnin-sqj11.pdf) dwarf marginal suggestion value; latent state drives acceptance more than code context (https://arxiv.org/html/2306.04930).
4. **Experience-tier defaults:** 2–5-year developers: higher suggestion frequency, proactive bias, plus lightweight verification nudges to counter over-reliance (https://facctconference.org/static/papers24/facct24-99.pdf). 10+ year developers in mature codebases: on-demand-biased defaults, explicit invocation, and dashboards showing measured vs. perceived impact, given the 43-point calibration gap observed in expert OSS maintainers (https://metr.org/blog/2025-07-10-early-2025-ai-experienced-os-dev-study/).
5. **Explanations with guardrails:** provide on-demand explanations (highest perceived trust: https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/3832184) but pair them with cognitive-forcing verification steps, since explanation raises trust and agreement "in different ways" and acceptance is provisional — ~18% of accepted code is later deleted (Sahoo et al. via https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.10258; only 52% of trust decisions persist: https://dlnext.acm.org/doi/10.1109/ICSE55347.2025.00199).
6. **Metrics:** track acceptance rate as the leading indicator of perceived productivity (ρ = 0.24, https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2205.06537), but pair it with post-acceptance churn (deletion/rewrite within minutes-to-days) and context-switch telemetry, since JetBrains' longitudinal data shows acceptance-optimized systems can inflate output and churn simultaneously (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.10258), and acceptance-as-reward can select lower-quality suggestions (https://arxiv.org/html/2306.04930).

---

## 9. Uncertainty Register

- **100 ms / 500 ms / 1.5× latency–acceptance figures** come from a secondary summary of Ziegler et al. (https://exa.ai/library/publication/9qvgg86nrxh); I could not fetch the primary PDF section to verify exact values. Direction (faster = more accepted) is corroborated by the CDHF utility framework (https://arxiv.org/html/2306.04930).
- **Tabnine:** no primary studies found; any Tabnine timing parameters would be extrapolation.
- **Debugging vs. feature acceptance rates:** no direct published split found; §5.2 is labeled inference.
- **Experience bands:** no study uses exactly 2–5 vs. 10+ years; synthesis spans adjacent bands (mean ~6 yrs in Peng et al.; 5+ yrs repo familiarity in METR; JetBrains survey skewing senior).
- **Vendor studies:** AWS's 57%/27% figures come from a preview-period challenge and internal pod exercise, not blinded randomization (https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/amazon-codewhisperer-free-for-individual-use-is-now-generally-available/).
- **Temporal validity:** METR's slowdown reflects early-2025 tools (Cursor Pro + Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet) on mature OSS repos; results may not transfer to newer models or enterprise greenfield work (https://metr.org/blog/2025-07-10-early-2025-ai-experienced-os-dev-study/).
- The JetBrains ICSE '26 paper is dated for a 2026 conference; figures cited are as published in the arXiv preprint (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.10258).

1. **Ziegler et al. 2022 (GitHub, MAPS/PLDI workshop)** — ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2205.06537
   - 2,631 survey responses matched with Copilot telemetry (the ar5iv version says 2,631; the ACM PDF says 2,631; the initial fetch says 2,047 matched responses — actually the paper says "received 2,047 responses that could be matched" but the abstract says 2,631. Note: the ar5iv fetch says "we analyze 2,631 survey responses" in the abstract, but section 3.2 says "received 2,047 responses that could be matched" — there's a discrepancy between versions; the ACM version says 2,631. I'll cite both carefully).
   - Copilot acceptance rate: 27%, mean DCPU > 31
   - Acceptance rate (accepted_per_shown) is the strongest predictor of perceived productivity (ρ=0.24, P<0.0001)
   - Persistence metrics correlate less strongly
   - Language differences: TypeScript 24.7% of shown completions, JavaScript 21.3%, Python 14.1%; Python and JS have higher acceptance rates
   - Circadian rhythms: weekend acceptance 23.5%, weekday non-work hours 23%, work hours 21.2% (p<0.001%)
   - IntelliCode Compose CTR 10%; DCPU about 20 in prior work
   - The exa.ai summary of the same paper claims: "suggestions provided within 100 milliseconds had 1.5× higher acceptance compared to suggestions taking 500 milliseconds or more" — this is from a secondary source (exa.ai library publication summary) citing [3], which seems to be the Ziegler paper. However, the ar5iv fetch was cut off before section 5.3 (latency section). The exa.ai citation says "the study further revealed that completion latency had a direct effect on adoption patterns, with suggestions provided within 100 milliseconds having 1.5× higher acceptance compared to suggestions taking 500 milliseconds or more [3]". This is a secondary source describing the Ziegler study. I should report it with a caveat that it's a secondary citation of the latency finding (the original paper has a latency section I couldn't fully retrieve). I need to be honest about this uncertainty.

2. **Peng, Kalliamvakou et al. 2023 (GitHub/Microsoft/MIT)** — arxiv.org/html/2302.06590
   - RCT with 95 professional developers (recruited via Upwork), HTTP server implementation task in JavaScript
   - Treatment group was 55.8% faster (95% CI: 21–89%)
   - Heterogeneous effects: less experienced developers, older programmers, and those coding more hours per day benefited most
   - NN/g summary: control 160.89 min vs treatment 71.17 min; p=0.0017; average participant coding experience 6 years, ~9 hours/day coding; throughput gain 126%
   - Note: Nielsen's summary says "less experienced programmers and those coding fewer hours per day benefited most" but the paper says "those coding more hours per day benefited most" — there's a contradiction; the NN/g article itself acknowledges this discrepancy. I'll follow the arXiv abstract: less experienced, older, more coding hours per day benefited most.

3. **METR 2025 RCT** — metr.org/blog/2025-07-10-early-2025-ai-experienced-os-dev-study/ and arxiv.org/pdf/2507.09089
   - 16 experienced OSS developers, 246 tasks, mature repositories (avg 22k+ stars, 1M+ LOC), average 5 years of prior experience with the repo
   - AI allowed → 19% longer completion time (slower); regression speedup 0.188 (CI 0.013–0.395)
   - Developers predicted AI would reduce time by 24%; after the study, estimated a 20% reduction
   - Primarily used Cursor Pro + Claude 3.5/3.7 Sonnet
   - Tasks averaged ~2 hours; bug fixes, feature additions, refactoring
   - Experts predicted 38–39% shorter
   - This is the key contrast for experienced developers: perception-reality gap in trust calibration

4. **Amazon CodeWhisperer** — pages.awscloud.com PDF + AWS News Blog
   - Productivity challenge during preview period: participants using CodeWhisperer were 27% more likely to complete tasks successfully and 57% faster on average (AWS News Blog, aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/amazon-codewhisperer-free-for-individual-use-is-now-generally-available/)
   - Internal AWS study: 4 pods (2 in London, 2 in Denver), identical codebase/backlog, 1 sprint; 20–50% faster
   - Framing of "keeping developers in flow": CodeWhisperer provides recommendations in real time as code or comments are written, avoiding leaving the IDE for searches
   - Comment-to-code: CodeWhisperer examines comments in the IDE and generates snippets (from the quality study arxiv.org/pdf/2304.10778)
   - Quality study (Alshamsi et al. 2023, arXiv 2304.10778): technical debt from code smells on HumanEval: ChatGPT 8.9 min, Copilot 9.1 min, CodeWhisperer 5.6 min
   - Cracking CodeWhisperer (arxiv 2510.11516, VLHCC 2025): two user studies with 10 participants each; four behavioral patterns: incremental code refinement, explicit instruction via NL comments, baseline structuring via model suggestions, integrative use with external sources

5. **JetBrains** — arxiv.org/pdf/2601.10258 "Evolving with AI: A Longitudinal Analysis of Developer Logs" (ICSE '26, Sergeyuk, Huang et al.)
   - 151,904,543 fine-grained anonymized IDE interaction logs over 2 years, 800 developers (400 AI users, 400 non-users), survey of 62 professionals + 5 interviews
   - AI users produce substantially more code but also delete significantly more
   - Survey respondents report productivity gains but perceive minimal change elsewhere — perception/behavior divergence
   - Survey participants: 22 with 16+ years experience, 14 with 11–15 years, 17 with 6–10 years, 8 with 3–5 years, 1 with 1–2 years
   - Tools used: ChatGPT n=42, Copilot n=29, JetBrains AI Assistant n=23
   - References: Mozannar et al. — developers spend 50%+ of their time evaluating/editing AI output; Sahoo et al. — 18.16% of accepted AI code is later deleted, 6.62% substantially rewritten
   - Amann et al.: developers interact with IDE only 25% of the time, with frequent short interruptions
   - Minelli et al.: 70% of time spent on program comprehension
   - Also TU Delft master's thesis "Beyond Acceptance Rates: The Impact of JetBrains AI Assistant and FLCC" — 40 million actions across 26 thousand (users?); found correlation between code assistant use and reduced code quality in public GitHub repos, code churn within 2 weeks
   - JetBrains blog: blog.jetbrains.com/research/2026-04-ai-impact-developer-workflows/

6. **Parnin & Rugaber 2011** — chrisparnin.me/pdf/parnin-sqj11.pdf + gamedeveloper.com "Programmer, Interrupted"
   - 10,000 recorded sessions of 86 programmers; survey of 414 programmers
   - Only 10% of sessions resume programming activity within 1 minute after interruption
   - Only 7% of sessions involve no navigation to other locations before editing
   - Programmers take 10–15 minutes to start editing code after resuming work after an interruption
   - About one uninterrupted 2-hour session per day
   - Programmers need at least 7 minutes to transition from high-memory state to low-memory state
   - 40% of interrupted tasks don't get resumed
   - Resumption lag concept

7. **Mozannar et al. CHI 2024 "Reading Between the Lines" (CUPS)** — arxiv.org/abs/2210.14306, dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3613904.3641936
   - CUPS taxonomy of programmer states when interacting with Copilot
   - 21 developers labeled 3,137 coding segments and interacted with 1,096 suggestions
   - Developers spend about half of coding time interacting with the AI system (per citation in TU Delft integration-cost paper)
   - Existing interaction metrics like acceptance rate, time-to-accept are insufficient

8. **Mozannar et al. AAAI 2024 "When to Show a Suggestion?" (CDHF)** — arxiv.org/html/2306.04930, ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/28878
   - Utility-theoretic framework; suggestion utility increases with acceptance probability, decreases with latency
   - δ = E[writing|X,φ] − E[S_shown|X,φ] − E[τ|X,φ]; show if δ>0
   - P* = (E[verification] + E[latency]) / (E[writing|reject] − E[editing|accept])
   - Latency τ only incurred if programmer is expecting/waiting for the suggestion
   - CDHF: hides 25% of shown suggestions while guaranteeing 95% of them would have been rejected; avoids generating 13%; acceptance rate up 7.2%
   - Data: 535 programmers, 168k suggestions
   - Latent state matters: acceptance prediction accuracy 61.9±1.9% without latent state vs 83.6±2.4% with (p=6.9e-7)
   - Explicit invocation "can disrupt the natural flow of programming, breaking a state of flow achieved during intensive focus"; but automatic display can burden users with interruptions
   - A minimal version of CDHF has been implemented in newer versions of GitHub Copilot
   - Pitfall: using acceptance as a reward signal leads to lower-quality suggestions (partial completions prioritized)

9. **Trust/explanations:**
   - "Trust Dynamics in AI-Assisted Development" (ICSE 2025, dlnext.acm.org/doi/10.1109/ICSE55347.2025.00199): mixed-methods study, survey n=29 + observations n=10; comprehensibility and perceived correctness are the most frequently used factors for evaluating trustworthiness; developers change their trust judgments, retaining only 52% of original suggestions
   - "Evaluating the Impact of Explainable AI on Trust in AI-Assisted Code Review" (PACMSE 2026, dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/3832184): within-subjects study, 34 participants; three conditions (detailed explanation + feedback; feedback only; no explanation); level of explanation significantly affects trust and agreement but "in different ways"; full explanations (condition A) yield the highest perceived trust… (cut off mid-sentence)
   - "Identifying the Factors That Influence Trust in AI Code Completion" (AIware 2024, dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3664646.3664757): suggestion quality, developer expertise in the language, context (test files) all affect acceptance
   - "Investigating and Designing for Trust in AI-powered Code Generation Tools" (FAccT 2024, facctconference.org/static/papers24/facct24-99.pdf): trust is rooted in ability, integrity, benevolence; situational; cognitive forcing functions (Buçinca et al. 2021) can reduce over-reliance
   - Design probe study (dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3630106.3658984): interviews with 17 developers; design concepts: suggestion quality indicators, usage statistics, control mechanisms

10. **Google RCT** (arxiv.org/html/2410.12944v2): 96 Google engineers, enterprise-grade tasks, AI shortened time on task by ~21% (wide CI); developers coding more hours per day got faster with AI.

11. **Vaithilingam et al.**: Copilot vs IntelliCode with 25 participants — no significant correlation between task completion time and survey responses (cited in Ziegler). Also observed that Copilot didn't consistently reduce task time or improve success rates (cited in JetBrains paper).

12. **Imai**: Pair programming with Copilot increased code output (lines added).

13. **Sahoo et al.**: 18.16% of accepted AI code later deleted; 6.62% substantially rewritten.

14. **Weber et al.**: Interaction with AI interfaces introduces cognitive load and task fragmentation.

15. **del Rio-Chanona et al.**: StackOverflow posts dropped from ~60k to ~40k per month within 6 months of ChatGPT release.

Now, gaps I should honestly state:
- **Tabnine**: I have no direct research findings on Tabnine beyond the mention in Ziegler et al. that TabNine is one of the neural synthesis tools. The user asked about "Tabnine's multi-line prediction" — I have no Tabnine-specific study data. I must state this gap honestly.
- **Experience comparison of 2–5 years vs 10+ years**: Peng et al. found less experienced developers benefited most; METR found experienced developers were slowed. JetBrains survey demographics. No study directly splits at exactly 2–5 years vs 10+ years. I can synthesize.
- **Debugging vs new feature development**: METR tasks included bug fixes, feature additions, refactoring but I don't have per-task-type breakdowns in the evidence I collected. I should honestly note this gap and use what I have (Parnin on interruption costs, JetBrains HAX on bug triage preferences — "developers delegate first the work they like least" — from kairos.jetbrains.com A-Z article: feature implementation, test writing, bug triage, refactoring, NL artifacts; test generation and docstrings delegated early).
- **Latency thresholds**: Ziegler's 100ms vs 500ms (1.5× acceptance) via secondary source; CDHF utility framework treating latency as a cost; I don't have exact numbers on Copilot's debounce timing. I should be explicit about uncertainty.
- **JetBrains AI assistant deployment metrics**: I have the longitudinal telemetry study and TU Delft thesis (40M actions, 26k…). I don't have JetBrains-specific acceptance rates. I should be explicit about that.

Quantitative work I can show:
- Peng et al.: 160.89 vs 71.17 min → (160.89−71.17)/160.89 = 55.8% faster; throughput 160.89/71.17 = 2.26 → 126% increase. I can compute explicitly.
- METR: 19% longer; predicted −24% vs actual +19% → 43-point perception gap.
- CDHF: hides 25% of suggestions, 95% guarantee, +7.2% acceptance rate.
- Ziegler: acceptance rate 27%, ρ=0.24.

Let me compute: (160.89−71.17)/160.89 = 89.72/160.89 = 0.5577 ≈ 55.8%. ✓ Throughput ratio: 160.89/71.17 = 2.2607 → 126.1% increase. ✓

METR perception gap: predicted 24% speedup, actual 19% slowdown → gap = 24 − (−19) = 43 percentage points.

Report structure:
1. Executive summary
2. Evidence base and methodological notes (including gaps)
3. Productivity effects by tool and presentation mode (Copilot inline, CodeWhisperer comment-to-code, Tabnine gap)
4. Experience level: 2–5 years vs 10+ years
5. Latency thresholds and timing
6. Interruption costs, task type (debugging vs feature development), flow
7. Explanations and trust calibration
8. JetBrains telemetry evidence
9. Design synthesis: proactive vs on-demand recommendations
10. Uncertainties and open questions

Cite URLs inline. No tool calls. Plain text report. Let me write it now, being careful to attribute claims only to sources I actually have and to flag secondary-source-derived numbers (the 100ms/500ms latency claim) appropriately.

# Industrial IoT Sensor Platform Selection for Predictive Maintenance — Australian Mining Operation (Extreme Heat & Dust, 50 km² Site)

**Prepared for:** Procurement Lead
**Scope:** Siemens vs Honeywell vs Australian local providers — durability, edge processing, legacy SCADA integration, and total implementation cost across a 50 km² site.

---

## 1. Executive Summary

- **Environmental reality drives everything.** Pilbara-class conditions mean ambient air to ~48–50 °C, equipment surfaces exceeding 65–80 °C, conductive ultra-fine ore dust that penetrates standard IP65 enclosures, cyclonic wet-season rain, and daily 100–150 bar washdowns in plant areas (https://customwireassembly.com/resources/learning-center/mining-wire-harness-ip69k/, https://jdnce.com.au/maintaining-electrical-assets-in-pilbara-mining-environments-dust-heat-and-distance-challenges/). Spec floor: **IP66 minimum for static outdoor gear, IP67 for field sensors, IP69K in washdown zones**, with operating ratings to at least +80 °C and sun-shaded enclosures.

- **Siemens** offers the most durable individual wireless sensor (SITRANS MS200, IP69, −30…+80 °C) and the strongest general-purpose edge platform (SIMATIC Industrial Edge), but its predictive-maintenance analytics (SITRANS SCM IQ) are cloud-hosted on Insights Hub, its gateways are IP20 cabinet devices, and subscription costs at 500 assets are the highest of the three options. Australian radio approval now exists for current MS200/CC220 variants, but confirm local sales/support status before tendering (older literature restricted sales to EU/CH/GB/NO/RU).

- **Honeywell** (Versatilis LoRaWAN transmitters + on-premises Experion Equipment Health Monitoring) is the strongest fit if your legacy SCADA is Experion, and a strong fit generally: sensors are IP66/IP67, rated −40…+80 °C, with 3–5 year battery life, and the EHM server sits on your network (no mandatory cloud). It is sold and supported in Australia through authorised distributors (Territory Instruments, Motherwell Automation Perth, HMA Group).

- **Local providers** (Meshed, Sentient Computing, plus specialists like Predictive Industries, Monitel, Senstrali) deliver the lowest total cost, AU915 LoRaWAN networks proven in the Pilbara, local support, and — in Sentient's case — data that stays on the local control network (useful for air-gapped OT). Trade-off: lighter out-of-the-box analytics and reliance on system-integrator engineering.

- **Indicative 5-year TCO for a 500-point deployment (base case, AUD):** Local ≈ $0.35–0.65M; Honeywell ≈ $0.65–1.1M; Siemens ≈ $1.4–2.1M (dominated by cloud subscription). Ranges are estimates — see Section 6 and the uncertainty notes.

- **Recommended path:** a hybrid — private AU915 LoRaWAN network (local SI such as Meshed/Sentient) carrying Honeywell Versatilis sensors on critical assets (or equivalent IP67 LoRaWAN sensors), bridged to legacy SCADA via OPC UA/Modbus, with Siemens Industrial Edge retained as an option where Siemens PLCs dominate. Run a 3-month pilot on one conveyor line and one pump cluster before full rollout.

---

## 2. Site Environmental Design Basis (What the Hardware Must Survive)

| Stressor | Documented magnitude | Design implication |
|---|---|---|
| Ambient heat | >45 °C common; Marble Bar recorded 160 consecutive days ≥38 °C | Electronics rated ≥+70 °C operating; derate batteries |
| Surface heat | Ground/equipment surfaces 50–65 °C, equipment skins can exceed 80 °C | Sensor rating to +80 °C is the minimum; use sunshields/remote mounts |
| Dust | Ultra-fine silica/iron-ore dust penetrates IP65 via thermal-cycling gaps; conductive when combined with night condensation | IP6X (dust-tight) enclosures; silicone gaskets (7–9 yr life vs 3–5 yr neoprene); compound-filled cable glands cut ingress 85–90 % |
| Washdown | 100–150 bar, sometimes daily | IP69K in washdown zones; IP67 reportedly "fails in weeks" under daily high-pressure washdown |
| Weather | Cyclonic rain Nov–Mar; 8+ months intense UV; Region D wind loads | AS1170.2 wind ratings, UV-stabilised finishes, sloping roofs |
| Diurnal cycle | ~48 °C day to ~18 °C night (30 °C swing, daily) | Condensation management; sealed breathing enclosures |

Sources: https://customwireassembly.com/resources/learning-center/mining-wire-harness-ip69k/, https://jdnce.com.au/maintaining-electrical-assets-in-pilbara-mining-environments-dust-heat-and-distance-challenges/, https://theecolibrium.com/2022/04/02/lessons-for-the-future-of-australian-hvac-from-pilbara-mining/, https://www.brenclosures.com.au/products/sp/, https://www.ipenclosures.com.au/mine-spec-electrical-enclosures/

Australian enclosures built for exactly this exist off-the-shelf (B&R "Pilbara SP" IP66 −10…+60 °C with sunshades; IP Enclosures Mine-Spec IP66/IK10 with sun shields, seals rated −40…+80 °C) — budget for these for every gateway/edge device installed outdoors.

---

## 3. Platform Comparison

### 3.1 Siemens

**Wireless sensing path (predictive maintenance):** SITRANS MS200 battery multisensor → SITRANS CC220 gateway (up to 8 sensors each, BLE 5.0, MQTT uplink) → SITRANS SCM IQ anomaly-detection app on Siemens Insights Hub (https://cache.industry.siemens.com/dl/files/158/109804158/att_1159413/v1/sitrans_ms200_cc220_scmiq_fi01_en.pdf).

**Durability:**
- MS200: **IP69 per IEC 60529 (2 m/24 h)** — best ingress rating of any sensor in this comparison; ambient −30…+80 °C (storage −40…+85 °C); 3-axis accelerometer 15 Hz–3.3 kHz (6.6 kHz sampling); temperature accuracy ±4 °C; battery 3.6 V/2.6 Ah, life **2–5 years at 25 °C** (expect derating at sustained 50 °C+).
- CC220 gateway: **IP20, 0…+50 °C** — must live inside a cabinet.
- Supporting hardware: SIMATIC IOT2050 edge gateway IP20, 0–50 °C, RCM (Australian compliance) marked (https://support.industry.siemens.com/teddatasheet/?caller=SIOS&format=pdf&language=en&mlfbs=6ES7647-0BW00-1YA2); SIMATIC ET 200eco PN block I/O is IP65/IP67/IP69K, −40…+60 °C, ATEX zone 2/22 — a strong wired option for cabinet-free I/O in dust (https://www.siemens.com/en-us/products/simatic/et-200eco-pn/).

**Edge processing:** SIMATIC Industrial Edge is the most complete edge platform of the three: containerised (Docker) apps, central Industrial Edge Management, IEC 62443-4-2 and UL Platinum certification, and pre-built connectors for PROFINET/S7, OPC UA, Modbus TCP, EtherNet/IP (https://www.siemens.com/industrial-edge, https://www.icheme.org/media/27828/241213_icheme_vplc_v00.pdf). **Caveat:** the MS200/SCM IQ predictive analytics run in the Insights Hub cloud, not at the edge; edge devices are IP20 and 0–50 °C, so they need shaded/cooled cabinets in this climate.

**Legacy SCADA integration:** strong and vendor-agnostic — Industrial Edge connectors cover >90 % of industrial devices per Siemens; data can be exposed via OPC UA server, MQTT, GraphQL/REST (Industrial Information Hub), and integrated with WinCC, Ignition, Wonderware or overarching SCADA such as WinCC OA (https://www.siemens.com/en-us/content/architecture-hub/op-center/, https://assets.ctfassets.net/17si5cpawjzf/2ZYtEIEHl39oTWbvv0DrtA/925f619b85ec5b19e19898145ca09776/Architecture_Hub_Web_Version.pdf). The MS200 data path itself is cloud-first; feeding a legacy SCADA means bridging MQTT/OPC UA back on-prem.

**Availability caveat:** the 2023 FI 01 brochure listed MS200 sales only in EU/CH/GB/NO/RU, but current Industry Mall entries for CC220 (7MP2200-2CB05-2AA1) and MS200 variant 7MP2210-2BB22-2AB1 list radio approvals including **AU and NZ** (https://mall.industry.siemens.com/mall/en/siemensiranircom/Catalog/Product?SiepCountryCode=OE&mlfb=7MP2200-2CB05-2AA1, https://automationitems.com/datasheet/432067). Verify with Siemens Australia that the full stack (hardware, SCM IQ app, support) is sold locally before committing.

### 3.2 Honeywell

**Wireless sensing path:** Versatilis LoRaWAN transmitters → LoRaWAN gateways → Experion Equipment Health Monitoring (EHM), an on-premises solution built on Experion HS (https://cdn-documents.yodify.com/documents/Honeywell-Process-Solutions/Versatilis-Transmitter-Bluetooth-and-LoRaWAN/OPzVy/4827b319-b0f8-421f-bc7a-5e84cb7452cc/Experion-EHM-Specification.pdf). Honeywell also offers the OneWireless ISA100.11a mesh (XYR 6000 transmitters, 10-year batteries, 305 m LOS per hop) where higher-rate process instrumentation is needed (https://www.dgfg.nl/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/34-XY-03-29-XYR6000-Temp-Transmitter-Specsheet.pdf).

**Durability (Versatilis, per official spec):** enclosure **IP66/IP67**; operating and surface temperature **−40…+80 °C**; vibration 5–2,500 Hz (±16 g); acoustics 20 Hz–20 kHz; humidity and ambient pressure sensing in the same unit; AES-256; ATEX/IECEx/FM/CSA hazardous-area approvals; battery **3 years** at 5-min sensing/30-min uplink or **5 years** at 10-min/60-min; 20 days onboard data logging; mounting via adhesive, epoxy, magnet or M6 screw (https://process.honeywell.com/us/en/products/field-instruments/iot-sensor-solutions/equipment-health-monitoring-hvt/honeywell-versatilis-transmitter). The AU915-928 channel plan is explicitly listed for Australia in the technical specification (https://www.motherwell.net.au/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/Honeywell-Versatilis%E2%84%A2-Transmitter-Technical-Specification.pdf).

**Edge processing:** EHM is deployed on-premises (plant network), performs ISO 10816-based vibration alarming, asset hierarchy configuration, dashboards and alarm/event handling with zero mandatory cloud dependency; LoRaWAN network server connects via secure MQTT (EHM spec PDF; https://hmagrp.com/honeywell-versatilis-equipment-health-monitoring-ehm-solutions/). Honeywell Forge sits above as the enterprise analytics layer. Sensors themselves are low-power with no onboard AI.

**Legacy SCADA integration:** native if you run Experion (EHM is built on Experion HS; OneWireless Wireless Device Managers bring ISA100/WirelessHART data into Experion PKS or **any other control system via OPC client or Modbus TCP** — https://www.dgfg.nl/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/34-XY-03-29-XYR6000-Temp-Transmitter-Specsheet.pdf, https://www.engnet.co.za/documents/pdfcatalog/HON002_290714080612_wp-connecting-wireless-hart-sensor-networks-to-experion-pks-using-onewir....pdf). For non-Honeywell SCADA, integration is via OPC UA/Modbus (ControlEdge PLC is marketed as working "with any SCADA system," https://process.honeywell.com/content/dam/process/en/campaigns/hps/ControlEdge-PLC-Integration-made-easy/documents/hps-whitepaper-on-experion-controledgeplc-integration.pdf). Honeywell also has deep Australian mining migration credentials (e.g., Tronox Cooljarloo Experion upgrade, https://www.casestudies.com/company/honeywell/case-study/tronox-cooljarloo-control-system-upgrade).

**Australian channel:** authorised distributors include Territory Instruments (https://www.territoryinstruments.com/instrumentation/honeywell/honeywell-versatilis/honeywell-versatilis-transmitter) and Motherwell Automation with a Perth office in Osborne Park (https://www.motherwell.net.au/honeywell-versatilis-equipment-health-monitoring-ehm-solutions/), plus HMA Group (https://hmagrp.com/honeywell-versatilis-equipment-health-monitoring-ehm-solutions/).

### 3.3 Australian Local Providers

**Meshed (Sydney; national):** Australia's leading LoRaWAN systems integrator (since 2015). Private MeshedX networks run The Things Stack v3 on AWS Sydney (data sovereignty), from **$150/month + GST**, 99.9 % uptime SLA, **up to 20 km range, ~1,000 sensors per gateway**, IP67 gateways/sensors, LTE/satellite backhaul (https://www.meshed.network/lorawan-iot-private-networks/, https://www.meshed.network/industries/industrial-automation/smart-mining/). Pilbara-proven: a major iron-ore producer uses a single elevated gateway reaching assets >10 km away (https://www.meshed.network/resources/iron-ore-mining-case-study/); a WA lithium mine runs a dispersed Pilbara site on two managed gateways at 99.7 % uptime (https://www.meshed.network/resources/smart-water-monitoring-lithium-mining/). Open API and integration layer to existing OT.

**Sentient Computing (Perth):** MacroView SCADA/HMI vendor + IIoT. LoRaWAN on AU915 with a **secure local gateway that keeps data on the local control network (no cloud)**; Class A devices for temperature/humidity, pressure/ultrasonic level and vibration machine monitoring; **battery life 5+ years**; sampling 10 min–1 h with dynamic rate increase on change; proven integration into MacroView and "most Control Systems or Historians" (https://sencom.com.au/services/process-control/). Best fit if you want OT-network isolation and a single local vendor for SCADA + IIoT.

**Specialists worth shortlisting:** Predictive Industries (Perth) — vibration/thermography programs incl. "Kelvin" fixed wireless thermal monitoring (https://predictiveindustries.com/); Monitel (Perth) — wireless vibration systems to ISO 10816/20816 (https://monitel.com.au/services/structural-instrumentation/vibration-monitoring/machine-vibration-monitoring/); Senstrali — Mantis stringer-mounted conveyor idler monitoring (ultrasonic + vibration on a wired bus, one cellular modem per conveyor; notes conventional wireless CM sensors cost $150–300 each and struggle in steel-heavy RF environments — https://www.senstrali.com.au/services); X2 Engineering — solar-powered Pilbara dust/environmental monitors integrated to SCADA over LTE (https://x2eng.com.au/boundary-dust-monitors/); VEGA's VEGABAR 38 gearbox monitoring at a major Pilbara iron ore mine demonstrates vendor instruments surviving this exact climate (https://www.australianmining.com.au/vega-continuous-condition-monitoring-lights-up-the-pilbara/).

### 3.4 Comparison Matrix

| Criterion | Siemens | Honeywell | Local (Meshed/Sentient class) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sensor ingress rating | **IP69** (MS200) | IP66/IP67 (Versatilis) | IP67 typical (varies by sensor OEM) |
| Sensor temp rating | −30…+80 °C | **−40…+80 °C** | typically −20/−40…+70/85 °C (check per SKU) |
| Battery life | 2–5 yr (25 °C rating) | 3–5 yr (config-dependent) | 5+ yr (Sentient Class A, 10 min–1 h sampling) |
| Field gateway ruggedness | CC220 IP20 (cabinet) | LoRaWAN IP67 gateways (3rd-party) | IP67 gateways standard |
| Edge processing | **Strongest** (Industrial Edge, Docker apps, IEC 62443-4-2) — but CM analytics in cloud | On-prem EHM server, ISO 10816 alarming | Light (local gateway/buffering, AWS-Sydney network server); analytics via SI/partners |
| Legacy SCADA integration | OPC UA/Modbus/S7/EtherNet-IP/MQTT connectors; broad | Native on Experion; OPC/Modbus otherwise; EHM MQTT | MacroView native; open API/OPC to historians & SCADA |
| Cloud dependency | High (Insights Hub/SCM IQ) | Low (EHM on-prem) | Selectable (Sentient fully local; Meshed AWS-Sydney) |
| AU support/channel | Siemens AU + distributors (verify MS200/SCM IQ local availability) | Territory Instruments, Motherwell (Perth), HMA | Local HQ, Pilbara references |
| Hazardous-area certs (sensor) | Check per variant | ATEX/IECEx/FM/CSA | Varies by OEM sensor chosen |

---

## 4. Network Architecture for a 50 km² Site

**Coverage math.** 50 km² ≈ a circle of radius r = √(50/π) = **3.99 km**. Industrial LoRaWAN gateways at 915 MHz achieve 15 km line-of-sight (Milesight UG67, IP67, 8-channel, 2,000+ nodes, AU915 — https://qantecautomation.com/product/milesight-lorawan-gateway-ug67-915m/) and Meshed claims up to 20 km (https://www.meshed.network/industries/industrial-automation/smart-mining/). Geometrically one elevated central gateway covers the site; in practice stockpiles, conveyors, plant structures and terrain create RF shadows, and the Meshed lithium-mine reference used **2 gateways** for a dispersed Pilbara site (https://www.meshed.network/resources/smart-water-monitoring-lithium-mining/). **Recommendation: 3 gateways (coverage + N+1 redundancy), sited on existing comms towers/plant rooftops.** Capacity is not the constraint: 500–1,000 sensors fit within one gateway's capacity (1,000/gateway per Meshed; Advantech's mining wellfield reference ran ~700 nodes on 10 gateways for density/redundancy reasons, with 10+ km open-area range — https://www.advantech.com/en-au/resources/case-study/advantech-and-pace-establish-a-lorawan-solution-for-general-mining-wellfield-monitoring).

**Siemens BLE architecture caveat:** MS200 sensors talk BLE to CC220 gateways (short range, ~tens of metres), each CC220 serving ≤8 sensors. At 500 points that means **~63 CC220 gateways in field cabinets across the site**, each needing power, an IP66 sun-shaded enclosure and plant-LAN or cellular backhaul — a materially larger field-infrastructure footprint than a LoRaWAN design.

**Design rules for this climate** (from Section 2 sources): gateways in IP66 sun-shaded sloping-roof enclosures (B&R Pilbara SP or IP Enclosures Mine-Spec class); silicone gaskets; compound-filled cable glands; solar+battery power where mains is unavailable (X2 Engineering precedent); AU915/ACMA-compliant hardware (https://wz-it.com/en/blog/iot-solutions-australia-remote-monitoring-lorawan/).

---

## 5. Durability Verdict for This Site

1. **All three options meet the +80 °C sensor ceiling with near-zero margin** on sun-exposed or machinery-mounted assets — mandate sunshields, shaded mounting, or remote temperature probes; expect battery-life derating versus 25 °C lab ratings (Siemens explicitly rates MS200 battery life at 25 °C).
2. **Dust:** IP6X dust-tight is mandatory. MS200 (IP69) > Versatilis (IP66/67) ≥ typical local IP67 sensors. For washdown zones (100–150 bar), only IP69K-rated hardware should be specified.
3. **Enclosures matter as much as sensors:** budget Mine-Spec IP66/IK10 sun-shaded enclosures for every non-IP67 field device; this is standard Australian mining practice (https://www.ipenclosures.com.au/mine-spec-electrical-enclosures/).
4. Vibration alarm baselines should be set to **ISO 10816 / ISO 20816** (used by Honeywell EHM and Australian CM providers such as Monitel).

---

## 6. Total Implementation Cost Model (50 km², 500 monitored points base case)

**Assumptions (stated plainly):** mid-size operation with ~500 critical bearing/asset points (crushers, conveyor drives, screens, pumps, motors, gearboxes, fans). Sensitivity scenarios: 200 / 500 / 1,000 points. Currency conversions at ~1 USD = 1.50 AUD, 1 EUR = 1.60 AUD (approximate). Items marked *(est.)* are engineering estimates without a published source — treat ±40 %.

**Sensor unit prices found:**
- Siemens MS200: €286–€356 list/reseller (https://siserv.de/onlineshop/sitrans-ms200, https://shop.osd-schenck.de/Siemens-SITRANS-MS200-7MP2210-2AB21-2AB1); USD 417–652 (https://automation-warehouse.com/en-mena/products/7mp2210-2ab21-2ab1, https://electricals-shop.com/product/7mp2210-2ab21-2ab1-siemens/) → **~AUD 450–1,000; use 650.**
- Honeywell Versatilis: "from USD 488" (https://www.lesman.com/honeywell-versatilis-transmitters-for-equipment-health-monitoring); AU distributor quote-only → **~AUD 700–900; use 750.**
- Local LoRaWAN vibration/temp sensors: **AUD 150–300** typical per Senstrali's market statement (https://www.senstrali.com.au/services); premium units to ~500 → **use 350.**

### 6.1 CAPEX (AUD, 500 points)

| Item | Siemens | Honeywell | Local |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sensors | 500 × $650 = **$325,000** | 500 × $750 = **$375,000** | 500 × $350 = **$175,000** |
| Field gateways | 63 × CC220 @ ~$1,200 *(est.)* = **$75,600** | 3 × IP67 LoRaWAN GW @ ~$3,500 = **$10,500** | 3 × IP67 GW @ ~$3,000 = **$9,000** |
| Enclosures, poles, power, install | 63 CC220 → ~25 Mine-Spec cabinets @ ~$3,500 *(est.)* = **$87,500** | 3 sites × $15,000 *(est.)* = **$45,000** | 3 sites × $15,000 *(est.)* = **$45,000** |
| Servers/software licences (upfront) | Industrial Edge device(s) + IEM *(est.)* **$40,000–80,000** | EHM server/licence *(est., quote-only)* **$50,000–150,000** | Local gateway/server **$10,000–30,000** |
| SCADA integration engineering (OPC UA/Modbus bridging, graphics, alarms) | **$150,000–300,000** *(est.)* | **$100,000–250,000** *(est.)* | **$80,000–200,000** *(est.)* |
| **CAPEX subtotal** | **≈ $680k–920k** | **≈ $580k–830k** | **≈ $320k–460k** |

### 6.2 OPEX (AUD/yr)

| Item | Siemens | Honeywell | Local |
|---|---|---|---|
| Analytics/platform subscription | Insights Hub Essentials €6,299.98/yr covers only 25 assets (https://www.itechguides.com/products/siemens-insights-hub/pricing/); excess-asset usage fees €180–€360/asset/yr (https://assets.ctfassets.net/17si5cpawjzf/4Q7tKIX6RQk5HpepNpaIv8/5294234493e73194fff91511b040c4d4/MSPH_PriceList_for_Offerings_with_Usage-based_Fees_v2.1__1_.pdf). 475 excess assets → **€85.5k–171k ≈ $137k–274k/yr** (enterprise deals are custom-quoted; AWS Marketplace reference lists a $300k/yr enterprise tier: https://aws.amazon.com/marketplace/pp/prodview-enwtljpzoc7pu) | EHM support *(est.)* **$20k–50k** | MeshedX from $150/mo (https://www.meshed.network/lorawan-iot-private-networks/) scaling with size → **$2k–15k** |
| Batteries | ~125–250 swaps/yr (2–5 yr life) @ ~$100–150 *(est.)* = $15k–35k | ~100–165 swaps/yr (3–5 yr life) ≈ **$12k–19k** | ~100/yr (5 yr life) ≈ $10k–15k |
| Network/connectivity | LTE backhaul/SIMs *(est.)* $5k–15k | $5k–15k | $5k–15k |
| **OPEX/yr** | **≈ $160k–320k** | **≈ $40k–85k** | **≈ $20k–45k** |

### 6.3 5-Year TCO Summary (AUD, 500 points)

- **Local: ≈ $0.42M–$0.69M** (CAPEX $320–460k + 4 yrs OPEX $80–180k)
- **Honeywell: ≈ $0.74M–$1.17M**
- **Siemens: ≈ $1.32M–$2.20M** (subscription-dominated)

**Scale sensitivity (CAPEX hardware only, linear model):** at 200 points → Local ~$130k, Honeywell ~$155k, Siemens ~$270k (CC220 count = 25); at 1,000 points → Local ~$360k, Honeywell ~$760k, Siemens ~$730k (CC220 count = 125; Siemens gateway cost becomes a major driver). Conveyor-dense operations should separately quote Senstrali-style wired-bus monitoring, which materially cuts per-point cost on long conveyors (https://www.senstrali.com.au/services).

---

## 7. Key Uncertainties (stated plainly)

1. **No binding quotes exist in public sources** — Siemens MS200 street prices varied ~2.3× across resellers; Honeywell Versatilis AU pricing is quote-only; EHM, Industrial Edge licensing and all SI engineering rates are unpriced here and marked *(est.)*.
2. **Siemens MS200/SCM IQ Australian commercial availability** must be confirmed with Siemens Australia (older literature restricted sales regions; current mall data shows AU radio approval but not necessarily sales/support).
3. **Battery life figures are lab-condition ratings**; sustained 50–80 °C exposure will shorten them — pilot measurement is essential.
4. **Sensor count (500) is an assumption**; TCO scales roughly linearly (Section 6.3).
5. RF coverage claims (15–20 km) are line-of-sight; a site RF survey is required before fixing gateway count.
6. Exchange rates and subscription price lists (checked against 2025–2026 published versions) will shift.

## 8. Procurement Recommendation

1. **Issue an RFQ for a 3-month pilot**: one conveyor line + one pump cluster (~30–50 points), dual-vendor — Honeywell Versatilis on a private AU915 LoRaWAN network (Meshed or Sentient) vs the local provider's own sensor line; include Siemens MS200 if Siemens Australia confirms availability. Measure: packet delivery vs heat/dust cycles, battery drain, washdown survival, and SCADA data flow via OPC UA/Modbus.
2. **Select the production platform on**: (a) proven ≥+70 °C sustained operation, (b) IP67 minimum/IP69K in washdown zones, (c) on-prem or AU-hosted data path, (d) 5-yr TCO including subscriptions and battery labour.
3. **Preferred architecture**: local LoRaWAN network (3 gateways, IP67, sun-shaded) + IP67 multisensors (Versatilis-class) + on-prem health analytics bridged to legacy SCADA via OPC UA; reserve Siemens Industrial Edge for Siemens-PLC-heavy plant areas; engage Predictive Industries/Monitel for diagnostics interpretation regardless of platform.
4. **Contract terms**: require IP/temperature test evidence (IEC 60529), battery-life guarantees derated for 50 °C ambient, AU data sovereignty, and SLA-backed network uptime (≥99.5 %) — benchmarks already demonstrated by Australian providers in the Pilbara.
