# Monitoring Strategy, Authorization Pathway, and Escalation Thresholds for a 68-Year-Old Man With Symptomatic Bradycardia, Progressive First-Degree AV Block, and Uncaptured Dropped Beats

## Executive Summary

This patient has recurrent presyncopal symptoms (four ED visits in six weeks, ≈ one presentation every 10–11 days), sinus bradycardia (HR 52), a PR interval that has prolonged from 200 to 240 ms in three weeks, and "occasional dropped beats" whose mechanism was never captured. The clinical question is whether he has intermittent high-grade or Mobitz II AV block (a Class I pacemaker indication regardless of symptoms under the 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS bradycardia guideline) versus benign blocked premature atrial complexes or drug/vagal-mediated Wenckebach. The monitoring strategy that best fits both the evidence and Medicare/commercial coverage policy is a **30-day auto-triggering external loop recorder or, preferably, mobile cardiac outpatient telemetry (MCOT/MCT) with 24-hour attended surveillance**, ordered under the ambulatory electrocardiography (AECG) benefit for "symptoms suggestive of cardiac arrhythmia" — not contingent on a pre-existing documented arrhythmia. The payer's denial of a Holter "without documented arrhythmia" inverts the purpose of the test as defined in CMS NCD 20.15 and is appealable. Any documentation of Mobitz II, high-grade AV block, third-degree AV block, alternating bundle-branch block, or symptomatic bradycardia with hemodynamic compromise should bypass the three-month outpatient wait and trigger urgent electrophysiology/pacemaker consultation.

---

## 1. Clinical Risk Stratification: Why This Cannot Simply Wait Three Months

**Guideline framing.** The 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on the Evaluation and Management of Patients With Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay defines first-degree AV block as PR >200 ms with 1:1 conduction, and high-grade (advanced) AV block as "≥2 consecutive P waves at a constant physiologic rate that do not conduct to the ventricles with evidence for some atrioventricular conduction" (Table 3, Guidelines Made Simple, https://www.acc.org/-/media/Non-Clinical/Files-PDFs-Excel-MS-Word-etc/Guidelines/2018/Guidelines%5FMade%5FSimple%5F2018%5FBradycardia.pdf). Its central pacing statement: "In patients with acquired second-degree Mobitz type II atrioventricular block, high-grade atrioventricular block, or third-degree atrioventricular block not caused by reversible or physiologic causes, permanent pacing is recommended regardless of symptoms. For all other types of atrioventricular block… permanent pacing should generally be considered only in the presence of symptoms that correlate with atrioventricular block" (https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2018.10.044; https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/full/10.1161/CIR.0000000000000628). The 2021 ESC pacing guideline concurs and adds that "conservatively treated (i.e., non-paced) patients with high-degree AVB have notably poorer survival compared with pacemaker-treated patients" (https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/42/35/3427/6358547).

**What the dropped beats could be.** The differential for an isolated nonconducted P wave includes true Mobitz II (invariably infranodal, a pacemaker indication), Mobitz I/Wenckebach (often nodal and benign unless symptomatic), 2:1 block, blocked premature atrial complexes, and "pseudo-AV block" from concealed His-bundle or junctional extrasystoles. A 2024 Frontiers in Cardiovascular Medicine review emphasizes that Mobitz II is "a commonly overdiagnosed and misinterpreted arrhythmia": an unchanged PR after the blocked beat, a stable sinus rate, and at least two consecutive conducted P waves are required for the diagnosis, and concealed His extrasystoles or vagal surges can mimic it (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/cardiovascular-medicine/articles/10.3389/fcvm.2024.1450705/full; see also https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6020181/ and https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9811016/). Because management diverges completely (pacemaker vs. reassurance), the rhythm strip must be captured and over-read — telemetry that noted "dropped beats" without saving the strip is nondiagnostic.

**The beta-blocker confounder — and why it should not provide false reassurance.** Metoprolol 50 mg BID, started eight weeks ago (temporally concordant with symptom onset), is listed by the 2018 guideline among medications that "can induce/exacerbate bradycardia or conduction disorders" (Table 4, beta-blockers; https://www.acc.org/-/media/Non-Clinical/Files-PDFs-Excel-MS-Word-etc/Guidelines/2018/Guidelines%5FMade%5FSimple%5F2018%5FBradycardia.pdf). However, the landmark prognostic study of drug-associated AV block (Amigoni et al., JACC 2004) found that among patients with second- or third-degree AV block on beta-blockers or non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers, drug discontinuation resolved AV block in only 41%, 56% of those responders had recurrence off therapy, and only ~15% had AV block "truly caused by drugs" — concluding that drug-associated AV block usually "unmasks the presence of serious underlying AV conduction disease" (https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2004.03.057). A Spanish ED cohort of 127 patients with high-grade AV block in the setting of bradycardic drugs found AV block resolved in 47% after drug withdrawal, but 67% of those recurred and **84.3% ultimately required a pacemaker**; independent predictors of pacing need were heart rate <35 bpm (OR 8.12), wide QRS (OR 5.65), and presentation with symptoms other than syncope (OR 4.09) (https://www.revespcardiol.org/en-atrioventricular-block-in-patients-under-articulo-S1885585719304165-pdf-file). The 2021 ESC guideline similarly lists adverse drug effects among reversible causes (accounting for 21% of ED bradycardia presentations in one series) but insists on demonstrating actual resolution before attributing block to a drug (https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/42/35/3427/6358547).

**Implication for this patient:** holding or halving metoprolol is appropriate (see Section 5), but a normal ECG after washout does not exclude dangerous paroxysmal block, and persistent PR prolongation or any recurrent dropped beats off drug is evidence of intrinsic conduction disease. His PR has already progressed 200 → 240 ms (+40 ms, +20%) in three weeks while electrolytes (K 4.3, Mg 2.0), renal function (Cr 1.1), and TSH (2.8) are all normal — a trajectory that raises concern for progressive AV nodal or infranodal disease. A key missing datum is QRS duration: a wide QRS would shift the pretest probability strongly toward infranodal disease and higher risk (wide QRS OR 5.65 for pacemaker need in the Spanish cohort).

---

## 2. Recommended Monitoring Strategy

### 2.1 First-line: 30-day mobile cardiac outpatient telemetry (MCOT/MCT) with auto-trigger detection and 24-hour attended monitoring

**Why this modality fits the clinical problem:**
- **Symptom frequency matches the device.** The guideline evaluation algorithm directs ambulatory ECG monitoring (Class I, LOE B-NR) for suspected bradycardia, "with the specific type of cardiac monitor chosen based on the frequency and nature of symptoms" (https://www.ecgsmart.com/blog/bradycardia-diagnosis-ecg-monitoring/, quoting the 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS recommendation; full guideline at https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2018.10.044). With episodes roughly every 10 days, a 24–48 h Holter samples only ~2–5% of a typical symptom interval (see Section 6), whereas a 30-day service spans ~3 expected episodes. CMS's own LCD states a 24–48 h monitor "is most appropriate for patients with daily or near daily symptoms"; otherwise the provider should select the device matching symptom frequency (LCD L39492, https://www.cms.gov/medicare-coverage-database/view/lcd.aspx?lcdid=39492&ver=7).
- **It captures events the patient cannot trigger.** Presyncope can impair a patient's ability to press a button, and brief paroxysmal block often ends before activation. CMS explicitly warns that purely patient-activated event recorders are "medically unnecessary for any patient who is… unable to recognize symptoms, or activate the recorder" (LCD L40257, https://www.cms.gov/medicare-coverage-database/view/lcd.aspx?lcdId=40257). An auto-triggering device with pre-symptom memory loop satisfies both the clinical need and the LCD device definition ("patient/event activated… provide either presymptom memory loop or post-symptom recording"; LCD L33952, https://www.cms.gov/medicare-coverage-database/view/lcd.aspx?DocID=L33952&LCDId=33952).
- **It provides real-time safety surveillance for a patient who lives alone.** The covered service requires "a 24-hour attended monitoring station… technicians should have immediate, 24-hour access to a physician… instructed as to when and how to contact available facilities to assist the patient in case of emergencies" (LCD L33952 and L40257, URLs above). For a man with no family nearby who drives daily, this is the only outpatient modality that can actively summon help when high-grade block or long pauses are detected — converting the monitor from a diagnostic tool into a safety net.
- **Evidence of superior yield.** In the pivotal 17-center randomized trial (n=266; patients with syncope/presyncope/palpitations and a nondiagnostic Holter), MCOT made a diagnosis in 88% vs 75% for loop event monitors (P=0.008); in the syncope/presyncope subgroup, 89% vs 69% (P=0.008); and it detected clinically significant arrhythmias in 41% vs 15% (P<0.001) (Rothman et al., https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17318994/; https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1540-8167.2006.00729.x; trial registration NCT00295204, industry-sponsored — a limitation to note). A large proprietary-database comparison found MCOT significantly outperformed autotrigger loop recorders for asymptomatic bradycardia (ventricular rate ≤40 bpm) and pauses ≥3 s, with earlier time to diagnosis (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28940881/). A 2026 Europace analysis of 37,406 syncope patients on MCOT showed diagnostic yield rising with wear time — 4.3% (0–2 days), 10.5% (3–7 days), 15.1% (8–14 days), 20.6% (>14 days) — and used exactly the alert criteria relevant here: urgent = pause ≥3 s, bradycardia <35 bpm >30 s, 2nd-degree AV block; emergent = pause ≥10 s, 3rd-degree AV block (https://academic.oup.com/europace/article/28/Supplement_1/euag105.030/8716745).

**Order specifics that matter:** 30-day continuous wear; auto-trigger arrhythmia detection programmed to flag bradycardia, pauses, and second-/third-degree AV block; pre-symptom loop memory; patient symptom diary and event button; 24-hour attended monitoring center with physician escalation and ED-direction protocol; full over-read of any saved strip by the ordering clinician to adjudicate true AV block vs blocked PACs/pseudo-block (per the misdiagnosis literature in Section 1).

### 2.2 Acceptable fallback: 30-day external loop recorder (ELR) with auto-trigger

If the plan authorizes only a standard event/loop recorder (CPT-defined 30-day packaged cardiac event detection service), ensure it is an **auto-triggering looping recorder, not a post-symptom transtelephonic recorder** (the latter "represents old technology… no memory loop," NCD 20.15, https://www.cms.gov/medicare-coverage-database/view/ncd.aspx?ncdid=179&ncdver=2). The same LCD coverage criteria apply (LCD L33952/L34573). Yield will be lower than MCOT for asymptomatic events (see numbers above), and there is no real-time rescue function — a meaningful drawback for a patient who lives alone.

### 2.3 Escalation if 30-day monitoring is nondiagnostic

- **Repeat/extend one 30-day cycle only if symptoms recur** — CMS states testing beyond 30 consecutive days is "only rarely medically necessary" and failure to capture during one period "is not sufficient justification to reimburse a second or subsequent test" without new/recurrent symptoms (LCD L33952/L40257).
- **Implantable cardiac monitor (ICM/ILR).** The 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS algorithm assigns ICM a Class IIa role when symptoms are infrequent (>30 days apart) and external monitoring is nondiagnostic (Figure 1, https://www.acc.org/-/media/Non-Clinical/Files-PDFs-Excel-MS-Word-etc/Guidelines/2018/Guidelines%5FMade%5FSimple%5F2018%5FBradycardia.pdf); the 2021 ESC guideline gives ILR a Class I/A recommendation for infrequent (<1/month) unexplained symptoms suspected to be bradycardic after comprehensive evaluation (https://www.ecgsmart.com/blog/bradycardia-diagnosis-ecg-monitoring/; https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/42/35/3427/6358547). NCD 20.15 describes the ILR as appropriate "when syncope is thought to be cardiac-related, but is too infrequent to be detected by either a Holter monitor or a traditional pre-symptom MLR," with other uses left to MAC discretion (https://www.cms.gov/medicare-coverage-database/view/ncd.aspx?ncdid=179&ncdver=2).
- **Electrophysiology study** is reasonable when intermittent symptoms suggestive of bradycardia (lightheadedness, syncope) cannot be captured on monitoring, particularly to assess infranodal conduction (HV interval) in suspected conduction-system disease (secondary summary of the 2018 guideline, https://www.clinician.com/articles/143828-a-review-of-updated-guidelines-regarding-bradycardia-and-cardiac-conduction-delay). This becomes more attractive if QRS is wide.

### 2.4 A built-in therapeutic diagnostic: the metoprolol challenge

In parallel with monitoring, the prescriber should **taper/hold metoprolol** (it was started for hypertension, for which many non–AV-nodal alternatives exist) and repeat ECG after washout. Guideline basis: beta-blockers are named reversible causes of bradycardia/conduction delay (2018 guideline Table 4), and both US and European guidelines direct identification and treatment of reversible causes before labeling block permanent (https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2018.10.044; https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/42/35/3427/6358547). Interpret results using the JACC 2004 priors: only ~41% of drug-associated AV block resolves with discontinuation and only ~15% is truly drug-caused — so resolution supports but does not prove a benign diagnosis (56% recur), and persistence or recurrence off drug is strong evidence of intrinsic disease warranting pacing evaluation. If a compelling indication for beta-blockade later emerges (e.g., HFrEF), the guideline pathway of pacing to enable essential rate-slowing therapy exists (Class I for symptomatic bradycardia consequent to guideline-directed therapy with no alternative; https://www.ctxheart.com/guidelines/pacemaker-guidelines/sinus-node-dysfunction).

---

## 3. Authorization Pathway: Getting the Monitor Approved

### 3.1 The payer's stated denial rationale is inconsistent with Medicare policy

CMS NCD 20.15 covers AECG services "when there are documented signs and symptoms or other clinical indications," explicitly listing symptoms that "may correlate with intermittent cardiac arrhythmias," including **"syncope, dizziness, chest pain, palpitations, or shortness of breath,"** and additionally covering AECG "to evaluate patient response to initiation, revision, or discontinuation of arrhythmic drug therapy" (https://www.cms.gov/medicare-coverage-database/view/ncd.aspx?ncdid=179&ncdver=2). Requiring a *documented arrhythmia before* authorizing the test used to document arrhythmia contradicts the NCD's stated purpose. MAC LCDs restate this: cardiac event detection is covered for "detection, characterization, and documentation of symptomatic transient arrhythmias, when the frequency of the symptoms is limited and use of a 24-hour ambulatory EKG is unlikely to capture and document the arrhythmia" (LCD L33952, https://www.cms.gov/medicare-coverage-database/view/lcd.aspx?DocID=L33952&LCDId=33952; L34573, https://www.cms.gov/medicare-coverage-database/view/lcd.aspx?=&lcdid=34573&ver=30), and the newer TNACMD LCD covers monitoring when "symptoms suggestive of cardiac arrhythmia (such as palpitations, dizziness, presyncope, syncope…) occur infrequently (>24 hours between symptomatic episodes)" (LCD L40257, https://www.cms.gov/medicare-coverage-database/view/lcd.aspx?lcdId=40257). LCD L39492 covers AECG "for patients experiencing unexplained syncope, near syncope, episodic dizziness…" (https://www.cms.gov/medicare-coverage-database/view/lcd.aspx?lcdid=39492&ver=7).

### 3.2 Prior-authorization submission: documentation checklist

Build the PA (and any peer-to-peer) around these elements, each of which maps to a policy criterion:

1. **Covered indication (NCD 20.15):** recurrent lightheadedness/presyncope (4 ED visits in 6 weeks) — "dizziness/presyncope" are enumerated covered symptoms; add the second covered indication of evaluating response to discontinuation of a bradycardic drug (metoprolol).
2. **Symptom frequency satisfies the event-monitor criterion:** episodes ≈ every 10–11 days, i.e., ">24 hours between symptomatic episodes" (LCD L40257) and "frequency of symptoms is limited" such that "a 24-hour ambulatory EKG is unlikely to capture" the arrhythmia (LCD L33952). State explicitly: symptoms are too infrequent for Holter and too frequent/safety-critical to defer.
3. **Objective ECG abnormalities already documented:** sinus bradycardia HR 52; first-degree AV block with PR progression 200 → 240 ms over 3 weeks; dropped beats noted on ED telemetry but not captured. This rebuts any "screening" characterization — LCDs deny monitoring that is "routine… in the absence of treatable symptoms" or duplicative of a diagnostic ECG (LCD L40257/L33952); here there is a documented, undiagnosed abnormality requiring characterization.
4. **Why Holter is inadequate (addresses the plan's own logic):** LCD L39492 states 24–48 h monitoring is for daily/near-daily symptoms; a 24-h Holter covers ~2.4% of this patient's average 10.5-day symptom interval (Section 6).
5. **Device capability justification:** request auto-trigger detection with pre-symptom loop memory because presyncope may prevent patient activation — CMS itself deems purely patient-activated devices inappropriate for patients unable to reliably activate them (LCD L40257/L33952).
6. **24-hour attended monitoring / MCOT justification:** patient lives alone with no local support and drives daily; the covered MCOT service includes a 24-hour attended station with physician access and instructions "as to when and how to contact available facilities to assist the patient in case of emergencies" (LCD L33952/L40257) — i.e., the service is simultaneously diagnostic and a safety bridge until the cardiology appointment.
7. **Guideline support:** cite the 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Class I recommendation that ambulatory cardiac rhythm monitoring is indicated to correlate rhythm with symptoms in suspected bradycardia/conduction disorders, with monitor choice based on symptom frequency (https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2018.10.044; https://www.ecgsmart.com/blog/bradycardia-diagnosis-ecg-monitoring/), and the Class I pacing indication for Mobitz II/high-grade/third-degree AV block that makes capturing the rhythm clinically urgent.
8. **Ordering clinician requirement:** the test must be ordered by the treating physician/NPP (42 CFR 410.32 as quoted in LCD L33952) — have the PCP or ED attending place the order with the above note attached rather than relying on a standing referral.
9. **Diagnosis coding:** use codes for the documented findings (e.g., ICD-10 family for atrioventricular block/bradycardia, R55 syncope/presyncope, R42 dizziness as applicable); LCD billing articles tie covered ICD-10 codes to medical necessity, so code to the documented ECG findings plus symptoms rather than to "hypertension." (Verify the exact supported code list in the billing/coding article attached to the applicable MAC LCD, since LCD code tables were not retrievable in this review.)

### 3.3 If denied: escalation sequence

1. **Peer-to-peer review** with the plan's medical director, reading back NCD 20.15's symptom-based coverage language and the LCD's own ">24 hours between episodes" criterion; ask for the specific plan policy used to deny and the clinical rationale for requiring pre-existing arrhythmia documentation.
2. **Formal appeal** with the documentation package above plus the ED records showing four nondiagnostic visits (each visit is evidence that shorter/absent monitoring has failed). For Medicare, standard sequential appeal rights apply (redetermination by the MAC, then Qualified Independent Contractor reconsideration); for commercial plans, internal appeal followed by external independent review. (Appeal-step mechanics are standard benefit administration and were not independently re-verified in this review; confirm with the plan.)
3. **While the appeal is pending, maintain safety via the ED/hospital route:** LCDs expressly exclude ambulatory event monitoring for patients "in hospitals, emergency rooms, skilled nursing facilities" (LCD L33952/L40257) — meaning that if symptoms escalate, inpatient/observation telemetry is the covered and appropriate setting, not a second attempt at outpatient authorization. If the patient has another significant episode (syncope, near-syncope with injury, HR <40), ED evaluation with admission for telemetry monitoring is defensible and guideline-consistent, and any captured high-grade block then triggers Section 4.
4. **Expedited cardiology access:** ask the PCP/ED physician to call the cardiology group's triage line to request an urgent-slot or cancellation-list appointment, or referral to an electrophysiologist, attaching the ECG progression; many systems triage documented progressive AV conduction disease ahead of routine new-patient waits. (Practical step; not policy-derived.)

---

## 4. Clinical Thresholds That Should Prompt Immediate Pacemaker Consultation Rather Than Outpatient Workup

The following findings, if documented at any point (ED telemetry, monitor transmission, or repeat ECG), should bypass the three-month wait and trigger urgent electrophysiology consultation, with admission and temporary-pacing capability as indicated:

**A. Rhythm diagnoses that are Class I pacing indications regardless of symptoms (2018 ACC/AHA/HRS; concordant 2021 ESC):**
- Acquired **second-degree Mobitz type II AV block** (verified true Mobitz II — constant PR before/after the blocked P wave, stable sinus rate, ≥2 consecutive conducted P waves; exclude pseudo-AV block from concealed His/junctional extrasystoles and blocked PACs per Section 1) (https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2018.10.044; https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/cardiovascular-medicine/articles/10.3389/fcvm.2024.1450705/full).
- **High-grade/advanced AV block** — ≥2 consecutive nonconducted P waves at a physiologic rate (2018 guideline definition, Table 3).
- **Third-degree (complete) AV block** (https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2018.10.044; https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/42/35/3427/6358547).
- **Alternating bundle-branch block** (listed among Class I indications in guideline summaries; https://www.firstpasspa.com/diagnoses/av-blocks/; ESC 2021 also treats new alternating BBB as a high-risk conduction marker).
- These apply **even if the episode is attributed to metoprolol**, until resolution is actually demonstrated off drug — given only 41% resolution and 15% "truly drug-caused" rates (https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2004.03.057) and 84% eventual pacing in the Spanish high-grade cohort (https://www.revespcardiol.org/en-atrioventricular-block-in-patients-under-articulo-S1885585719304165-pdf-file).

**B. Symptom–rhythm combinations requiring urgent inpatient evaluation:**
- **Syncope or near-syncope with documented AV block or bradycardia** (symptomatic AV block is a pacing pathway; Class I when symptoms correlate with block, Class IIa for symptomatic first-degree/Mobitz I clearly attributable to block; https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2018.10.044; https://www.firstpasspa.com/diagnoses/av-blocks/).
- **Hemodynamic compromise** (hypotension, heart failure, altered mentation) with second-/third-degree block: guideline acute pathway is atropine for nodal-level block, beta-agonist infusion if needed, temporary transvenous pacing reasonable when refractory to medical therapy (Class IIa, LOE B-NR), transcutaneous pacing as a bridge (Class IIb), then permanent pacing (2018 guideline acute management, summarized at https://www.wikidoc.org/index.php/Paroxysmal_AV_block_interventions and https://wikidoc.org/index.php/Conduction_system_disease). Conversely, temporary pacing should not be used in patients with minimal symptoms without hemodynamic compromise (Class III: Harm) — supporting outpatient monitored management while he remains stable.
- **Monitor-defined alert thresholds** used in telemetry services: pause ≥3 s, bradycardia <35 bpm sustained, any 2nd-degree AV block (urgent); pause ≥10 s or 3rd-degree AV block (emergent) (https://academic.oup.com/europace/article/28/Supplement_1/euag105.030/8716745). ESC syncope/pacing guidance similarly uses asystolic pauses >3 s if symptomatic or >6 s if asymptomatic as decision thresholds in reflex/asystolic syncope (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8785099/). The BioTelemetry comparison study used ventricular rate ≤40 bpm and pauses ≥3 s as its bradycardia detection criteria (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28940881/).
- **Persistent high-grade or second-degree block after metoprolol washout** — converts a "possibly reversible" finding into a non-reversible one, activating the Class I indication.
- **New wide QRS, new bifascicular block, or alternating BBB with symptoms** — markers of infranodal disease; the 2018 guideline recommends echocardiography for newly identified LBBB, Mobitz II, high-grade, or third-degree AV block (Class I, LOE B-NR; https://www.acc.org/-/media/Non-Clinical/Files-PDFs-Excel-MS-Word-etc/Guidelines/2018/Guidelines%5FMade%5FSimple%5F2018%5FBradycardia.pdf), and wide QRS independently predicts pacing need (OR 5.65; https://www.revespcardiol.org/en-atrioventricular-block-in-patients-under-articulo-S1885585719304165-pdf-file).
- **Recurrent ED visits with escalating symptom severity** (injury, prolonged episodes, exertional presyncope) even without captured block — consider inpatient telemetry or EP study rather than continued outpatient waiting.

**C. What does NOT by itself mandate a pacemaker:** isolated first-degree AV block (even PR 240 ms), asymptomatic Mobitz I/Wenckebach, blocked PACs, sinus bradycardia at 52 bpm without symptom correlation, and nocturnal bradycardia (2018 guideline: pacing should generally be considered only with symptom–block correlation; nocturnal bradycardia is not itself an indication — screen for sleep apnea instead; https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2018.10.044; https://www.cardioguide.ca/bradycardia/).

---

## 5. Interim Safety Plan for a Man Who Lives Alone and Drives Daily

1. **Driving restriction now.** He has had four episodes of unexplained presyncope in six weeks and the workup is incomplete. UK DVLA standards — a commonly referenced framework — hold that cardiovascular syncope warrants no driving for 4 weeks (Group 1), unexplained recurrent syncope 6 months, and arrhythmias liable to cause sudden incapacity require control before driving resumes (https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/690c6d0a68fffdd77951aab0/assessing-fitness-to-drive-november-2025.pdf; comparative review at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6528027/). US rules are state-specific (e.g., Maine's medical advisory framework ties restriction to the likelihood that arrhythmia recurrence causes alteration/loss of consciousness, https://www.maine.gov/sos/sites/maine.gov.sos/files/content/assets/Cardiovascular-20Conditions.pdf), but the clinical counseling obligation is the same: advise him not to drive until the rhythm is characterized or the block is treated, and document that counseling. Given he drives daily, this is the single highest-yield harm-reduction step available today.
2. **Medication safety:** taper/hold metoprolol with prescriber oversight; avoid adding any other AV-nodal blockers (non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers, digoxin, other beta-blockers) and review OTC/supplement use (2018 guideline Table 4 lists multiple bradycardia-inducing agents).
3. **Monitoring-as-safety-net:** select MCOT specifically for its 24-hour attended station; confirm the vendor's protocol for emergent findings (pause ≥10 s, 3rd-degree AV block) includes direct patient contact and ED direction (LCD-mandated capability; https://www.cms.gov/medicare-coverage-database/view/lcd.aspx?DocID=L33952&LCDId=33952).
4. **Solo-living contingencies:** explicit written return precautions (syncope, near-syncope, new confusion, chest pain, worsening fatigue → ED, not clinic); keep a phone within reach; consider a medical-alert device; identify a neighbor/friend for daily check-ins; arrange rides for essential trips while driving is restricted. (Practical measures; not guideline-graded.)
5. **Follow-up cadence:** PCP review of monitor transmissions at least weekly; repeat 12-lead ECG 5–7 days after metoprolol hold to document PR response; echocardiogram if any Mobitz II/high-grade/complete block or new LBBB is captured (Class I, 2018 guideline).

---

## 6. Quantitative Appendix (explicit calculations)

- **Symptom periodicity:** 4 presentations over 6 weeks (42 days) → mean interval 42/4 = **10.5 days between episodes**. A 24-h Holter samples 1/10.5 ≈ **9.5%** of one inter-symptom interval at best (2.4% of the 42-day window); a 48-h Holter ≈ 19%. A 30-day monitor spans 30/10.5 ≈ **2.9 expected episode intervals**. This is exactly the LCD scenario: symptoms ">24 hours between episodes," Holter "unlikely to capture" (LCD L40257, L33952).
- **PR progression:** 200 → 240 ms = **+40 ms (+20%) in 21 days** ≈ +1.9 ms/day on average — measurable conduction deterioration on a stable background of normal K (4.3), Mg (2.0), Cr (1.1), TSH (2.8).
- **MCOT vs loop event monitor RCT (n=266):** diagnosis 88% vs 75% → absolute risk reduction (ARR) 13%, number needed to monitor (NNM) ≈ 1/0.13 = **7.7**; syncope/presyncope subgroup 89% vs 69% → ARR 20%, NNM = **5.0**; clinically significant arrhythmias 41% vs 15% → ARR 26%, NNM ≈ **3.8** (computed from https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17318994/).
- **Yield vs wear time (MCOT, 37,406 syncope patients):** actionable-arrhythmia yield 4.3% (0–2 d) → 10.5% (3–7 d) → 15.1% (8–14 d) → **20.6% (>14 d)**; >14-day wear roughly doubles yield vs 3–7 days (https://academic.oup.com/europace/article/28/Supplement_1/euag105.030/8716745).
- **Drug-associated AV block priors:** resolution after drug stop **41%**; recurrence off drug **56%**; truly drug-caused **~15%** (JACC 2004, https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2004.03.057); Spanish high-grade cohort: resolution 47.2%, recurrence among resolvers 66.6%, eventual pacemaker **84.3%**; predictors HR <35 bpm OR 8.12 (95% CI 1.82–36.17), wide QRS OR 5.65 (1.77–18.04), non-syncopal symptoms OR 4.09 (1.18–14.13) (https://www.revespcardiol.org/en-atrioventricular-block-in-patients-under-articulo-S1885585719304165-pdf-file).

---

## 7. Stated Uncertainties and Limitations

- **QRS duration is not provided** and is the most important missing modifier: a wide QRS would substantially raise the probability of infranodal block and lower the threshold for admission/EP study.
- **The mechanism of the "dropped beats" is unknown**; they may be benign blocked PACs or pseudo-AV block rather than true Mobitz II. All escalation decisions in Section 4 assume over-read confirmation.
- **Symptom–rhythm correlation is not yet established**; guidelines require it for pacing in all AV block types except Mobitz II/high-grade/third-degree.
- **Coverage specifics vary by payer and MAC jurisdiction.** The NCD/LCD language cited governs Medicare (NCD 20.15; LCDs L40257, L33952/L34573, L39492); commercial plans often mirror it but may apply different prior-authorization forms and code lists. Exact CPT/HCPCS codes for the 30-day packaged service should be confirmed against the applicable LCD's billing article, which was not retrievable in this review.
- **The MCOT superiority RCT was industry-sponsored** (CardioNet/BioTelemetry), and the large database comparisons are proprietary-data retrospective analyses; effect sizes may overstate real-world advantages, though direction and the duration–yield relationship are consistent across studies.
- **Driving rules cited are primarily UK (DVLA) plus one US state framework**; the patient's actual state law must be checked for mandatory reporting and specific restriction periods.
- The 2026 Europace MCOT yield data are a conference abstract (retrospective registry), not yet peer-reviewed in full.

**Bottom line:** order a 30-day auto-triggering external loop recorder or MCOT with 24-hour attended surveillance today, justify it under NCD 20.15/LCD criteria as evaluation of infrequent presyncopal symptoms plus drug-discontinuation monitoring (not as screening), hold metoprolol and recheck the ECG, restrict driving until the rhythm is defined, and treat any captured Mobitz II, high-grade, or complete AV block — on or off metoprolol — as an urgent pacemaker consultation rather than an outpatient appointment three months away.

4. Clinical thresholds prompting immediate pacemaker consultation/admission (rather than outpatient workup):
From 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS + ESC 2021 + StatPearls + Europace alert criteria:
- Documented Mobitz II second-degree AV block (true, not pseudo) — Class I pacing regardless of symptoms.
- High-grade/advanced AV block (≥2 consecutive nonconducted P waves) — Class I.
- Third-degree/complete AV block — Class I.
- Alternating bundle branch block (Class I per guideline summaries — from wikidoc/FirstPassPA: "alternating bundle branch block" listed as Class I; also ESC).
- Symptomatic bradycardia/AV block with hemodynamic instability refractory to medical therapy → temporary pacing (Class IIa) and urgent permanent pacing.
- Syncope attributable to AV block; pauses — ESC urgent/emergent criteria: pauses ≥3 s symptomatic / ≥6 s asymptomatic (from ESC 2021 summary in PMC8785099: "asystolic pauses (>3 s if symptomatic or >6 s if asymptomatic)" in syncope context); Europace MCOT urgent: pauses ≥3 s, bradycardia <35 bpm >30 s, 2nd degree AV block; emergent: pauses ≥10 s, 3rd degree AV block.
- New wide QRS/bifascicular block + syncope or HV ≥70 ms (EP study context) — guideline: neuromuscular disease HV≥70; for general bifascicular block, ESC recommends pacing with documented symptomatic block. Keep to what's sourced: newly identified LBBB/Mobitz II/high-grade/third-degree → echo Class I; EP study reasonable when symptoms remain uncaptured.
- Heart rate thresholds: HR <35 bpm predictor of pacing need (OR 8.12) in bradycardic drug cohort; wide QRS OR 5.65.
- Clinical: syncope, presyncope with injury, worsening frequency, hypotension, heart failure symptoms, ventricular rate <40 or pauses ≥3 s while awake (per BioTelemetry study bradycardia definition ≤40), documented block while off AV nodal blockers.
- Also: if block persists after metoprolol withdrawal → strong indication; if high-grade block documented on monitor → ED/admission + temporary pacing capability, don't wait 3 months.
- Also mention: 2018 guideline Class I pacing for symptomatic AV block when correlation documented; for first-degree/Mobitz I with symptoms clearly attributable, pacing is Class IIa (per FirstPassPA/ecgsmart summary).

5. Interim safety plan until definitive evaluation:
- Driving restriction: advise not to drive until evaluation complete given unexplained presyncope with daily driving; cite DVLA/UK guidance and US state variability (PMC6528027: cardiovascular syncope Group 1 no driving for 4 weeks; unexplained recurrent syncope 6 months; Maine guideline). Frame as clinician counseling + state DMV rules.
- Medication: reassess metoprolol — taper/hold with prescriber; avoid other AV nodal blockers; monitor for resolution (only 41% resolve with drug discontinuation).
- Remote monitoring alerts: MCOT with 24-hour center can direct patient to ED for emergent criteria (LCD requires technicians to have instructions on when/how to contact facility to assist patient).
- Safety-net instructions: ED return precautions for syncope, near-syncope, worsening symptoms; home safety since lives alone — consider medical alert, phone access, inform neighbor/friend; (practical, low evidence — frame as practical).
- Bridge if high-risk but stable: some centers admit for telemetry; guideline says temporary pacing not for minimal symptoms (Class III harm) — so outpatient with MCOT is appropriate if stable.

6. Explicit quantitative work:
- Symptom interval: 4 visits / 6 weeks → average interval 42 days / 4 = 10.5 days between presentations; Holter window 1–2 days = 2.4–4.8% of interval → low capture probability; hence LCD ">24 h between episodes" → event monitor/MCT appropriate.
- PR progression: 200 → 240 ms = +40 ms (+20%) in 3 weeks.
- MCOT vs LOOP: diagnosis 88% vs 75% (ARR 13%, NNT ~7.7); presyncope/syncope subgroup 89% vs 69% (ARR 20%, NNT 5); clinically significant arrhythmia 41% vs 15% (ARR 26%, NNT ~3.8). Compute precisely: 1/0.13 = 7.69; 1/0.20 = 5.0; 1/0.26 = 3.85.
- Europace yield: 20.6% at >14 days vs 10.5% at 3–7 days (≈2×).
- Drug-induced: 41% resolution with discontinuation; 56% recurrence; only 15% truly drug-induced; 84.3% ultimately paced in Spanish cohort.

Uncertainties to state:
- QRS duration unknown (key modifier: wide QRS → infranodal, higher risk).
- Mechanism of dropped beats unknown (blocked PACs vs Mobitz II vs pseudo-block) — monitoring must capture.
- Whether symptoms correlate with bradycardia not yet established.
- Insurance details (Medicare vs commercial) change exact LCD applicability; NCD 20.15 applies to Medicare; commercial plans often mirror but vary.
- Metoprolol contribution uncertain; don't attribute fully to drug.
- State driving law varies.

Citations: include URLs inline.

Report structure:
- Bottom line / executive summary
- 1. Clinical risk stratification (what we know, what the dropped beats could mean, beta-blocker confounder with numbers)
- 2. Recommended monitoring strategy (first choice MCOT, alternative, escalation to ILR, what to program/monitor, medication challenge)
- 3. Authorization pathway (medical necessity documentation, NCD/LCD citations, PA letter elements, peer-to-peer/appeal, addressing Holter denial)
- 4. Thresholds for immediate pacemaker consultation (table)
- 5. Interim safety plan (driving, meds, living alone, ED return precautions)
- 6. Quantitative appendix
- 7. Uncertainties

Length: comprehensive but focused. Now let me write.

final.content:
# UCC Acceptance and Cure Analysis: Buyer v. Vendor (Legal-Size Paper Delivery)

## 1. Issue

Whether, on summary judgment, Buyer rightfully rejected 500 reams of legal-size copy paper on November 30, 2024, or whether Buyer accepted the goods under UCC Article 2 — leaving Vendor entitled to the price and, alternatively, entitled to cure by substituting letter-size stock within five business days.

## 2. Governing Framework

This is a contract for the sale of goods (copy paper), so UCC Article 2 governs. Four clusters of provisions control.

**Perfect tender (UCC § 2-601).** If goods or the tender of delivery "fail in any respect to conform to the contract," the buyer may reject the whole, accept the whole, or accept any commercial unit(s) and reject the rest (https://www.nolo.com/legal-encyclopedia/sellers-performance-under-the-ucc.html; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_tender_rule). The common-law doctrine of substantial performance does not apply to sales of goods; the UCC revived the perfect-tender rule for single-delivery contracts, mitigated only by the cure and revocation provisions (https://scholarship.law.wm.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1814&context=wmlr; https://digitalcommons.lib.uconn.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1053&context=law_review; Ramirez v. Autosport, 88 N.J. 277, 440 A.2d 1345 (1982), https://law.justia.com/cases/new-jersey/supreme-court/1982/88-n-j-277-0.html). Goods conform when they are "in accordance with the obligations under the contract" (Ramirez).

**Acceptance (UCC § 2-606).** Acceptance occurs when the buyer, after a reasonable opportunity to inspect: (a) signifies that the goods are conforming or that it will retain them despite nonconformity; (b) fails to make an effective rejection under § 2-602(1); or (c) "does any act inconsistent with the seller's ownership" (wrongful acts count only if ratified by the seller). Acceptance of part of a commercial unit is acceptance of the entire unit (https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-606; https://nebraskalegislature.gov/laws/ucc.php?code=2-606). Under the Kansas annotation, acceptance under (1)(c) requires that the buyer knew or should have known of the defect, and rejection requires affirmative action — silence is not rejection (https://www.ksrevisor.gov.ksrevisor.org/statutes/chapters/ch84/084_002_0606.html). Nebraska annotations hold that commingling or consuming delivered goods are acts inconsistent with the seller's ownership (Johnson v. Holdrege Coop. Equity Exchange, 206 Neb. 568 (1980); Fabricators, Inc. v. Farmers Elevator, Inc., 203 Neb. 150 (1979), https://nebraskalegislature.gov/laws/ucc.php?code=2-606).

**Rejection (UCC § 2-602).** Rejection "must be within a reasonable time after their delivery or tender" and "is ineffective unless the buyer seasonably notifies the seller." After rejection, any exercise of ownership over any commercial unit is wrongful against the seller (https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-602). Courts distinguish *ineffective* rejections (procedurally defective under § 2-602(1), which operate as acceptance and support an action for the price) from *wrongful* rejections (effective but unjustified) (Integrated Circuits Unlimited, Inc. v. E.F. Johnson Co., 691 F. Supp. 630 (E.D.N.Y. 1988), https://openjurist.org/691/fsupp/630/integrated-circuits-unlimited-inc-v-e-f-johnson-co-1813808). Timeliness is generally a jury question, but summary judgment is proper "when only one inference may be drawn as to the reasonableness of the time" (J.N.K. Mach. Corp. v. TBW, Ltd., 2011 NY Slip Op 01192, http://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/3dseries/2011/2011_01192.htm).

**Effect of acceptance and cure (UCC §§ 2-607, 2-508).** The buyer must pay at the contract rate for goods accepted; acceptance "precludes rejection of the goods accepted" and, if made with knowledge of a nonconformity, cannot be revoked unless the buyer reasonably assumed the nonconformity would be seasonably cured; the buyer bears the burden of establishing any breach as to accepted goods (https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-607). Under § 2-508(1), if the contract time has not expired, the seller may seasonably notify and make a conforming delivery; under § 2-508(2), where the buyer rejects a tender "which the seller had reasonable grounds to believe would be acceptable with or without money allowance," the seller may, on seasonable notice, have "a further reasonable time to substitute a conforming tender" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-508). A seller has such reasonable grounds where, for example, a reasonably prudent seller would not have known of the nonconformity, or trade usage or course of dealing supported the tender; the provision exists to prevent "surprise rejection" (Kansas Comment, https://ksrevisor.gov/statutes/chapters/ch84/084_002_0508.html).

## 3. Application

### A. The tender was nonconforming — but that alone does not end the case

The October 15 purchase order specified letter size; Vendor delivered 500 reams that were all legal size. Because the purchase order terms are part of the contract, the tender "fail[ed] in any respect to conform" under § 2-601, and Buyer was entitled at the moment of delivery to reject. Vendor's argument that legal-size paper has "equivalent value" is legally insufficient to defeat the perfect-tender rule — equivalence of market value is not the standard; conformity to contract terms is (Ramirez, 88 N.J. 277). The contract's undefined phrase "standard office paper" does not cure the defect, because the PO's express letter-size specification controls over a vague generic label.

However, perfect tender governs only the *initial* right to reject. That right is lost if the buyer accepts, and acceptance is determined by § 2-606.

### B. Buyer accepted the goods by acts inconsistent with Vendor's ownership (§ 2-606(1)(c))

The facts establish acceptance by conduct as to essentially the entire shipment:

1. **Consumption of 180 reams (36% of the shipment).** Over three weeks Buyer's staff used 180 reams for internal drafts and overflow projects. Consuming goods in ordinary operations is a paradigmatic act of ownership that no bailee or rejecting buyer may do. Analogously, in Mooresville Gen. Contr. v. Basepoint, Inc. (Va. 1997), the buyer's installation of nonconforming cabinets was held to be "an act inconsistent with the seller's ownership" constituting acceptance that could not be revoked (https://www.casemine.com/judgement/us/591481feadd7b0493448e289). Nebraska's commingling/consumption annotations point the same way (https://nebraskalegislature.gov/laws/ucc.php?code=2-606). Consumed reams cannot be returned at all.

2. **Knowledge of the defect during use.** The Kansas annotation requires knowledge (actual or imputed) of the defect for conduct-based acceptance (https://www.ksrevisor.gov.ksrevisor.org/statutes/chapters/ch84/084_002_0606.html). Here, employees "complained about reformatting documents" during the three-week usage period — Buyer's staff knew the paper was the wrong size almost from the start, yet Buyer continued drawing down the stock for three weeks instead of rejecting. Continued use with knowledge of the nonconformity is the strongest form of conduct-based acceptance.

3. **Printing letterhead and logo on the remaining 320 reams (64%).** Customizing the remaining stock with Buyer's proprietary letterhead and logo is an act of dominion even more inconsistent with Vendor's ownership than ordinary use: the paper is physically altered and rendered unusable for Vendor's resale to anyone else. Modification/alteration of goods is treated as acceptance because the seller can no longer meaningfully reclaim them (https://legalclarity.org/ucc-2-606-what-constitutes-acceptance-of-goods/). This act occurred with full knowledge of the size discrepancy (it necessarily postdated the employee complaints and the three-week usage period).

4. **The ratification proviso does not save Buyer.** § 2-606(1)(c) provides that acts "wrongful as against the seller" count as acceptance only if ratified. But under § 2-602(2)(a), exercise of ownership becomes wrongful only *after* rejection (https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-602). Buyer's first rejection occurred November 30 — all consumption and all letterhead printing preceded it. Pre-rejection use of nonconforming goods is therefore not wrongful and operates directly as acceptance.

5. **Commercial-unit point.** Under § 2-606(2), acceptance of part of a commercial unit is acceptance of that entire unit (https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-606). At minimum, each consumed ream (or each opened ream) was accepted in full. But because the remaining 320 reams were independently accepted by the letterhead printing, acceptance extends to the whole 500-ream delivery regardless of how "commercial unit" is defined.

### C. Buyer also accepted by failing to reject within a reasonable time (§ 2-606(1)(b); § 2-602(1))

Delivery was Friday, November 8, 2024; Buyer's first notification of rejection was Saturday, November 30, 2024 — **22 calendar days later**. The nonconformity was patent, not latent: paper size is immediately visible on opening any ream, and Buyer's own office manager took delivery and stocked the closet the same day. Buyer had a reasonable opportunity to inspect on or about November 8. See Import Traders, Inc. v. Frederick Mfg. Corp. (N.Y. Civ. Ct. 1983), where five months of silence after a reasonable opportunity to inspect constituted acceptance, and the court emphasized that acceptance "precludes their subsequent rejection" (https://exa.ai/library/legal/opinion/mq6z01lp0db).

Twenty-two days of silence, combined with heavy affirmative use (180 reams consumed) and alteration of the remainder, permits only one inference: Buyer did not reject within a reasonable time. Under J.N.K. Mach., that is precisely the situation where timeliness may be resolved on summary judgment rather than left to a jury (http://www.nycourts.gov/reporter/3dseries/2011/2011_01192.htm).

### D. Consequences: the November 30 "rejection" is ineffective; revocation fails

Because acceptance occurred no later than during the three-week usage period (and certainly upon letterhead printing), § 2-607(2) "precludes rejection of the goods accepted" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-607). Buyer's November 30 demand for return of payment can therefore be analyzed only as an attempted **revocation of acceptance** under § 2-608 — and it fails on every prong:

- **No substantial impairment.** Revocation requires a nonconformity that substantially impairs the value of the goods to the buyer. The paper functioned for its intended purpose: Buyer itself used 180 reams for real work over three weeks. Employee complaints about reformatting are inconvenience, not substantial impairment, and Buyer "cannot quantify hours lost."
- **Knowledge.** Buyer used the goods with full awareness of the size discrepancy; acceptance made with knowledge of a nonconformity cannot be revoked unless it was induced by a reasonable assumption that the nonconformity would be seasonably cured (§ 2-607(2)). There is no evidence Buyer accepted on any such assumption — it simply consumed and customized the stock.
- **Timing and restitution.** Even if revocation were available, Buyer cannot return what it consumed (36%) and physically altered the rest (64%), making restoration impossible.

Buyer's proper remedy after acceptance was damages under § 2-714 for the nonconformity of accepted goods — but § 2-607(4) places the burden of proving breach and loss on the buyer (https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-607), and Buyer concedes it cannot quantify its loss. Unquantified "workflow disruption" creates no triable damages issue.

### E. Alternative ground: Vendor's right to cure (§ 2-508)

Even if a court treated the November 30 demand as a timely, effective rejection, Vendor's contemporaneous offer to exchange the remaining stock for letter size within five business days invokes § 2-508:

- **Reasonable grounds to believe the tender acceptable (§ 2-508(2)).** The written contract said only "standard office paper" without defining dimensions. That ambiguity is exactly the situation the Kansas comment describes: a reasonably prudent seller might not know that legal size would be deemed nonconforming, or might reasonably rely on the generic term (https://ksrevisor.gov/statutes/chapters/ch84/084_002_0508.html). Vendor therefore had "reasonable grounds to believe" the tender would be acceptable, at least "with ... money allowance."
- **Seasonable notice and further reasonable time.** Vendor made the exchange offer the same day as Buyer's rejection (November 30), proposing substitution within five business days — by my calculation, no later than Friday, December 6, 2024. For a commodity good like copy paper, five business days is a "further reasonable time." See Bartus v. Riccardi, 55 Misc. 2d 3, 284 N.Y.S.2d 222 (Utica City Ct. 1967), holding that § 2-508(2) "extends the contract period beyond the date set forth in the contract itself" and that a buyer who rejects a nonconforming tender must give the seller the opportunity to substitute a conforming one (https://syfert.com/new-york/cases/55-misc-2d-3/bartus-v-riccardi; https://opencasebook.org/casebooks/477-contracts-casebook-digital-version/resources/5.3.1.5-bartus-v-riccardi/). See also Wilson v. Scampoli, 228 A.2d 848 (D.C. 1967): a seller of goods it reasonably believed acceptable is entitled to cure — by adjustment, repair, or substitution — and the buyer may not refuse all cure and insist on rescission, so long as cure works "without subjecting the buyer to any great inconvenience, risk or loss" (https://exa.ai/library/legal/opinion/y92m8nmnfcx; https://www.plainsite.org/opinions/nx25eyrd/wilson-v-scampoli/). Ramirez likewise confirms that "because of the seller's right to cure ... the buyer's rejection does not necessarily discharge the contract" (https://law.justia.com/cases/new-jersey/supreme-court/1982/88-n-j-277-0.html).
- **Buyer's blanket refusal was improper.** Buyer "demanded return of payment and refused" the exchange. Under Wilson and Bartus, a buyer who refuses a seasonable, non-burdensome cure offer forfeits its right to rescind. Swapping boxed paper in five business days imposes no great inconvenience, and any interim inconvenience is offset by the fact that Buyer had already put the goods to productive use.

Cure is thus a fallback: the primary holding is that there was nothing left to reject because acceptance had already occurred. Note also that cure could reach only the 320 unaltered reams (the 180 consumed cannot be exchanged), which further confirms that acceptance, not cure, is the dispositive doctrine.

### F. Evidentiary side-issues

- **Vendor's incomplete delivery records / missing packing slips for four other accounts.** These facts bear on Vendor's general record-keeping credibility but do not create a genuine dispute of material fact about *this* transaction: the delivery, the size mismatch, the acceptance into the closet, the consumption of 180 reams, and the letterhead printing are all undisputed. They would not, standing alone, defeat summary judgment.
- **Buyer's unquantified disruption claim.** A claim of lost staff time with no quantification fails the burden imposed by § 2-607(4) and supplies no evidence of substantial impairment for revocation purposes.
- **Office manager's signature on delivery.** Receipt and storage are not themselves acceptance (acceptance requires a reasonable opportunity to inspect), but the size defect was patent, so inspection opportunity existed immediately on November 8.

## 4. Quantitative Summary

Verified by date arithmetic (Python datetime):

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Purchase order date | Tuesday, October 15, 2024 |
| Delivery date | Friday, November 8, 2024 (24 days after PO) |
| Usage period | ~3 weeks; 180 of 500 reams consumed = **36%** |
| Remaining stock printed with letterhead | 320 of 500 reams = **64%** |
| Rejection demand | Saturday, November 30, 2024 — **22 days after delivery** |
| Cure deadline (5 business days from Nov 30) | Friday, December 6, 2024 |

## 5. Conclusion — Summary Judgment Outcome

**Buyer did not rightfully reject; Buyer must be deemed to have accepted the goods, and Vendor prevails.**

1. The tender was nonconforming under § 2-601 (legal instead of letter size), so Buyer had an initial right to reject — but only for a reasonable time and only without exercising ownership.
2. Buyer accepted the entire delivery under § 2-606(1)(c): it consumed 36% of the reams over three weeks with knowledge of the size problem and physically altered the remaining 64% by printing its letterhead and logo on them — acts wholly inconsistent with Vendor's ownership, undertaken before any rejection and therefore not "wrongful" under § 2-602(2)(a). Independently, Buyer accepted under § 2-606(1)(b) by failing to reject a patent defect for 22 days after a reasonable opportunity to inspect.
3. Under § 2-607(1)–(2), Buyer must pay the contract rate for accepted goods, and its November 30 demand cannot operate as a rejection. It also fails as a revocation of acceptance under § 2-608: no substantial impairment (the paper was used productively for weeks), acceptance with knowledge, no assumption of cure, and no possibility of restitution.
4. In the alternative, even treating November 30 as an effective rejection, Vendor's same-day offer to substitute letter-size paper within five business days (by December 6, 2024) was a seasonable cure under § 2-508(2): the contract's undefined "standard office paper" language gave Vendor reasonable grounds to believe the tender acceptable, and Buyer's refusal of a non-burdensome commodity exchange bars rescission under Bartus and Wilson.
5. Buyer's only surviving remedy is damages for nonconformity of accepted goods, on which it bears the burden (§ 2-607(4)) and which it admits it cannot quantify.

**Uncertainty stated plainly:** (a) jurisdiction is unspecified; all cited UCC provisions are uniform in substance across adopting states, but local numbering and precedent could vary slightly; (b) a factfinder could theoretically find that "standard office paper" plus course of dealing or trade usage made legal size conforming under § 1-303/§ 2-106 principles — but that would help Vendor, not Buyer; (c) the precise day within the three weeks when staff first noticed the size error is not fixed by the facts, though the letterhead printing indisputably occurred with knowledge; (d) whether each ream, each carton, or the whole shipment is the "commercial unit" (§ 2-105(6)) does not change the outcome, since conduct-based acceptance reached all 500 reams either way.

**Sources:** UCC §§ 2-601, 2-602, 2-606, 2-607, 2-508 (https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-606, https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-602, https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-607, https://www.law.cornell.edu/ucc/2/2-508); Nebraska UCC annotations (https://nebraskalegislature.gov/laws/ucc.php?code=2-606); Kansas UCC and comments (https://www.ksrevisor.gov.ksrevisor.org/statutes/chapters/ch84/084_002_0606.html, https://ksrevisor.gov/statutes/chapters/ch84/084_002_0508.html); Ramirez v. Autosport, 88 N.J. 277 (1982) (https://law.justia.com/cases/new-jersey/supreme-court/1982/88-n-j-277-0.html); Bartus v. Riccardi, 55 Misc. 2d 3 (1967) (https://syfert.com/new-york/cases/55-misc-2d-3/bartus-v-riccardi); Wilson v. Scampoli, 228 A.2d 848 (D.C. 1967) (https://exa.ai/library/legal/opinion/y92m8nmnfcx); Mooresville Gen. Contr. v. Basepoint (1997) (https://www.casemine.com/judgement/us/591481feadd7b0493448e289); Import Traders, Inc. v. Frederick Mfg. Corp. The user is asking me to write a final report based only on the evidence gathered so far. Let me organize what I have:

**Facts:**
- October 15, 2024 (Tuesday): Purchase order specifying letter size
- November 8, 2024 (Friday): Vendor delivers 500 reams, all legal size
- Contract says "standard office paper" without defining dimensions
- Buyer's office manager accepted the delivery and stored it in the supply closet
- Over three weeks, staff used 180 reams (36%) for internal drafts and overflow projects; employees complained about document reformatting
- Buyer printed the company's standard letterhead and logo on the remaining 320 reams (64%)
- November 30, 2024 (Saturday): Buyer demanded return of payment and refused Vendor's offer to exchange the remaining inventory for letter size within 5 business days (5 business days from Nov 30 = approximately Dec 6, Friday)
- Vendor's delivery records are incomplete; packing slips are missing for 4 other accounts
- Buyer claims workflow disruption and staff time waste but cannot quantify the lost time
- Vendor argues that legal size has equivalent value and that Buyer's extensive use constitutes acceptance

**Legal framework gathered:**

1. UCC 2-601 (perfect tender): If goods "fail in any respect to conform to the contract," buyer may reject the whole, accept the whole, or accept part and reject the rest. Sources: Nolo article, Connecticut Law Review article, Wikipedia, Ramirez v. Autosport.

2. UCC 2-606 (acceptance): three routes — (a) express indication of acceptance after reasonable opportunity to inspect; (b) failure to make an effective rejection after reasonable opportunity to inspect; (c) any act inconsistent with seller's ownership (wrongful acts count only if ratified). (2) Acceptance of part of a commercial unit is acceptance of the whole unit. Sources: LII, Nebraska legislature, Kansas statute with comments.

3. UCC 2-602 (rejection): Must be within a reasonable time after delivery/tender; ineffective unless buyer seasonably notifies seller. After rejection, any exercise of ownership over any commercial unit is wrongful against seller. Source: LII.

4. UCC 2-607 (effect of acceptance): Buyer must pay at contract rate for goods accepted; acceptance precludes rejection of accepted goods; acceptance with knowledge of nonconformity cannot be revoked unless acceptance was based on reasonable assumption that nonconformity would be seasonably cured; buyer must notify seller of breach within reasonable time; burden on buyer to establish breach as to accepted goods. Source: LII.

5. UCC 2-508 (cure): (1) If time for performance not expired, seller may seasonably notify and cure within contract time; (2) If buyer rejects nonconforming tender that seller had "reasonable grounds to believe" would be acceptable with or without money allowance, seller may, if seasonably notifies, have further reasonable time to substitute conforming tender. Source: LII.

6. Kansas comment on 2-508: Seller has reasonable grounds to believe tender acceptable when (1) seller knows of nonconformity but has reason such as trade usage or prior course of dealing to believe tender is acceptable, or (2) reasonably prudent seller would not know of nonconformity. Purpose is to avoid "surprise rejection."

7. Bartus v. Riccardi, 55 Misc. 2d 3, 284 N.Y.S.2d 222 (Utica City Ct. 1967): hearing aid case; 2-508(2) extends cure beyond contract time; seller permitted to cure by substitution; buyer must allow seller opportunity to cure. (I know facts from training: hearing aid ordered, wrong model delivered, buyer used it for some hours, then rejected; court held seller had reasonable grounds to believe tender acceptable and could cure by substitution. From search snippets I got the court's discussion of 2-508(1) and (2).)

8. Wilson v. Scampoli, 228 A.2d 848 (D.C. 1967): color TV with reddish tint; court held retail dealer had reasonable grounds to believe new crated TV would be acceptable; seller may cure by minor repair/adjustment or replacement; buyer cannot insist on brand new replacement and refuse all cure; policy is to avoid injustice from surprise rejection. From exa.ai snippet: "A retail dealer would certainly expect and have reasonable grounds to believe that merchandise like color television sets, new and delivered as crated at the factory, would be acceptable as delivered and that, if defective in some way, he would have the right to substitute a conforming tender." And Hawkland quote: seller should be able to cure "in those cases in which he can do so without subjecting the buyer to any great inconvenience, risk or loss."

9. Ramirez v. Autosport, 88 N.J. 277, 440 A.2d 1345 (1982): camper van with minor defects; UCC retains perfect tender rule via 2-601 but mitigates harshness through revocation of acceptance and cure (2-608, 2-508). Before acceptance, buyer may reject for any nonconformity; seller's right to cure means rejection does not necessarily terminate contract. Within time for performance, seller's right to cure is unconditional.

10. Moore Moore Gen. Contr. v. Basepoint, Inc., 254 Va. 59 (1997) (CaseMine): buyer's installation of nonconforming cabinets constituted act inconsistent with seller's ownership = acceptance under 2-606(1)(c); acceptance of nonconforming goods could not be revoked.

11. Import Traders, Inc. v. Frederick Mfg. Corp., 121 Misc.2d 300, 468 N.Y.S.2d 296 (N.Y. Civ. Ct. 1983): silence for 5 months after reasonable opportunity to inspect constituted acceptance; acceptance precludes later rejection; return only via revocation under 2-608.

12. Integrated Circuits Unlimited, Inc. v. E.F. Johnson Co., 691 F. Supp. 630 (E.D.N.Y. 1988): distinction between ineffective rejection (procedurally defective under 2-602(1) → acceptance) and wrongful rejection (effective rejection, even if unjustified, bars acceptance); remedy for ineffective rejection is action for price.

13. J.N.K. Mach. Corp. v. TBW, Ltd., 2011 NY Slip Op 01192: failure to reject timely = acceptance under 2-606(1)(b); timeliness of rejection is generally question of fact, but summary judgment appropriate where only one inference can be drawn.

14. Nebraska annotations: commingling of grain = act inconsistent with ownership (Johnson v. Holdrege Coop.); acceptance occurs upon failure to make effective rejection after reasonable opportunity to inspect (Fabricators, Inc. v. Farmers Elevator).

15. Kansas comment on 2-606: acceptance under (1)(c) requires buyer to know of defect or be deemed to know through failure to inspect. Rejection requires affirmative action; silence is not rejection. Rejection may be effective yet wrongful.

16. Michigan Law Review article (repository.law.umich.edu) on 2-508 and 2-608 as limits on perfect tender rule.

17. Connecticut Law Review article on good faith rejection in falling markets; perfect tender applies to one-shot contracts; installment contracts have substantial impairment standard.

**Quantitative work (from bash):**
- PO date: Tue Oct 15, 2024; delivery: Fri Nov 8, 2024; rejection: Sat Nov 30, 2024 (22 days after delivery); 24 days from PO to delivery
- 180/500 = 36% consumed; 320/500 = 64% remaining
- 5 business days from Nov 30 (Sat) → approximately Dec 6 (Fri)

**Analysis structure:**

I. Governing law: UCC Article 2 applies (sale of goods, paper). Perfect tender under 2-601: if goods fail in any respect to conform, buyer may reject whole, accept whole, or accept part/reject part. Substantial performance doctrine does not apply to sales of goods (William & Mary Law Review article; Connecticut Law Review; Nolo).

II. Was the tender conforming? Contract says "standard office paper" without defining dimensions; PO (Oct 15) specifies letter size. Under 2-106, goods conform when they are in accordance with obligations under contract (Ramirez). The PO is part of the contract; letter size is the specification. Legal ≠ letter (8.5" x 14" vs 8.5" x 11" — common knowledge, can state as generally known). So tender nonconforming; Vendor's "equivalent value" argument does not defeat perfect tender — 2-601 permits rejection for any nonconformity, even minor. But note ambiguity of "standard office paper" could be argued as course of dealing/trade usage issue; still, PO specified letter.

III. Acceptance analysis — the heart of the case.

A. 2-606(1)(c): Act inconsistent with seller's ownership. Buyer consumed 180 reams (36%) over 3 weeks for internal drafts and overflow projects, and printed letterhead/logo on remaining 320 reams. Consumption and printing/customization are classic acts of ownership. Moore Moore (installation of nonconforming cabinets = acceptance); LegalClarity guide (modification/alteration, use in manufacturing); Kansas comment (buyer must know of defect — here, employees complained about reformatting, so Buyer knew size was wrong from early use, yet continued using for three weeks). Printing letterhead on paper makes it non-returnable/non-resalable as generic stock — strongly inconsistent with Vendor's ownership.

Note the ratification proviso: if act is "wrongful as against seller," it counts as acceptance only if ratified. But 2-602(2)(a) makes exercise of ownership wrongful only "after rejection." Here, use occurred before any rejection (rejection came Nov 30, 22 days later). So pre-rejection use is not wrongful; it is acceptance.

B. 2-606(1)(b): Failure to make effective rejection within reasonable time. Delivery Nov 8; rejection Nov 30 — 22 days later. Defect was patent (size is immediately discoverable on inspection; office manager accepted and stored). Reasonable opportunity to inspect existed on Nov 8. Whether 22 days is reasonable is usually a fact question (J.N.K. Mach.), but where only one inference can be drawn, summary judgment is proper. Import Traders: 5 months of silence = acceptance. Here, Buyer not only remained silent but used extensively. Three weeks of use with knowledge of the defect (employee complaints) strongly indicates acceptance.

C. 2-606(2): Acceptance of part of a commercial unit is acceptance of whole unit. Each ream is likely a commercial unit; use of 180 reams = acceptance of those units at minimum. But printing letterhead on remaining 320 reams also constitutes act inconsistent with ownership as to those.

D. Effect: 2-607(1)-(2): Buyer must pay at contract rate for goods accepted; acceptance precludes rejection; acceptance with knowledge of nonconformity cannot be revoked unless based on reasonable assumption that nonconformity would be seasonably cured. There's no indication Buyer accepted on assumption Vendor would cure; Buyer simply used the paper. So Nov 30 "rejection" is legally ineffective — it is an attempted revocation that fails under 2-608 (no substantial impairment — paper functionally works for drafts/overflow; Buyer used it for three weeks; complaints about reformatting do not establish substantial impairment of value; and Buyer cannot quantify damages).

E. Nuance: could acceptance have occurred only as to some units? The 180 consumed reams are certainly accepted. As to the 320 remaining: printing letterhead/logo is an act inconsistent with Vendor's ownership (customized goods cannot be returned to Vendor's stock). So acceptance extends to all 500.

IV. Cure under 2-508 — in case rejection was effective.

Even assuming Buyer made an effective rejection on Nov 30, Vendor has cure rights. Time for performance: no delivery deadline stated; delivery was Nov 8. If contract time had not expired, 2-508(1) gives unconditional right to cure with seasonable notice. More likely analysis: 2-508(2) — did Vendor have "reasonable grounds to believe" legal-size tender would be acceptable? Contract said "standard office paper" without defining dimensions — ambiguous term. Vendor could argue it reasonably believed either standard size would satisfy; Kansas comment recognizes this category (reasonably prudent seller would not know of nonconformity, or trade usage). Ambiguity of contract language supports reasonable grounds. Seasonable notice: Vendor offered exchange within 5 business days contemporaneously with Nov 30 rejection — that is seasonable. Five business days is a "further reasonable time" for paper, a readily available commodity.

Wilson v. Scampoli: seller entitled to cure by substitution or repair; buyer cannot refuse all cure and demand refund. Bartus v. Riccardi: 2-508(2) extends cure beyond contract time; buyer must permit cure. Ramirez: rejection does not necessarily terminate contract because of seller's cure right.

But — cure's relevance is secondary because acceptance has already occurred. If Buyer accepted, cure is moot as to accepted goods; Vendor's exchange offer is gratuitous. Buyer's remedy is under 2-607/2-714 (damages for nonconformity of accepted goods) with burden on buyer (2-607(4)) — and Buyer cannot quantify damages.

V. Evidentiary / summary judgment considerations:
- Vendor's incomplete delivery records / missing packing slips for 4 other accounts: relevant to credibility/pattern but does not change the acceptance analysis as to this delivery, where delivery and use are undisputed. Might defeat summary judgment only if it creates genuine dispute about what was delivered (e.g., whether packing slip matched), but here size mismatch is undisputed.
- Buyer's unquantified workflow disruption: insufficient to create fact issue on substantial impairment or damages.
- Standard of review: J.N.K. Mach. — timeliness of rejection usually fact question but summary judgment proper where only one inference can be drawn.

VI. Conclusion: On summary judgment, Buyer did not rightfully reject. Buyer accepted all 500 reams (at least the 180 consumed; the letterhead printing accepted the 320) through acts inconsistent with Vendor's ownership under 2-606(1)(c) and through failure to reject seasonably under 2-606(1)(b)/(2-602(1)). Nov 30 demand for return of payment is ineffective as rejection; it fails as revocation of acceptance under 2-608 because no substantial impairment and acceptance was not induced by assumption of cure. Even if rejection were effective, Vendor's seasonable 5-business-day exchange offer triggers 2-508(2) cure right given contract ambiguity ("standard office paper") gave Vendor reasonable grounds to believe tender acceptable. Result: judgment for Vendor on Buyer's refund claim; Buyer owes contract price for accepted goods (2-607(1)), subject only to offset for provable damages — which Buyer has not quantified.

Let me double-check the 5-business-day calculation: Nov 30, 2024 is Saturday. 5 business days: Dec 2 (Mon), 3 (Tue), 4 (Wed), 5 (Thu), 6 (Fri) → Dec 6, 2024, Friday. Bash confirmed Dec 6 is Friday.

Also: 22 days from delivery to rejection; 24 days from PO to delivery.

Uncertainty to state: jurisdiction not specified (UCC section numbering varies slightly by state but substantively identical); whether "standard office paper" ambiguity could make tender conforming under trade usage (2-106, course of dealing) — but PO specified letter size; exact timing of when office manager/employees first noticed size mismatch (facts say employees complained during the 3 weeks — knowledge arose during use, but certainly before Nov 30); whether each ream is a "commercial unit" (2-105(6)) — likely, but even if whole shipment is one commercial unit, result is same (acceptance of part = acceptance of whole).

Also note: office manager's acceptance of delivery and storage in supply closet is receipt, not necessarily acceptance (acceptance requires reasonable opportunity to inspect). But size was patent.

One more point on the "wrongful act only if ratified" proviso of 2-606(1)(c): Kansas comment says buyer must know of defect for (1)(c) acceptance. Here, initial use may have begun before size issue was discovered (employees complained about reformatting — suggests discovery happened during early use). But continued use for three weeks with knowledge, plus letterhead printing (which necessarily occurred with knowledge of size since letterhead is printed on the paper in hand and complaints had already arisen), satisfies the knowledge requirement.

Also 2-607(3)(a) notice of breach: Buyer gave no notice until Nov 30 — 22 days. Even assuming notice was sufficient, remedy is limited to damages.

Now, structure of the report:

1. Issue presented
2. Governing framework (UCC Article 2, perfect tender, acceptance, rejection, cure)
3. Application
   A. Conforming goods / perfect tender — tender nonconforming; substantial performance inapplicable
   B. Acceptance by conduct (2-606(1)(c)) — 180 consumed + 320 letterhead printed
   C. Acceptance by failure to reject (2-606(1)(b); 2-602(1)) — 22 days, patent defect
   D. Effect of acceptance (2-607) — precludes rejection; revocation unavailable (2-608)
   E. Vendor's cure right (2-508) — alternative holding
   F. Evidentiary issues — Vendor's record-keeping, Buyer's unquantified damages
   G. Summary judgment standard
4. Conclusion
5. Quantitative appendix
6. Sources
