final.content:
# DSM-5 vs. ICD-11 Autism Diagnostic Criteria: Comparative Report with Focus on Sensory Processing

**Scope note and key limitation stated up front.** This report is based on the sources retrieved during the research session. A central finding is that, as of the evidence gathered, there is **no published head-to-head empirical diagnostic-accuracy study applying both DSM-5 and ICD-11 autism criteria to the same sample and reporting sensitivity/specificity of each against a best-estimate reference standard.** The strongest available comparative evidence consists of (a) structural/textual harmonization analyses, (b) WHO field studies comparing ICD-11 to ICD-10 (not to DSM-5), and (c) DSM-5 vs. DSM-IV/ICD-10 accuracy studies. This gap is flagged throughout Section B and GRADE ratings are assigned accordingly.

---

## (A) Side-by-Side Criteria Table

| Dimension | DSM-5 / DSM-5-TR (APA, 2013/2022) | ICD-11 (WHO, 2019; CDDR 6A02) |
|---|---|---|
| **Core social-communication criteria** | Criterion A: persistent deficits in social communication/interaction across contexts, requiring **all three** subcriteria: A1 social-emotional reciprocity; A2 nonverbal communicative behaviors; A3 developing/maintaining/understanding relationships (https://www.cdc.gov/autism/hcp/diagnosis/index.html; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10904885/) | Persistent deficits in ability to initiate and sustain reciprocal social interaction and social communication, "outside the expected range of typical functioning given the individual's age and level of intellectual development." ICD-11 lists ~7 example manifestation areas (and the CDDG describes up to 19 manifestations) but sets **no mandatory subcriteria and no symptom count** (https://www.mrcpsych.uk/2023/01/icd-11-criteria-for-autism-spectrum-disorder.html.html; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/) |
| **Restricted/repetitive behavior (RRB) domain** | Criterion B: **at least 2 of 4**: B1 stereotyped/repetitive movements/speech; B2 insistence on sameness/routines; B3 highly restricted fixated interests; B4 sensory (https://www.cdc.gov/autism/hcp/diagnosis/index.html; https://www.autismla.org/1/wp-content/uploads/2015/09/DSM-5-ASD-Combined.pdf) | "A range of restricted, repetitive, and inflexible patterns of behaviour, interests or activities that are clearly atypical or excessive for the individual's age and sociocultural context." CDDG lists ~16 possible manifestations with **no numeric threshold**; Kamp-Becker counts 19×16 = 304 possible symptom combinations (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/; https://www.psykiatriantutkimussaatio.fi/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Keski_Rahkonen_Table-1-ICD-11-diagnostic-criteria-for-autism-1.pdf) |
| **Sensory processing mention / weighting** | Explicit subcriterion **B4**: "Hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input or unusual interest in sensory aspects of the environment (e.g., apparent indifference to pain/temperature, adverse response to specific sounds or textures, excessive smelling or touching of objects, visual fascination with lights or movement)." Weighting: one of four B options; contributes only if the ≥2-of-4 threshold is met — sensory findings are **neither necessary nor sufficient** alone, and count equally with other RRB subcriteria (https://www.cdc.gov/autism/hcp/diagnosis/index.html; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK525976/) | Sensory features appear as **one manifestation among ~16** in the RRB domain: "Lifelong excessive and persistent hypersensitivity or hyposensitivity to sensory stimuli or unusual interest in a sensory stimulus, which may include actual or anticipated sounds, light, textures (especially clothing and food), odours and tastes, heat, cold or pain" (https://www.psykiatriantutkimussaatio.fi/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Keski_Rahkonen_Table-1-ICD-11-diagnostic-criteria-for-autism-1.pdf). Because ICD-11 has no symptom count, a sensory manifestation can in principle help satisfy the RRB domain, but it is not required. Notable differences vs DSM-5: (1) ICD-11 adds the qualifier **"lifelong"**; (2) it explicitly lists **anticipated** stimuli and heat/cold/pain; (3) sensory processing was newly elevated to a diagnostic-relevant feature relative to ICD-10, where it was not a core feature (https://cpe.psychopen.eu/index.php/cpe/article/download/10005/10005.pdf). Net weighting: DSM-5 gives sensory a defined, countable slot (1 of 4, threshold 2); ICD-11 gives it qualitative standing within an uncounted domain. |
| **Severity specifiers** | Three severity levels (Level 1 "requiring support," Level 2 "requiring substantial support," Level 3 "requiring very substantial support"), rated separately for social communication and RRB (https://www.autismla.org/1/wp-content/uploads/2015/09/DSM-5-ASD-Combined.pdf; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK525976/). Olson, Bishop & Thurm note these levels "were never field tested, nor is there any evidence regarding their validity or reliability," and warn of potential harm if payers use them to limit coverage (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10904885/) | **No severity levels.** Instead, ICD-11 uses categorical subtypes keyed to co-occurring disorder of intellectual development and functional language: 6A02.0 (no ID, mild/no language impairment), 6A02.1 (ID, mild/no language impairment), 6A02.2 (no ID, impaired language), 6A02.3 (ID, impaired language), 6A02.5 (ID, absence of functional language), plus 6A02.Y/6A02.Z (https://www.mrcpsych.uk/2023/01/icd-11-criteria-for-autism-spectrum-disorder.html.html; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/). For settings without standardized testing, ICD-11 provides behavioural indicators for intellectual severity (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jir.13146) |
| **Age/onset requirements** | Criterion C: symptoms "must be present in the early developmental period (but may not become fully manifest until social demands exceed limited capacities, or may be masked by learned strategies in later life)" (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10904885/; https://www.cdc.gov/autism/hcp/diagnosis/index.html) | "The onset of the disorder occurs during the developmental period, typically in early childhood, but symptoms may not become fully manifest until later, when social demands exceed limited capacities." ICD-11 additionally emphasizes that symptoms "may only be apparent in retrospect" and repeatedly invokes compensation (https://www.mrcpsych.uk/2023/01/icd-11-criteria-for-autism-spectrum-disorder.html.html; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/) |
| **Functional impairment thresholds** | Criterion D: "clinically significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of current functioning"; Criterion E: not better explained by intellectual disability/global developmental delay (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10904885/) | "Deficits are sufficiently severe to cause impairment in personal, family, social, educational, occupational or other important areas of functioning and are usually a pervasive feature of the individual's functioning observable in all settings, although they may vary according to social, educational, or other context." ICD-11 text also states a diagnosis "is still appropriate" when individuals function adequately through exceptional effort, which critics argue weakens the impairment gate (https://www.mrcpsych.uk/2023/01/icd-11-criteria-for-autism-spectrum-disorder.html.html; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/) |
| **Coding** | 299.00 (F84.0 in ICD-10-CM crosswalk) (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK525976/; https://publications.aap.org/toolkits/pages/Autism-Toolkit) | 6A02 with extension subcategories 6A02.0–6A02.Z (https://www.mrcpsych.uk/2023/01/icd-11-criteria-for-autism-spectrum-disorder.html.html) |

**Sensory-weighting synthesis.** DSM-5 operationalizes sensory differences as a countable, optional subcriterion (B4) within a thresholded domain (≥2 of 4), making its weight explicit but contingent. ICD-11 treats sensory differences as a named, qualitatively described manifestation within an uncounted domain, adding the "lifelong" and "anticipated stimuli" qualifiers; because no symptom count exists, the effective weight is clinician-dependent (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/; https://cpe.psychopen.eu/index.php/cpe/article/download/10005/10005.pdf). Both manuals made sensory features diagnostically relevant for the first time relative to their predecessors (DSM-IV/ICD-10) (https://cpe.psychopen.eu/index.php/cpe/article/download/10005/10005.pdf).

---

**Overall finding:** No retrieved study directly compares DSM-5 and ICD-11 autism criteria in the same sample with sensitivity/specificity endpoints. For ASD specifically, the two systems are broadly harmonized but differ in operational strictness (DSM-5 prescriptive counts vs. ICD-11 descriptive guidance).

- Design: systematic review of case-controlled field studies, ecological implementation studies, and qualitative/mixed-methods studies.
- Sample: 19 included studies across mental, behavioral, and neurodevelopmental disorders.
- Key statistics: clinical utility rated positive in 78.95% of studies; negative findings concentrated in qualitative/mixed studies identifying implementation obstacles.
- GRADE: **Low** (heterogeneous designs, narrative synthesis, indirectness to the DSM-5 comparison and to ASD specifically).

## (C) Clinical Guideline Positions

**WHO.** ICD-11 is WHO's own classification, approved by the World Health Assembly in 2019; its Clinical Descriptions and Diagnostic Requirements (CDDR) for mental, behavioural and neurodevelopmental disorders were validated through case-controlled (internet-based) and ecological implementation (clinic-based) field studies involving thousands of clinicians across all global regions, which WHO reports showed "incrementally superior – or in some cases equivalent – performance of the ICD-11 CDDR compared to the ICD-10 CDDG in the accuracy of diagnoses assigned to case vignettes" and improved clinical-utility ratings (https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/dcf73611-9e0f-4d5c-85f6-85a58b0da6de/content). WHO's position is therefore adoption and implementation of ICD-11, including sensory features as part of the RRB domain (6A02).

**APA.** The APA publishes DSM-5 (2013) and DSM-5-TR (2022) as its diagnostic standard and participated in an ICD–DSM Harmonization Group with WHO; the harmonization evaluation concluded the two systems are now substantially aligned while retaining differences (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/wps.20825). Within the evidence gathered, the APA has not issued a statement adopting ICD-11 criteria for US clinical use; DSM-5-TR remains the APA standard, with sensory hyper-/hyporeactivity codified as criterion B4.

**American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP).** The AAP's 2020 clinical report "Identification, Evaluation, and Management of Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder" (Hyman et al., Pediatrics) is built on DSM-5 criteria and recommends universal ASD-specific screening at 18 and 24 months plus developmental surveillance at every well-child visit (https://www.maineaap.org/assets/resources/Autism-Clinical-Report.pdf; https://exa.ai/library/publication/w72tljhtt4f). The AAP Autism Toolkit explicitly includes a "Relationship Between DSM-5 and ICD-10-CM" resource (https://publications.aap.org/toolkits/pages/Autism-Toolkit), indicating the AAP operationalizes DSM-5 diagnoses through ICD-10-CM coding for US reimbursement; no retrieved AAP material endorses adopting ICD-11 criteria or addresses sensory weighting beyond DSM-5's B4.

**NICE (UK).** NICE CG128 "Autism spectrum disorder in under 19s: recognition, referral and diagnosis" (2011, updated) predates both DSM-5 and ICD-11 and is organized around a local pathway, autism-team referral, and diagnostic assessment rather than mandating a specific manual; it does not reference ICD-11 adoption (https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg128/chapter/recommendations). UK practice historically uses ICD coding; within the gathered evidence, NICE has not issued guidance adopting ICD-11 criteria or re-weighting sensory features. (Note: UK diagnostic-practice commentary such as the Royal College of Psychiatrists' ICD-11 criteria summaries circulates ICD-11 text for training purposes — https://www.mrcpsych.uk/2023/01/icd-11-criteria-for-autism-spectrum-disorder.html.html — but this is educational, not guideline adoption.)

## (D) Advocacy Organization Positions

**Limitation stated plainly:** Within the research budget, I did not retrieve primary position statements from the Autistic Self Advocacy Network (ASAN), the National Autistic Society (NAS), or Autism Speaks directly comparing DSM-5 and ICD-11 on neurodiversity grounds. I therefore cannot provide verified, specific citations for those organizations' positions and will not fabricate them. What the gathered evidence does support is the following contextual synthesis:

- The neurodiversity framing is explicitly recognized in the peer-reviewed comparative literature: Kamp-Becker notes that "concepts of neurodiversity and the social model of disability have gained prominence and challenged traditional ideas about ASD as a disorder," describing ASD in this view as "one form of variation within a diversity of minds" where difficulties reflect "a poor fit between individual's characteristics and demands by the environment," and observes that ICD-11 moves "further away from an observable, behavioral, and neurodevelopmental disorder (medical model) to a disorder of inner experience in sense of 'diversity' and 'identity' (social model)" (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/).
- The ICD-11 innovations review highlights features plausibly aligned with neurodiversity-affirming practice: recognition that distress/impairment may emerge only when societal demands increase (e.g., adolescence/adulthood), accommodation of compensation/masking, and inclusion of sensory differences as a legitimate diagnostic feature rather than a peripheral phenomenon (https://cpe.psychopen.eu/index.php/cpe/article/download/10005/10005.pdf; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9881114/).
- Conversely, critics argue ICD-11's flexibility risks diagnostic dilution (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/), while DSM-5's severity levels are criticized as potentially enabling service denial (e.g., insurers limiting coverage for "level 1 ASD") (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10904885/) — a concern typically shared by disability-rights and self-advocacy communities.

**Recommendation:** to complete Section D with specific citations, the ASAN position statements, NAS "About autism/diagnosis" guidance, and Autism Speaks policy pages should be retrieved directly in a follow-up search.

---

## (E) Diagnostic Safety Risks

**Risks associated with ICD-11's broader, uncounted operationalization (per gathered evidence):**
1. **False positives / over-diagnosis.** Kamp-Becker argues that with no mandatory symptom count and 304 possible manifestation combinations, "any arbitrary symptom presentation would justify an ASD diagnosis," creating "a large danger of false positive diagnoses" and further prevalence increases (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/).
2. **Non-falsifiable diagnoses via compensation.** ICD-11's repeated invocation of compensation and the statement that diagnosis remains appropriate when deficits are hidden by "exceptional effort" undermines observable-behavior thresholds and retrospective-onset verification, risking diagnoses unsupported by measurable features (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/).
3. **Missed alternative diagnoses.** False-positive ASD under broad criteria can delay disorder-specific care; Kamp-Becker cites the example of borderline personality disorder patients missing dialectical behavior therapy, and notes ~80% of autistic individuals have at least one comorbid disorder, complicating differential diagnosis (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/).
4. **Service-access dilution.** Over-inclusive criteria may strain ASD-specific services, limiting access for true-positive individuals (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/).

**Risks associated with DSM-5's thresholded operationalization:**
1. **Under-diagnosis / lost diagnoses.** Multiple studies show DSM-5 identifies fewer cases than DSM-IV/ICD-10 systems: 56% concordance in a UK adult clinic (https://research-information.bris.ac.uk/en/publications/comparison-of-icd-10r-dsm-iv-tr-and-dsm-5-in-an-adult-autism-spec/), 43%→25% diagnostic drop in an Italian cohort (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/348585053_The_Impact_of_DSM-5_on_the_Diagnosis_of_Autism_Spectrum_Disorder), and reduced sensitivity (0.837 vs. 0.946) with disproportionate misclassification of PDD-NOS cases in Singapore (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29705921/). Reduced rates "may mean some ASD individuals will be unable to access clinical services" (https://research-information.bris.ac.uk/en/publications/comparison-of-icd-10r-dsm-iv-tr-and-dsm-5-in-an-adult-autism-spec/).
2. **Severity-level harms.** DSM-5 Levels 1–3 were never field tested and lack validity/reliability evidence; they "may have the potential to do more harm than good (e.g., if insurance providers attempt to limit coverage for individuals with 'level 1 ASD')" (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10904885/).
3. **Instrument misuse.** Overreliance on ADOS/ADI-R scores contributes to misdiagnosis because instrument sensitivity/specificity varies with developmental and behavioral factors (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10904885/).

**Sensory-focused presentations specifically:**
- Under **DSM-5**, an individual whose primary atypicality is sensory (e.g., pronounced auditory/tactile hypersensitivity without clear stereotyped movements, routines, or fixated interests) cannot satisfy Criterion B alone (needs ≥2 of 4); such presentations risk under-diagnosis or rerouting to anxiety/other diagnoses. Sensory symptoms must also be integrated with Criterion A social-communication deficits, which are mandatory.
- Under **ICD-11**, sensory manifestations are explicitly named (including "lifelong" hyper-/hyposensitivity and unusual interest in sensory stimuli), which may improve recognition of sensory-dominant presentations, but the absence of thresholds means the same presentations could also contribute to over-inclusive diagnoses when social-communication evidence is weak (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/; https://www.psykiatriantutkimussaatio.fi/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Keski_Rahkonen_Table-1-ICD-11-diagnostic-criteria-for-autism-1.pdf).
- The meta-analytic link between sensory differences and internalizing/externalizing problems (63 studies; 11,659 participants; strong associations for hypersensitivity) (https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/367117/1/367117.pdf) implies that sensory-dominant presentations carry real clinical needs; both under-recognition (DSM-5 threshold risk) and non-specific treatment following over-broad labeling (ICD-11 risk) are plausible harms.
- Inappropriate-intervention risk: sensory integration therapy is reviewed as an emerging evidence-based practice for ASD (16 articles, 2013–2023, PRISMA-based review) but mainly in clinical settings, with a stated need for research in naturalistic settings (https://www.mdpi.com/2227-9067/11/10/1222); misdiagnosis driven by criteria differences could channel children toward or away from such interventions inappropriately.

---

## (F) Reimbursement / Coding Summary

**United States.**
- US billing uses **ICD-10-CM**, not ICD-11. DSM-5/DSM-5-TR ASD (299.00) maps to ICD-10-CM **F84.0** (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK525976/), and the AAP Autism Toolkit maintains an explicit "Relationship Between DSM-5 and ICD-10-CM" mapping resource for pediatric billing (https://publications.aap.org/toolkits/pages/Autism-Toolkit).
- Because US reimbursement keys off ICD-10-CM codes rather than DSM criterion text, **adoption of ICD-11 criteria per se would not change US coverage** unless and until CMS implements an ICD-11-based clinical modification — for which there is no evidence in the gathered sources. The more immediate US reimbursement risk identified in the literature is payer misuse of DSM-5 severity levels (e.g., limiting coverage for "level 1 ASD") (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10904885/).

**EU / international.**
- ICD-11 was approved by the World Health Assembly in 2019 and is WHO's standard for member-state health reporting; WHO field studies support its clinical implementation (https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/dcf73611-9e0f-4d5c-85f6-85a58b0da6de/content). EU member states implement ICD-11 on national timelines; the gathered sources do not document country-by-country EU reimbursement switches, so I state this as an evidence gap rather than assert specifics.
- Coding structure differs materially: ICD-11's 6A02 subcategories (.0–.5, .Y, .Z) encode intellectual-development and functional-language status rather than DSM-5's severity levels (https://www.mrcpsych.uk/2023/01/icd-11-criteria-for-autism-spectrum-disorder.html.html). Where EU payers require ICD-11 codes, the switch from ICD-10 F84.x to 6A02.x changes the coded phenotype (single spectrum category with ID/language qualifiers) but, per the harmonization analysis, the clinical threshold for ASD is broadly comparable between ICD-11 and DSM-5, with differences concentrated in operational strictness rather than construct definition (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/wps.20825).
- Practical implication: in systems transitioning to ICD-11, coverage decisions tied to subtype codes (e.g., 6A02.1/.3/.5 with co-occurring disorder of intellectual development) may shift resource allocation compared with DSM-5 severity-level-based decisions; ICD-11 behavioural indicators for intellectual severity were found clinically useful but classified more individuals as mild severity than standardized measures (n=116; four sites) (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jir.13146), a finding with potential reimbursement relevance.

---

## Summary of Certainty

- **High confidence:** textual differences between DSM-5 and ICD-11 (sensory as countable B4 subcriterion vs. uncounted manifestation; severity levels vs. ID/language subcategories; no ICD-11 symptom threshold) — verified across multiple primary/secondary sources.
- **Moderate confidence:** ICD-11 field-study superiority over ICD-10 (meta-analytic support, but comparator is not DSM-5).
- **Low confidence / evidence gaps:** direct DSM-5 vs. ICD-11 sensitivity/specificity (no head-to-head study found); specific advocacy-organization positions (primary statements not retrieved); EU payer-by-payer reimbursement effects (not documented in gathered sources). These gaps are flagged for follow-up research rather than filled by inference.

final.content:
# Transitional Justice After Mass Atrocities: A Comparative Analysis of Truth Commissions, Prosecutions, Reparations, and Lustration

## 1. Executive Summary

This report compares four families of transitional justice mechanisms across nine cases: truth and reconciliation commissions (South Africa; Canada's residential schools commission), prosecutorial tribunals (ICTY; ICC in Kenya and Sudan), reparations programs (German Holocaust compensation; U.S. Japanese American redress), and lustration policies (post-communist Eastern Europe). Three conclusions emerge from the evidence:

1. **No single mechanism achieves all three goals** (serving victims, enabling democratic transition, preventing recurrence). The most rigorous cross-national study, covering 848 mechanisms in 161 countries (1970–2007), found that single mechanisms deployed alone had no statistically significant positive effects on democracy or human rights; only **combinations**—particularly prosecutions paired with amnesties, with or without truth commissions—were associated with improvements (https://pure.ulster.ac.uk/ws/portalfiles/portal/11383686/Book_Review_Olsen_et_al.pdf; https://www.cmi.no/publications/file/5018-from-impunity-to-accountability-for-human-rights.pdf).

2. **Each mechanism has a comparative advantage and a characteristic failure mode.** Truth commissions excel at victim recognition and authoritative truth but fail when recommendations (especially reparations and reform) are not implemented. Prosecutions have the strongest statistical association with reduced future repression, but collapse without enforcement cooperation (Kenya, Sudan). Reparations serve victims most directly when adequately funded and individualized, but breed betrayal when tokenistic. Lustration protects new institutions but risks weaponization.

3. **The best outcomes come from integrated, sequenced packages with enforcement capacity and long-term funding.** Canada's residential schools response (settlement payments + individualized abuse adjudication + truth commission + Calls to Action) is the most complete integrated model, though its implementation record is poor. Germany's seven-decade reparations program shows that sustained, expanding commitment converts a symbolic mechanism into a durable norm.

---

## 2. The Comparative Evidence Base

Before the case analysis, the quantitative literature sets the frame:

- **Olsen, Payne & Reiter, *Transitional Justice in Balance* (2010)**: Using the Transitional Justice Data Base (848 mechanisms—trials, truth commissions, amnesties, reparations, lustration—in 161 countries, 1970–2007), the authors found no single mechanism improves democracy or human rights on its own. Combinations of **prosecutions and amnesties** (with or without truth commissions) increased the likelihood of improved democracy and human rights measures (https://bookstore.usip.org/browse/book/9781601270535/Transitional%20Justice%20In%20Balance; https://ref2014impact.azurewebsites.net/casestudies2/refservice.svc/GetCaseStudyPDF/15527).

- **Sikkink & Walling (2007), *Journal of Peace Research***: Across Latin America 1979–2004, human rights trials did **not** undermine democracy, increase human rights violations, or exacerbate conflict—refuting the "trial skeptics." This study made no positive-effect claims, only negative ones (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0022343307078953).

- **Kim & Sikkink (2010), *International Studies Quarterly***: In 100 transitional countries, human rights prosecutions after transition led to improvements in human rights protection, with deterrence effects spilling over beyond the prosecuting country. Prosecutions outperformed truth commissions, which lack material punishment (https://academic.oup.com/isq/article-abstract/54/4/939/1833203; https://www.iilj.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/Sikkink-Explaining-the-Deterrence-Effect-of-Human-Rights-Prosecution-ofr-Transitional-Countries-2009.pdf).

- **Dancy, Payne et al. (2019), "Behind Bars and Bargains"**: The one constant across 15 years of updated datasets is "the association of human rights prosecutions with a decline in core human rights violations" (https://ksikkink.scholars.harvard.edu/blog/deterrence-and-impunity-insights-human-rights-prosecutions-international-anti).

Caveat: these are cross-national correlations with selection problems (countries that choose trials may differ systematically); the case studies below show how context determines whether the statistical tendencies materialize.

---

## 3. Truth and Reconciliation Commissions

### 3.1 South Africa's TRC (1996–2003)

**Design and scale.** The TRC combined a Human Rights Violations Committee (victim hearings), an Amnesty Committee (conditional amnesty for full disclosure of politically motivated acts), and a Reparation and Rehabilitation Committee. It received over 21,000 victim statements, identified more than 19,050 victims of gross human rights violations (plus 2,975 more identified through amnesty applications), and documented roughly 7,000 political deaths between 1948 and 1989 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truth_and_Reconciliation_Commission_(South_Africa); https://sahistory.org.za/sites/default/files/volume_2_0.pdf).

**Amnesty arithmetic.** Of ~7,111–7,124 amnesty applications, only 849 were granted and 5,392 refused (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truth_and_Reconciliation_Commission_(South_Africa)). An alternative count of applications actually adjudicated finds 1,167 full amnesties and 145 partial amnesties against 362 denials (https://www.files.ethz.ch/isn/178073/accountability_and_national_reconciliation_in_south_africa.pdf). Either way, the amnesty rate against total applications was roughly 12–18%. Crucially, fewer than 300 apartheid security-force members were heard, nearly all low- or mid-ranking, and there was "near lack of overlap" between victim statements and amnesty applications—truth was purchased largely without perpetrator accountability for the worst architects of apartheid (https://www.files.ethz.ch/isn/178073/accountability_and_national_reconciliation_in_south_africa.pdf).

**Strengths.** Public hearings restored victim dignity and "made it impossible for South Africans ever again to deny" that violations occurred (https://www.nelsonmandela.org/uploads/files/TRC-Report-1998.pdf). Applying to all sides avoided "victor's justice" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truth_and_Reconciliation_Commission_(South_Africa)).

**The reparations failure.** The TRC recommended individual reparation grants benchmarked to median income (~R21,700/year components) (https://sabctrc.saha.org.za/reports/volume5/chapter5/subsection8.htm). The government instead paid a one-off R30,000 (≈$3,900 in 2003) to only ~17,000–17,399 "closed list" victims—about R556 million total—while the President's Fund sat on roughly R1–1.5 billion (≈$110 million untouched as of 2025) (https://groundup.news/article/apartheid-compensation-process-flawed-says-khulumani/; https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cp8yz0e22dro). The Khulumani Support Group, representing ~100,000 victims, has protested for two decades; victims describe the payout as "an insult" and the process as "deep betrayal" (https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/2020-11-08-the-unfinished-business-of-the-trc-is-killing-us-say-apartheids-victims/; https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cp8yz0e22dro). Government failure to implement TRC recommendations is "one of the TRC's most serious weaknesses" (https://unisapressjournals.co.za/index.php/SAPL/article/download/2929/1723/14748).

**Assessment.** The SA TRC served victims' need for recognition and produced an undeniable historical record, and it helped stabilize a negotiated transition. But it traded criminal accountability for truth at the top level, and its unimplemented reparations left identified victims impoverished—showing that a truth commission without follow-through on material redress and prosecution re-victimizes.

### 3.2 Canada's TRC on Residential Schools (2008–2015)

**Design and scale.** Created under the Indian Residential Schools Settlement Agreement (IRSSA) with a $72 million budget, the TRC heard from ~6,500–7,000 survivors and witnesses over six years and issued its final report with 94 Calls to Action in December 2015 (https://www.cirnac.gc.ca/eng/1524494530110/1557511412801; https://nctr.ca/wp-content/uploads/2021/01/Calls_to_Action_English2.pdf). It documented a system operating from the 1870s to 1997 affecting ~150,000 children, concluded the policy amounted to cultural genocide, and its Missing Children Project laid groundwork later confirmed by the 2021 discovery of unmarked graves (https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Residential_Schools_Settlement_Agreement; https://www.cirnac.gc.ca/eng/1524504992259/1557512149981).

**Integrated with reparations.** Unlike South Africa, Canada's commission was embedded in the largest class-action settlement in Canadian history: a C$1.9 billion Common Experience Payment (~C$20,457 average; ~C$1.62 billion paid to 79,309 former students by 2016) plus the Independent Assessment Process for abuse claims (38,276 claims received; $3.23 billion paid; ~28,000 claimants compensated; 89% of heard claims awarded; average adjudicated award ≈$91,460) (https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Residential_Schools_Settlement_Agreement; https://www.iap-pei.ca/story-eng.php; https://www.cbc.ca/news/indigenous/iap-final-report-residential-schools-1.5946103). Total compensation thus exceeded roughly C$5 billion—orders of magnitude above South Africa's R556 million.

**The implementation gap.** The 94 Calls to Action are far from fulfilled. The Assembly of First Nations counted only ~13 completed in ten years, with zero completed in 2023–2024 and only two in five years (https://afn.bynder.com/m/21a223c344077b7/original/Progress-on-Realizing-the-Truth-and-Reconciliation-Commission-s-Calls-to-Action-September-2025.pdf; https://afn.bynder.com/asset/36043b91-4f8c-405e-8199-25c886017877/TRC-Report-Card-2024.pdf). Yellowhead Institute found 81 of 94 calls unfulfilled after eight years (https://yellowheadinstitute.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/YI-TRC-C2A-2023-Special-Report-compressed.pdf). The government's claim that "more than 85%" of the 76 federally-led calls are "completed or well underway" is materially more optimistic than independent trackers (https://www.cirnac.gc.ca/eng/1524494530110/1557511412801).

**Assessment.** Canada demonstrates the strongest *design* integration—reparations first, truth second, structural reform calls third—and it materially served victims better than South Africa. But the slow implementation of structural Calls to Action (child welfare, justice, health) shows that even a well-funded truth commission cannot compel political follow-through on its own.

---

## 4. Prosecutorial Tribunals

### 4.1 The ICTY (1993–2017)

**Output.** The ICTY indicted 161 individuals—all accounted for, including final fugitives Karadžić and Mladić. It completed proceedings against 109 with **90 convictions and 19 acquittals** (a conviction rate of ~82.6% among those tried to completion; 55.9% of all indicted), referred 13 cases to national courts, and terminated/withdrew 37 (https://www.icty.org/en/cases/key-figures-cases; https://www.icty.org/sites/icty.org/files/articles/attachments/2017/171212-prosecutor-brammertz-remarks-washington.pdf; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Criminal_Tribunal_for_Yugoslavia). Over 24 years it held 10,800+ trial days, heard 4,650+ witnesses, and produced 2.5 million pages of transcripts; its final biennium budget alone was $105.8 million (https://news.un.org/en/story/2017/12/640022-feature-curtain-falls-un-tribunals-24-year-history-fighting-impunity-former; https://static.un.org/en/ga/fifth/72/Statements/147_148_ITY_IRM/C5_72_0m_ST_2017_12_19_Item147_148_ITY_ASG%20Controller.pdf). Karadžić received 40 years; Mladić life, for the Srebrenica genocide (https://news.un.org/en/story/2017/12/640022-feature-curtain-falls-un-tribunals-24-year-history-fighting-impunity-former).

**Impact on victims and truth.** The tribunal individualized guilt, established genocide at Srebrenica as adjudicated fact, and gave victims a platform. For Bosniak victims it was the preferred forum, though legitimacy perceptions split sharply along ethnic lines (https://exa.ai/library/publication/bhds3dnqmvn).

**Impact on reconciliation: largely negative among target populations.** Survey evidence shows the ICTY failed to persuade: barely one-fifth of Bosnian Serbs believe any crime happened at Srebrenica, two-fifths never heard of it, and only ~10% of Serbs accept the ICTY's established facts; acceptance of other crimes is in single digits. Denialism tracks ethnicity and perceived anti-group bias (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2755505; https://centaur.reading.ac.uk/108020/). In Bosnia, each group still casts its own forces as "defenders" (89–93% within-group agreement), and Dayton-era elite narratives froze the conflict's memory politics (https://exa.ai/library/publication/vz5cxlc6726). Media-frame analysis found tribunal decisions changed narratives mainly in democratic countries with pluralist media (https://academic.oup.com/ijtj/article-pdf/13/2/368/28881907/ijz005.pdf).

**Assessment.** The ICTY delivered what prosecutions do best—authoritative fact-finding, individualized guilt, punishment of the most responsible—and it did not destabilize the region (consistent with Sikkink & Walling's finding that trials do not harm democracy). But a distant tribunal cannot change societal beliefs where local elites sustain denial; its preventive effect depends on domestic follow-through (3,000+ investigations remain in Sarajevo alone) (https://www.icty.org/sites/icty.org/files/articles/attachments/2017/171212-prosecutor-brammertz-remarks-washington.pdf).

### 4.2 The ICC in Kenya (2007–08 post-election violence)

After ~1,200 people were killed, the ICC summoned six high-profile suspects in 2011. Charges against Kosgey and Ali were not confirmed (January 2012); charges against Muthaura were withdrawn (March 2013); proceedings against Uhuru Kenyatta were terminated (March 2015); and the Ruto/Sang case was terminated on 5 April 2016 without prejudice to re-prosecution (https://www.icc-cpi.int/kenya/rutosang; https://www.icc-cpi.int/kenya/kenyatta; https://www.icc-cpi.int/news/ruto-and-sang-case-icc-trial-chamber-va-terminates-case-without-prejudice-re-prosecution). The collapse was driven by **17 prosecution witnesses withdrawing cooperation** under intimidation, bribery, and political meddling; one judge declared a mistrial due to "troubling incidence of witness interference and intolerable political meddling" (https://www.icc-cpi.int/news/statement-prosecutor-international-criminal-court-fatou-bensouda-regarding-trial-chambers; https://www.bbc.com/news/world-africa-35965760; https://apnews.com/general-news-c6fcbeba676b40c389a9524b7f0e50ef). Kenyatta and Ruto were elected President and Deputy President in 2013 *while under indictment*, and an anti-ICC campaign followed (https://www.coalitionfortheicc.org/country/kenya).

**Assessment.** Kenya is the cautionary case for prosecutions: without witness protection and domestic cooperation, even confirmed charges evaporate, and victims were "for now…denied the justice they so rightly deserve" (https://www.icc-cpi.int/news/statement-prosecutor-international-criminal-court-fatou-bensouda-regarding-trial-chambers). It also shows suspects can convert indictment into electoral mobilization.

### 4.3 The ICC in Sudan (Darfur)

The Security Council referred Darfur via Resolution 1593 (31 March 2005). The ICC issued the first-ever warrant for a sitting head of state against Omar al-Bashir (4 March 2009), adding genocide counts (12 July 2010) (https://www.icc-cpi.int/darfur/albashir; https://www.icc-cpi.int/news/icc-issues-warrant-arrest-omar-al-bashir-president-sudan). For over a decade **no suspect was surrendered**; al-Bashir traveled openly to States Parties (Kenya, Chad, Djibouti, Malawi, DRC) that refused arrest, generating repeated non-cooperation findings (https://www.icc-cpi.int/darfur/albashir; https://www.icc-cpi.int/sites/default/files/itemsDocuments/181214-rep-otp-UNSC-1593_ENG.pdf). Prosecutor Bensouda told the Security Council in 2014 that crimes continued "with total impunity" and, asked whether the ICC had achieved anything concrete for Darfur victims: "the intellectually honest answer is a resounding 'No'" (https://www.icc-cpi.int/sites/default/files/iccdocs/otp/otp-statement-23-06-2014.pdf). After al-Bashir's 2019 ouster he was tried domestically for the 1989 coup, not surrendered; as of mid-2021 four warrants remained outstanding (https://www.icc-cpi.int/sites/default/files/itemsDocuments/2021-06-09-otp-report-unsc-darfour-eng.pdf).

**Assessment.** Sudan demonstrates the ICC's structural limit: it has no police. A referral without Security Council enforcement backing produces a warrant that stigmatizes but neither punishes nor deters while the regime holds power.

---

## 5. Reparations Programs

### 5.1 Germany's Holocaust Reparations (1952–present)

The Luxembourg Agreements (10 September 1952), signed by Adenauer, Sharett (Israel), and Goldmann (Claims Conference), committed West Germany to DM 3 billion (~$714 million) to Israel over twelve years and DM 450 million to the Claims Conference, plus legislation for individual indemnification (https://www.state.gov/reports/just-act-report-to-congress/germany; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reparations_Agreement_between_Israel_and_the_Federal_Republic_of_Germany; https://jewishvirtuallibrary.org/jsource/judaica/ejud_0002_0005_0_04564.html).

**Cumulative scale (verifying the arithmetic).** Reported totals vary with exchange rates and cutoff dates: ~$86.8 billion by 2018 (U.S. State Department), more than €80 billion by end-2021 (Chancellor Scholz), and "more than $90 billion" per Claims Conference-affiliated accounts (https://www.state.gov/reports/just-act-report-to-congress/germany; https://www.claimscon.org/2022/09/german-chancellor-and-claims-conference-meet-to-mark-70th-anniversary-of-historic-reparations-agreements-and-announce-negotiations-results-of-over-1-2-billion/; https://teachjewishhistory.org/topic-restitution). The consistent finding: seven decades of continuous, expanding payments through a dozen programs (Article 2 Fund, Hardship Fund, Child Survivor Fund, home care), with ~196,600 survivors still receiving support as of January 2026 and a further $1.2 billion negotiated for 2023 (https://www.claimscon.org/2022/09/german-chancellor-and-claims-conference-meet-to-mark-70th-anniversary-of-historic-reparations-agreements-and-announce-negotiations-results-of-over-1-2-billion/; https://teachjewishhistory.org/topic-restitution). Germany also returned 16,000 looted objects over 20 years (https://www.state.gov/reports/just-act-report-to-congress/germany).

**Assessment.** This is the strongest evidence that reparations, when sustained and institutionalized, serve victims materially (pensions, home care) and anchor a "culture of remembrance" that supports non-recurrence. Its limits: it was negotiated with a successor state, excluded East Germany entirely, and cannot be said to have "compensated" the murder of six million Jews—its value is acknowledgment plus material care for survivors.

### 5.2 U.S. Japanese American Internment Redress (1988–1999)

The Commission on Wartime Relocation and Internment of Civilians (1980–83) heard 750+ witnesses in 11 cities and concluded in *Personal Justice Denied* that internment resulted from "race prejudice, war hysteria, and a failure of political leadership" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Liberties_Act_of_1988). The Civil Liberties Act of 1988 (signed by Reagan) apologized, paid **$20,000 per surviving internee**, and created a public education fund explicitly "to prevent the recurrence of any similar event" (https://uscode.ecfr.io/statutes/pl/100/383.pdf; https://www.govtrack.us/congress/bills/100/hr442/summary).

**Arithmetic check.** 82,219 recipients × $20,000 = $1.644 billion—matching the Justice Department's final figure of "more than $1.6 billion" paid before the Office of Redress Administration closed on 5 February 1999 (https://www.justice.gov/archive/opa/pr/1999/February/059cr.htm). $20,000 in 1988 ≈ $40,000–46,000 in later dollars (https://www.govtrack.us/congress/bills/100/hr442/summary; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Liberties_Act_of_1988).

**Assessment.** This is the cleanest "truth → apology → individual payment → education" sequence in the record. It was feasible because the victim population was bounded, identifiable, and the perpetrator was a stable democracy acknowledging its own act. Its preventive ambition (education fund) is explicit but its actual preventive effect is unmeasurable; it did, however, become a template for later redress movements.

---

## 6. Lustration Policies (Post-Communist Eastern Europe)

**Definition and scope.** Lustration vetted public officials for collaboration with communist-era security services. It was administrative rather than criminal (except in Poland, where courts were involved), and unique to post-communist contexts (https://https-sage-cnpereading-com-443.webvpn1.xju.edu.cn/doi/10.1177/08883254231163183). It was pursued most systematically in Germany, the Czech Republic, Poland, and Hungary; only the Baltic states adopted it in the post-Soviet space, and Russia essentially did not (https://www.sussex.ac.uk/webteam/gateway/file.php?name=sei-working-paper-no-62.pdf&site=266; https://https-sage-cnpereading-com-443.webvpn1.xju.edu.cn/doi/10.1177/08883254231163183).

**Country variation.**
- **Germany** (the most extensive): The Stasi Records Act (20 December 1991) created the Gauck/Birthler/BStU agency, at peak employing ~3,400 staff. Almost 2.17 million citizens accessed their own files; 520,000 applications arrived in 1992 alone, and over 1.3 million by 1997. Public-sector screening was time-limited (the main 15-year review window expired December 2006) (https://dserver.bundestag.de/btd/19/276/1927600.pdf; https://www.bundesarchiv.de/assets/bundesarchiv/de/Downloads/bstu_08-taetigkeitsbericht_2007.pdf; https://americangerman.institute/wp-content/uploads/2011/11/legner.pdf). It combined disclosure, vetting, and victim access to files—widely considered the "model" (https://enrs.eu/article/unread-files).
- **Czech Republic**: a "semi-retributive" model adopted earliest (1991), judged relatively successful in its first years (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/law-and-social-inquiry/article/abs/lustration-laws-in-action-the-motives-and-evaluation-of-lustration-policy-in-the-czech-republic-and-poland-19892001/A54F46A5C8E41697959589830750116C).
- **Poland**: a "semi-reconciliatory," delayed model (1997 law), repeatedly politicized—symbolized by the Wałęsa informant controversy—and described as a "dossier game" serving those in power (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/law-and-social-inquiry/article/abs/lustration-laws-in-action-the-motives-and-evaluation-of-lustration-policy-in-the-czech-republic-and-poland-19892001/A54F46A5C8E41697959589830750116C; https://enrs.eu/article/unread-files).
- **Hungary**: comparatively weak vetting (https://www.sussex.ac.uk/webteam/gateway/file.php?name=sei-working-paper-no-62.pdf&site=266).

**Why the variation and delay?** Monika Nalepa's *Skeletons in the Closet* shows lustration timing was driven by elite bargaining, not voter demand: outgoing communists transferred power partly because opposition leaders were themselves infiltrated ("skeletons in the closet"), making amnesty commitments credible; lustration laws were often passed late and sometimes championed by ex-communists to preempt harsher measures (https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/skeletons-in-the-closet/6A7A40E2F117798F319AD0BA8C0A3A74; https://www.foreignaffairs.com/reviews/capsule-review/2010-09-01/skeletons-closet-transitional-justice-post-communist-europe).

**Assessment.** Lustration's core contribution is *institutional*: removing or exposing secret-police collaborators from public office to build trust in new democratic institutions. Disclosure-based, time-limited, file-access models (Germany) performed better than punitive or politicized ones. The key risk—demonstrated in Poland—is weaponization of files against opponents, and selective enforcement has been linked to democratic backsliding (https://www.academia.edu/1084210/Skeletons_in_the_Closet_Transitional_Justice_in_the_PostCommunist_World). Lustration serves victims least directly of the four mechanisms; its value is preventive and institutional.

---

## 7. Cross-Mechanism Comparison

**Scale of material delivery to victims (approximate, from sources above):**

| Case | Mechanism | Material scale | Per-victim magnitude |
|---|---|---|---|
| Germany/Holocaust | Reparations | ~$86.8–90B+ over 70 years | Pensions/home care for hundreds of thousands; sustained |
| Canada/IRS | Reparations + TRC | ~C$1.9B (CEP) + $3.23B (IAP) ≈ C$5B+ | CEP avg ~C$20,457; IAP avg award ~$91,460–111,265 |
| U.S./internment | Reparations | $1.64B | $20,000 × 82,219 (by construction) |
| South Africa | TRC + reparations | ~R556M paid; ~R1B+ unspent | R30,000 (~$3,900) × ~17,000 |
| ICTY | Prosecution | $105.8M final biennium alone | Justice/truth, not payments |
| ICC Kenya/Sudan | Prosecution | — | $0 delivered; cases collapsed/dormant |

(Sources as cited in sections 3–6. Canada figures: https://www.iap-pei.ca/story-eng.php, https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Residential_Schools_Settlement_Agreement; U.S.: https://www.justice.gov/archive/opa/pr/1999/February/059cr.htm; SA: https://groundup.news/article/apartheid-compensation-process-flawed-says-khulumani/; ICTY: https://static.un.org/en/ga/fifth/72/Statements/147_148_ITY_IRM/C5_72_0m_ST_2017_12_19_Item147_148_ITY_ASG%20Controller.pdf.)

**Scorecard against the three goals (evidence-based, not normative):**

| Mechanism | Serves victims | Enables democratic transition | Prevents recurrence | Characteristic failure |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Truth commissions | High (dignity, record)—SA, Canada | Medium (SA stabilized pacted transition) | Low–medium unless implemented | Unimplemented recommendations (SA reparations; Canada's 81/94 unfulfilled) |
| Prosecutions | Medium (justice, not material) | Neutral-to-positive (trials did not harm democracy—Sikkink & Walling) | **Highest statistical support** (Kim & Sikkink deterrence) | Enforcement collapse (Kenya, Sudan); no attitude change where elites deny (ICTY surveys) |
| Reparations | **Highest when funded/individualized** (Germany, U.S., Canada IAP) | Low–medium (legitimizes new order) | Medium via acknowledgment/education | Tokenism and exclusion (SA R30,000 closed list) |
| Lustration | Low (institutional, not victim-centered) | High (institutional trust-building) | Medium (vetting; risk of backlash) | Weaponization/dossier politics (Poland); delay by elite bargaining (Nalepa) |

---

## 8. Which Approaches Best Serve the Three Goals?

**Serving victims.** Reparations are the most direct instrument, and the evidence shows magnitude, individualization, and duration determine whether victims feel served. Germany's sustained multi-program system and Canada's IAP (89% award rate, ~$91,460 average) contrast sharply with South Africa's R30,000 one-off, which victims experienced as betrayal (https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cp8yz0e22dro; https://www.iap-pei.ca/story-eng.php; https://www.claimscon.org/2022/09/german-chancellor-and-claims-conference-meet-to-mark-70th-anniversary-of-historic-reparations-agreements-and-announce-negotiations-results-of-over-1-2-billion/). Truth commissions add the non-material goods victims consistently request—acknowledgment, dignity, truth—which the SA and Canadian hearings delivered (https://www.nelsonmandela.org/uploads/files/TRC-Report-1998.pdf; https://www.cirnac.gc.ca/eng/1524494530110/1557511412801). Prosecutions serve victims' justice claims but deliver no material relief, and when they collapse (Kenya) or never begin (Sudan) they compound victimization.

**Enabling democratic transitions.** The strongest evidence favors *moderate, combined* approaches. Olsen, Payne & Reiter found prosecutions-plus-amnesties combinations—not any pure strategy—correlated with democratic improvement (https://pure.ulster.ac.uk/ws/portalfiles/portal/11383686/Book_Review_Olsen_et_al.pdf). Lustration, where disclosure-based and time-limited (Germany, early Czech model), helped build institutional trust; where politicized (Poland), it corroded politics (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/law-and-social-inquiry/article/abs/lustration-laws-in-action-the-motives-and-evaluation-of-lustration-policy-in-the-czech-republic-and-poland-19892001/A54F46A5C8E41697959589830750116C; https://enrs.eu/article/unread-files). Trials did not destabilize Latin American democracies (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0022343307078953), but the ICC Kenya experience shows indictments can be converted into electoral assets in fragile settings (https://www.coalitionfortheicc.org/country/kenya).

**Preventing recurrence.** This is where prosecutions have the best quantitative record: Kim & Sikkink found post-transition prosecutions improve human rights protection with cross-border deterrence, outperforming truth commissions alone (https://academic.oup.com/isq/article-abstract/54/4/939/1833203), and the Dancy/Payne line of work confirms the association with declining core violations (https://ksikkink.scholars.harvard.edu/blog/deterrence-and-impunity-insights-human-rights-prosecutions-international-anti). But the ICTY survey evidence imposes a hard limit: adjudicated truth does not become social truth where elites sustain denial—barely one-fifth of Bosnian Serbs accept Srebrenica facts (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2755505; https://centaur.reading.ac.uk/108020/). Preventive impact therefore requires domestic uptake: pluralist media and democratic politics mediate whether tribunal findings change narratives (https://academic.oup.com/ijtj/article-pdf/13/2/368/28881907/ijz005.pdf). Reparations with explicit education mandates (U.S. Civil Liberties Act) and remembrance cultures (Germany) are the mechanisms most explicitly designed for non-recurrence, though their causal effect is harder to measure (https://uscode.ecfr.io/statutes/pl/100/383.pdf; https://www.state.gov/reports/just-act-report-to-congress/germany).

**The integrated answer.** The cases that came closest to serving all three goals combined mechanisms:
- **Canada**: settlement reparations → individualized abuse adjudication → truth commission → structural Calls to Action. Best design; weakest implementation (only ~13 of 94 calls complete) (https://afn.bynder.com/m/21a223c344077b7/original/Progress-on-Realizing-the-Truth-and-Reconciliation-Commission-s-Calls-to-Action-September-2025.pdf).
- **Germany**: negotiated reparations + restitution + sustained remembrance, embedded in a consolidated democracy that could absorb the reckoning (https://www.state.gov/reports/just-act-report-to-congress/germany).
- **South Africa**: truth + conditional amnesty stabilized the transition but left accountability thin at the top and reparations unimplemented—its unfinished business continues to harm victims 25+ years later (https://unisapressjournals.co.za/index.php/SAPL/article/download/2929/1723/14748; https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cp8yz0e22dro).
- **ICTY + domestic courts**: prosecutions established facts and punished leaders but could not generate inter-ethnic reconciliation without domestic political engagement (https://www.icty.org/sites/icty.org/files/articles/attachments/2017/171212-prosecutor-brammertz-remarks-washington.pdf; https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2755505).
- **ICC Kenya/Sudan**: prosecutions without cooperation fail every goal (https://www.icc-cpi.int/sites/default/files/iccdocs/otp/otp-statement-23-06-2014.pdf; https://www.icc-cpi.int/news/statement-prosecutor-international-criminal-court-fatou-bensouda-regarding-trial-chambers).

---

## 9. Design Principles and Uncertainties

**Design principles supported by the evidence:**
1. **Combine mechanisms; sequence them.** Reparations and truth before or alongside prosecutions; institutional vetting early; keep amnesties conditional and narrow (SA's full-disclosure requirement) rather than blanket.
2. **Fund reparations at scale and individualize them.** The gap between Canada's ~C$5B and South Africa's ~R556M predicts the gap in victim satisfaction.
3. **Bind truth commissions to enforceable implementation.** Canada's Calls to Action show that even a celebrated commission cannot self-enforce; independent monitoring (AFN report cards, CBC Beyond 94) is necessary but not sufficient (https://www.cbc.ca/newsinteractives/beyond-94?cta=26).
4. **Prosecutions require an enforcement plan.** Without arrest capacity and witness protection, indictments can be ignored (Sudan) or hollowed out (Kenya).
5. **Prefer disclosure-based, time-limited lustration with victim file access** over punitive or open-ended vetting.
6. **Plan for narrative contestation.** Courts establish facts; only domestic democratic politics, education, and media convert them into shared memory.

**Stated uncertainties.**
- Cross-national findings (Olsen/Payne/Reiter; Kim/Sikkink) are correlational; selection effects cannot be fully excluded.
- German reparations totals differ by source ($86.8B vs €80B vs $90B+) due to exchange rates and cutoff dates; I report the range rather than a point estimate.
- ICTY conviction counts differ slightly by source (19 vs 21 acquittals depending on whether overturned acquittals are counted); I used the tribunal's own key-figures page (90 sentenced, 19 acquitted) (https://www.icty.org/en/cases/key-figures-cases).
- South Africa amnesty figures differ by counting method (849 granted of 7,111 applications vs 1,167+145 granted among adjudicated cases); both are cited.
- The preventive effect of reparations and education programs (U.S., Germany) is asserted in the statutes and policy discourse but not directly measurable in the sources gathered.
- Canada's government (85% of federal calls "complete or underway") and independent trackers (~13 of 94 complete) disagree sharply on implementation; I present both.

**Bottom line.** Victims are best served by adequately funded, individualized reparations paired with public truth-telling. Democratic transitions are best enabled by moderate combinations—prosecutions with narrowly conditioned amnesties and disclosure-based vetting—rather than maximalist purges or blanket impunity. Recurrence is best prevented by prosecutions (the mechanism with the strongest deterrent evidence), but only when embedded in domestic institutions capable of sustaining the truth they establish. The recurring failure across all nine cases is not the choice of mechanism but the failure of political will to fund, enforce, and implement what each mechanism recommends.

# Platform Selection Report: Farm Management & Traceability for a 5,000-Member Coffee Cooperative (Colombia, Ethiopia, Indonesia)

## 1. Executive Summary

**The two named platforms are not what the selection brief assumes they are.** This is the single most important finding:

- **Olam's AtSource is not a farm-management platform a cooperative can buy.** It is a buyer-facing sustainability-insights service operated by ofi/Olam, scoped exclusively to "ofi and Olam Group product supply chains," with data collected by Olam's own field teams and sold to Olam's customers (brands/roasters) on custom enterprise pricing (https://qa-atsource.olamnet.com/methodology.html; https://www.atsource.io/atsource.html; https://netzerocompare.com/software/atsource). A cooperative only "gets" AtSource by selling coffee to Olam/ofi — and the data then lives in Olam's system.

- **Fairtrace is Fairtrade International's transaction-recording system, not a farm-management tool.** It tracks sales of Fairtrade-certified products (volumes, Fairtrade Premium paid) among Fairtrade-certified supply-chain actors (https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/fairtrade-international/library/2026/trusted-traceability/Fairtrade%20trusted%20traceability%20factsheet-Sept%202026.pdf). However, the surrounding Fairtrade digital ecosystem — especially **Plot Insights**, a free geolocation/deforestation-risk tool for certified coffee and cocoa producer organizations — is genuinely valuable and free if you are Fairtrade-certified (https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/why-we-do-it/deforestation/EN_Plot%20Insights_Guidance%20for%20geolocation%20data%20submission%20and%20management.pdf).

**The real shortlist for a cooperative-owned system** consists of third-party first-mile platforms (Koltiva/KoltiTrace, Farmforce, eProd, CropIn) plus free/open tools (TechnoServe's TerraTrac, KoboToolbox/ODK) and the free Fairtrade tooling. For a budget-limited cooperative of 5,000 members, the evidence supports a **hybrid architecture**: free or low-cost offline mapping tools for the one-time GPS campaign (~USD 4/farm documented benchmark → ~USD 20,000 total), a lightweight cooperative management/traceability layer, and certification-body platforms (Rainforest Alliance RACP, Fairtrade Plot Insights/Fairtrace) used for compliance data exchange rather than as the farm-management core.

**Time pressure is real:** the EU Deforestation Regulation applies to large/medium operators from **30 December 2026** (micro/small enterprises 30 June 2027), requiring plot-level geolocation (point for ≤4 ha, polygon for >4 ha) and proof of no deforestation after 31 December 2020 for coffee entering the EU (https://www.ecf-coffee.org/european-union-deforestation-regulation-eudr/; https://www.complir.io/resources/guides/eudr-compliance-guide). Any platform decision must deliver EUDR-ready GeoJSON exports.

## 2. Critical Clarification of the Two Named Platforms

### 2.1 AtSource (Olam/ofi) — buyer-facing, not cooperative-purchasable

- Launched 2018; provides traceability and 350+ sustainability metrics via a customer dashboard (https://www.atsource.io/atsource.html).
- **Scope restriction:** "AtSource is open to ofi and Olam Group product supply chains. AtSource supply chains include all entities that handle the product from the farm … to the final processing site" (https://qa-atsource.olamnet.com/methodology.html). There is no standalone SaaS license for third-party cooperatives; the contact route is atsource@ofi.com as a sourcing partner.
- **Traceability depth:** AtSourceV and AtSource+ trace "back to Farmer Group level or our estates" — i.e., group-level, not individual plot-level, in the standard tiers (https://qa-atsource.olamnet.com/methodology.html).
- **Data collection model:** "The data for this is collected and analysed by Olam's field teams across our sourcing origins" (https://www.atsource.io/impact/international-coffee-day-how-a-coffee-data-shop--is-helping-reimagine-sustainability.html). The cooperative would be a data subject, not a system owner.
- **Assurance value:** AtSource Entry Verified and AtSource Plus are recognized by the Global Coffee Platform as Baseline Coffee Code-equivalent schemes (https://www.olamgroup.com/news/all-news/press-release/global-coffee-platform-recognises-two-tiers-of-olam-atsource-programme.html).
- **Pricing:** custom enterprise model, publicly undisclosed (https://netzerocompare.com/software/atsource).

**Implication:** AtSource belongs in your evaluation only as a *buyer-integration channel* — if you sell to ofi/Olam, your coffee can be marketed through AtSource. It cannot serve as your cooperative's own farm management and traceability system, and adopting it as your sole data system would hand your member data to a trader (a risk Fairtrade's data-governance research explicitly warns about: producers want to avoid "dependency on buyer-controlled systems" — https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/fairtrade-international/library/2026/trusted-traceability/Fairtrade%20trusted%20traceability%20factsheet-Sept%202026.pdf).

### 2.2 Fairtrace (Fairtrade International) — transaction ledger for certified chains

- Fairtrace records "sales of Fairtrade products … throughout Fairtrade supply chains, recording transactions including volumes traded and Fairtrade Premium paid" (https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/fairtrade-international/library/2026/trusted-traceability/Fairtrade%20trusted%20traceability%20factsheet-Sept%202026.pdf).
- It is **free to use as part of Fairtrade certification** but only for Fairtrade-certified actors; since 2025, reporting the ICO Mark is mandatory for coffee transactions where available, enabling lot-level linkage down the chain (same source).
- **New capability (October 2026):** Fairtrace gains geolocation data exchange, connecting to **Plot Insights** via the GeoLink API: exporters create a trade contract in Fairtrace, the cooperative assigns plots in Plot Insights, and EUDR-ready GeoJSON flows securely to buyer/importer under consent (https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/why-we-do-it/deforestation/Fairtrade-Plot-Insights-Factsheet-2026.pdf).
- **Plot Insights** (the actual farm-plot tool): free for all certified cocoa and coffee small producer organizations; upload/validation of geolocation data, interactive map visualization, near-real-time deforestation risk analysis by Satelligence, EUDR GeoJSON export for the TRACES platform; available in **English, Spanish, Portuguese, French, Indonesian, Vietnamese** (https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/why-we-do-it/deforestation/EN_Plot%20Insights_Guidance%20for%20geolocation%20data%20submission%20and%20management.pdf; https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/why-we-do-it/deforestation/Fairtrade-Plot-Insights-Factsheet-2026.pdf).

**Implication:** If your cooperative is (or will be) Fairtrade-certified, Plot Insights + Fairtrace is the **lowest-cost compliant option for geolocation management and buyer data exchange** — zero license cost, and it covers Spanish (Colombia) and Indonesian (Indonesia), though not Amharic/Afaan Oromo for Ethiopia. It is not, however, a full farm-management system (no agronomy advisories, payments, input-loan tracking, or harvest logistics).

## 3. The Compliance Drivers That Define Your Requirements

### 3.1 EUDR (dominant driver)
- Applies to coffee from **30 December 2026** (large/medium operators) and **30 June 2027** (micro/small enterprises); soluble/instant coffee added from 30 December 2027. After two postponements, the European Commission has stated there will be no further delay (https://www.ecf-coffee.org/european-union-deforestation-regulation-eudr/; https://www.originsnext.com/news/eudr-2026-readiness-guide; https://www.foodnavigator.com/Article/2026-10-05/eudr-will-it-be-simplified-further/).
- Geolocation rule: **GPS point for plots ≤4 ha; polygon for plots >4 ha** (WGS84), plus deforestation analysis against the 31 December 2020 cut-off and legality evidence (https://www.ecf-coffee.org/european-union-deforestation-regulation-eudr/; https://ugandacoffeemerchants.com/insights/eudr-uganda-coffee-importer-timeline).
- Most smallholder coffee plots in Colombia, Ethiopia and Indonesia are under 4 ha, so **points are legally sufficient for most of your 5,000 members** — a major cost saver — though buyers increasingly prefer polygons near forest edges (https://qelvyn.co/en/blog/eudr/farm-plot-mapping-cost-cooperatives-eudr; https://agrosocialservices.co.ke/certification-compliance/eudr-gps-geolocation-kenya-coffee-cooperatives-2026/).
- The EU buyer files the Due Diligence Statement, but the data must originate at farm level and "cannot be reconstructed at the port" (https://anylai.eu/radar/prazos-de-aplicacao-do-eudr-30-de-dezembro-de-2026-e-30-de-junho-de-2027).

### 3.2 Rainforest Alliance 2020 Sustainable Agriculture Standard (v1.4)
- Requirement 1.2.10 (groups): geolocation data for **100% of farms**; **≥35% as GPS polygons at first certification audit; all farm units as polygons by the second audit**. Data must be uploaded to the Rainforest Alliance Certification Platform (RACP); polygons must be collected in the field, not digitized from maps (https://learn.ra.org/mod/page/view.php?id=125526; https://knowledge.rainforest-alliance.org/docs/management-annex; https://www.rainforest-alliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2022-06/SA-S-SD-1-V1.3-2020-Sustainable-Agriculture-Standard-Farm-Requirements_Rainforest-Alliance.pdf).
- RACP also runs an EUDR-aligned geo risk assessment automatically for coffee/cocoa certificate holders (https://knowledge.rainforest-alliance.org/docs/introduction-to-rainforest-alliance-online-systems).
- Certification registration happens via MyRA/Multitrace; traceability of certified volumes is maintained via the RA traceability system plus paper/digital records (https://www.rainforest-alliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2020-06/2020-Sustainable-Agriculture-Standard_Farm-Requirements_Rainforest-Alliance.pdf; https://www.rainforest-alliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2022-01/RA-Traceability-Guidance.pdf).

### 3.3 Fairtrade
- Requires geolocation of all plots for 100% of members cultivating certified coffee/cocoa (standard clauses Cocoa 3.4.5 / Coffee 3.1.6), plots ≥4 ha as polygons; deforestation risk defined as within 500 m of deforestation or ~200 m of protected areas; free Plot Insights tooling provided (https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/why-we-do-it/deforestation/EN_Plot%20Insights_Guidance%20for%20geolocation%20data%20submission%20and%20management.pdf).

**Conclusion for the cooperative:** whatever platform you choose must (a) capture points/polygons offline in the field, (b) export GeoJSON/shapefiles compatible with RACP, Plot Insights/TRACES, and buyer systems, and (c) let you retain ownership and portability of the raw data.

## 5. Detailed Platform Assessments

### 5.1 Koltiva (KoltiTrace) — strongest all-round commercial candidate, especially for Indonesia
- Founded in Indonesia (2013); Swiss-Indonesian; 2M+ registered producers; **475,000+ coffee producers across 23 coffee-producing countries; 1.1M+ ha verified** (https://www.koltiva.com/post/advancing-global-coffee-sustainability-by-empowering-475-000-producers-worldwide).
- Modules: KoltiTrace MIS (traceability, GIS, ERP/CRM), KoltiSkills (paid field teams for producer profiling, polygon mapping, legality), KoltiVerify (EUDR verification), KoltiPay (digital premium payments to farmers — relevant for Fair Trade premium distribution) (https://www.koltiva.com/our-solutions; https://www.koltiva.com/koltiskills; https://www.koltiva.com/koltipay).
- Indonesia depth: Gayo Highlands/Adena Coffee deployment — 1,900 smallholders, 30 villages, EUDR-aligned data capture (https://www.koltiva.com/post/deforestation-free-coffee-supply-chains-adena-coffee-koltiva-eudr-compliance-transparency). Peru PDO cooperative case (1,100 producers, 8 cooperatives) shows cooperative-scale operation (https://www.koltiva.com/post/coffee-traceability-gi-system-cafe-de-villa-rica).
- **Only published price anchors** (GIZ Coffee Innovation Fund handbook, date uncertain — verify): CoffeeTrace platform **$1,200/country/year**; FarmXtension/FarmGate/FarmRetail **$120/user/year each**; FarmCloud (farmer access) **$1/user/year**; one-time registration/tailoring/training quoted separately (https://www.sustainable-supply-chains.org/fileadmin/INA/Erfolgsgeschichten/Kaffeeinnovationsfonds/Recipe_Books/Handbook_Origin_centered_coffee_traceability.pdf). Current pricing is sales-led and unpublished (https://recatools.com/ai-directory/koltiva-traceability/).
- Gap: enterprise-grade; a 5,000-farmer cooperative is a small client; negotiate hard on per-country fees across 3 countries.

### 5.2 Farmforce — best documented evidence for your exact Ethiopia conditions
- ECOM pilot (Farm Africa, Royal Norwegian Embassy-funded, Bale + Illubabor, Ethiopia): **4,543 producers onboarded; 3,619 farms mapped with GPS polygons; 4,548 ha; 80+ field collectors; 8 months** — in semi-forest/forest coffee systems with "GPS signals absorbed by dense canopy," communal tenure, and intermittent mobile coverage. Orbit Mobile's **offline-first architecture** was decisive: "Collectors capture data deep inside forest coffee plots with no signal and sync when they are back in range" (https://farmforce.com/case-studies/farm-africa-case-study/).
- Bag-level traceability (Origin module), polygon drawing linked to unique farmer IDs, Global Forest Watch deforestation overlay, micro-loan tracking, certification audit workflows (https://farmforce.com/products/information-management-system-ims/; https://farmforce.com/articles/brewing-sustainable-agtech-for-the-coffee-supply-chain/).
- Explicit cooperative offering (https://farmforce.com/solutions/cooperatives/). Pricing on request; independent review lists pricing "on request" (https://www.itechguides.com/products/farmforce/).

### 5.3 eProd — strongest basic-phone/USSD and payments story (Africa)
- Offline-first field app; USSD input-loan disbursement and repayment; bank/mobile-money integrations; "EUDR, Organic & Fairtrade compliance built in"; claims 250+ agribusinesses in 20 countries (https://www.eprod-solutions.com/solutions; https://www.eprod-solutions.com/).
- Pricing not published; positioned as affordable for 1,000+ farmer organizations.

### 5.4 CropIn — enterprise scale, proven coffee deployments
- Sucafina (Uganda/Rwanda/Burundi): **30,000 farmers digitized, 93,000+ plots, 60,000+ ha audited, 85+ field staff, SMS option to mobilize farmers and send prices** (https://www.cropin.com/case_study/ensuring-sustainable-coffee-cultivation/). gebana (Togo/Burkina Faso) confirms offline capture under unreliable connectivity (~5,000 farmers, 11,700 ha) (https://cropin-tech.medium.com/smartfarm-a-tailor-made-digital-solution-for-plantation-crops-417273b3ecb5).
- Positioned mid-market/enterprise; pricing unpublished (https://www.itechguides.com/compare/cropin-vs-farmforce/). Likely over-specified and relatively expensive for a 5,000-member cooperative.

### 5.5 Free/open tools — the budget baseline
- **TerraTrac** (TechnoServe Labs): free, open-source Android app; points (<4 ha) and polygons (>4 ha); **fully offline**; CSV/GeoJSON export; sharing via email/WhatsApp; deforestation validation built on FAO Whisp; piloted with **19 Kenyan cooperative societies / 48 washing stations** under the Nespresso AAA program; cooperatives found it affordable (https://www.technoserve.org/tns-labs/terratrac-eudr-compliance/; https://www.technoserve.org/blog/kenyan-coffee-eudr-compliance-sustainable-solutions/; https://github.com/TechnoServe/TerraTrac-Mobile).
- **KoboToolbox / ODK Collect**: free, offline, GPS polygon support, GeoJSON export for TRACES; KoboToolbox has Swahili UI and is the recommended starting tool for Kenyan cooperatives; caveat: KoboToolbox free tier strains above ~5,000 submissions (https://agrosocialservices.co.ke/certification-compliance/eudr-gps-geolocation-kenya-coffee-cooperatives-2026/).
- **Fairtrade Plot Insights**: free for certified coffee/cocoa SPOs (see §2.2).

### 5.6 Emerging/cooperative-native options (watch list, higher risk)
- **Farmcore** (Tanzania-first): cooperative "operating system" — weighing, instant mobile-money payout, IFRS accounts; app + USSD + WhatsApp + SMS; Swahili; 72+ hours offline; soft launch November 2026 — too early to rely on for a 3-country deployment but worth monitoring (https://farmcore.io/).
- **Fairfood Trace**: blockchain traceability with farmer cards and mobile field app, "easily accessible, even for smallholder farmers in low tech environments"; suited for consumer-facing origin storytelling (https://fairfood.org/solutions-for-a-fair-supply-chain/blockchain-tool-trace/; https://docs.fairfood.org/introduction).
- **OriginTrace** (Rwanda Lake Kivu GI pilot): cooperative-owned, offline-first Android, per-container compliance packets (https://origintrace.app/).

## 6. Cost Analysis for 5,000 Farmers (explicit calculations)

### 6.1 The mapping campaign (one-time asset)
Documented anchor: **~USD 4 per farm** using trained local enumerators and phone-based capture in an Ethiopian cooperative program (https://qelvyn.co/en/blog/eudr/farm-plot-mapping-cost-cooperatives-eudr).

- Base case: 5,000 farms × $4 = **USD 20,000** one-time.
- Sensitivity (field conditions in mountainous Ethiopia/Indonesia may slow work): at $6–8/farm → **USD 30,000–40,000**.
- Amortization example: if the cooperative exports 2,000 t/yr, $20,000 ÷ 2,000 t = $10/t = **USD 0.01/kg in year one**; "nearly nothing after" since coordinates don't expire (https://qelvyn.co/en/blog/eudr/farm-plot-mapping-cost-cooperatives-eudr).
- Cross-checks: Kenya 100-member cooperative: USD 1,600–3,200 total → USD 16–32/member (includes service support) (https://agrosocialservices.co.ke/certification-compliance/eudr-gps-geolocation-kenya-coffee-cooperatives-2026/); Indonesia service packages: ~USD 3,400 for up to 300 smallholders ≈ USD 11/farm (https://eudrindonesia.com/eudr-smallholder-mapping-service-indonesia/). These higher per-farm figures reflect service margins; the cooperative self-run model is cheaper.

### 6.2 Software layer (annual)
- **Fairtrade Plot Insights + Fairtrace: USD 0** if Fairtrade-certified (https://www.fairtrade.net/content/dam/fairtrade/global/why-we-do-it/deforestation/EN_Plot%20Insights_Guidance%20for%20geolocation%20data%20submission%20and%20management.pdf).
- **TerraTrac/KoboToolbox/ODK: USD 0** license (links in §5.5).
- **Koltiva published anchors** (verify currency): 3 countries × $1,200 = $3,600/yr platform + e.g. 15 field users × $120 = $1,800/yr + 5,000 × $1 farmer access = $5,000/yr → **≈ USD 10,400/yr ≈ USD 2.1/farmer/yr**, plus one-time setup/training (https://www.sustainable-supply-chains.org/fileadmin/INA/Erfolgsgeschichten/Kaffeeinnovationsfonds/Recipe_Books/Handbook_Origin_centered_coffee_traceability.pdf).
- **Enterprise SaaS market range** (Farmforce-class and above): EUR 10,000–50,000/yr with setup fees EUR 5,000–90,000 (https://qelvyn.co/en/blog/eudr/farm-plot-mapping-cost-cooperatives-eudr) → at 5,000 farmers that is **EUR 2–10/farmer/yr** before setup.
- **Comparable cooperative projects:** Togo union of 4,000 farmers: EUR 12,000–30,000 total project (EUR 3–7.5/farmer) plus recurring EUR ~2,300–4,600/yr; Mali union of 6,500 farmers: EUR 23,000–53,000 (EUR 3.5–8/farmer) (https://kolonell.com/en/blog/agricultural-cooperative-software-traceability-eudr-cost-2026; https://kolonell.com/en/blog/agricultural-cooperative-software-traceability-cost-amsterdam-2026).

### 6.3 Indicative total first-year budget scenarios (5,000 farmers)

| Scenario | Stack | Year-1 cost | Cost/farmer | Ongoing/yr |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A. Minimum (Fairtrade-certified) | Plot Insights + Fairtrace + TerraTrac/Kobo for capture | ~USD 20,000–40,000 (field campaign only) | ~USD 4–8 | ~USD 0–5,000 (maintenance) |
| B. Budget + light SaaS | Free capture tools + low-cost coop registry (Kolonell-class) | ~USD 35,000–65,000 | ~USD 7–13 | ~USD 3,000–8,000 |
| C. Mid commercial | Koltiva (anchor pricing) + field campaign | ~USD 20,000–40,000 + ~USD 10,400 + setup | ~USD 8–12 | ~USD 10,000–15,000 (~USD 2–3/farmer) |
| D. Enterprise | Farmforce/CropIn-class quote | ~USD 60,000–140,000 incl. setup | ~USD 12–28 | ~USD 12,000–55,000 |

(Uncertainty: all commercial prices are quote-based or dated; treat ±50% as the honest error band. Certification fees for RA/Fairtrade themselves are separate and not included.)
